As soon as he had finished bathing his beautiful feet, he dried them with a towel he pulled from under the montera, and when he took the cap off he raised his face — and the watchers got a view of beauty so exquisite that Cardenio whispered to the curate:
“Since this is not Luscinda, this is no human creature; it's a divine being.”

Then the youth removed the montera, and as he shook his head from side to side, a mass of hair broke loose and tumbled out — hair the beams of the sun themselves might have envied. By this they realized that the apparent peasant was actually a lovely woman; indeed, the most beautiful that two of them had ever laid eyes on, and even the most beautiful Cardenio had ever seen, had he not seen and known Luscinda — for he later declared that only Luscinda's beauty could rival hers. Her long auburn tresses not only covered her shoulders; they were so long and so abundant that they hid her entire body beneath their masses, so that nothing of her figure was visible except her feet. She now used her hands as a comb, and if her feet had looked like pieces of crystal in the water, her hands among her locks looked like handfuls of driven snow — all of which increased not only the admiration of the three watchers but also their eagerness to learn who she was. With that aim they decided to show themselves, and at the noise they made getting to their feet, the lovely girl raised her head, parted the hair from her eyes with both hands, and looked to see who had made the sound. The moment she saw them she sprang up, and without pausing to put on her shoes or gather her hair, she hastily snatched up a bundle, apparently of clothes, that lay beside her and, frightened and alarmed, tried to run. But before she had gone six paces she fell to the ground, her delicate feet unable to bear the roughness of the stones. Seeing this, the three hurried toward her, and the curate spoke to her first:

“Stop, señora, whoever you may be. The men you see here want only to be of service to you. There is no need for such a reckless attempt to flee — your feet cannot endure it, and we will not allow it.”
Caught off guard and bewildered, she made no reply to these words. They came toward her anyway, and the curate, taking her hand, went on to say:

“What your clothes would conceal, señora, your hair reveals to us — clear proof that it can be no small matter that has disguised your beauty in a costume so unworthy of it and sent it into a wilderness like this, where we have had the good luck to find you, if not to relieve your distress, then at least to offer you comfort. For no distress, while life lasts, can be so crushing, or reach such an extreme, that the sufferer should refuse to listen to comfort offered with good intentions. And so, señora — or señor, or whatever you prefer to be — set aside the fear our appearance has caused you and tell us about your fortunes, good or bad; from all of us together, or from each of us alone, you will find sympathy in your trouble.”

While the curate spoke, the disguised young woman stood as if spellbound, staring at them without opening her lips or saying a word — exactly like a village rustic who has suddenly been shown some strange thing he has never seen before. But when the curate addressed a few more words to the same effect to her, she sighed deeply, broke her silence, and said:

“Since the solitude of these mountains has failed to hide me, and since my loosened, disheveled hair will not let my tongue tell lies, it would be pointless for me to keep up any further pretense now — anything you believed of it, you would believe out of courtesy rather than for any other reason. That being so, I say that I thank you, sirs, for the offer you have made me, which obliges me to comply with what you have asked; though I fear the account I give of my misfortunes will stir in you as much concern as compassion, since you will be unable to suggest anything to remedy them, or any consolation to ease them. Even so — so that my honor will not be left in doubt in your minds, now that you have discovered I am a woman and can see that I am young, alone, and dressed like this, circumstances that together or separately would be enough to destroy any good reputation — I feel bound to tell you what I would gladly keep secret if I could.”

She who was now revealed to be a lovely woman delivered all this without any hesitation, so fluently and in so sweet a voice that they were as charmed by her intelligence as by her beauty. And when they repeated their offers and their pleas that she keep her promise, she needed no further urging. First modestly covering her feet and gathering up her hair, she seated herself on a stone with the three men placed around her, and after an effort to hold back some tears that came to her eyes, she began her story in a clear, steady voice:

“Here in Andalusia there is a town from which a duke takes his title, making him one of those they call Grandees of Spain. This nobleman has two sons: the elder, heir to his rank and apparently to his good qualities; the younger, heir to I don't know what, unless it is the treachery of Vellido and the deceit of Ganelon. My parents are vassals of this lord — humble in origin, but so wealthy that if their birth had given them as much as their fortune did, they would have had nothing left to wish for, and I would have had no reason to fear a misfortune like the one I am in now; for it may well be that my bad luck springs from theirs, in not having been nobly born. It is true they are not so lowly that they have any reason to be ashamed of their station, but neither are they so high as to rid my mind of the suspicion that my disaster comes from their humble birth. They are, in short, farmers, plain ordinary people, with no strain of disreputable blood in them — old rusty Christians, as the saying goes — but so rich that their wealth and open-handed way of living are gradually earning them the standing of gentlefolk by birth, and even by position. Yet the wealth and nobility they prized most was having me as their daughter; and since they have no other child to make their heir, and are devoted parents, I was one of the most pampered daughters that parents ever pampered.

“I was the mirror in which they saw themselves, the staff of their old age, and — with all submission to Heaven — the single object of all their wishes; and mine never strayed from theirs, because I knew their worth. And just as I was mistress of their hearts, so I was also mistress of their property. Through me they hired and dismissed their servants; the accounts and records of everything sown and harvested passed through my hands; the oil mills, the wine presses, the tally of the flocks and herds, the beehives — everything, in short, that a rich farmer like my father owns or could own, I had in my care, and I served as steward and mistress with a diligence on my part, and a satisfaction on theirs, that I cannot adequately describe to you. The leisure hours left to me, after giving the necessary orders to the head shepherds, the overseers, and the other laborers, I spent on pursuits that are not only permissible but necessary for young girls — the ones the needle, the embroidery cushion, and the spinning wheel usually provide — and if I set them aside for a while to refresh my mind, I found recreation in reading some devotional book or playing the harp, for experience had taught me that music calms a troubled mind and relieves weariness of spirit. That was the life I led in my parents' house, and if I have painted it in such detail, it is not out of vanity, or to let you know that I am rich, but so that you can see how, through no fault of my own, I have fallen from the happy condition I have described into the misery I am in now. The truth is that while I was leading this busy life, in a seclusion that could rival a convent's, unseen — as I believed — by anyone except the household servants (for when I went to Mass it was so early in the morning, and I was so closely escorted by my mother and the women of the house, and so heavily veiled and so shy, that my eyes scarcely saw more ground than my feet stepped on), despite all this, the eyes of love — or more accurately, of idleness — eyes a lynx cannot match, found me out, aided by the persistence of Don Fernando; for that is the name of the duke's younger son I told you about.”

The moment the speaker mentioned the name Don Fernando, Cardenio's color changed and he broke into a sweat, with such visible signs of distress that the curate and the barber, who noticed it, feared that one of the mad fits they had heard came over him from time to time was about to strike. But Cardenio showed no further agitation and stayed quiet, studying the peasant girl with fixed attention, because he was beginning to suspect who she was. She, without noticing his agitation, continued her story, and went on to say:

“And his eyes had hardly found me when — as he admitted afterwards — he was struck with a violent passion for me, as the way it displayed itself made perfectly plain. But to shorten the long account of my sorrows, I will pass over in silence all the schemes Don Fernando used to declare his feelings for me. He bribed the entire household; he gave and offered gifts and presents to my parents; every day in our street was like a holiday or a festival; at night nobody could sleep for the music; the love letters that reached my hand — no one knew how — were beyond counting, crammed with tender pleadings and pledges, containing more promises and oaths than they had letters in them. None of it softened me; instead it hardened my heart against him, as though he were my mortal enemy and everything he did to make me yield had been done with the opposite intention. Not that Don Fernando's aristocratic bearing displeased me, or that I found his attentions tiresome; it gave me a certain kind of satisfaction to find myself so pursued and prized by such a distinguished gentleman, and I was not sorry to read my own praises in his letters — for however plain we women may be, it seems to me we are always pleased to hear ourselves called beautiful. What stood against all this was my own sense of what was right, along with the repeated advice of my parents, who by now saw Don Fernando's purpose very clearly, since he hardly cared whether the whole world knew it. They told me they were entrusting their honor and good name to my virtue and integrity alone, and asked me to consider the gap in rank between Don Fernando and myself — from which I could conclude that his intentions, whatever he might claim to the contrary, aimed at his own pleasure rather than my good. And they said that if I wanted to put any obstacle in the way of his unreasonable pursuit, they were ready to marry me at once to anyone I preferred, whether among the leading families of our own town or any of the neighboring ones; with their wealth and my good reputation, a match could be looked for anywhere. This offer, and their sound advice, strengthened my resolve, and I never gave Don Fernando a single word in reply that could offer him even the remotest hope of success.

“All this caution of mine, which he must have taken for disdain, apparently only sharpened his lustful appetite — for that is the name I give to his passion for me; if it had been what he claimed it was, you would never have heard of it, because there would have been no occasion to tell you about it. Eventually he learned that my parents were arranging a marriage for me, to put an end to his hopes of possessing me, or at least to give me additional protectors to watch over me; and that news, or suspicion, drove him to do what you are about to hear. One night I was in my room with no other company than the maid who attended me, the doors carefully locked so that no carelessness could endanger my honor — and I do not know, I cannot imagine, how it happened, but despite all this seclusion and all these precautions, in the solitude and silence of my retreat, I found him standing in front of me. The sight so stunned me that it robbed my eyes of sight and my tongue of speech. I had no strength to cry out, and I do not think he would have given me time to anyway, because he came straight to me, took me in his arms (since, overwhelmed as I was, I had, as I say, no power to defend myself), and began making such declarations to me that I still do not understand how lies could have the skill to dress themselves up to look so much like truth. And the traitor arranged for his tears to vouch for his words, and his sighs for his sincerity.

“I was a poor young thing, alone, untrained by my upbringing in matters like this; and somehow, I do not know how, I began to believe all those lying declarations were true — though his sighs and tears moved me to nothing more than simple compassion. And so, as the first shock of bewilderment wore off and I began to recover myself a little, I said to him, with more courage than I thought I possessed: 'Señor, if instead of being in your arms I were in the claws of a savage lion, and I could win my freedom by doing or saying anything that damaged my honor, I could no more do it or say it than the past could be made never to have happened. So if you hold my body clasped in your arms, I hold my soul secured by virtuous intentions, very different from yours, as you will see if you try to force them through. I am your vassal, but I am not your slave; your noble blood has no right — and should have none — to dishonor or degrade my humble birth; and low-born peasant though I am, I have my self-respect as much as you, a lord and a gentleman. Your violence will get you nowhere with me, your wealth will carry no weight, your words will have no power to deceive me, and your sighs and tears no power to soften me. If I saw any of the things I am describing in the man my parents gave me as a husband, my will would bend to his and never stray beyond it; and with my honor preserved, even if my desires were not, I would willingly give him what you, señor, are now trying to obtain by force. I say all this so you will not imagine that anyone but my lawful husband will ever win anything from me.' 'If that,' said this disloyal gentleman, 'is the only scruple holding you back, loveliest Dorothea' (for that is the name of this unhappy creature), 'look — here and now I give you my hand to be yours, and let Heaven, from which nothing is hidden, and this image of Our Lady that you have here, be witnesses to my pledge.'”

When Cardenio heard her say her name was Dorothea, he showed fresh agitation, now convinced that his earlier suspicion was correct; but he did not want to interrupt the story, wishing to hear the end of what he already nearly knew, so he said only:

“What — your name is Dorothea, señora? I have heard of another woman of the same name whose misfortunes may perhaps match yours. But go on; in due course I may tell you something that will astonish you as much as it will move you to pity.”

Dorothea was struck by Cardenio's words, and by his strange, wretched clothing, and she begged him, if he knew anything about her situation, to tell her at once; for if fortune had left her one blessing, it was the courage to bear whatever calamity might fall on her, since she felt certain that none could come that would add in the slightest degree to what she suffered already.

“I would not let the moment pass, señora,” Cardenio replied, “without telling you what I think — if what I suspect were certain. But so far the right opportunity has not come, and it is not of any importance to you to know it yet.”

“Be that as it may,” Dorothea replied, “what happened next in my story was that Don Fernando took an image that stood in the room and set it up as a witness to our betrothal, and with the most binding words and the most extravagant oaths he gave me his promise to become my husband — though before he had even finished pledging himself, I told him to consider carefully what he was doing, and to think of the anger his father would feel at seeing him married to a peasant girl, one of his own vassals. I told him not to let my beauty, such as it was, blind him, since it was not enough to provide an excuse for his offense; and that if the love he bore me made him want to do me any kindness, it would be to leave my lot to run its course at the level my station required, because marriages so unequal never bring happiness, and the pleasure they begin with never lasts for long.

“All this that I have just repeated I said to him, and much more that I cannot remember; but none of it persuaded him to abandon his purpose — a man who has no intention of paying does not worry himself about the difficulties when he is striking the bargain. Meanwhile I argued the matter over briefly in my own mind, telling myself: 'I will not be the first woman who has risen through marriage from a humble station to a high one, nor will Don Fernando be the first man whom beauty — or more likely, blind infatuation — has led to take a partner beneath his rank. Since I am starting no new custom or practice, I might as well accept the honor that chance is offering me; for even if his feelings for me last no longer than the satisfaction of his desires, I will still, after all, be his wife before God. And if I try to drive him off with scorn, I can see that, when fair means fail, he is in a mood to use force, and I will be left dishonored and with no way of proving my innocence to those who cannot know how innocently I came to be in this situation. What arguments could ever convince my parents that this gentleman entered my room without my consent?'

“All these questions and answers ran through my mind in an instant; but what swayed me most, and began to drag me unawares toward my ruin, were Don Fernando's oaths, the witnesses he called on, the tears he shed, and finally his graceful person and aristocratic charm, which, accompanied by so many signs of genuine love, might well have conquered a heart even freer and more guarded than mine. I called my waiting maid to me, so that there would be a witness on earth besides those in Heaven; and Don Fernando renewed and repeated his oaths once again, invoked new saints as witnesses on top of the earlier ones, called down a thousand future curses on himself if he failed to keep his promise, summoned more tears, redoubled his sighs, and pressed me tighter in his arms, from which he had never once let me escape. And so, when my maid left the room, I stopped being one, and he became a traitor and a perjurer.

“The day that followed the night of my misfortune did not arrive, I imagine, as quickly as Don Fernando wished, for once desire has obtained what it wanted, the greatest pleasure is to get away from the scene of the pleasure. I say this because Don Fernando was in a great hurry to leave me, and through the cunning of my maid — who was in fact the one who had let him in — he was out in the street before daybreak. On taking leave of me he told me, though not with the same earnestness and passion as when he arrived, that I could rest assured of his faithfulness and of the sanctity and sincerity of his oaths; and to seal his words he drew a rich ring from his finger and placed it on mine. Then he left, and I was left behind — whether sad or happy, I cannot say; all I can tell you is that I was left agitated and troubled in mind and almost dazed by what had happened, and I either lacked the spirit, or it simply did not occur to me, to scold my maid for the treachery she had committed in hiding Don Fernando in my room; for I still could not make up my mind whether what had befallen me was good or bad. I told Don Fernando as he left that, since I was now his, he could see me on other nights in the same way, until he chose to let the matter become public. But except for the following night, he never came again, and for more than a month I could not catch a glimpse of him in the street or at church, though I exhausted myself watching for one; I knew he was in town, and that nearly every day he went out hunting, a pastime he was very fond of. I remember well how sad and dreary those days and hours were for me; I remember well how, as they passed, I began to doubt, and even to lose confidence in Don Fernando's word; and I remember, too, how my maid then heard the words rebuking her insolence that she had not heard before, and how I had to force a restraint on my tears and on the expression of my face, so as not to give my parents reason to ask why I was so unhappy and drive me to invent lies in answer. But all of this came to a sudden end, when the moment arrived in which all such considerations were swept aside, all thought of honor was abandoned, my patience gave out, and the secret of my heart became known abroad. The reason was that a few days later a report spread through the town that in a nearby city Don Fernando had married a young woman of extraordinary beauty, the daughter of parents of distinguished position, though not so rich that her dowry would have entitled her to expect so brilliant a match. It was said her name was Luscinda, and that at the betrothal some strange things had happened.”

Cardenio heard the name Luscinda, but he did nothing except shrug his shoulders, bite his lips, and knit his brows — and before long two streams of tears spilled from his eyes. Dorothea, however, did not break off her story, but continued in these words:

“When this grim news reached my ears, instead of freezing my heart it set it blazing with such rage and fury that I could barely stop myself from running out into the streets, shouting aloud and openly proclaiming the betrayal and treachery I had suffered. But that surge of rage was checked, for the moment, by a plan I formed to carry out that very night: to put on these clothes, which I got from one of my father's servants — one of the zagals, as they are called on farms — to whom I confided the whole of my misfortune and whom I begged to go with me to the city where I had heard my enemy was. He scolded me for my recklessness and condemned my decision, but when he saw that I was set on my purpose, he offered to keep me company, as he put it, to the end of the world. I immediately packed a woman's dress into a linen pillowcase, along with some jewels and money for emergencies, and in the silence of the night, without alerting my treacherous maid, I left the house, accompanied by my servant and a crowd of anxieties, and set out on foot for the city — though my eagerness to reach it practically carried me on wings, if not to prevent what I assumed was already done, then at least to demand of Don Fernando with what conscience he had done it. I reached my destination in two and a half days, and on entering the city I asked the way to the house of Luscinda's parents. The first person I asked gave me more in answer than I had wanted to know. He pointed out the house and told me everything that had happened at the betrothal of the family's daughter — an affair so notorious in the city that it was the gossip of every cluster of idlers in the street. He said that on the night Don Fernando was betrothed to Luscinda, the moment she had consented to be his bride by saying 'Yes,' she was overcome by a sudden fainting fit; and that when the bridegroom came to unlace the bosom of her dress to give her air, he found a paper in her own handwriting, in which she stated and declared that she could not be Don Fernando's bride because she was already Cardenio's — who, by this man's account, was a gentleman of distinction in the same city — and that if she had accepted Don Fernando, it was only out of obedience to her parents. In short, he said, the words of the paper made it clear that she had meant to kill herself when the betrothal was completed, and gave her reasons for ending her life — all of which, it was said, was confirmed by a dagger they found somewhere in her clothing. On seeing this, Don Fernando, convinced that Luscinda had fooled, slighted, and toyed with him, attacked her before she had recovered from her faint and tried to stab her with the very dagger that had been found — and he would have succeeded if her parents and the others present had not stopped him. It was said, moreover, that Don Fernando left at once, and that Luscinda did not come out of her collapse until the next day, when she told her parents that she was truly the bride of that Cardenio I mentioned. I learned besides that Cardenio, according to report, had been present at the betrothal, and that on seeing her promised to another — something he had never expected — he had left the city in despair, leaving behind a letter declaring the wrong Luscinda had done him and announcing his intention of going where no one would ever see him again. All this was common knowledge throughout the city, and everyone was talking about it — all the more when it became known that Luscinda had disappeared from her father's house and from the city, for she was nowhere to be found, leaving her parents beside themselves, not knowing what steps to take to recover her. What I learned revived my hopes, and I was happier not to have found Don Fernando at all than to have found him married, because it seemed to me that the door to relief in my case was not yet completely shut. I told myself that Heaven might have placed this obstacle in the way of the second marriage to bring him to recognize his obligations under the first, and to reflect that as a Christian he was bound to put his soul above all human concerns. All this turned over in my mind, and I tried to comfort myself though there was no comfort, indulging in faint, far-off hopes of clinging to this life that I now despise.

“But while I was in the city, unsure what to do since I could not find Don Fernando, I heard a public crier announce a large reward for anyone who found me, giving the details of my age and a description of the very clothes I was wearing; and I heard it said that the boy who had come with me had taken me away from my father's house — a thing that cut me to the heart, showing how far my good name had fallen: it was not enough that I should lose it by running away; they had to add who I had supposedly fled with — someone so far beneath me and so unworthy of my regard. The instant I heard the announcement I left the city with my servant, who was already beginning to show signs that his loyalty to me was wavering, and that same night, fearing discovery, we entered the most thickly wooded part of these mountains. But, as the saying goes, one evil summons another, and the end of one misfortune tends to be the beginning of a greater one — and so it proved in my case. My good servant, until then so faithful and reliable, once he found me in that lonely place, was moved more by his own villainy than by my beauty, and decided to seize the opportunity these solitudes seemed to offer him; with little shame, less fear of God, and no respect for me, he began making advances to me. And when he found that I answered the impudence of his propositions with the justly harsh language it deserved, he set aside the pleading he had tried at first and began to use force.

“But just Heaven, which rarely fails to watch over and assist good intentions, assisted mine, so that with my slight strength, and without much effort, I pushed him over a precipice, where I left him — whether dead or alive, I do not know. Then, faster than seemed possible given my terror and exhaustion, I made my way into these mountains, with no other thought or plan than to hide myself in them and escape my father and the men he had sent out searching for me on his orders. I do not know how many months it has been since I came here with that aim. I met a herdsman who took me on as his servant at a place deep in the heart of this Sierra, and all this time I have been working for him as a herder, trying to stay always out in the fields to hide this hair that has now betrayed me when I least expected it. But all my care and effort came to nothing, because my master discovered that I was not a man, and conceived the same vile designs as my servant had; and since fortune does not always provide a remedy for every difficulty, and I had no cliff or ravine at hand down which to throw the master and cure his passion, as I had in the servant's case, I judged it the lesser evil to leave him and hide once more among these crags rather than test my strength or my arguments against him. So, as I say, I went into hiding again, looking for some place where, with sighs and tears, I might beg Heaven to take pity on my misery and grant me the help and strength to escape it — or else let me die in these solitudes, leaving no trace of an unhappy woman who, through no fault of her own, has given people material for gossip and scandal at home and abroad.”

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 29
paragraphs: About the droll device and method used to extricate our love-stricken knight from the severe penance he had imposed on himself

"Such, sirs, is the true story of my sad adventures: judge for yourselves now whether the sighs and lamentations you heard, and the tears that flowed from my eyes, had not sufficient cause even if I had indulged in them more freely; and if you consider the nature of my misfortune you will see that consolation is idle, since there is no possible remedy for it. All I ask of you is what you may easily and reasonably do: show me where I may pass my life unharassed by the fear and dread of discovery by those who are in search of me; for though the great love my parents bear me makes me sure of being kindly received by them, so great is my feeling of shame at the mere thought that I cannot present myself before them as they expect, that I had rather banish myself from their sight for ever than look them in the face with the reflection that they beheld mine stripped of that purity they had a right to expect in me."

With these words she fell silent, and the colour that overspread her face showed plainly the pain and shame she was suffering at heart. In theirs the listeners felt as much pity as wonder at her misfortunes; but as the curate was just about to offer her some consolation and advice, Cardenio forestalled him, saying, "So then, señora, you are the fair Dorothea, the only daughter of the rich Clenardo?" Dorothea was astonished at hearing her father's name, and at the miserable appearance of the man who mentioned it, for it has already been said how wretchedly clad Cardenio was; so she said to him:
"And who may you be, brother, who seem to know my father's name so well? For so far, if I remember rightly, I have not mentioned it in the whole story of my misfortunes."

"I am that unhappy being, señora," replied Cardenio, "whom, as you have said, Luscinda declared to be her husband; I am the unfortunate Cardenio, whom the wrong-doing of him who has brought you to your present condition has reduced to the state you see me in — bare, ragged, bereft of all human comfort, and, what is worse, of reason, for I only possess it when Heaven is pleased to restore it to me for some short while. I, Dorothea, am he who witnessed the wrong done by Don Fernando, and waited to hear the 'Yes' uttered by which Luscinda owned herself his betrothed: I am he who had not courage enough to see how her fainting fit ended, or what came of the paper that was found in her bosom, because my heart had not the fortitude to endure so many strokes of ill fortune at once; and so losing patience I quitted the house, and leaving a letter with my host, which I entreated him to place in Luscinda's hands, I betook myself to these solitudes, resolved to end here the life I hated as if it were my mortal enemy. But fate would not rid me of it, contenting itself with robbing me of my reason — perhaps to preserve me for the good fortune I have had in meeting you; for if what you have just told us be true, as I believe it to be, it may be that Heaven still has in store for both of us a happier outcome to our misfortunes than we look for. Because, seeing that Luscinda cannot marry Don Fernando, being mine, as she has herself so openly declared, and that Don Fernando cannot marry her as he is yours, we may reasonably hope that Heaven will restore to us what is ours, since it is still in existence and not yet alienated or destroyed. And as we have this consolation springing from no very visionary hope or wild fancy, I entreat you, señora, to form new resolutions in your better mind, as I mean to do in mine, preparing yourself to look forward to happier fortunes; for I swear to you by the faith of a gentleman and a Christian not to desert you until I see you in possession of Don Fernando; and if I cannot by words bring him to recognise his obligation to you, in that case to avail myself of the right which my rank as a gentleman gives me, and with just cause challenge him on account of the injury he has done you, not regarding my own wrongs, which I shall leave to Heaven to avenge, while I on earth devote myself to yours."

Cardenio's words completed Dorothea's astonishment, and not knowing how to return thanks for such an offer, she attempted to kiss his feet; but Cardenio would not permit it, and the licentiate replied for both, commended the sound reasoning of Cardenio, and lastly begged, advised, and urged them to come with him to his village, where they might furnish themselves with what they needed and take measures to discover Don Fernando, or restore Dorothea to her parents, or do what seemed to them most advisable. Cardenio and Dorothea thanked him, and accepted the kind offer he made them; and the barber, who had been listening to all attentively and in silence, on his part also said some kindly words, and with no less good will than the curate offered his services in any way that might be of use to them. He also explained to them in a few words the object that had brought them there, and the strange nature of Don Quixote's madness, and how they were waiting for his squire, who had gone in search of him. Like the recollection of a dream, the quarrel he had had with Don Quixote came back to Cardenio's memory, and he described it to the others; but he was unable to say what the dispute was about.

At this moment they heard a shout, and recognised it as coming from Sancho Panza, who, not finding them where he had left them, was calling aloud to them. They went to meet him, and in answer to their inquiries about Don Quixote, he told them how he had found him stripped to his shirt, lank, yellow, half dead with hunger, and sighing for his lady Dulcinea; and although he had told him that she commanded him to quit that place and come to El Toboso, where she was expecting him, he had answered that he was determined not to appear in the presence of her beauty until he had done deeds to make him worthy of her favour. If this went on, Sancho said, he ran the risk of not becoming an emperor as in duty bound, or even an archbishop — which was the least he could be — for which reason they ought to consider what was to be done to get him away from there. The licentiate in reply told him not to be uneasy, for they would fetch him away in spite of himself. He then told Cardenio and Dorothea what they had proposed to do to cure Don Quixote, or at any rate take him home; on which Dorothea said that she could play the distressed damsel better than the barber, especially as she had there the dress in which to do it to the life, and that they might trust to her acting the part in every particular required for carrying out their scheme, since she had read a great many books of chivalry and knew exactly the style in which afflicted damsels begged boons of knights-errant.

"In that case," said the curate, "there is nothing more required than to set about it at once, for beyond a doubt fortune is declaring itself in our favour, since it has so unexpectedly begun to open a door for your relief and smoothed the way for us to our object."

Dorothea then took out of her pillow-case a complete petticoat of some rich stuff, and a green mantle of some other fine material, and a necklace and other ornaments out of a little box, and with these in an instant she so arrayed herself that she looked like a great and rich lady. All this, and more, she said, she had taken from home in case of need, but that until then she had had no occasion to make use of it. They were all highly delighted with her grace, air, and beauty, and declared Don Fernando to be a man of very little taste when he rejected such charms. But the one who admired her most was Sancho Panza, for it seemed to him (and indeed it was true) that in all the days of his life he had never seen such a lovely creature; and he asked the curate with great eagerness who this beautiful lady was, and what she wanted in these out-of-the-way quarters.

"This fair lady, brother Sancho," replied the curate, "is no less a personage than the heiress in the direct male line of the great kingdom of Micomicon, who has come in search of your master to beg a boon of him — namely, that he redress a wrong or injury that a wicked giant has done her; and given the fame as a good knight that your master has acquired far and wide, this princess has come from Guinea to seek him out."

"A lucky seeking and a lucky finding!" said Sancho Panza at this; "especially if my master has the good fortune to redress that injury, and right that wrong, and kill that son of a bitch of a giant your worship speaks of — as kill him he will if he meets him, unless of course he happens to be a phantom, for my master has no power at all against phantoms. But one thing among others I would beg of you, señor licentiate: to prevent my master taking a fancy to be an archbishop, which is what I'm afraid of, your worship would recommend him to marry this princess at once; for in this way he'll be disabled from taking archbishop's orders, and will easily come into his empire, and I to the end of my desires. I've been thinking the matter over carefully, and by what I can make out I find it will not do for me that my master should become an archbishop, because I am no good for the Church, as I am married; and for me now, having a wife and children, to set about obtaining dispensations to enable me to hold a place of profit under the Church, would be endless work. So that, señor, it all turns on my master marrying this lady at once — for as yet I do not know her grace, and so I cannot call her by her name."
"She is called the Princess Micomicona," said the curate; "for as her kingdom is Micomicon, it is clear that must be her name."

"There's no doubt of that," replied Sancho, "for I have known many to take their name and title from the place where they were born, and call themselves Pedro of Alcalá, Juan of Úbeda, and Diego of Valladolid; and it may be that over there in Guinea queens have the same way of taking the names of their kingdoms."

"So it may," said the curate; "and as for your master's marrying, I will do all in my power to bring it about" — with which Sancho was as much pleased as the curate was amazed at his simplicity, and at seeing what a hold the absurdities of his master had taken of his fancy, for he had evidently persuaded himself that he was going to be an emperor.

By this time Dorothea had seated herself on the curate's mule, and the barber had fitted the ox-tail beard to his face; and they now told Sancho to conduct them to where Don Quixote was, warning him not to say that he knew either the licentiate or the barber, as his master's becoming an emperor entirely depended on his not recognising them. Neither the curate nor Cardenio, however, thought fit to go with them: Cardenio lest he remind Don Quixote of the quarrel he had had with him, and the curate as there was no need for his presence just yet. So they let the others go on ahead, while they themselves followed slowly on foot. The curate did not forget to instruct Dorothea how to act, but she said they might set their minds at ease, as everything would be done exactly as the books of chivalry required and described.

They had gone about three-quarters of a league when they discovered Don Quixote in a wilderness of rocks, by this time clothed but without his armour; and as soon as Dorothea saw him and was told by Sancho that that was Don Quixote, she whipped her palfrey, the well-bearded barber following her, and on coming up to him her squire sprang from his mule and came forward to receive her in his arms. She, dismounting with great ease of manner, advanced to kneel at the feet of Don Quixote; and though he strove to raise her up, she, without rising, addressed him in this fashion:

"From this spot I will not rise, valiant and doughty knight, until your goodness and courtesy grant me a boon, which will redound to the honour and renown of your person and render a service to the most disconsolate and afflicted damsel the sun has seen; and if the might of your strong arm matches the repute of your immortal fame, you are bound to aid the helpless being who, led by the savour of your renowned name, hath come from far-distant lands to seek your aid in her misfortunes."
"I will not answer a word, beauteous lady," replied Don Quixote, "nor will I listen to anything further concerning you, until you rise from the earth."
"I will not rise, señor," answered the afflicted damsel, "unless of your courtesy the boon I ask is first granted me."
"I grant and accord it," said Don Quixote, "provided that without detriment or prejudice to my king, my country, or her who holds the key of my heart and freedom, it may be complied with."

"It will not be to the detriment or prejudice of any of them, my worthy lord," said the afflicted damsel; and here Sancho Panza drew close to his master's ear and said very softly, "Your worship may very safely grant the boon she asks; it's nothing at all — only to kill a big giant; and she who asks it is the exalted Princess Micomicona, queen of the great kingdom of Micomicon of Ethiopia."

"Let her be who she may," replied Don Quixote, "I will do what is my bounden duty, and what my conscience bids me, in accordance with what I have professed"; and turning to the damsel he said, "Let your great beauty rise, for I grant the boon you would ask of me."

"Then what I ask," said the damsel, "is that your magnanimous person accompany me at once wherever I will conduct you, and that you promise not to engage in any other adventure or quest until you have avenged me of a traitor who against all human and divine law has usurped my kingdom."

"I repeat that I grant it," replied Don Quixote; "and so, lady, you may from this day forth lay aside the melancholy that distresses you, and let your failing hopes gather new life and strength; for with the help of God and of my arm you will soon see yourself restored to your kingdom, and seated on the throne of your ancient and mighty realm, notwithstanding and despite the felons who would gainsay it. And now to work, for in delay there is apt to be danger."

The distressed damsel strove with great persistence to kiss his hands; but Don Quixote, who was in all things a polished and courteous knight, would by no means allow it, but made her rise and embraced her with great courtesy and politeness, and ordered Sancho to look to Rocinante's girths and to arm him without a moment's delay. Sancho took down the armour, which was hung up on a tree like a trophy, and having seen to the girths armed his master in a trice, who as soon as he found himself in his armour exclaimed:
"Let us be gone, in the name of God, to bring aid to this great lady."

The barber was all this time on his knees at great pains to hide his laughter and not let his beard fall, for had it fallen perhaps their fine scheme would have come to nothing; but now, seeing the boon granted, and the promptness with which Don Quixote prepared to set out in compliance with it, he rose and took his lady's hand, and between them they placed her on the mule. Don Quixote then mounted Rocinante, and the barber settled himself on his beast, Sancho being left to go on foot — which made him feel anew the loss of his Dapple, finding the want of him now. But he bore it all with cheerfulness, being persuaded that his master had now fairly started and was just on the point of becoming an emperor; for he had no doubt at all that he would marry this princess and be king of Micomicon at least. The only thing that troubled him was the reflection that this kingdom was in the land of the blacks, and that the people they would give him for vassals would all be black; but for this he soon found a remedy in his fancy, and he said to himself, "What is it to me if my vassals are blacks? What more have I to do than make a cargo of them and carry them to Spain, where I can sell them and get ready money for them, and with it buy some title or office in which to live at ease all the days of my life? Not unless you go to sleep and haven't the wit or skill to turn things to account, and sell three, six, or ten thousand vassals while you'd be talking about it! By God I'll stir them up, big and little, or as best I can, and let them be ever so black I'll turn them into white or yellow. Come, come, what a fool I am!" And so he jogged on, so occupied with his thoughts and so easy in his mind that he forgot all about the hardship of travelling on foot.

Cardenio and the curate were watching all this from among some bushes, not knowing how to join company with the others; but the curate, who was very fertile in devices, soon hit upon a way of accomplishing their purpose. With a pair of scissors he had in a case he quickly cut off Cardenio's beard, and putting on him a grey jerkin of his own he gave him a black cloak, leaving himself in his breeches and doublet; and Cardenio's appearance was so different from what it had been that he would not have known himself had he seen himself in a mirror. Having done this, although the others had gone on ahead while they were disguising themselves, they easily came out onto the high road before them, for the brambles and rough places they encountered did not allow those on horseback to go as fast as those on foot. They then posted themselves on the level ground at the outlet of the Sierra, and as soon as Don Quixote and his companions emerged from it the curate began to examine him very deliberately, as though he were trying to recognise him, and after having stared at him for some time he hastened toward him with open arms exclaiming, "A happy meeting with the mirror of chivalry, my worthy compatriot Don Quixote of La Mancha, the flower and cream of high breeding, the protection and relief of the distressed, the quintessence of knights-errant!" And so saying he clasped in his arms the knee of Don Quixote's left leg. Don Quixote, astonished at the stranger's words and behaviour, looked at him attentively, and at length recognised him, very much surprised to see him there, and made great efforts to dismount. This, however, the curate would not allow, on which Don Quixote said, "Permit me, señor licentiate, for it is not fitting that I should be on horseback and so reverend a person as your worship on foot."

"On no account will I allow it," said the curate; "your mightiness must remain on horseback, for it is on horseback you achieve the greatest deeds and adventures that have been beheld in our age; as for me, an unworthy priest, it will serve me well enough to mount on the haunches of one of the mules of these gentlefolk who accompany your worship, if they have no objection, and I will fancy I am mounted on the steed Pegasus, or on the zebra or charger that bore the famous Moor Muzaraque, who to this day lies enchanted in the great hill of Zulema, a little distance from the great Complutum."

"Nor even that will I consent to, señor licentiate," answered Don Quixote, "and I know it will be the good pleasure of my lady the princess, out of love for me, to order her squire to give up the saddle of his mule to your worship, and he can sit behind if the beast will bear it."
"It will, I am sure," said the princess, "and I am sure too that I need not order my squire, for he is too courteous and considerate to allow a Churchman to go on foot when he might be mounted."

"That he is," said the barber, and at once dismounting, he offered his saddle to the curate, who accepted it without much entreaty; but unfortunately as the barber was mounting behind, the mule — being as it happened a hired one, which is the same thing as saying ill-conditioned — lifted its hind hoofs and let fly a couple of kicks in the air, which would have made Master Nicholas wish his expedition in quest of Don Quixote at the devil had they caught him on the breast or head. As it was, they so took him by surprise that he came to the ground, giving so little heed to his beard that it fell off, and all he could do when he found himself without it was to cover his face hastily with both his hands and moan that his teeth were knocked out. Don Quixote, when he saw all that bundle of beard detached, without jaws or blood, from the face of the fallen squire, exclaimed:
"By the living God, but this is a great miracle! It has knocked off and plucked away the beard from his face as if it had been shaved off deliberately."

The curate, seeing the danger of discovery that threatened his scheme, at once pounced on the beard and hastened with it to where Master Nicholas lay, still uttering moans, and drawing his head to his breast had it on in an instant, muttering over him some words which he said were a certain special charm for sticking on beards, as they would see; and as soon as he had it fixed he left him, and the squire appeared well-bearded and whole as before, at which Don Quixote was beyond measure astonished, and begged the curate to teach him that charm when he had the opportunity, since he was persuaded its virtue must extend beyond the sticking-on of beards — for it was clear that where the beard had been stripped off the flesh must have remained torn and lacerated, and when it could heal all that, it must be good for more than beards.

"And so it is," said the curate, and he promised to teach it to him on the first opportunity. They then agreed that for the present the curate should mount, and that the three of them should ride by turns until they reached the inn, which might be about six leagues from where they were.
Three then being mounted — that is to say, Don Quixote, the princess, and the curate — and three on foot — Cardenio, the barber, and Sancho Panza — Don Quixote said to the damsel:
"Let your highness, lady, lead on wherever is most pleasing to you"; but before she could answer the licentiate said:
"Toward what kingdom would your ladyship direct our course? Is it perchance toward that of Micomicon? It must be, or else I know little about kingdoms."
She, being ready on all points, understood that she was to answer "Yes," so she said, "Yes, señor, my way lies toward that kingdom."

"In that case," said the curate, "we must pass right through my village, and there your worship will take the road to Cartagena, where you will be able to embark, fortune favouring; and if the wind be fair and the sea smooth and tranquil, in somewhat less than nine years you may come in sight of the great lake Meona — I mean Meotides — which is little more than a hundred days' journey this side of your highness's kingdom."

"Your worship is mistaken, señor," said she; "for it is not two years since I set out from it, and though I never had good weather, nevertheless I am here to behold what I so longed for — and that is my lord Don Quixote of La Mancha, whose fame came to my ears as soon as I set foot in Spain and impelled me to go in search of him, to commend myself to his courtesy and entrust the justice of my cause to the might of his invincible arm."

"Enough; no more praise," said Don Quixote at this, "for I hate all flattery; and though this may not be so, still language of the kind is offensive to my chaste ears. I will only say, señora, that whether it has might or not, that which it may or may not have shall be devoted to your service even to death; and now, leaving this to its proper season, I would ask the señor licentiate to tell me what it is that has brought him into these parts, alone, unattended, and so lightly clad that I am filled with amazement."

"I will answer that briefly," replied the curate; "you must know then, Señor Don Quixote, that Master Nicholas, our friend and barber, and I were going to Seville to receive some money that a relative of mine who went to the Indies many years ago had sent me — and not such a small sum but that it was over sixty thousand pieces of eight, full weight, which is something. Passing by this place yesterday we were attacked by four footpads, who stripped us even to our beards — and them they stripped off so that the barber found it necessary to put on a false one, and even this young man here" — pointing to Cardenio — "they completely transformed. But the best of it is, the story goes in the neighbourhood that those who attacked us belong to a number of galley slaves who, they say, were set free almost on the very same spot by a man of such valour that, in spite of the commissary and the guards, he released the whole lot of them; and beyond all doubt he must have been out of his senses, or he must be as great a scoundrel as they, or some man without heart or conscience to let the wolf loose among the sheep, the fox among the hens, the fly among the honey. He has defrauded justice and opposed his king and lawful master, since he opposed his just commands; he has, I say, robbed the galleys of their feet, stirred up the Holy Brotherhood, which for many years past has been quiet, and lastly has done a deed by which his soul may be lost without any gain to his body." Sancho had told the curate and the barber of the adventure of the galley slaves, which his master had achieved so much to his glory, and hence the curate in alluding to it made the most of it to see what would be said or done by Don Quixote, who changed colour at every word, not daring to say that it was he who had been the liberator of those worthy people. "These, then," said the curate, "were they who robbed us; and God in his mercy pardon him who would not let them go to the punishment they deserved."

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 30
paragraphs: About the cleverness shown by the fair Dorothea, with other pleasant and entertaining matters

The curate had hardly finished speaking when Sancho said, "On my faith, then, señor licentiate, the one who did that deed was my master; and it wasn't for lack of my warning him beforehand and telling him to be careful, that it was a sin to set them free, since they were all on the march there because they were special scoundrels."

"Blockhead!" said Don Quixote at this. "It is no business or concern of knights-errant to inquire whether the persons in distress, chained, or oppressed whom they meet on the high roads go that way and suffer in that condition because of their faults or because of their misfortunes. The only thing that concerns us is to help them as people in need, with regard to their suffering and not to their crimes. I came across a chaplet — a string of miserable, unfortunate people — and did for them what my sense of duty demands, and as for the rest, let it be as it may. Whoever objects to it — saving the sacred dignity of the señor licentiate and his honoured person — I say he knows little about chivalry and lies like a whoreson villain, and I will make him understand this to the fullest extent with my sword." And with that he settled himself in his stirrups and pressed down his morion — for the barber's basin, which to him was Mambrino's helmet, he carried hanging at the saddle-bow until he could repair the damage the galley slaves had done to it.

Dorothea, who was shrewd and quick-witted, by now thoroughly understood Don Quixote's crazy turn and that everyone except Sancho Panza was playing along; so as not to be outdone, when she saw his irritation she said to him, "Sir Knight, remember the favour you have promised me, and that under its terms you must not engage in any other adventure, however urgent. Calm yourself; if the licentiate had known that the galley slaves had been set free by that unconquered arm, he would have sewed up his mouth three times over, or even bitten his tongue three times before he said a word that smacked of disrespect to your worship."
"That I swear heartily," said the curate, "and I would even have plucked out a whisker of my moustache."

"I will hold my peace, señora," said Don Quixote, "and curb the natural anger that had risen in my chest, and I will proceed in peace and quiet until I have fulfilled my promise. But in return for this restraint I entreat you to tell me — if you have no objection — what is the nature of your trouble, and how many, who, and what kind of persons they are from whom I am to demand satisfaction and on whom I am to take vengeance on your behalf."
"I'll do that with all my heart," replied Dorothea, "if it doesn't tire you to listen to miseries and misfortunes."

"It will not tire me, señora," said Don Quixote. To which Dorothea replied, "Well, if that's so, give me your attention." As soon as she said this, Cardenio and the barber drew close to her side, eager to hear what kind of story the quick-witted Dorothea would invent for herself; and Sancho did the same, for he was as much taken in by her as his master. She settled herself comfortably in the saddle, and with the help of a few coughs and other preliminaries to give herself time to think, she began with great spirit in this fashion.

"First of all, sirs, I would have you know that my name is —" and here she stopped for a moment, because she'd forgotten the name the curate had given her. But he came to her rescue, seeing her difficulty, and said, "It's no wonder, señora, that your highness should be confused and embarrassed when telling the tale of your misfortunes; such afflictions often have the effect of depriving the sufferers of memory, so that they cannot even remember their own names, as is the case now with your ladyship, who has forgotten that she is called the Princess Micomicona, lawful heiress of the great kingdom of Micomicon. With this cue your highness may now recall to your sorrowful memory everything you wish to tell us."

"That is the truth," said the damsel, "but I think from here on I shall need no further prompting, and I shall bring my true story safely into port. Here it is. The king my father, who was called Tinacrio the Sapient, was very learned in what they call the magic arts, and by his craft he became aware that my mother, who was called Queen Jaramilla, was to die before he did, and that soon after he too was to depart this life, and I would be left an orphan without father or mother. But all this, he declared, did not grieve or distress him as much as the certain knowledge that a prodigious giant — the lord of a great island close to our kingdom, Pandafilando of the Scowl by name (for it's said that, although his eyes are properly placed and straight, he always looks sideways as if he squinted, and he does it out of malice, to strike fear and terror into those he looks at) — that he knew, I say, that this giant, on becoming aware of my orphaned condition, would overrun my kingdom with a mighty force and strip me of everything, not leaving me even a small village to shelter in; but that I could avoid all this ruin and misfortune if I were willing to marry him. However, as far as he could see, he never expected me to consent to such an unequal marriage; and he spoke no more than the truth in this, since it has never entered my mind to marry that giant, or any other, however great or enormous he may be. My father said, too, that when he was dead and I saw Pandafilando about to invade my kingdom, I was not to wait and try to defend myself, for that would be the ruin of me; instead I should leave the kingdom entirely open to him if I wished to avoid the death and total destruction of my good and loyal vassals, since there would be no way of defending myself against the giant's devilish power. He told me I should at once set out with some of my followers for Spain, where I would find relief in my distress on finding a certain knight-errant whose fame by then would extend over the whole kingdom, and who would be called, if I remember rightly, Don Azote or Don Gigote."
"He must have said 'Don Quixote,' señora," Sancho put in at this, "otherwise known as the Knight of the Rueful Countenance."

"That's it," said Dorothea. "He said, moreover, that the knight would be tall of stature and lank of feature; and that on his right side under the left shoulder, or thereabouts, he would have a grey mole with hairs like bristles."
On hearing this, Don Quixote said to his squire, "Here, Sancho my son, lend a hand and help me strip, because I want to see if I'm the knight that sage king foretold."
"What does your worship want to strip for?" said Dorothea.
"To see if I have the mole your father spoke of," answered Don Quixote.
"There's no need to strip," said Sancho. "I know your worship has just such a mole in the middle of your backbone, which is the mark of a strong man."

"That's enough," said Dorothea. "With friends we must not look too closely into trifles, and whether it's on the shoulder or on the backbone matters little; what counts is that there's a mole, wherever it may be, since it's all the same flesh. No doubt my good father hit the truth in every particular, and I have made a lucky hit in commending myself to Don Quixote — for he is the one my father spoke of, since the features of his face correspond with those given to this knight by that wide fame he has earned not only in Spain but in all La Mancha. I had hardly landed at Osuna when I heard such accounts of his exploits that at once my heart told me he was the very one I had come in search of."
"But how did you land at Osuna, señora," asked Don Quixote, "when it's not a seaport?"
Before Dorothea could reply, the curate cut in and said, "The princess means that after she had landed at Málaga, the first place where she heard of your worship was Osuna."
"That is what I meant to say," said Dorothea.
"And that would be only natural," said the curate. "Will your majesty please go on?"

"There's nothing more to add," said Dorothea, "except that in finding Don Quixote I have had such good fortune that I already count and consider myself queen and mistress of all my domains, since out of his courtesy and magnanimity he has granted me the favour of accompanying me wherever I may lead him — which will be only to bring him face to face with Pandafilando of the Scowl, so that he may kill him and restore to me what has been unjustly taken from me. All this must come about satisfactorily, since my good father Tinacrio the Sapient foretold it; he also left it stated in writing, in Chaldee or Greek characters (for I cannot read them), that if this predicted knight, after cutting the giant's throat, should be willing to marry me, I was to offer myself at once without protest as his lawful wife, and yield him possession of my kingdom together with my person."
"What do you think now, friend Sancho?" said Don Quixote at this. "Do you hear that? Didn't I tell you so? Look — we already have a kingdom to govern and a queen to marry!"

"On my oath that's so," said Sancho, "and bad luck to anyone who won't marry after slitting Señor Pandahilado's windpipe! And then, how ill-favoured the queen is! I wish the fleas in my bed were that kind!"

And with that he cut a couple of capers in the air with every sign of extreme satisfaction, then ran to seize the bridle of Dorothea's mule, and pulling it up he fell on his knees before her, begging her to give him her hand to kiss in acknowledgement that he accepted her as his queen and mistress. Which of the bystanders could have helped laughing to see the madness of the master and the simplicity of the servant? Dorothea therefore gave him her hand and promised to make him a great lord in her kingdom, when Heaven should be good enough to allow her to recover and enjoy it; for which Sancho returned his thanks in words that set them all laughing again.

"This, sirs," Dorothea continued, "is my story. It only remains to tell you that of all the attendants I took with me from my kingdom, I have none left except this well-bearded squire, for all the others were drowned in a great tempest we encountered when in sight of port. He and I came to land on a couple of planks as if by a miracle; and indeed the whole course of my life is a miracle and a mystery, as you may have noticed. If I have been over-detailed about any of it, or not as precise as I should have been, blame it on what the licentiate said at the beginning of my tale — that constant and excessive troubles deprive the sufferers of their memory."

"They shall not deprive me of mine, exalted and worthy princess," said Don Quixote, "however great and unparalleled those I endure in your service may be. Here I confirm anew the favour I have promised you, and I swear to go with you to the ends of the earth until I find myself in the presence of your fierce enemy, whose haughty head I trust by the strength of my arm to cut off with the edge of this — I will not say good sword, thanks to Ginés de Pasamonte who carried off mine" — (this he muttered between his teeth, and then went on) — "and when it has been cut off and you have been put in peaceful possession of your realm, it shall be left to your own decision to dispose of your person as may please you most; for so long as my memory is occupied, my will enslaved, and my understanding enthralled by her — I say no more — it's impossible for me even for a moment to contemplate marriage, even with a Phoenix."
His master's last words about not wanting to marry were so disagreeable to Sancho that, raising his voice, he exclaimed with great irritation:

"By my oath, Señor Don Quixote, you are not in your right senses; how can your worship possibly refuse to marry such an exalted princess as this? Do you think Fortune will offer you behind every stone a piece of luck like this one? Is my lady Dulcinea more beautiful, perhaps? Not she; not half as beautiful; I'll even go so far as to say she doesn't come up to the shoe of this one here. A poor chance I have of getting that county I'm waiting for, if your worship goes hunting for delicacies at the bottom of the sea. In the devil's name, marry, marry, and take this kingdom that comes to hand without any trouble; and when you're king, make me a marquis or governor of a province, and the rest can go to the devil."

When Don Quixote heard such blasphemies uttered against his lady Dulcinea, he could not bear it, and lifting his pike, without saying anything to Sancho or uttering a word, he gave him two such whacks that he knocked him to the ground; and if Dorothea hadn't shouted at him to spare him, he would no doubt have taken his life on the spot.

"Do you think," he said to him after a pause, "you scurvy clown, that you are always to be interfering with me, and that you are always to be giving offence and I always to be pardoning? Don't get any such idea, you impious scoundrel — for that's beyond all doubt what you are, since you've set your tongue going against the peerless Dulcinea. Don't you know, you lout, vagabond, beggar, that were it not for the strength she pours into my arm I wouldn't have the power to kill a flea? Tell me, scoffer with a viper's tongue, what do you think has won this kingdom and cut off this giant's head and made you a marquis (for I count all this as already done and decided) but the might of Dulcinea, using my arm as the instrument of her achievements? She fights in me and conquers in me, and I live and breathe in her, and owe my life and being to her. O whoreson scoundrel, how ungrateful you are! You see yourself raised from the dust of the earth to be a titled lord, and the return you make for so great a benefit is to speak ill of her who has conferred it on you!"
Sancho was not so stunned that he didn't hear everything his master said, and getting up with some quickness he ran to place himself behind Dorothea's palfrey, and from there he said to his master:

"Tell me, señor — if your worship is resolved not to marry this great princess, it's plain the kingdom won't be yours; and if it's not, how can you bestow favours on me? That's what I complain of. Let your worship at any rate marry this queen, now that we have her here as if showered down from heaven, and afterwards you can go back to my lady Dulcinea; there must have been kings in the world who kept mistresses. As to beauty, I have nothing to do with that; to tell the truth, I like them both, though I have never seen the lady Dulcinea."
"What? Never seen her, you blasphemous traitor!" exclaimed Don Quixote. "Didn't you just now bring me a message from her?"
"I mean," said Sancho, "that I did not see her at such leisure that I could take particular notice of her beauty, or of her charms piece by piece; but taken in the lump, I like her."
"Now I forgive you," said Don Quixote, "and you forgive me the injury I have done you, for our first impulses are not in our control."
"That I see," replied Sancho, "and with me the wish to speak is always the first impulse, and I cannot help saying, at least once, whatever's on the tip of my tongue."
"All the same, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "watch what you say, because the pitcher goes so often to the well — I need say no more."
"Well, well," said Sancho, "God is in heaven, and he sees all the tricks, and will judge who does more harm — me by not speaking right, or your worship by not doing it."

"That's enough," said Dorothea. "Run, Sancho, kiss your lord's hand and beg his pardon, and from now on be more careful with your praise and abuse; and say nothing in disparagement of that lady of El Toboso, of whom I know nothing except that I am her servant. Put your trust in God, and you'll not fail to obtain some position that will let you live like a prince."

Sancho came forward hanging his head and begged his master's hand, which Don Quixote presented with dignity, giving him his blessing as soon as he had kissed it. He then told him to come on ahead a little, as he had questions to ask and matters of great importance to discuss with him. Sancho obeyed, and when the two had gone some distance ahead, Don Quixote said to him, "Since your return I have had no opportunity or time to ask you many particulars concerning your mission and the answer you brought back; now that chance has granted us the time and opportunity, don't deny me the happiness you can give me with such good news."
"Let your worship ask whatever you want," answered Sancho, "and I'll find a way out of all of it, as I found a way in; but I beg you, señor, not to be so vengeful in future."
"Why do you say that, Sancho?" said Don Quixote.

"I say it," he returned, "because those blows just now were more for the quarrel the devil stirred up between us the other night than for what I said against my lady Dulcinea, whom I love and revere as I would a relic — though there's nothing relic-like about her — merely as something belonging to your worship."
"Say no more on that subject, for your life, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "for it displeases me. I have already pardoned you for it, and you know the common saying, 'for a fresh sin a fresh penance.'"

While this was going on they saw, coming along the road they were following, a man mounted on an ass. When he came close he seemed to be a gypsy; but Sancho Panza, whose eyes and heart were wherever he saw asses, had no sooner laid eyes on the man than he knew him for Ginés de Pasamonte; and by the thread of the gypsy he got at the ball — his ass. For it was, in fact, Dapple who was carrying Pasamonte, who to escape recognition and sell the ass had disguised himself as a gypsy, being able to speak the gypsy language, and many others, as well as if they were his own. Sancho saw him and recognised him, and the instant he did so he shouted at him, "Ginesillo, you thief, give up my treasure, release my life, don't trouble yourself with my repose, leave my ass, leave my delight, get out, scoundrel, get gone, thief, and give back what isn't yours!"

There was no need for so many words or curses, for at the first one Ginés jumped down, and at a sprinter's pace made off and got clear of them all. Sancho hurried to his Dapple, and embracing him said, "How have you been, my treasure, Dapple of my eyes, my comrade?" — all the while kissing him and caressing him as if he were a human being. The ass held his peace, and let himself be kissed and caressed by Sancho without answering a single word. The others all came up and congratulated him on having found Dapple, Don Quixote especially, who told him that despite this he would not cancel the order for the three ass-colts; for which Sancho thanked him.

While the two had been going along talking like this, the curate remarked to Dorothea that she had shown great cleverness, both in the story itself and in its conciseness, and in how closely it resembled the kind found in the books of chivalry. She said she had often amused herself reading them, but that she didn't know the location of the provinces or seaports, and so she had said at random that she had landed at Osuna.

"So I saw," said the curate, "and that's why I made haste to say what I did, by which it was all set right. But isn't it a strange thing to see how readily this unhappy gentleman believes all these fictions and lies, simply because they're in the style and manner of the absurdities in his books?"
"It is," said Cardenio, "and so uncommon and unparalleled that if anyone tried to invent and concoct it as fiction, I doubt there's any wit keen enough to imagine it."

"But another strange thing about it," said the curate, "is that, apart from the silly things this worthy gentleman says in connection with his obsession, on any other subject he can discuss things in a perfectly rational way, showing that his mind is quite clear and composed. So provided his chivalry is not touched on, no one would take him for anything but a man of thoroughly sound understanding."
While they were having this conversation, Don Quixote continued his with Sancho, saying:

"Friend Panza, let's forgive and forget our quarrels, and now tell me, putting aside any anger or irritation, where, how, and when did you find Dulcinea? What was she doing? What did you say to her? What did she answer? How did she look when she was reading my letter? Who copied it out for you? — and everything in the matter that seems to you worth knowing, asking, and learning. Neither add to it nor falsify to please me, nor cut it short and deprive me of any of it."
"Señor," replied Sancho, "if the truth is to be told, nobody copied out the letter for me, because I carried no letter at all."

"It's as you say," said Don Quixote, "for the notebook in which I wrote it I found in my own possession two days after you left, which gave me very great vexation, since I had no idea what you would do on finding yourself without any letter; I felt sure you would come back from the spot where you first noticed it was missing."

"I should have done that," said Sancho, "if I hadn't got it by heart when your worship read it to me — so that I repeated it to a sacristan, who copied it out from hearing it, so exactly that he said in all the days of his life, though he had read many a letter of excommunication, he had never seen or read so pretty a letter as that one."
"And have you got it still in your memory, Sancho?" said Don Quixote.

"No, señor," replied Sancho, "because as soon as I had repeated it, seeing there was no further use for it, I set about forgetting it; and if I recall any of it, it's that bit about 'Scrubbing' — I mean to say 'Sovereign Lady' — and the end, 'Yours till death, the Knight of the Rueful Countenance;' and between those two I put more than three hundred 'my souls' and 'my life's' and 'my eyes.'"

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 31
paragraphs: About the delightful conversation between Don Quixote and Sancho Panza, his squire, together with other incidents

"None of that is unsatisfactory to me," said Don Quixote. "Go on; you reached her — and what was that queen of beauty doing? Surely you found her stringing pearls, or embroidering some device in gold thread for this her enslaved knight."
"I didn't," said Sancho. "I found her winnowing two bushels of wheat in the yard of her house."
"Then depend on it," said Don Quixote, "the grains of that wheat were pearls when touched by her hands. And did you look, friend? Was it white wheat or brown?"
"It was neither — it was red," said Sancho.

"Then I promise you," said Don Quixote, "that, winnowed by her hands, beyond a doubt the bread it made was of the whitest. But go on; when you gave her my letter, did she kiss it? Did she place it on her head? Did she perform any ceremony worthy of it, or what did she do?"

"When I went to give it to her," replied Sancho, "she was hard at it, swaying from side to side with a lot of wheat she had in the sieve, and she said to me, 'Lay the letter, friend, on top of that sack, for I can't read it until I've finished sifting all this.'"

"Discreet lady!" said Don Quixote. "That was so she could read it at her leisure and enjoy it. Go on, Sancho — while she was busy with her work, what conversation did she hold with you? What did she ask about me, and what did you answer? Hurry up; tell me everything, and let not an atom be left in the ink-bottle."

"She asked me nothing," said Sancho. "But I told her how your worship was left doing penance in her service, naked from the waist up, in among these mountains like a savage, sleeping on the ground, not eating bread off a tablecloth nor combing your beard, weeping and cursing your fortune."

"In saying I cursed my fortune you said wrong," said Don Quixote. "Rather, I bless it, and shall bless it all the days of my life for having made me worthy of aspiring to love so lofty a lady as Dulcinea del Toboso."
"And so lofty she is," said Sancho, "that she stands more than a hand's-breadth taller than I am."
"What? Sancho," said Don Quixote, "did you measure yourself against her?"
"I measured this way," said Sancho. "Going to help her put a sack of wheat on the back of an ass, we came so close together that I could see she stood more than a good palm over me."

"Well!" said Don Quixote. "And does she not in truth accompany and adorn this stature with a thousand million charms of mind? But one thing you will not deny, Sancho — when you came close to her, did you not catch a Sabaean fragrance, an aromatic scent, a — I know not what — something delicious that I cannot name; a redolence, an exhalation, as if you were in the shop of some fine glover?"
"All I can say," said Sancho, "is that I did catch a little odour, something goatish — it must have been that she was all in a sweat with hard work."

"It cannot be that," said Don Quixote. "You must have had a cold in the head, or smelled yourself; for I know well what would be the scent of that rose among thorns, that lily of the field, that dissolved amber."
"Maybe so," replied Sancho. "There often comes from me that same odour which then seemed to me to come from her grace the lady Dulcinea; but that's no wonder — one devil is like another."
