"Well then," Don Quixote continued, "now she has finished sifting the corn and sent it to the mill — what did she do when she read the letter?"

"As for the letter," said Sancho, "she didn't read it, because she said she could neither read nor write. Instead she tore it up into small pieces, saying she didn't want to let anyone read it for fear her secrets might be known in the village, and that what I had told her by word of mouth about the love your worship bore her, and the extraordinary penance you were doing for her sake, was enough; and, to make an end of it, she told me to tell your worship that she kissed your hands, and that she had a greater desire to see you than to write to you; and that therefore she begged and commanded you, on sight of this present message, to come out of these thickets and have done with carrying on absurdities, and to set out at once for El Toboso — unless something more important came up — for she had a great longing to see your worship. She laughed a great deal when I told her how your worship was called the Knight of the Rueful Countenance. I asked her if that Biscayan from the other day had been there, and she told me he had, and that he was an honest fellow; I asked her too about the galley slaves, but she said she had not seen any as yet."

"So far so good," said Don Quixote. "But tell me, what jewel did she give you on taking your leave, in return for your news of me? It's a customary and ancient practice with knights and ladies errant to give the squires, damsels, or dwarfs who bring tidings of their ladies to the knights, or of their knights to the ladies, some rich jewel as a reward for good news and acknowledgement of the message."

"That sounds very likely," said Sancho, "and a good custom too, to my mind; but that must have been in days gone by, because nowadays it seems the custom is to give only a piece of bread and cheese — which is what my lady Dulcinea gave me over the top of the yard-wall when I took leave of her. And, for added proof, it was sheep's-milk cheese."

"She is generous in the extreme," said Don Quixote, "and if she didn't give you a jewel of gold, no doubt it was because she didn't have one to hand to give you; but sleeves are good after Easter — I shall see her and all will be put right. But do you know what amazes me, Sancho? It seems to me you must have gone and come through the air, since you took little more than three days to go to El Toboso and return, even though it's more than thirty leagues from here to there. From which I'm inclined to think that the sage magician who is my friend, and watches over my interests (for there must necessarily be such a one, or else I wouldn't be a true knight-errant) — that this same magician, I say, must have helped you travel without your knowing it. Because some of these sages will catch up a knight-errant sleeping in his bed, and without his knowing how or in what way it happened, he wakes up the next day more than a thousand leagues from where he went to sleep. If it weren't for this, knights-errant could not come to one another's aid in peril, as they do at every turn. A knight, say, is fighting in the mountains of Armenia with some dragon, or fierce serpent, or another knight, and gets the worst of the battle, and is at the point of death; but when he least expects it, there appears across from him on a cloud, or chariot of fire, another knight, a friend of his, who just before had been in England, who takes his side and saves him from death; and at night he finds himself in his own quarters, supping very much to his satisfaction; and yet from one place to the other will have been two or three thousand leagues. All this is done by the craft and skill of the sage enchanters who take care of those valiant knights; so, friend Sancho, I have no difficulty in believing that you may have gone from this place to El Toboso and returned in such a short time, since, as I have said, some friendly sage must have carried you through the air without your noticing."
"That must have been it," said Sancho, "because Rocinante really did go like a gypsy's ass with quicksilver in his ears."

"Quicksilver!" said Don Quixote. "Yes, and what is more, a legion of devils — folk that can travel and make others travel without weariness, exactly as the whim takes them. But setting this aside, what do you think I should do about my lady's command to go and see her? Because, while I feel I am bound to obey her order, I feel too that I'm prevented by the boon I have granted to the princess accompanying us, and the law of chivalry compels me to honour my word in preference to my inclination. On the one hand, the desire to see my lady pursues and harasses me; on the other, my solemn promise and the glory I'll win in this enterprise urge and call to me. But what I think I'll do is travel with all speed and reach the place where this giant is as soon as possible, and on my arrival I'll cut off his head and settle the princess peacefully in her realm, and then immediately return to behold the light that illuminates my senses, to whom I will make such excuses that she'll be led to approve of my delay, since she will see that it entirely tends to increase her glory and fame — for all that I have won, am winning, or shall win by arms in this life, comes to me by the favour she extends to me, and because I am hers."

"Oh, what a sad state your worship's brains are in!" said Sancho. "Tell me, señor, do you mean to travel all that way for nothing, and to let slip and lose so rich and grand a match as this — where they give as a dowry a kingdom that in sober truth I have heard is more than twenty thousand leagues around, and abounds with everything necessary to support human life, and is bigger than Portugal and Castile put together? Peace, for the love of God! Blush for what you've said, and take my advice, and forgive me, and marry at once in the first village where there's a curate; if not, here's our licentiate, who will do the job beautifully. Remember, I'm old enough to give advice, and this advice comes pat to the purpose — for a sparrow in the hand is better than a vulture on the wing, and he who has the good in his hand and chooses the bad has no right to complain when the good doesn't come to him."

"Look here, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "If you're advising me to marry so that immediately upon killing the giant I'll become king and be able to confer favours on you and give you what I have promised — let me tell you I shall be able to satisfy your desires very easily without marrying; for before going into battle I'll make it a condition that, if I come out of it victorious, even if I don't marry, they shall give me a portion of the kingdom so I may bestow it on whomever I choose; and when they give it to me, on whom would you have me bestow it but you?"

"That's plain speaking," said Sancho. "But let your worship take care to choose it on the seacoast, so that if I don't like the life, I can ship off my black vassals and deal with them as I've said. Don't mind going to see my lady Dulcinea now — go and kill this giant and let's finish off this business; for by God it strikes me it will be a matter of great honour and great profit."

"I hold that you're right, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and I'll take your advice about accompanying the princess before going to see Dulcinea. But I caution you not to say anything to anyone, including those who are with us, about what we have considered and discussed. Since Dulcinea is so discreet that she does not want her thoughts known, it is not right that I, or anyone on my behalf, should disclose them."

"Well then, if that's the case," said Sancho, "how is it that your worship makes everyone you defeat by your arm go and present themselves before my lady Dulcinea — which is the same as signing your name to it that you love her and are her lover? And since those who go must kneel before her and say they come from your worship to submit themselves to her, how can the thoughts of either of you be hidden?"

"Oh, how foolish and simple you are!" said Don Quixote. "Don't you see, Sancho, that this only adds to her greater glory? You must know that, according to our way of thinking in chivalry, it's a high honour to a lady to have many knights-errant in her service, whose thoughts go no further than serving her for her own sake, and who look for no other reward for their great and true devotion than that she should be willing to accept them as her knights."

"It's with that kind of love," said Sancho, "that I have heard preachers say we ought to love our Lord — for himself alone, without being moved by the hope of glory or the fear of punishment; though for my part, I would rather love and serve him for what he could do."
"The devil take you for a clown!" said Don Quixote. "What shrewd things you say at times! One would think you'd studied."
"In faith, then, I cannot even read."

Master Nicholas called out to them at this point to wait a while, as they wanted to stop and drink at a little spring there was nearby. Don Quixote drew up, much to the satisfaction of Sancho, who by this time was weary of telling so many lies and afraid his master would catch him tripping; for though he knew that Dulcinea was a peasant girl of El Toboso, he had never seen her in his life. Cardenio had now put on the clothes Dorothea was wearing when they found her, and though they weren't very good, they were far better than the ones he took off. They dismounted together by the side of the spring, and with what the curate had provided himself with at the inn they appeased, though not very well, the keen appetite they had all brought with them.

While they were so occupied, a youth happened to come by on his way along the road; stopping to examine the party at the spring, the next moment he ran to Don Quixote and, clasping him around the legs, began to weep freely, saying, "Oh, señor, do you not know me? Look at me well; I am that lad Andrés that your worship released from the oak-tree where I was tied."

Don Quixote recognised him, and taking his hand, he turned to those present and said: "So that your worships may see how important it is to have knights-errant in the world to redress the wrongs and injuries done by tyrannical and wicked men, I tell you that some days ago, passing through a wood, I heard cries and pitiful complaints as of a person in pain and distress; I immediately hurried, driven by my bounden duty, to the quarter from which the plaintive sounds seemed to come, and I found this lad now before you tied to an oak — which I rejoice at in my heart, for his testimony will not permit me to depart from the truth in any particular. He was, I say, tied to an oak, naked from the waist up, and a clown, whom I later found to be his master, was scoring him with lashes from the reins of his mare. As soon as I saw him I asked the reason for so cruel a flogging. The boor replied that he was flogging him because he was his servant, and because of carelessness that proceeded more from dishonesty than stupidity; at which this boy said, 'Señor, he flogs me only because I ask for my wages.' The master made I-don't-know-what speeches and explanations, which, though I listened, I didn't accept. In short, I forced the clown to unbind him and to swear he would take him with him and pay him real by real, and perfumed into the bargain. Isn't that all true, Andrés my son? Didn't you notice with what authority I commanded him, and with what humility he promised to do all I enjoined, specified, and required of him? Answer without hesitation; tell these gentlemen what took place, so they may see that it's as great an advantage as I say to have knights-errant abroad."
"All that your worship has said is quite true," answered the lad, "but the end of the business turned out just the opposite of what your worship supposes."
"What? The opposite?" said Don Quixote. "Did the clown not pay you, then?"

"Not only did he not pay me," replied the lad, "but as soon as your worship had passed out of the wood and we were alone, he tied me up again to the same oak and gave me a fresh flogging that left me like a flayed Saint Bartholomew; and every stroke he gave me he followed up with some joke or jeer about having made a fool of your worship — and but for the pain I was in, I should have laughed at the things he said. In short, he left me in such a state that I have been until now in a hospital getting cured of the injuries that rascally clown inflicted on me then — for which your worship is to blame. Because if you had gone your own way and not come where there was no call for you, nor meddled in other people's affairs, my master would have been content with giving me one or two dozen lashes and would then have untied me and paid me what he owed me. But when your worship abused him so out of all measure and gave him so many hard words, his anger was kindled; and since he couldn't take revenge on you, as soon as he saw you had left him, the storm burst on me in such a way that I feel I shall never be a man again."

"The mischief," said Don Quixote, "lay in my going away; for I should not have gone until I had seen you paid. Because I ought to have known well by long experience that there is no clown who will keep his word if he finds it doesn't suit him to keep it. But you remember, Andrés, that I swore if he didn't pay you I would go and seek him and find him, even if he hid himself in the whale's belly."
"That's true," said Andrés, "but it was no use."

"You shall see now whether it's of use or not," said Don Quixote. And so saying, he got up hastily and told Sancho to bridle Rocinante, who was grazing while they ate. Dorothea asked him what he meant to do. He replied that he meant to go in search of this clown and chastise him for such wicked conduct, and see Andrés paid to the last maravedí, in spite of all the clowns in the world. To which she replied that he must remember that, in accordance with his promise, he could not undertake any enterprise until he had finished hers; and that since he knew this better than anyone, he should restrain his ardour until his return from her kingdom.
"That's true," said Don Quixote, "and Andrés must have patience until my return, as you say, señora; but I once more swear and promise not to stop until I have seen him avenged and paid."

"I have no faith in those oaths," said Andrés. "I would rather have something now to help me get to Seville than all the revenges in the world. If you have anything to eat that I can take with me, give it to me, and God be with your worship and all knights-errant; and may their errands turn out as well for themselves as they have for me."
Sancho took a piece of bread and another of cheese out of his store and, giving them to the lad, said, "Here, take this, brother Andrés, since we all of us have a share in your misfortune."
"Why — what share have you got?"

"This share of bread and cheese I'm giving you," answered Sancho, "and God knows whether I shall feel the want of it myself or not. I'll have you know, friend, that we squires to knights-errant have to bear a great deal of hunger and hard fortune, and other things too more easily felt than told."

Andrés seized his bread and cheese, and seeing that nobody gave him anything more, bent his head and took to the road, as the saying is. Before leaving, however, he said, "For the love of God, sir knight-errant, if you ever meet me again, even if you see them cutting me to pieces, give me no aid or help, but leave me to my misfortune — which will not be so great but that a greater will come to me by being helped by your worship, on whom, and on all the knights-errant ever born, God send his curse."

Don Quixote was getting up to chastise him, but he took to his heels at such a pace that no one tried to follow him; and mightily crestfallen was Don Quixote at Andrés's story, and the others had to take great care to restrain their laughter so as not to put him entirely out of countenance.

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 32
paragraphs: About what befell Don Quixote's party at the inn

Their tasty meal finished, they saddled up at once, and without any adventure worth mentioning they reached the next day the inn — the object of Sancho Panza's fear and dread; but though he would rather not have gone in, there was no help for it. The landlady, the landlord, their daughter, and Maritornes, when they saw Don Quixote and Sancho coming, went out to welcome them with signs of hearty satisfaction, which Don Quixote received with dignity and gravity; and he told them to make up a better bed for him than the last time. To which the landlady replied that if he paid better than he did the last time, she would give him one fit for a prince. Don Quixote said he would, so they made up a tolerable one for him in the same garret as before; and he lay down at once, being sorely shaken and in want of sleep.
No sooner was the door shut on him than the landlady made for the barber, and seizing him by the beard, said:

"By my faith, you're not going to make a beard of my tail any longer; you must give me back my tail, for it's a shame the way that thing of my husband's is left tossing about on the floor — I mean the comb I used to stick in my good tail."

But for all she tugged at it, the barber would not give it up until the licentiate told him to let her have it, since there was no further need for that stratagem now: he could declare himself and appear in his own character and tell Don Quixote that he had fled to this inn when those thieves the galley slaves robbed him; and if he asked for the princess's squire, they could tell him that she had sent him on ahead to give notice to the people of her kingdom that she was coming, and bringing with her the deliverer of them all. At this the barber cheerfully restored the tail to the landlady, and at the same time they returned all the other items they had borrowed to bring about Don Quixote's deliverance. All the people of the inn were struck with astonishment at the beauty of Dorothea, and even at the comely figure of the shepherd Cardenio. The curate had them get ready such food as there was in the inn, and the landlord, in hope of better payment, served them up a tolerably good dinner. All this time Don Quixote was asleep, and they thought it best not to wake him, since sleeping would now do him more good than eating.

While at dinner, the company consisting of the landlord, his wife, their daughter, Maritornes, and all the travellers, they discussed the strange craze of Don Quixote and the way he had been found; and the landlady told them what had taken place between him and the carrier; and then, looking round to see if Sancho was there, when she saw he wasn't, she gave them the whole story of his blanketing, which they received with no little amusement. But when the curate observed that it was the books of chivalry Don Quixote had read that had turned his brain, the landlord said:

"I can't understand how that can be, for in truth to my mind there's no better reading in the world; I have here two or three of them, with other writings that are the very life — not only of me but of plenty of others. Because when it's harvest time, the reapers flock here on holidays, and there's always one among them who can read, and he takes up one of these books, and we gather round him, thirty or more of us, and stay listening to him with a delight that makes our grey hairs grow young again. At least I can say for myself that when I hear of what furious and terrible blows the knights deliver, the longing seizes me to do the same, and I would like to be hearing about them night and day."

"And so would I," said the landlady, "because I never have a quiet moment in my house except when you're listening to someone reading — for then you're so taken up that for the time being you forget to scold."

"That's true," said Maritornes; "and, faith, I greatly enjoy hearing these things too, for they are very pretty — especially when they describe some lady or other in the arms of her knight under the orange trees, and the duenna keeping watch for them is half dead with envy and fright; all this, I say, is as good as honey."
"And you, what do you think, young lady?" said the curate, turning to the landlord's daughter.

"I really don't know, señor," she said. "I listen too, and to tell the truth, though I don't understand it, I like hearing it. But it's not the blows that my father likes that I like — it's the laments the knights utter when they are separated from their ladies; and indeed they sometimes make me weep with the pity I feel for them."
"Then you would console them if it were for you they wept, young lady?" said Dorothea.

"I don't know what I should do," said the girl. "I only know that there are some of those ladies so cruel that they call their knights tigers and lions and a thousand other foul names; and Jesus! — I don't know what sort of folk they can be, so unfeeling and heartless that, rather than bestow a glance on a worthy man, they leave him to die or go mad. I don't know what's the good of such prudery; if it's for honour's sake, why not marry them? That's all they want."
"Hush, child," said the landlady. "It seems to me you know a great deal about these things, and it's not fitting for girls to know or talk so much."
"Since the gentleman asked me, I couldn't help answering him," said the girl.
"Well then," said the curate, "bring me those books, señor landlord, for I should like to see them."

"With all my heart," said he, and going into his own room he brought out an old valise secured with a little chain, which when opened the curate found to contain three large books and some manuscripts written in a very good hand. The first he opened he found to be _Don Cirongilio of Thrace_; the second, _Don Felixmarte of Hircania_; and the other, the _History of the Great Captain Gonzalo Hernández de Córdoba, with the Life of Diego García de Paredes_.
When the curate read the first two titles he looked over at the barber and said, "We could use my friend's housekeeper and niece here now."
"No," said the barber, "I can do just as well by carrying them out to the yard or to the hearth — and there's a very good fire there."
"What? Your worship would burn my books?" said the landlord.
"Only these two," said the curate, "_Don Cirongilio_ and _Felixmarte_."
"Are my books, then, heretics or phlegmatics, that you want to burn them?" said the landlord.
"Schismatics, you mean, friend," said the barber, "not phlegmatics."

"That's it," said the landlord; "but if you want to burn any, let it be the one about the Great Captain and that Diego García — because I'd rather have a child of mine burnt than either of the other two."

"Brother," said the curate, "those two books are made up of lies and are full of folly and nonsense; but this one about the Great Captain is true history, and contains the deeds of Gonzalo Hernández of Córdoba, who by his many and great achievements earned the title all over the world of the Great Captain — a famous and illustrious name, deserved by him alone. And this Diego García de Paredes was a distinguished knight of the city of Trujillo in Estremadura, a most gallant soldier, of such bodily strength that with one finger he stopped a mill-wheel in full motion; and posted with a two-handed sword at the foot of a bridge he kept a whole vast army from passing across it, and achieved such other exploits that if, instead of his relating them himself with the modesty of a knight and of one writing his own history, some free and impartial writer had recorded them, they would have put in the shade all the deeds of the Hectors, Achilleses, and Rolands."

"Tell that to my father!" said the landlord. "There's a thing to be astonished at — stopping a mill-wheel! By God, your worship should read what I have read of Felixmarte of Hircania, how with one single backstroke he cleft five giants asunder through the middle as if they had been made of bean-pods like the little friars the children make; and another time he attacked a very great and powerful army of more than a million six hundred thousand soldiers, all armed from head to foot, and he routed them all as if they had been flocks of sheep."

"And then, what do you say to the good Cirongilio of Thrace, who was so stout and bold? — as may be seen in the book, where it's told that as he was sailing along a river there came up out of the middle of the water against him a fiery serpent, and as soon as he saw it he flung himself on it and got astride its scaly shoulders, and squeezed its throat with both hands with such force that the serpent, finding it was being throttled, had nothing for it but to let itself sink to the bottom of the river, carrying with it the knight, who would not let go his hold; and when they got down there he found himself among palaces and gardens so beautiful it was a wonder to see; and then the serpent changed itself into an old ancient man, who told him things never heard before. Hold your peace, señor; if you were to hear this you would go mad with delight. A couple of figs for your Great Captain and your Diego García!"
Hearing this, Dorothea said in a whisper to Cardenio, "Our landlord is almost fit to play a second part to Don Quixote."

"I think so," said Cardenio, "because, as he shows, he accepts it as a certainty that everything those books relate happened exactly as it's written down; and the barefoot friars themselves could not persuade him to the contrary."

"But consider, brother," said the curate again, "there never was any Felixmarte of Hircania in the world, nor any Cirongilio of Thrace, or any of the other knights of the same sort that the books of chivalry talk about. The whole thing is the fabrication and invention of idle wits, devised by them for the purpose you describe — of passing the time, as your reapers do when they read. For I swear to you in all seriousness, there never were any such knights in the world, and no such exploits or nonsense ever happened anywhere."

"Try that bone on another dog!" said the landlord. "As if I didn't know how many make five, and where my shoe pinches me. Don't think to feed me with pap, for by God I'm no fool. It's a fine joke for your worship to try to convince me that everything these good books say is nonsense and lies, when they're printed by license of the Lords of the Royal Council — as if they were people who would allow such a load of lies to be printed all together, and so many battles and enchantments that they take away one's senses."

"I have told you, friend," said the curate, "that it's done to divert our idle thoughts; and just as in well-ordered states games of chess, fives, and billiards are allowed for the diversion of those who don't care to work, or aren't obliged to, or can't, so books of this kind are allowed to be printed, on the supposition — which is in fact the truth — that there can be nobody so ignorant as to take any of them for true stories. And if I were allowed now, and the present company wished it, I could say something about the qualities books of chivalry should possess to be good ones, which would be to the advantage and even to the taste of some; but I hope the time will come when I can communicate my ideas to someone who might be able to mend matters. In the meantime, señor landlord, believe what I have said, and take your books and make up your mind about their truth or falsehood; and much good may they do you — and God grant you may not fall lame of the same foot your guest Don Quixote limps on."

"No fear of that," replied the landlord. "I shall not be so mad as to make a knight-errant of myself; I see well enough that things are not now as they used to be in those days when, they say, those famous knights roamed about the world."

Sancho had appeared in the middle of this conversation, and he was very much troubled and downcast by what he heard said about knights-errant being no longer in vogue, and all books of chivalry being folly and lies. He resolved in his heart to wait and see what came of this journey of his master's, and if it didn't turn out as happily as his master expected, he determined to leave him and go back to his wife and children and his ordinary work.

The landlord was carrying away the valise and the books when the curate said to him, "Wait — I want to see what those papers are that are written in such a good hand." The landlord took them out and handed them to him to read, and he saw it was a work of about eight sheets of manuscript, with, in large letters at the beginning, the title _Novel of the Ill-Advised Curiosity_. The curate read three or four lines to himself and said, "I must say the title of this novel doesn't seem bad to me, and I feel an inclination to read it all." To which the landlord replied, "Then your reverence will do well to read it, because I can tell you that some guests who have read it here have been much pleased with it and have begged it from me very earnestly. But I wouldn't give it, meaning to return it to the person who forgot the valise, books, and papers here — since maybe he'll come back here some time or other. And though I know I shall miss the books, faith I mean to return them; for though I am an innkeeper, still I am a Christian."
"You are quite right, friend," said the curate, "but for all that, if the novel pleases me you must let me copy it."
"With all my heart," replied the host.
While they were talking, Cardenio had taken up the novel and begun to read it, and forming the same opinion of it as the curate, he begged him to read it so they might all hear it.
"I would read it," said the curate, "if the time wouldn't be better spent in sleeping."
"It will be rest enough for me," said Dorothea, "to while away the time by listening to some tale, for my spirits are not yet calm enough to let me sleep when it would be seasonable."
"Well then, in that case," said the curate, "I will read it, if only out of curiosity; perhaps it may contain something pleasant."

Master Nicholas added his entreaties to the same effect, and Sancho too; seeing which, and considering that he would give pleasure to all and receive it himself, the curate said, "Well then, everyone attend, for the novel begins like this."

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 33
paragraphs: In which is told the novel of "The Ill-Advised Curiosity"

In Florence, a rich and famous city of Italy in the province called Tuscany, there lived two gentlemen of wealth and quality, Anselmo and Lothario, such great friends that by way of distinction they were called by everyone who knew them "The Two Friends." They were unmarried, young, of the same age, and of the same tastes — which was enough to account for the mutual friendship between them. Anselmo, it's true, was somewhat more inclined to seek pleasure in love than Lothario, for whom the pleasures of the chase had more attraction; but on occasion Anselmo would forgo his own tastes to yield to Lothario's, and Lothario would surrender his to fall in with Anselmo's, and in this way their inclinations kept pace with one another with a harmony so perfect that the best-regulated clock could not have surpassed it.

Anselmo was deep in love with a high-born and beautiful maiden of the same city, the daughter of parents so estimable, and so estimable herself, that he resolved — with the approval of his friend Lothario, without whom he did nothing — to ask her of them in marriage; and did so, Lothario being the bearer of the request and conducting the negotiation so much to his friend's satisfaction that in a short time he was in possession of the object of his desires, and Camilla was so happy in having won Anselmo for her husband that she gave thanks unceasingly to heaven, and to Lothario, by whose means such good fortune had come to her. The first few days, those of a wedding being usually days of celebration, Lothario frequented his friend Anselmo's house as he had been accustomed, striving to do honour to him and to the occasion, and to gratify him in every way he could; but when the wedding days were over and the round of visits and congratulations had slackened, he began purposely to leave off going to Anselmo's house. It seemed to him, as it would naturally seem to any sensible man, that friends' houses ought not to be visited after marriage with the same frequency as in their masters' bachelor days — because, though true and genuine friendship cannot and should not be in any way suspicious, still a married man's honour is a thing so delicate that it is held liable to injury even from brothers, let alone from friends. Anselmo noticed the cessation of Lothario's visits, and complained to him about it, saying that if he had known marriage was going to keep him from enjoying his company as before, he would never have married; and that if, by the thorough harmony that had existed between them while he was a bachelor, they had earned so sweet a name as that of "The Two Friends," he should not allow a title so rare and so delightful to be lost through a needless anxiety to be circumspect; and so he begged him — if such a phrase was allowable between them — to be once more master of his house, and to come in and go out as before, assuring him that his wife Camilla had no other desire or inclination than that which he would wish her to have, and that knowing how sincerely they loved one another she was grieved to see such coldness in him.

To all this and much more that Anselmo said to Lothario to persuade him to come to his house as he had been in the habit of doing, Lothario replied with so much prudence, sense, and judgement that Anselmo was satisfied of his friend's good intentions, and it was agreed that on two days of the week, and on holidays, Lothario would come to dine with him. But although this arrangement was made between them, Lothario resolved to observe it no further than he judged compatible with his friend's honour, whose good name was more to him than his own. He said, and rightly, that a married man on whom heaven had bestowed a beautiful wife should consider as carefully what friends he brought to his house as what female friends his wife associated with — because what cannot be done or arranged in the market-place, in church, at public festivals or at stations (opportunities that husbands cannot always deny their wives) may be easily managed in the house of the female friend or relative in whom most confidence is placed. Lothario said, too, that every married man should have some friend who would point out to him any negligence he might be guilty of in his conduct — for it will sometimes happen that owing to the deep affection the husband bears his wife, either he does not caution her or, so as not to vex her, refrains from telling her to do or not to do certain things, the doing or avoiding of which may be a matter of honour or reproach to him; and errors of this kind he could easily correct if warned by a friend. But where is such a friend to be found as Lothario describes — so judicious, so loyal, and so true?

In truth, I don't know; Lothario alone was such a one, for with the utmost care and vigilance he watched over the honour of his friend, and strove to reduce, cut down, and limit the number of days for going to his house according to their agreement, lest the visits of a young man — wealthy, high-born, and with the attractions he was conscious of possessing — at the house of a woman as beautiful as Camilla, should be regarded with suspicion by the inquisitive and malicious eyes of the idle public. Because, though his integrity and reputation might bridle slanderous tongues, still he was unwilling to risk either his own good name or that of his friend; and for this reason on most of the days agreed upon he devoted himself to some other business which he pretended was unavoidable, so that a great portion of the day was taken up with complaints on one side and excuses on the other. It happened, however, that on one occasion when the two were walking together outside the city, Anselmo addressed the following words to Lothario.

"You may imagine, Lothario my friend, that I am unable to give sufficient thanks for the favours God has done me in making me the son of such parents as mine were, and bestowing on me with no stingy hand what are called the gifts of nature as well as those of fortune — and above all for what he has done in giving me you for a friend and Camilla for a wife: two treasures that I value, if not as highly as I should, at least as highly as I am able. And yet, with all these good things — which are commonly all that men need to live happily — I am the most discontented and dissatisfied man in the whole world. For some time now, I have been harassed and oppressed by a desire so strange and so unusual that I wonder at myself and blame and chide myself when I'm alone, and try to stifle it and hide it from my own thoughts — and with no better success than if I were deliberately trying to publish it to all the world. And since, in short, it must come out, I would confide it to your safe keeping, feeling sure that by this means, and by your readiness as a true friend to help me, I shall soon find myself freed from the distress it causes me, and that your care will give me happiness in the same degree as my own folly has caused me misery."

Anselmo's words struck Lothario with astonishment, unable as he was to guess the purport of such a long preamble; and though he tried to imagine what desire it could be that so troubled his friend, his guesses were all far from the truth. To relieve the anxiety this perplexity was causing him, he told him he was doing a flagrant injustice to their great friendship in seeking circuitous ways of confiding to him his most hidden thoughts — for he well knew he could count on his counsel in turning them aside, or on his help in carrying them into effect.

"That is the truth," replied Anselmo, "and relying on that I will tell you, friend Lothario, that the desire which harasses me is to know whether my wife Camilla is as good and as perfect as I think her to be; and I cannot satisfy myself of the truth on this point except by testing her in such a way that the trial may prove the purity of her virtue as fire proves that of gold. Because I am persuaded, my friend, that a woman is virtuous only in proportion as she is or is not tempted; and that she alone is strong who does not yield to the promises, gifts, tears, and importunities of earnest lovers. For what thanks does a woman deserve for being good if no one urges her to be bad, and what wonder is it that she is reserved and circumspect to whom no opportunity is given of going wrong, and who knows she has a husband that will take her life the first time he catches her in an impropriety? So I do not hold her who is virtuous through fear or want of opportunity in the same estimation as her who comes out of temptation and trial with a crown of victory. And so, for these reasons and many others I could give you to justify and support the opinion I hold, I desire that my wife Camilla should pass this crisis, and be refined and tested by the fire of finding herself wooed, and by one worthy to set his affections on her; and if she comes out, as I know she will, victorious from this struggle, I shall look upon my good fortune as unequalled, I shall be able to say that the cup of my desire is full, and that the virtuous woman of whom the sage says 'Who shall find her?' has fallen to my lot. And if the result is the opposite of what I expect, in the satisfaction of knowing I was right in my opinion, I shall bear without complaint the pain that my so dearly bought experience will naturally cause me. And since nothing you can urge against my wish will avail to keep me from carrying it out, it is my desire, friend Lothario, that you consent to become the instrument for effecting this purpose I am bent on. For I will afford you opportunities to that end, and nothing shall be lacking that I may think necessary for the pursuit of a virtuous, honourable, modest and high-minded woman. And among other reasons, I am led to entrust this hard task to you by the consideration that if Camilla is conquered by you, the conquest will not be pushed to extremes, but only far enough to count as accomplished what from a sense of honour will be left undone; thus I shall not be wronged in anything beyond intention, and my wrong will remain buried in the integrity of your silence, which I know well will be as lasting as that of death where it concerns me. If, then, you would have me enjoy what can be called life, you will at once engage in this love-struggle — not lukewarmly nor sluggishly, but with the energy and zeal my desire demands, and with the loyalty our friendship assures me of."

These were the words Anselmo addressed to Lothario, who listened to them with such attention that, apart from what's already been mentioned, he did not open his lips until the other had finished. Then perceiving that he had no more to say, after looking at him for a while as one would regard something never before seen that excited wonder and amazement, he said to him, "I cannot persuade myself, Anselmo my friend, that what you have said to me is not in jest; if I had thought you were speaking seriously, I would not have allowed you to go so far, but would have put a stop to your long harangue by not listening to you. I truly suspect that either you do not know me, or I do not know you; but no, I know well you are Anselmo, and you know I am Lothario. The misfortune is, it seems to me, that you are not the Anselmo you were, and you must have thought I am not the Lothario I should be; for the things you've said to me are not those of the Anselmo who was my friend, nor are those you demand of me what should be asked of the Lothario you know. True friends will prove their friends and make use of them, as a poet has said, _usque ad aras_ — by which he meant that they will not make use of their friendship in things that are contrary to God's will. If this, then, was a heathen's feeling about friendship, how much more should it be a Christian's, who knows that the divine must not be forfeited for the sake of any human friendship? And if a friend should go so far as to put aside his duty to Heaven to fulfil his duty to his friend, it should not be in matters that are trifling or of little moment, but in such as concern the friend's life and honour. Now tell me, Anselmo, in which of these two are you imperilled, that I should hazard myself to gratify you, and do a thing as detestable as the one you ask of me? Neither, in fact; on the contrary, you ask me, as far as I understand, to strive and labour to rob you of honour and life, and to rob myself of them at the same time. For if I take away your honour, it's plain I take away your life, since a man without honour is worse than dead; and being the instrument, as you would have it, of so much wrong to you, shall not I too be left without honour, and consequently without life? Listen to me, Anselmo my friend, and don't be impatient to answer me until I have said what occurs to me about the object of your desire — there will be time enough left for you to reply and for me to hear."
"So be it," said Anselmo. "Say what you will."

Lothario then went on to say, "It seems to me, Anselmo, that yours is just now the temper of mind that's always that of the Moors, who can never be brought to see the error of their creed by quotations from the Holy Scriptures, or by reasons that depend upon examination of the understanding or are founded on the articles of faith — they must have examples that are tangible, easy, intelligible, capable of proof, not admitting of doubt, with mathematical demonstrations that cannot be denied, such as, '_If equals be taken from equals, the remainders are equal;_' and if they do not understand this in words — and indeed they do not — it has to be shown to them with the hands, and put before their eyes, and even with all this nobody succeeds in convincing them of the truth of our holy religion. This same procedure I shall have to adopt with you, since the desire that has sprung up in you is so absurd and so remote from anything resembling reason that I feel it would be a waste of time to spend any in reasoning with your simplicity — for at present I'll call it by no other name. I'm even tempted to leave you in your folly as punishment for your pernicious desire; but the friendship I bear you, which will not allow me to abandon you in such manifest danger of destruction, keeps me from dealing so harshly with you. And so that you may clearly see this — tell me, Anselmo, haven't you told me that I must force my suit upon a modest woman, decoy one that is virtuous, make overtures to one that is pure-minded, pay court to one that is prudent? Yes, you have told me so. Then, if you know you have a wife who is modest, virtuous, pure-minded, and prudent, what is it that you seek? And if you believe she will come forth victorious from all my attacks — as no doubt she would — what higher titles than those she possesses now do you think you can bestow on her then, or in what will she be better then than she is now? Either you do not hold her to be what you say, or you don't know what you're asking. If you don't hold her to be what you say, why do you seek to test her, instead of treating her as guilty in whatever way may seem best to you? But if she is as virtuous as you believe, it is an unwarranted proceeding to put truth itself on trial — for after the trial, it will but be in the same estimation as before. So it is conclusive that to attempt things from which harm rather than good may come to us is the part of unreasoning and reckless minds, especially when they are things we are not forced or compelled to attempt, and which show from afar that it is plainly madness to attempt them.

"Difficulties are attempted either for the sake of God or for the sake of the world, or for both: those undertaken for God's sake are those the saints undertake when they attempt to live the lives of angels in human bodies; those undertaken for the sake of the world are those of the men who cross such a vast expanse of water, such a variety of climates, so many strange countries, to acquire what are called the blessings of fortune; and those undertaken for the sake of God and the world together are those of brave soldiers, who no sooner see in the enemy's wall a breach as wide as a cannonball could make than, casting aside all fear, without hesitating or heeding the manifest peril that threatens them, borne onward by the desire of defending their faith, their country, and their king, they fling themselves dauntlessly into the midst of the thousand deaths that await them. Such are the things that men are accustomed to attempt, and there is honour, glory, gain in attempting them, however full of difficulty and peril they may be. But what you say it is your wish to attempt and carry out will win you neither the glory of God, nor the blessings of fortune, nor fame among men. For even if the issue is as you would have it, you will be no happier, richer, or more honoured than you are at this moment; and if it is otherwise, you will be reduced to misery greater than can be imagined — for then it will avail you nothing to reflect that no one knows of the misfortune that has befallen you; it will suffice to torture and crush you that you know it yourself. And in confirmation of the truth of what I say, let me repeat to you a stanza by the famous poet Luigi Tansillo at the end of the first part of his _Tears of Saint Peter_, which says this:

The anguish and the shame but greater grew / In Peter's heart as morning slowly came; / No eye was there to see him, well he knew, / Yet he himself was to himself a shame; / Exposed to all men's gaze, or screened from view, / A noble heart will feel the pang the same; / A prey to shame the sinning soul will be, / Though none but heaven and earth its shame can see.

Thus by keeping it secret you will not escape your sorrow; rather, you will shed tears unceasingly — if not tears of the eyes, tears of blood from the heart, like those shed by that simple doctor our poet tells us of, who tried the test of the cup, which the wise Rinaldo, better advised, refused to do. For though this may be a poetic fiction, it contains a moral lesson worthy of attention, study, and imitation. Moreover, by what I am about to say to you, you will be led to see the great error you would commit.

"Tell me, Anselmo: if Heaven or good fortune had made you the master and lawful owner of a diamond of the finest quality, with the excellence and purity of which all the jewellers who had seen it had been satisfied, saying with one voice and common consent that in purity, quality, and fineness it was all that a stone of the kind could possibly be — you yourself too being of the same belief, since you knew nothing to the contrary — would it be reasonable for you to want to take that diamond and place it between an anvil and a hammer, and by sheer force of blows and strength of arm test whether it was as hard and as fine as they said? And if you did, and if the stone survived so silly a test, that would add nothing to its value or reputation; and if it were broken, as it might be, would not all be lost? Undoubtedly it would, leaving its owner to be reckoned a fool in the opinion of all. Consider, then, Anselmo my friend, that Camilla is a diamond of the finest quality, both in your estimation and in that of others, and that it is contrary to reason to expose her to the risk of being broken. For if she remains intact, she cannot rise to a higher value than she now possesses; and if she give way and be unable to resist, think now how you will be deprived of her, and with what good reason you will reproach yourself for having been the cause of her ruin and your own. Remember there is no jewel in the world so precious as a chaste and virtuous woman, and that the whole honour of women consists in reputation; and since your wife's is of that high excellence you know, why should you seek to call that truth in question? Remember, my friend, that woman is an imperfect creature, and that impediments are not to be placed in her way to make her trip and fall, but should be removed, and her path left clear of all obstacles, so that without hindrance she may run her course freely to attain the perfection she lacks, which consists in being virtuous. Naturalists tell us that the ermine is a little animal that has a fur of purest white, and that when the hunters wish to take it, they use this trick. Having found out the places it frequents and passes, they block the way to them with mud, and then rousing it, drive it towards the spot; and as soon as the ermine comes to the mud it halts, and allows itself to be taken captive rather than pass through the mire and spoil and sully its whiteness, which it values more than life and liberty. The virtuous and chaste woman is an ermine, and whiter and purer than snow is the virtue of modesty; and he who wishes her not to lose it but to keep and preserve it must adopt a course different from the one used with the ermine — he must not put before her the mire of the gifts and attentions of persistent lovers, because perhaps — and even without a perhaps — she may not have sufficient virtue and natural strength in herself to pass through and trample these impediments underfoot; they must be removed, and the brightness of virtue and the beauty of a fair name must be set before her. A virtuous woman, too, is like a mirror of clear shining crystal, liable to be tarnished and dimmed by every breath that touches it. She must be treated as relics are — adored, not touched. She must be protected and prized as one protects and prizes a fair garden full of roses and flowers, the owner of which lets no one trespass or pluck a blossom; enough for others that from afar and through the iron grating they may enjoy its fragrance and its beauty. Finally, let me repeat to you some verses that come to my mind; I heard them in a modern play, and it seems to me they bear upon the point we are discussing. A prudent old man was giving advice to another, the father of a young girl, to lock her up, watch over her, and keep her in seclusion, and among other arguments he used these:
Woman is a thing of glass; / But her brittleness 'tis best / Not too curiously to test: / Who knows what may come to pass?
Breaking is an easy matter, / And it's folly to expose / What you cannot mend to blows; / What you can't make whole to shatter.
This, then, all may hold as true, / And the reason's plain to see; / For if Danaës there be, / There are golden showers too.

"All that I have said to you so far, Anselmo, has concerned what touches you; now it's right that I should say something of what regards myself; and if I am long-winded, pardon me, for the labyrinth into which you have entered and from which you would have me extricate you makes it necessary.

"You reckon me your friend, and you would rob me of honour — a thing wholly inconsistent with friendship; and not only do you aim at this, but you would have me rob you of it also. That you would rob me of it is clear, for when Camilla sees that I pay court to her as you require, she will certainly regard me as a man without honour or right feeling, since I attempt and do a thing so much opposed to what I owe to my own position and to your friendship. That you would have me rob you of it is beyond doubt — for Camilla, seeing that I press my suit on her, will suppose that I have noticed something light in her that has encouraged me to disclose my base desire to her; and if she holds herself dishonoured, her dishonour touches you as belonging to her. And from this arises what so commonly takes place — that the husband of the adulterous woman, though he may not be aware of, or have given any cause for, his wife's failure in her duty, or (being careless or negligent) have had it in his power to prevent his dishonour, is nevertheless stigmatised by a vile and reproachful name, and in a manner regarded with eyes of contempt instead of pity by all who know of his wife's guilt — though they see that he is unfortunate not by his own fault, but by the lust of a vicious consort. But I'll tell you why with good reason dishonour attaches to the husband of the unchaste wife, even though he does not know she is so, nor is to blame, nor has done anything or given any provocation to make her so; and don't be tired of listening to me, for it will be for your good.

"When God created our first parent in the earthly paradise, the Holy Scripture says that he caused sleep to fall on Adam, and while he slept took a rib from his left side, of which he formed our mother Eve; and when Adam awoke and beheld her he said, 'This is flesh of my flesh, and bone of my bone.' And God said, 'For this shall a man leave his father and his mother, and they shall be two in one flesh;' and then was instituted the divine sacrament of marriage, with such ties that death alone can loose them. And such is the force and virtue of this miraculous sacrament that it makes two different persons one and the same flesh; and even more than this, when the virtuous are married — for though they have two souls they have but one will. And so it follows that as the flesh of the wife is one and the same with that of her husband, the stains that may come upon it, or the injuries it incurs, fall upon the husband's flesh, even though he, as has been said, may have given no cause for them. For just as the pain of the foot or of any member of the body is felt by the whole body, because all is one flesh, as the head feels the hurt to the ankle without having caused it, so the husband, being one with her, shares the dishonour of the wife; and since all worldly honour or dishonour comes of flesh and blood, and the erring wife's is of that kind, the husband must necessarily bear his part of it, and be held dishonoured without knowing it. Consider, then, Anselmo, the peril you are running in seeking to disturb the peace of your virtuous consort; consider for what an empty and ill-advised curiosity you would rouse up passions that now rest in quiet in the breast of your chaste wife. Reflect that what you are staking everything to win is little, and what you will lose is so much that I leave it undescribed, not having the words to express it. But if all I have said is not enough to turn you from your vile purpose, you must seek some other instrument for your dishonour and misfortune — for I will not consent to be one, though I lose your friendship, the greatest loss I can conceive."

Having said this, the wise and virtuous Lothario was silent, and Anselmo, troubled in mind and deep in thought, was unable for a while to utter a word in reply; but at length he said, "I have listened, Lothario my friend, attentively, as you have seen, to what you have chosen to say to me, and in your arguments, examples, and comparisons I have seen the high intelligence you possess and the perfection of true friendship you have reached; and likewise I see and confess that if I am not guided by your opinion but follow my own, I am running from the good and pursuing the evil. This being so, you must remember that I am now suffering from that infirmity women sometimes suffer from, when the craving seizes them to eat clay, plaster, charcoal, and things even worse, disgusting to look at, much more to eat. So it will be necessary to have recourse to some artifice to cure me; and this can easily be done if only you will begin, even though it be in a lukewarm and make-believe way, to pay court to Camilla, who will not be so yielding that her virtue gives way at the first attack. With this mere attempt I shall rest satisfied, and you will have done what our friendship binds you to do, not only in giving me life but in persuading me not to discard my honour. And you are bound to do this for one reason alone: that, being as I am resolved to apply this test, it is not for you to permit me to reveal my weakness to another, and so imperil that honour you are striving to keep me from losing. And if yours may not stand as high as it should in Camilla's estimation while you are paying court to her, that is of little or no importance — because before long, on finding in her that constancy we expect, you can tell her the plain truth about our stratagem, and so regain your place in her esteem. And since you are venturing so little, and by the venture can give me so much satisfaction, do not refuse to undertake it, even if further difficulties present themselves — for, as I have said, if you will only make a beginning I will count the issue decided."

Lothario, seeing the fixed determination of Anselmo, and not knowing what further examples to offer or arguments to urge to dissuade him from it, and perceiving that he threatened to confide his pernicious scheme to someone else, decided — to avoid a greater evil — to gratify him and do what he asked, intending to manage the business so as to satisfy Anselmo without corrupting Camilla's mind. So in reply he told him not to communicate his purpose to anyone else, for he would undertake the task himself and would begin as soon as he pleased. Anselmo embraced him warmly and affectionately, and thanked him for his offer as if he had bestowed some great favour on him; and it was agreed between them to set about it the next day, Anselmo affording opportunity and time to Lothario to converse alone with Camilla, and furnishing him with money and jewels to offer and present to her. He suggested, too, that he should treat her to music, and write verses in her praise; and if he was unwilling to take the trouble of composing them, he offered to do it himself. Lothario agreed to all this, with an intention very different from what Anselmo supposed; and with this understanding they returned to Anselmo's house, where they found Camilla awaiting her husband anxiously and uneasily, since he was later than usual in returning that day. Lothario went back to his own house, and Anselmo remained in his, as well satisfied as Lothario was troubled in mind — for he could see no satisfactory way out of this ill-advised business. That night, however, he thought of a plan by which he might deceive Anselmo without any injury to Camilla. The next day he went to dine with his friend, and was welcomed by Camilla, who received and treated him with great cordiality, knowing the affection her husband felt for him. When dinner was over and the cloth removed, Anselmo told Lothario to stay there with Camilla while he attended to some pressing business, and that he would return in an hour and a half. Camilla begged him not to go, and Lothario offered to accompany him, but nothing could persuade Anselmo, who on the contrary pressed Lothario to remain waiting for him, as he had a matter of great importance to discuss with him. At the same time he told Camilla not to leave Lothario alone until he came back. In short, he contrived to put so good a face on the reason — or the folly — of his absence that no one could have suspected it was a pretence.

Anselmo took his departure, and Camilla and Lothario were left alone at the table, for the rest of the household had gone to dinner. Lothario saw himself in the lists according to his friend's wish, and facing an enemy who by her beauty alone could vanquish a squadron of armed knights — judge whether he had good reason to fear. But what he did was to lean his elbow on the arm of the chair, and his cheek on his hand, and, asking Camilla's pardon for his bad manners, he said he wished to take a little sleep until Anselmo returned. Camilla in reply said he could rest more comfortably in the reception-room than in his chair, and begged him to go in and sleep there; but Lothario declined, and there he remained asleep until Anselmo's return. Anselmo, finding Camilla in her own room and Lothario asleep, imagined that he had stayed away long enough to have afforded them time enough for conversation and even for sleep, and was all impatience until Lothario should wake up, that he might go out with him and question him as to his success. Everything fell out as he wished; Lothario awoke, and the two at once left the house, and Anselmo asked what he was anxious to know. Lothario in answer told him that he had not thought it advisable to declare himself entirely the first time, and therefore had only praised the charms of Camilla, telling her that the whole city spoke of nothing else but her beauty and wit — for this seemed to him an excellent way of beginning to gain her goodwill and prepare her to listen to him with pleasure the next time, thus availing himself of the device the devil resorts to when he would deceive someone who is on the watch: for being the angel of darkness, he transforms himself into an angel of light, and under cover of a fair appearance discloses himself at last, and accomplishes his purpose if at the beginning his wiles are not discovered. All this gave great satisfaction to Anselmo, and he said he would afford the same opportunity every day, but without leaving the house — for he would find things to do at home so that Camilla shouldn't detect the plot.

And so several days went by, and Lothario, without uttering a word to Camilla, reported to Anselmo that he had talked with her and that he had never been able to draw from her the slightest indication of consent to anything dishonourable, nor even a sign or shadow of hope; on the contrary, he said she would inform her husband of it.

"So far so good," said Anselmo. "Camilla has so far resisted words; we must now see how she will resist deeds. Tomorrow I'll give you two thousand crowns in gold for you to offer or even present, and as many more to buy jewels to lure her — for women are fond of being smartly dressed and going about gaily attired, all the more so if they are beautiful, however chaste they may be. And if she resists this temptation, I'll rest satisfied and give you no more trouble."

Lothario replied that now that he had begun, he would carry on the undertaking to the end, even though he perceived he was going to come out of it wearied and vanquished. The next day he received the four thousand crowns, and with them four thousand perplexities — for he didn't know what to say by way of a new falsehood; but in the end he made up his mind to tell him that Camilla stood as firm against gifts and promises as against words, and that there was no use in taking any further trouble, since the time was all being spent to no purpose.

But chance, directing things in a different manner, so arranged it that Anselmo, having left Lothario and Camilla alone as on other occasions, shut himself into a chamber and posted himself to watch and listen through the keyhole to what passed between them, and perceived that for more than half an hour Lothario did not utter a word to Camilla, and would not have uttered a word if he had been there for an age. He came to the conclusion that what his friend had told him about Camilla's replies was all invention and falsehood, and to find out whether it was so, he came out, and calling Lothario aside asked him what news he had, and in what humour Camilla was. Lothario replied that he was not disposed to go on with the business, since she had answered him so angrily and harshly that he had no heart to say anything more to her.

"Ah, Lothario, Lothario!" said Anselmo, "how ill you meet your obligations to me, and the great confidence I place in you! I have just been watching through this keyhole, and I have seen that you have not said a word to Camilla — from which I conclude that on the previous occasions you have not spoken to her either; and if this is so, as no doubt it is, why do you deceive me, or why do you seek by trickery to deprive me of the means I might find of attaining my desire?"

Anselmo said no more, but he had said enough to cover Lothario with shame and confusion; and Lothario, feeling as it were his honour touched at being caught in a lie, swore to Anselmo that from that moment he would devote himself to satisfying him without any deception, as he would see if he had the curiosity to watch — though he need not take the trouble, for the pains he would take to satisfy him would remove all suspicions from his mind. Anselmo believed him, and to afford him an opportunity more free and less liable to surprise, he resolved to absent himself from his house for eight days, going to that of a friend who lived in a village not far from the city; and, the better to account for his departure to Camilla, he arranged for the friend to send him a very pressing invitation.

Unhappy, shortsighted Anselmo — what are you doing? What are you plotting? What are you devising? Consider: you are working against yourself, plotting your own dishonour, devising your own ruin. Your wife Camilla is virtuous; you possess her in peace and quiet; no one assails your happiness; her thoughts do not wander beyond the walls of your house; you are her heaven on earth, the object of her wishes, the fulfilment of her desires, the measure with which she measures her will, making it conform in all things to yours and Heaven's. If, then, the mine of her honour, beauty, virtue, and modesty yields you without labour all the wealth it contains and you can wish for, why will you dig the earth in search of fresh veins, of new unknown treasure, risking the collapse of all — since it rests only on the feeble props of her weak nature? Consider that from him who seeks impossibilities, that which is possible may with justice be withheld, as was better expressed by a poet who said:
'Tis mine to seek for life in death, / Health in disease seek I, / I seek in prison freedom's breath, / In traitors loyalty.
So Fate that ever scorns to grant / Or grace or boon to me, / Since what can never be I want, / Denies me what might be.

The next day Anselmo set off for the village, leaving instructions with Camilla that during his absence Lothario would come to look after his house and to dine with her, and that she was to treat him as she would himself. Camilla was distressed, as a discreet and right-minded woman would be, at the orders her husband left her, and reminded him that it was not becoming for anyone to occupy his seat at the table during his absence; and if he acted thus from not feeling confident she could manage his house, let him try her this time, and he would find by experience she was equal to greater responsibilities. Anselmo replied that it was his pleasure to have it so, and that she had only to submit and obey. Camilla said she would do so, though against her will.

Anselmo went, and the next day Lothario came to his house, where he was received by Camilla with a friendly and modest welcome; but she never let Lothario see her alone, for she was always attended by her men and women servants — especially by a handmaid of hers, Leonela by name, to whom she was much attached (for they had been brought up together from childhood in her father's house), and whom she had kept with her after her marriage to Anselmo. The first three days Lothario did not speak to her, though he might have done so when they removed the cloth and the servants retired to dine hastily; for such were Camilla's orders. Indeed, Leonela had instructions to dine earlier than Camilla and never to leave her side. She, however, having her thoughts fixed on other things more to her taste, and wanting that time and opportunity for her own pleasures, did not always obey her mistress's commands — on the contrary she left them alone, as if they had ordered her to do so. But the modest bearing of Camilla, the calmness of her face, the composure of her aspect were enough to bridle Lothario's tongue. Yet the influence the many virtues of Camilla exerted in imposing silence on Lothario's tongue proved mischievous for both of them: for if his tongue was silent his thoughts were busy, and could dwell at leisure on the perfections of Camilla's goodness and beauty one by one — charms enough to warm with love a marble statue, not to say a heart of flesh. Lothario gazed upon her when he might have been speaking to her, and thought how worthy of being loved she was; and so reflection began little by little to assail his loyalty to Anselmo, and a thousand times he thought of withdrawing from the city and going where Anselmo should never see him nor he see Camilla. But already the delight he found in gazing on her stepped in and held him fast. He put a constraint upon himself, and struggled to repel and repress the pleasure he found in contemplating Camilla; when alone he blamed himself for his weakness, called himself a bad friend, even a bad Christian; then he argued the matter and compared himself with Anselmo, always coming to the conclusion that Anselmo's folly and rashness had been worse than his own faithlessness, and that if he could excuse his intentions as easily before God as with man, he had no reason to fear any punishment for his offence.

In short, the beauty and goodness of Camilla, combined with the opportunity which the blind husband had placed in his hands, overthrew the loyalty of Lothario; and giving heed to nothing save the object towards which his inclinations led him, after Anselmo had been three days absent — during which he had been waging a continual struggle with his passion — he began to make love to Camilla with so much vehemence and warmth of language that she was overwhelmed with amazement, and could only rise from her place and retire to her room without answering him a word. But the hope that always springs up with love was not weakened in Lothario by this repelling demeanour; on the contrary, his passion for Camilla increased, and she, discovering in him what she had never expected, did not know what to do; and considering it neither safe nor right to give him the chance or opportunity of speaking to her again, she resolved to send — as she did that very night — one of her servants with a letter to Anselmo, in which she addressed the following words to him.

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 34
paragraphs: Continuing the novel of "The Ill-Advised Curiosity"

"They say an army looks wrong without its general and a castle without its castellan, and I'd add that a young married woman looks worse still without her husband — unless there are very good reasons for it. I feel so out of sorts without you, and so unable to bear this separation, that if you don't come back soon I'll have to go take refuge at my parents' house, even if it means leaving yours unguarded; for the guardian you left me — if he deserved that title at all — has, I suspect, more regard for his own pleasure than for anything that concerns you. You're a perceptive man; I don't need to say more, nor would it be proper for me to say more."

Anselmo received this letter and gathered from it that Lothario had already begun his task and that Camilla must have answered him exactly as he had hoped. Delighted beyond measure at the news, he sent word back to her not to leave the house on any account, since he would be returning very shortly. Camilla was astonished at Anselmo's reply, which left her in a worse bind than before, for she dared neither stay in her own house nor go to her parents'; staying put her virtue in danger, and leaving meant disobeying her husband. In the end she chose the worse course for herself — to remain — resolving not to flee Lothario's presence so as not to give her servants something to gossip about. She now regretted writing as she had to her husband, afraid he might imagine that Lothario had sensed in her some lightness that had encouraged him to drop the respect he owed her; but trusting her own rectitude she put her faith in God and her virtuous intentions, with which she hoped to resist Lothario's pursuits in silence and say nothing to her husband so as not to drag him into any quarrel or trouble. She even began to think how she might excuse Lothario to Anselmo when he asked what had made her write that letter. With these resolutions — more honourable than wise or effective — she sat through the next day listening to Lothario, who pressed his suit so hard that Camilla's firmness began to waver, and her virtue had its hands full keeping her eyes from betraying a certain tender pity that Lothario's tears and pleas had stirred in her heart. Lothario noticed all this, and it inflamed him further. In short, he felt that while Anselmo's absence gave him time and opportunity he had to press the siege of the fortress, so he attacked her self-esteem with praises of her beauty — for nothing levels the castle-walls of a fair woman's vanity faster than vanity itself on the tongue of flattery. With the most relentless persistence he undermined the rock of her purity with such engines that, had Camilla been bronze, she would still have fallen. He wept, he begged, he promised, he flattered, he pestered, he feigned with such feeling and apparent sincerity that he overthrew Camilla's virtuous resolves and won the triumph he least expected and most longed for. Camilla yielded; Camilla fell. But what wonder, if Lothario's own friendship could not stand firm? A clear proof to us that the passion of love is to be conquered only by fleeing from it, and that no one should engage in a struggle with so mighty an enemy; for divine strength is needed to defeat its human power. Only Leonela knew of her mistress's weakness, since the two false friends and new lovers could not hide it from her. Lothario did not tell Camilla what Anselmo's plan had been, nor that Anselmo himself had given him the opportunity to achieve such an outcome, for fear she would undervalue his love and think that he had courted her by accident and reluctantly, not of his own choice.

A few days later Anselmo returned home and did not see what had been lost — what he had so casually risked and so highly prized. He went at once to see Lothario, and found him in. They embraced, and Anselmo asked for the news of his life or his death.

"The news I have to give you, Anselmo my friend," said Lothario, "is that you possess a wife fit to be the model and crown of all good wives. The words I directed at her were swept away on the wind; my promises were despised; my presents were refused; the fake tears I shed were openly mocked. In short, just as Camilla is the essence of all beauty, she is the treasure-house of purity, and gentleness and modesty live in her along with every virtue that can bring a woman praise, honour, and happiness. Take back your money, my friend; here it is, and I never had to touch it, for Camilla's chastity does not bow to anything as cheap as gifts or promises. Be satisfied, Anselmo, and don't go testing her any further; you have crossed dryshod through the sea of those doubts and suspicions men commonly entertain about women — don't plunge again into the deep ocean of fresh embarrassments, or, with another pilot, test the soundness of the boat that Heaven has granted you for your passage across this life. Count yourself safe in port, moor yourself with the anchor of sound reflection, and rest in peace until you are summoned to pay that debt no nobility on earth can escape paying."

Anselmo was completely satisfied by Lothario's words and believed them as fully as if they had been spoken by an oracle; nevertheless, he begged him not to give the project up, if only for curiosity and amusement — though from now on he need not press as hard as before. All he wanted was for Lothario to write some verses praising her under the name of Chloris, for he himself would let her think Lothario was in love with a lady to whom he had given that name so that he could sing her praises with the decorum her modesty deserved; and if Lothario didn't want the trouble of writing the verses, he would compose them himself.

"That won't be necessary," said Lothario, "for the muses are not so hostile to me but that they visit me now and then in the course of a year. Tell Camilla what you propose about this pretended love of mine; as for the verses, I'll make them, and if they aren't as good as the subject deserves they will at least be the best I can produce." An agreement to this effect was reached between the friends — the ill-advised one and the treacherous one — and Anselmo, going home, asked Camilla the question she was already surprised he had not asked: what had made her write the letter she had sent him. Camilla replied that it had seemed to her Lothario looked at her somewhat more freely than when Anselmo had been at home, but that she was now undeceived and believed it had only been her own imagination, since Lothario now avoided seeing her or being alone with her. Anselmo told her she could be quite easy about that suspicion, because he knew Lothario was in love with a young lady of rank in the city whom he was celebrating under the name of Chloris, and that even if he were not, his loyalty and their great friendship left no room for fear. Had Camilla not already been warned by Lothario that this love for Chloris was a pretence — and that he had told Anselmo about it so as to be able sometimes to give voice to praise of Camilla herself — she would no doubt have fallen into the despairing toils of jealousy; but being forewarned she took the startling news without distress.

The next day, as the three of them were at table, Anselmo asked Lothario to recite something of what he had composed for his mistress Chloris; since Camilla did not know her, he could say whatever he liked.
