All that remains is to set out on our journey tomorrow, for today we could not make much way; and for the rest of the happy outcome I am looking forward to, I trust in God and the valour of your heart."

So said the sprightly Dorothea, and on hearing her Don Quixote turned to Sancho, and said to him with an angry air, "I declare, little Sancho, you are the greatest little villain in Spain. Tell me, thief and vagabond, didn't you just now tell me that this princess had been turned into a maiden called Dorothea, and that the head I am convinced I cut off from a giant was the bitch that bore you, and other nonsense that put me in the greatest perplexity I've ever been in in all my life? I swear" (and here he looked to heaven and ground his teeth) "I have a mind to play the mischief with you, in a way that will teach sense for the future to all lying squires of knights-errant in the world."

"Be calm, your worship, señor," returned Sancho; "it may well be that I've been mistaken about the change of the lady princess Micomicona; but as to the giant's head, or at least as to the piercing of the wine-skins, and the blood being red wine, I make no mistake, as sure as there's a God; because the wounded skins are there at the head of your worship's bed, and the wine has made a lake of the room; if not, you'll see when the eggs come to be fried — I mean when his worship the landlord calls for all the damages. For the rest, I'm heartily glad that her ladyship the queen is as she was, for it concerns me as much as anyone."
"I tell you again, Sancho, you are a fool," said Don Quixote; "forgive me, and that will do."

"That will do," said Don Fernando; "let's say no more about it; and as her ladyship the princess proposes to set out tomorrow because it's too late today, so be it. We'll spend the night in pleasant conversation, and tomorrow we'll all accompany Señor Don Quixote; for we wish to witness the valiant and unparalleled achievements he is about to perform in the course of this mighty enterprise he has undertaken."

"It is I who shall wait upon and accompany you," said Don Quixote; "and I am much gratified by the favour bestowed upon me and the good opinion entertained of me, which I shall strive to justify, or it shall cost me my life — or even more, if that is possible."

Many were the compliments and expressions of politeness that passed between Don Quixote and Don Fernando; but they were brought to an end by a traveller who at this moment entered the inn, and who seemed from his attire to be a Christian lately come from the country of the Moors. He was dressed in a short-skirted coat of blue cloth with half-sleeves and no collar; his breeches were also of blue cloth, and his cap of the same colour; he wore yellow buskins and had a Moorish cutlass slung from a baldric across his breast. Behind him, mounted on an ass, there came a woman dressed in Moorish fashion, with her face veiled and a scarf on her head, and wearing a little brocaded cap, and a mantle that covered her from her shoulders to her feet. The man was of a robust and well-proportioned frame, in age a little over forty, rather swarthy in complexion, with long moustaches and a full beard; in short, his appearance was such that if he had been well dressed he would have been taken for a person of quality and good birth. On entering he asked for a room, and when they told him there was none in the inn he seemed distressed, and approaching the woman who by her dress seemed to be a Moor, he took her down from the saddle in his arms. Luscinda, Dorothea, the landlady, her daughter, and Maritornes, attracted by the strange — and to them entirely new — costume, gathered round her; and Dorothea, who was always kindly, courteous, and quick-witted, sensing that both she and the man who had brought her were annoyed at not finding a room, said to her, "Don't be put out, señora, by the discomfort and lack of luxuries here, for it's the way of roadside inns to be without them; still, if you'll be pleased to share our lodging with us" (pointing to Luscinda), "perhaps you have had worse accommodations in the course of your journey."

To this the veiled lady made no reply; all she did was rise from her seat, cross her hands on her bosom, bow her head, and bend her body as a sign that she was returning thanks. From her silence they concluded she must be a Moor and unable to speak a Christian tongue.

At this moment the captive came up, having been until now otherwise engaged, and seeing that they all stood round his companion and that she made no reply to what they said to her, he said, "Ladies, this damsel hardly understands my language and can speak none but that of her own country, for which reason she does not and cannot answer what has been asked of her."

"Nothing has been asked of her," returned Luscinda; "she has only been offered our company for this evening and a share of the quarters we occupy, where she shall be made as comfortable as the circumstances allow, with the good will we are bound to show all strangers who stand in need of it, especially if it is a woman to whom the service is rendered."

"On her part and my own, señora," replied the captive, "I kiss your hands, and I esteem highly, as I ought, the favour you have offered, which, on such an occasion and coming from persons of your appearance, is — it is plain to see — a very great one."
"Tell me, señor," said Dorothea, "is this lady a Christian or a Moor? for her dress and her silence lead us to imagine she is what we could wish she were not."
"In dress and outwardly," he said, "she is a Moor, but at heart she is a thoroughly good Christian, for she has the greatest desire to become one."
"Then she has not been baptised?" returned Luscinda.

"There has been no opportunity for that," replied the captive, "since she left Algiers, her native country and home; and up to now she has not found herself in any such imminent danger of death as to make it necessary to baptise her before she has been instructed in all the ceremonies our holy mother Church ordains; but, please God, before long she shall be baptised with the solemnity befitting her, which is higher than her dress or mine indicates."

By these words he excited a desire in all who heard him to know who the Moorish lady and the captive were, but no one liked to ask just then, seeing that it was a fitter moment for helping them to rest themselves than for questioning them about their lives. Dorothea took the Moorish lady by the hand and, leading her to a seat beside herself, asked her to remove her veil. She looked at the captive as if to ask him what they meant and what she was to do. He said to her in Arabic that they were asking her to take off her veil, and thereupon she removed it and disclosed a face so lovely that to Dorothea she seemed more beautiful than Luscinda, and to Luscinda more beautiful than Dorothea; and all the bystanders felt that if any beauty could compare with theirs it was the Moorish lady's, and there were even those who were inclined to give it somewhat the preference. And as it is the privilege and charm of beauty to win the heart and secure goodwill, all at once became eager to show kindness and attention to the lovely Moor.

Don Fernando asked the captive what her name was, and he replied that it was Lela Zoraida; but the instant she heard him she guessed what the Christian had asked, and said hastily, with some displeasure and energy, "No, not Zoraida; Maria, Maria!" giving them to understand that she was called "Maria" and not "Zoraida." These words, and the touching earnestness with which she uttered them, drew more than one tear from some of the listeners, particularly the women, who are by nature tender-hearted and compassionate. Luscinda embraced her affectionately, saying, "Yes, yes, Maria, Maria," to which the Moor replied, "Yes, yes, Maria; Zoraida macange," which means "not Zoraida."

Night was now approaching, and by the orders of those who accompanied Don Fernando the landlord had taken care and pains to prepare for them the best supper that was in his power. The hour having arrived, they all took their seats at a long table like a refectory one — for round or square table there was none in the inn — and the seat of honour at the head of it, though he was for refusing it, they assigned to Don Quixote, who wanted the lady Micomicona to place herself by his side, since he was her protector. Luscinda and Zoraida took their places next to her; opposite them were Don Fernando and Cardenio, and next the captive and the other gentlemen; and by the side of the ladies, the curate and the barber. And so they supped in high enjoyment, which increased when they noticed Don Quixote leave off eating, and, moved by an impulse like the one that made him hold forth at such length when he supped with the goatherds, begin to address them:

"Truly, gentlemen, if we reflect upon it, great and marvellous are the things they see who profess the order of knight-errantry. Say, what being is there in this world, who entering the gate of this castle at this moment and seeing us as we are here, would suppose or imagine us to be what we are? Who would say that this lady beside me was the great queen we all know her to be, or that I am that Knight of the Rueful Countenance, trumpeted far and wide by the mouth of Fame? Now, there can be no doubt that this art and calling surpasses all those that mankind has invented, and is the more deserving of being held in honour the more it is exposed to peril. Away with those who maintain that letters have pre-eminence over arms; I will tell them, whoever they may be, that they don't know what they're talking about. For the reason such persons commonly give, and on which they chiefly rest, is that the labours of the mind are greater than those of the body, and that arms give employment to the body alone — as if the calling were a porter's trade, for which nothing more is required than sturdy strength; or as if, in what we who profess them call arms, there were not included acts of vigour for the execution of which high intelligence is required; or as if the soul of the warrior, when he has an army or the defence of a city under his care, did not exert itself as much in mind as in body. No; see whether by bodily strength it is possible to learn or divine the intentions of the enemy, his plans, stratagems, or obstacles, or to ward off impending mischief — for all these are the work of the mind, and in them the body has no share whatever. Since, therefore, arms have need of the mind as much as letters, let us see now which of the two minds — that of the man of letters or that of the warrior — has most to do; and this will be seen by the end and goal each seeks to attain, since that purpose is the more estimable which has for its aim the nobler object. The end and goal of letters — I am not speaking now of divine letters, the aim of which is to raise and direct the soul to Heaven, for with an end so infinite no other can be compared — I speak of human letters, the end of which is to establish distributive justice, give every man what is his, and see and take care that good laws are observed: an end undoubtedly noble, lofty, and deserving of high praise, but not such as should be given to that sought by arms, which have for their end and object peace, the greatest boon men can desire in this life. The first good news the world and mankind received was that which the angels announced on the night that was our day, when they sang in the air, 'Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to men of good will;' and the salutation which the great Master of heaven and earth taught his disciples and chosen followers when they entered any house was to say, 'Peace be on this house;' and many other times he said to them, 'My peace I give unto you, my peace I leave you, peace be with you;' a jewel and a precious gift given and left by such a hand: a jewel without which there can be no happiness either on earth or in heaven. This peace is the true end of war; and war is only another name for arms. Granted, then, that the end of war is peace, and that in this it has the advantage of the end of letters, let us turn to the bodily labours of the man of letters and those of him who follows the profession of arms, and see which are the greater."

Don Quixote delivered his discourse in such a manner and in such correct language that for the time being he made it impossible for any of his hearers to consider him a madman; on the contrary, as they were mostly gentlemen, to whom arms are an appurtenance by birth, they listened to him with great pleasure as he continued: "Here, then, I say, is what the student has to undergo: first of all, poverty — not that all are poor, but to put the case as strongly as possible. When I have said that he endures poverty, I think nothing more need be said about his hard fortune, since the man who is poor has no share of the good things of life. This poverty he suffers from in various ways — hunger, or cold, or nakedness, or all together; but for all that it is not so extreme that he doesn't get something to eat, though it may be at somewhat unseasonable hours and from the leavings of the rich; for the greatest misery of the student is what they themselves call 'going out for soup,' and there is always some neighbour's brazier or hearth for them, which, if it doesn't warm, at least tempers the cold; and lastly, they sleep comfortably at night under a roof. I won't go into other particulars, such as want of shirts and no superabundance of shoes, thin and threadbare garments, and gorging themselves to surfeit in their voracity when good luck has treated them to a banquet of some sort. By this road I have described — rough and hard, stumbling here, falling there, getting up again to fall again — they reach the rank they desire, and once it is attained, we have seen many who have passed these Syrtes and Scyllas and Charybdises as if borne flying on the wings of favouring fortune; we have seen them, I say, ruling and governing the world from a chair, their hunger turned into satiety, their cold into comfort, their nakedness into fine raiment, their sleep on a mat into repose on holland linen and damask — the justly earned reward of their virtue. But, contrasted and compared with what the warrior undergoes, all they have endured falls far short of it, as I am now about to show."

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 38
paragraphs: About the curious discourse Don Quixote delivered on arms and letters

Continuing his discourse, Don Quixote said: "As we began in the student's case with poverty and its accompaniments, let's see now if the soldier is richer, and we'll find that in poverty itself there is no one poorer; for he depends on his miserable pay, which comes late or never, or else on what he can plunder, seriously endangering his life and conscience; and sometimes his nakedness will be so great that a slashed doublet serves him for uniform and shirt, and in the depth of winter he has to defend himself against the inclemency of the weather in the open field with nothing better than the breath of his mouth — which, coming from an empty place, I need not say must come out cold, contrary to the laws of nature. To be sure, he looks forward to the coming of night to make up for all these discomforts on the bed that awaits him — which, unless by some fault of his own, never sins by being too narrow, since he can easily measure out on the ground as much as he likes and roll about in it to his heart's content without any fear of the sheets slipping away from him. Then, after all this, suppose the day and hour have come for him to take his degree in his calling; suppose the day of battle has arrived, when they invest him with the doctor's cap made of lint — to mend some bullet-hole, perhaps, that has gone through his temples, or left him with a crippled arm or leg. Or if this does not happen, and merciful Heaven watches over him and keeps him safe and sound, it may be he will be in the same poverty he was in before, and he will have to go through more engagements and more battles and come out victorious from all of them before he betters himself; but miracles of that sort are seldom seen. For tell me, sirs, if you have ever reflected on it: by how much do those who have gained by war fall short of the number of those who have perished in it? No doubt you will reply that there can be no comparison — that the dead cannot be numbered, while the living who have been rewarded may be summed up in three figures. All of which is the reverse in the case of men of letters; for by skirts (to say nothing of sleeves) they all find means of support; so that though the soldier has more to endure, his reward is much less. But against all this it may be urged that it is easier to reward two thousand soldiers, since the former may be remunerated by giving them places that must perforce be conferred on men of their calling, while the latter can only be recompensed out of the very property of the master they serve; but this impossibility only strengthens my argument.

"Setting that aside, however, for it's a puzzling question for which it's hard to find a solution, let us return to the superiority of arms over letters, a matter still undecided, so many are the arguments put forward on each side; for besides those I have mentioned, letters say that without them arms cannot maintain themselves, since war too has its laws and is governed by them, and laws belong to the domain of letters and men of letters. To this arms answer that without them laws cannot be maintained, since by arms states are defended, kingdoms preserved, cities protected, roads made safe, seas cleared of pirates; and, in short, if it were not for them, states, kingdoms, monarchies, cities, ways by sea and land would be exposed to the violence and confusion war brings with it so long as it lasts and is free to make use of its privileges and powers. And then it is plain that whatever costs most is valued and deserves to be valued most. To attain to eminence in letters costs a man time, watching, hunger, nakedness, headaches, indigestions, and other things of the sort, some of which I have already mentioned. But for a man to come in the ordinary course of things to be a good soldier costs him all the student suffers, and to an incomparably higher degree, for at every step he runs the risk of losing his life. For what dread of want or poverty that can reach or harass the student can compare with what the soldier feels, who, finding himself besieged in some stronghold mounting guard in some ravelin or cavalier, knows that the enemy is pushing a mine toward the post where he is stationed, and cannot under any circumstances retire or fly from the imminent danger that threatens him? All he can do is inform his captain of what's going on so that he may try to remedy it with a counter-mine, and then stand his ground in fear and expectation of the moment when he will fly up to the clouds without wings and descend into the deep against his will. And if this seems a trifling risk, let's see whether it is equalled or surpassed by the encounter of two galleys ramming each other prow to prow in the middle of the open sea, locked and entangled together, when the soldier has no more standing room than two feet of the plank of the spur; and yet, though he sees before him as many ministers of death threatening him as there are cannon of the foe pointed at him, not a lance length from his body, and sees too that with the first heedless step he will go down to visit the depths of Neptune's bosom, still with dauntless heart, urged on by the honour that nerves him, he makes himself a target for all that musketry, and struggles to cross that narrow path to the enemy's ship. And what is still more marvellous, no sooner has one gone down into the depths he will never rise from till the end of the world, than another takes his place; and if he too falls into the sea that waits for him like an enemy, another and another will succeed him without a moment's pause between their deaths — courage and daring the greatest that all the chances of war can show. Happy the blest ages that knew not the dread fury of those devilish engines of artillery, whose inventor I am persuaded is in hell receiving the reward of his diabolical invention, by which he made it easy for a base and cowardly arm to take the life of a gallant gentleman; so that when he knows not how or whence, in the height of the ardour and enthusiasm that fire and animate brave hearts, there should come some random bullet — discharged perhaps by one who fled in terror at the flash when he fired off his accursed machine — which in an instant puts an end to the projects and cuts off the life of one who deserved to live for ages to come. And so when I reflect on this, I am almost tempted to say that in my heart I repent of having adopted this profession of knight-errant in so detestable an age as the one we live in now; for though no peril can make me fear, still it gives me some uneasiness to think that powder and lead may rob me of the chance to make myself famous and renowned throughout the known earth by the might of my arm and the edge of my sword. But Heaven's will be done; if I succeed in my attempt I shall be all the more honoured, as I have faced greater dangers than the knights-errant of yore exposed themselves to."

All this lengthy discourse Don Quixote delivered while the others supped, forgetting to raise a morsel to his lips, though Sancho more than once told him to eat his supper, since he would have time enough afterwards to say all he wanted. It excited fresh pity in those who had heard him to see a man of apparently sound sense, and with rational views on every subject he discussed, so hopelessly wanting in all when his wretched, unlucky chivalry was in question. The curate told him he was quite right in all he had said in favour of arms, and that he himself, though a man of letters and a graduate, was of the same opinion.

They finished their supper, the cloth was removed, and while the hostess, her daughter, and Maritornes were getting Don Quixote of La Mancha's garret ready — in which it was arranged that the women were to be quartered by themselves for the night — Don Fernando begged the captive to tell them the story of his life, since it could not fail to be strange and interesting, to judge by the hints he had let fall on his arrival in company with Zoraida. To this the captive replied that he would very willingly comply with his request, only he feared his tale would not give them as much pleasure as he wished; nevertheless, not to be wanting in compliance, he would tell it. The curate and the others thanked him and added their entreaties, and finding himself so pressed, he said there was no need to ask where a command carried such weight, and added, "If your worships will give me your attention, you will hear a true story which perhaps fictitious ones constructed with ingenious and studied art cannot come up to." These words made them settle themselves in their places and preserve a deep silence, and he, seeing them waiting on his words in mute expectation, began in a pleasant, quiet voice:

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 39
paragraphs: In which the captive relates his life and adventures

My family had its origin in a village in the mountains of Leon, and nature had been kinder and more generous to it than fortune; though in the general poverty of those communities my father passed for being even a rich man, and he would have been so in reality had he been as clever in preserving his property as he was in spending it. This tendency of his to be liberal and lavish he had acquired from having been a soldier in his youth, for the soldier's life is a school in which the miser becomes free-handed and the free-handed prodigal; and if any soldiers are to be found who are misers, they are monsters of rare occurrence. My father went beyond liberality and bordered on prodigality, a disposition by no means advantageous to a married man with children to inherit his name and position. My father had three, all sons, and all of an age to make choice of a profession. Finding, then, that he was unable to resist his propensity, he resolved to divest himself of the instrument and cause of his prodigality and lavishness — to divest himself of wealth, without which Alexander himself would have seemed miserly. And so calling us all three aside one day into a room, he addressed us in words somewhat to the following effect:

"My sons, to assure you that I love you, no more need be known or said than that you are my sons; and to encourage a suspicion that I do not love you, no more is needed than the knowledge that I have no self-control as far as preservation of your patrimony is concerned. Therefore, that you may for the future feel sure that I love you like a father, and have no wish to ruin you like a stepfather, I propose to do with you what I have for some time back meditated, and after mature deliberation decided upon. You are now of an age to choose your line of life, or at least make choice of a calling that will bring you honour and profit when you are older; and what I have resolved to do is divide my property into four parts. Three I will give to you, to each his portion without making any difference, and the other I will retain to live upon and support myself for whatever remainder of life Heaven may be pleased to grant me. But I wish each of you, on taking possession of the share that falls to him, to follow one of the paths I shall indicate. In this Spain of ours there is a proverb, to my mind very true — as they all are, being short aphorisms drawn from long practical experience — and the one I refer to says, 'The church, or the sea, or the king's house;' as much as to say, in plainer language, whoever wants to flourish and become rich, let him follow the church, or go to sea, adopting commerce as his calling, or go into the king's service in his household; for they say, 'Better a king's crumb than a lord's favour.' I say so because it is my will and pleasure that one of you should follow letters, another trade, and the third serve the king in the wars; for it is a difficult matter to gain admission to his service in his household, and if war does not bring much wealth it confers great distinction and fame. Eight days from now I will give you your full shares in money, without defrauding you of a farthing, as you will see in the end. Now tell me if you are willing to follow out my idea and advice as I have laid it before you."

Having called on me as the eldest to answer, I, after urging him not to strip himself of his property but to spend it all as he pleased — for we were young men able to gain our own living — consented to comply with his wishes, and said that mine were to follow the profession of arms and thereby serve God and my king. My second brother, having made the same proposal, decided on going to the Indies, embarking the portion that fell to him in trade. The youngest, and in my opinion the wisest, said he would rather follow the church, or go to complete his studies at Salamanca. As soon as we had come to an understanding and made choice of our professions, my father embraced us all, and in the short time he mentioned carried into effect all he had promised; and when he had given each his share, which as well as I remember was three thousand ducats apiece in cash (for an uncle of ours bought the estate and paid for it down, not to let it go out of the family), we all three on the same day took leave of our good father. At the same time, as it seemed to me inhuman to leave my father with such scanty means in his old age, I induced him to take two of my three thousand ducats, since the remainder would be enough to provide me with all a soldier needed. My two brothers, moved by my example, gave him each a thousand ducats, so that there was left for my father four thousand ducats in money, besides three thousand, the value of the portion that fell to him, which he preferred to retain in land instead of selling it. Finally, as I said, we took leave of him, and of our uncle whom I have mentioned, not without sorrow and tears on both sides, they charging us to let them know whenever an opportunity offered how we fared, whether well or ill. We promised to do so, and when he had embraced us and given us his blessing, one set out for Salamanca, the other for Seville, and I for Alicante, where I had heard there was a Genoese vessel taking on a cargo of wool for Genoa.

It is now some twenty-two years since I left my father's house, and in all that time, though I have written several letters, I have had no news whatever of him or of my brothers; my own adventures during that period I will now relate briefly. I embarked at Alicante, reached Genoa after a prosperous voyage, and proceeded from there to Milan, where I provided myself with arms and a few soldier's accoutrements; from there it was my intention to go and take service in Piedmont, but as I was already on the road to Alessandria della Paglia I learned that the great Duke of Alva was on his way to Flanders. I changed my plans, joined him, served under him in the campaigns he made, was present at the deaths of the Counts Egmont and Horn, and was promoted to be ensign under a famous captain of Guadalajara, Diego de Urbina by name. Some time after my arrival in Flanders news came of the league that his Holiness Pope Pius V, of happy memory, had made with Venice and Spain against the common enemy, the Turk, who had just then with his fleet taken the famous island of Cyprus, which belonged to the Venetians, a loss deplorable and disastrous. It was known as a fact that the Most Serene Don John of Austria, natural brother of our good king Don Philip, was coming as commander-in-chief of the allied forces, and rumours were abroad of the vast warlike preparations being made, all of which stirred my heart and filled me with a longing to take part in the campaign that was expected. And though I had reason to believe, and almost certain promises, that at the first opportunity I should be promoted to be captain, I preferred to leave all and betake myself, as I did, to Italy; and it was my good fortune that Don John had just arrived at Genoa, and was going on to Naples to join the Venetian fleet, as he afterwards did at Messina. I may say, in short, that I took part in that glorious expedition, promoted by then to be a captain of infantry, an honourable charge to which my good luck rather than my merits raised me; and that day — so fortunate for Christendom, since then all the nations of the earth were disabused of the error under which they lay in imagining the Turks to be invincible at sea — on that day, I say, on which the Ottoman pride and arrogance were broken, among all that were there made happy (for the Christians who died that day were happier than those who remained alive and victorious) I alone was miserable; for, instead of some naval crown that I might have expected had it been Roman times, on the night that followed that famous day I found myself with fetters on my feet and manacles on my hands.

It happened in this way: El Uchali, the king of Algiers, a daring and successful corsair, having attacked and taken the leading Maltese galley (only three knights being left alive in it, and they badly wounded), the chief galley of John Andrea — on board of which I and my company were placed — came to its relief; and doing as was bound to be done in such a case, I leaped on board the enemy's galley, which, sheering off from the one that had attacked it, prevented my men from following me, and so I found myself alone in the midst of my enemies, who were in such numbers that I was unable to resist. In short, I was taken, covered with wounds; El Uchali, as you know, sirs, made his escape with his entire squadron, and I was left a prisoner in his power, the only sad being among so many filled with joy, and the only captive among so many free; for there were fifteen thousand Christians, all at the oar in the Turkish fleet, who regained their longed-for liberty that day.

They carried me to Constantinople, where the Grand Turk, Selim, made my master general at sea for having done his duty in the battle and carried off, as evidence of his bravery, the standard of the Order of Malta. The following year, which was the year seventy-two, I found myself at Navarino rowing in the leading galley with the three lanterns. There I saw and observed how the opportunity of capturing the whole Turkish fleet in harbour was lost; for all the marines and janizzaries that belonged to it made sure that they were about to be attacked inside the very harbour, and had their kits and pasamaques, or shoes, ready to flee at once on shore without waiting to be assailed, in such great fear did they stand of our fleet. But Heaven ordered it otherwise, not for any fault or neglect of the general who commanded on our side, but for the sins of Christendom, and because it was God's will and pleasure that we should always have instruments of punishment to chastise us. As it was, El Uchali took refuge at Modon, which is an island near Navarino, and landing forces fortified the mouth of the harbour and waited quietly until Don John retired. On this expedition the galley called the Prize was taken, whose captain was a son of the famous corsair Barbarossa. It was taken by the chief Neapolitan galley called the She-wolf, commanded by that thunderbolt of war, that father of his men, that successful and unconquered captain Don Álvaro de Bazan, Marquis of Santa Cruz; and I cannot help telling you what took place at the capture of the Prize.

The son of Barbarossa was so cruel, and treated his slaves so badly, that, when those who were at the oars saw the She-wolf galley bearing down on them and gaining on them, they all at once dropped their oars and seized their captain, who stood on the stage at the end of the gangway shouting to them to row lustily; and passing him on from bench to bench, from the poop to the prow, they so bit him that before he had got much past the mast his soul had already got to hell — so great, as I said, was the cruelty with which he treated them, and the hatred with which they hated him.

We returned to Constantinople, and the following year, seventy-three, it became known that Don John had seized Tunis and taken the kingdom from the Turks, and placed Muley Hamet in possession, putting an end to the hopes Muley Hamida — the cruellest and bravest Moor in the world — entertained of returning to reign there. The Grand Turk took the loss greatly to heart, and with the cunning all his race possess, he made peace with the Venetians (who were much more eager for it than he was), and the following year, seventy-four, he attacked the Goletta and the fort which Don John had left half built near Tunis. While all these events were occurring, I was labouring at the oar without any hope of freedom; at least I had no hope of obtaining it by ransom, for I was firmly resolved not to write to my father telling him of my misfortunes. At length the Goletta fell, and the fort fell, before which places there were seventy-five thousand regular Turkish soldiers, and more than four hundred thousand Moors and Arabs from all parts of Africa, and in the train of all this great host such munitions and engines of war, and so many pioneers that with their hands they might have covered the Goletta and the fort with handfuls of earth. The first to fall was the Goletta, until then reckoned impregnable, and it fell, not by any fault of its defenders, who did all that they could and should have done, but because experiment proved how easily entrenchments could be made in the desert sand there; for water used to be found at two palms' depth, while the Turks found none at two yards; and so by means of a quantity of sandbags they raised their works so high that they commanded the walls of the fort, sweeping them as if from a cavalier, so that no one was able to make a stand or maintain the defence.

It was a common opinion that our men should not have shut themselves up in the Goletta but should have waited in the open at the landing-place; but those who say so talk at random and with little knowledge of such matters. For if in the Goletta and in the fort there were barely seven thousand soldiers, how could such a small number, however resolute, sally out and hold their own against numbers like those of the enemy? And how is it possible to help losing a stronghold that is not relieved, above all when surrounded by a host of determined enemies in their own country? But many thought, and I thought so too, that it was a special favour and mercy which Heaven showed to Spain in permitting the destruction of that source and hiding place of mischief — that devourer, sponge, and moth of countless money, fruitlessly wasted there to no other purpose save preserving the memory of its capture by the invincible Charles V; as if, to make that eternal — as it is and will be — these stones were needed to support it. The fort also fell; but the Turks had to win it inch by inch, for the soldiers who defended it fought so gallantly and stoutly that the number of the enemy killed in twenty-two general assaults exceeded twenty-five thousand. Of three hundred who remained alive, not one was taken unwounded — a clear and manifest proof of their gallantry and resolution, and how sturdily they had defended themselves and held their post. A small fort or tower which was in the middle of the lagoon under the command of Don Juan Zanoguera, a Valencian gentleman and a famous soldier, capitulated on terms. They took prisoner Don Pedro Puertocarrero, commandant of the Goletta, who had done all in his power to defend his fortress, and took the loss of it so much to heart that he died of grief on the way to Constantinople, where they were carrying him a prisoner. They also took the commandant of the fort, Gabrio Cerbellon by name, a Milanese gentleman, a great engineer and a very brave soldier. In these two fortresses perished many persons of note, among whom was Pagano Doria, knight of the Order of St. John, a man of generous disposition, as was shown by his extreme liberality to his brother, the famous John Andrea Doria; and what made his death the more sad was that he was slain by some Arabs to whom, seeing that the fort was now lost, he entrusted himself, and who offered to conduct him in the disguise of a Moor to Tabarca, a small fort or station on the coast held by the Genoese employed in the coral fishery. These Arabs cut off his head and carried it to the commander of the Turkish fleet, who proved on them the truth of our Castilian proverb that "though the treason may please, the traitor is hated;" for they say he ordered those who brought him the present to be hanged for not having brought him alive.

Among the Christians who were taken in the fort was one named Don Pedro de Aguilar, a native of some place — I know not what — in Andalusia, who had been ensign in the fort, a soldier of great repute and rare intelligence, who had in particular a special gift for what they call poetry. I say so because his fate brought him to my galley and to my bench, and made him a slave to the same master; and before we left the port this gentleman composed two sonnets by way of epitaphs, one on the Goletta and the other on the fort. Indeed, I may as well repeat them, since I know them by heart, and I think they will be liked rather than disliked.

The instant the captive mentioned the name of Don Pedro de Aguilar, Don Fernando looked at his companions and they all three smiled; and when he came to speak of the sonnets one of them said, "Before your worship proceeds any further I entreat you to tell me what became of that Don Pedro de Aguilar you have spoken of."

"All I know is," replied the captive, "that after having been in Constantinople two years, he escaped in the disguise of an Arnaut, in company with a Greek spy; but whether he regained his liberty or not I cannot tell, though I fancy he did, because a year later I saw the Greek at Constantinople, though I was unable to ask him what the result of the journey was."
"Well then, you are right," returned the gentleman, "for that Don Pedro is my brother, and he is now in our village in good health, rich, married, and with three children."
"Thanks be to God for all the mercies he has shown him," said the captive; "for to my mind there is no happiness on earth to compare with recovering lost liberty."
"And what is more," said the gentleman, "I know the sonnets my brother made."
"Then let your worship repeat them," said the captive, "for you will recite them better than I can."
"With all my heart," said the gentleman; "that on the Goletta runs like this."

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 40
paragraphs: In which the captive's story continues
SONNET

"Blessed souls, set free from this mortal husk, rewarded for brave deeds and exalted, you now dwell above this lowly globe of ours, made heirs of heaven and immortality. With noble rage and burning ardour, while your strength was yours, you plied it in battle, and with your own blood and the enemy's stained the sandy soil and the encircling sea. It was the ebbing life-blood that failed your weary arms first; the stout hearts never quailed. Though defeated, you still earned the victor's crown: though mourned, your fall was still a triumph, for there, between sword and wall, you won glory in heaven and renown on earth."
"That is exactly it, as I recall," said the captive.
"Well then, the one about the fort," said the gentleman, "if my memory serves me, goes like this:"
SONNET

"Up from this wasted soil, this shattered shell, whose walls and towers lie here in ruin, three thousand soldier souls took wing on high to dwell in the bright mansions of the blessed. They tried in vain, with all the strength of their arms, to repel the enemy's onslaught, and when at last nothing remained but to die, the last defenders fell, wearied and few. And this same arid soil has always been the haunt of countless mournful memories, as much in our day as in days of old. But never yet, I think, has it sent to heaven from its hard bosom purer souls than these, or borne braver bodies on its surface."
The sonnets were not disliked, and the captive was glad of the news they gave him of his comrade. Continuing his tale, he went on:

With La Goletta and the fort now in their hands, the Turks gave orders to dismantle La Goletta — the fort was reduced to such a state that there was nothing left to level — and to do the work faster they mined it in three places. But nowhere were they able to blow up what seemed the weakest part, that is, the old walls, while everything left standing of the new fortifications the Fratin had built came down with the greatest ease. Eventually the fleet returned victorious and triumphant to Constantinople, and a few months later my master, El Uchali — otherwise Uchali Fartax, which in Turkish means "the scabby renegade" — died. He certainly was scabby; it is the Turks' custom to name people from some defect or virtue they possess, the reason being that among them there are only four surnames belonging to families tracing descent from the Ottoman house, and the rest, as I said, take their names and surnames from either bodily blemishes or moral qualities. This "scabby one" rowed at the oar as a slave of the Grand Signor's for fourteen years, and when he was past thirty-four, in resentment at having been struck by a Turk at the oar, he turned renegade and renounced his faith in order to take his revenge. And such was his valour that, without rising by the base methods most of the Grand Signor's favourites use, he came to be king of Algiers and afterwards general at sea, which is the third position of trust in the realm. He was a Calabrian by birth and a worthy man morally, and he treated his slaves with great humanity. He had three thousand of them, and after his death they were divided, as he directed in his will, between the Grand Signor (who is heir of all who die, sharing with the dead man's children) and his renegades. I fell to the lot of a Venetian renegade who, as a cabin boy on a ship, had been captured by Uchali and was so loved by him that he became one of his most favoured boys. He turned into the cruellest renegade I ever saw: his name was Hassan Aga, and he grew very rich and became king of Algiers. With him I went there from Constantinople, rather glad to be so much nearer Spain — not that I planned to write to anyone about my unhappy lot, but to try whether fortune would be kinder to me in Algiers than in Constantinople, where I had tried in a thousand ways to escape without ever finding the right moment or chance. In Algiers I resolved to look for other means of carrying out the purpose I cherished so dearly, for the hope of regaining my liberty never deserted me. When my plots and schemes and attempts did not turn out as I expected, instead of giving way to despair I would immediately look for or invent some new hope to keep me going, however faint or feeble it might be.

In this way I went on living, shut up in a building or prison the Turks call a baño, where they confine their Christian captives — those of the king's, those of private owners, and those they call "of the Almacen," meaning slaves of the municipality, who work on the city's public works and other jobs. Captives of this last kind recover their liberty only with great difficulty, because, being public property and having no particular master, there is no one to negotiate ransom with even if they have the means. To these baños, as I said, certain private individuals of the town are in the habit of bringing their captives, especially when they are being held for ransom, because there they can keep them safely and comfortably until the ransom arrives. The king's captives held for ransom likewise do not go out to work with the rest of the crew, unless their ransom is delayed; then, to make them write more urgently, they are forced to work and gather wood, which is no light labour.

I, however, was one of those held for ransom, because when it was discovered that I was a captain, although I declared my meagre means and lack of fortune, nothing would persuade them not to count me among the gentlemen and those awaiting ransom. They put a chain on me, more as a mark of this than for safekeeping, and so I passed my life in that baño with several other gentlemen and persons of quality singled out as held for ransom. Although at times — or rather almost always — we suffered from hunger and inadequate clothing, nothing distressed us so much as seeing and hearing at every turn the unparalleled and unheard-of cruelties my master inflicted on the Christians. Every day he hanged a man, impaled another, cut off someone's ears — all with so little provocation, or with none at all, that even the Turks acknowledged he did it just for the sake of doing it, since he was by nature murderously disposed towards the entire human race. The only one who fared at all well with him was a Spanish soldier, someone de Saavedra by name, to whom he never gave a blow himself or ordered one given, or addressed a harsh word, although he had done things that will dwell in the memory of the people there for many a year — all to recover his liberty. For the least of the many things he did, we all dreaded he would be impaled, and he himself feared it more than once; and only because time does not allow, I could tell you now things that soldier did which would interest and astonish you far more than the narration of my own tale.

To go on with my story: the courtyard of our prison was overlooked by the windows of the house of a wealthy Moor of high position. As is usual in Moorish houses, these were loopholes rather than windows, and besides were covered with thick, close lattice-work. It happened, then, that one day I was on the terrace of our prison with three other comrades, passing the time by seeing how far we could leap with our chains. We were alone, all the other Christians having gone out to work. I happened to raise my eyes, and from one of those little closed windows I saw a reed appear with a cloth attached to the end of it, and it kept waving and moving as if making signs to us to come and take it. We watched it, and one of those with me went and stood under the reed to see whether they would drop it or what they would do, but as he did so the reed was raised and moved from side to side, as if saying "no" by a shake of the head. The Christian came back, and the reed was lowered again, making the same movements as before. Another of my comrades went, and the same thing happened to him as to the first, and then the third went forward, with the same result. Seeing this I did not want to miss my own chance, and as soon as I came under the reed it was dropped and fell inside the baño at my feet. I hurried to untie the cloth, in which I noticed a knot, and inside it were ten cianis, which are coins of base gold current among the Moors, each worth ten reals of our money.

Needless to say I rejoiced over this windfall, and my joy was matched by my wonder as I tried to imagine how this good fortune could have come to us, and especially to me — for the evident unwillingness to drop the reed for anyone but me showed that the favour was intended for me. I took my welcome money, broke the reed, and returned to the terrace. Looking up at the window, I saw a very white hand put out, which opened and shut very quickly. From this we gathered, or imagined, that it must be some woman living in that house who had done us this kindness, and to show that we were grateful we made salaams in the Moorish fashion, bowing the head, bending the body, and crossing our arms on our chest. Shortly afterwards, at the same window, a small cross made of reeds was put out and immediately withdrawn. This sign led us to believe that some Christian woman was a captive in the house, and that it was she who had been so kind to us; but the whiteness of the hand and the bracelets we had glimpsed made us dismiss that idea. We thought instead that it might be one of those Christian renegades whom their masters often take as lawful wives, and gladly, since they prefer them to the women of their own nation. In all our guesses we were wide of the truth. From then on our sole occupation was watching and gazing at the window where the cross had appeared, as if it were our pole-star. But at least fifteen days passed without our seeing either it, or the hand, or any other sign. Meanwhile, though we tried with all our might to find out who lived in the house, and whether there was any Christian renegade in it, no one could tell us anything more than that the man living there was a rich Moor of high position called Hadji Morato, formerly alcaide of La Pata, an office of high dignity among them. But when we least expected any more cianis to rain from that quarter, we suddenly saw the reed appear again, this time with another cloth tied in a larger knot, and this at a moment when, as before, the baño was deserted and empty.

We tried as before, the same three going forward before me; but the reed was delivered to no one but me, and on my approach it was let drop. I untied the knot and found forty Spanish gold crowns and a paper written in Arabic, with a large cross drawn at the end. I kissed the cross, took the crowns, and returned to the terrace, and we all made our salaams. The hand appeared again, I signed that I would read the paper, and then the window was closed. We were all puzzled but filled with joy at what had taken place; and since none of us understood Arabic, our curiosity to know what the paper contained was great, and the difficulty of finding someone to read it even greater. At last I decided to confide in a renegade, a native of Murcia, who professed great friendship for me and had given pledges binding him to keep any secret I might entrust to him. It is the practice with some renegades, when they intend to return to Christian territory, to carry around certificates from notable captives stating, in whatever form they can, that such-and-such a renegade is a worthy man who has always shown kindness to Christians and is eager to escape on the first opportunity. Some obtain these testimonials with good intentions, others put them to cunning use: when they go raiding on Christian territory, if they are wrecked or captured they produce their certificates and say that these papers show why they came — to remain on Christian ground — and that this is why they had joined the Turks in their raid. By this means they escape the consequences of the first outburst and make peace with the Church before it does them any harm, and then, when they have the chance, they return to Barbary to become what they were before. Others, however, do procure these papers and use them honestly, and remain on Christian soil. This friend of mine was one of those renegades I have described: he had certificates from all our comrades, in which we testified for him as strongly as we could; and if the Moors had found the papers they would have burned him alive.

I knew he understood Arabic very well, and could not only speak but also write it; but before I disclosed the whole matter to him, I asked him to read for me this paper which I had, I said, found by accident in a hole in my cell. He opened it and spent some time examining it and muttering to himself as he translated. I asked him whether he understood it, and he said he did perfectly, and that if I wanted him to tell me its meaning word for word, I must give him pen and ink so that he could do it properly. We at once gave him what he asked for, and he set about translating it bit by bit. When he had finished he said:
"All that is here in Spanish is what the Moorish paper contains, and you must remember that when it says 'Lela Marien' it means 'Our Lady the Virgin Mary.'"
We read the paper, and it ran like this:

"When I was a child my father had a slave who taught me to say the Christian prayer in my own language, and told me many things about Lela Marien. The Christian woman died, and I know she did not go to the fire but to Allah, because since then I have seen her twice, and she told me to go to the land of the Christians to see Lela Marien, who has great love for me. I do not know how to go. I have seen many Christians, but except for you none has seemed to me a gentleman. I am young and beautiful, and have plenty of money to bring with me. See if you can contrive how we may go, and if you wish you shall be my husband there, and if not it will not distress me, because Lela Marien will find me someone to marry me. I myself have written this: take care to whom you give it to read; trust no Moor, for they are all treacherous. I am greatly troubled about this, because I would not have you confide in anyone — if my father knew of it he would at once throw me down a well and cover me with stones. I will tie a thread to the reed; fasten the answer to it, and if you have no one to write for you in Arabic, tell it to me by signs, for Lela Marien will make me understand you. May she and Allah and this cross, which I often kiss as the captive woman told me to, protect you."

Judge, sirs, whether we had reason to feel surprise and joy at the words of this paper. Both were so great that the renegade realised the paper had not been found by chance but had really been addressed to one of us; and he begged us, if his suspicion was correct, to trust him and tell him everything, because he would risk his life for our freedom. So saying, he took from his breast a metal crucifix and, with many tears, swore by the God it represented — in whom, sinful and wicked as he was, he truly and faithfully believed — to be loyal to us and to keep secret whatever we chose to reveal to him; for he thought, and almost foresaw, that through the woman who had written that paper he and all of us would obtain our liberty, and he himself would obtain what he so much desired, his restoration to the bosom of Holy Mother Church, from which by his own sin and ignorance he was now severed like a corrupt limb. The renegade said this with so many tears and such signs of repentance that we all agreed unanimously to tell him the whole truth, and so we gave him a full account, hiding nothing. We pointed out the window at which the reed had appeared, and by this means he took note of the house and resolved to find out with particular care who lived in it. We also agreed it would be wise to answer the Moorish lady's letter, and the renegade, without a moment's delay, took down the words I dictated, which were exactly what I shall tell you — for nothing of importance in this affair has escaped my memory, or ever will while life lasts. This, then, was the answer sent back to the Moorish lady:

"May the true Allah protect you, Lady, and that blessed Marien who is the true mother of God, and who has put it in your heart to go to the land of the Christians, because she loves you. Beg her to be pleased to show you how you can carry out what she commands, for she will, such is her goodness. On my part, and on the part of all these Christians with me, I promise to do all we can for you, even to death. Do not fail to write to me and tell me what you mean to do, and I will always answer; for the great Allah has given us a Christian captive who can speak and write your language well, as you can see from this paper. So without fear you can tell us anything you wish. As to your saying that if you reach the land of the Christians you will be my wife, I give you my promise on it as a good Christian; and know that Christians keep their promises better than the Moors do. May Allah and Marien his mother watch over you, my Lady."

With the paper written and folded, I waited two days until the baño was empty as before, and immediately took my usual walk on the terrace to see if there was any sign of the reed, which was not long in appearing. As soon as I saw it, although I could not make out who was holding it, I showed the paper as a sign to attach the thread; but the thread was already fixed to the reed, and to it I tied the paper. Shortly afterwards our star once more appeared with the white flag of peace — the little bundle. It was dropped, I picked it up, and found in the cloth, in gold and silver coins of all sorts, more than fifty crowns, which fifty times over strengthened our joy and doubled our hope of gaining our liberty. That very night our renegade returned and said he had learned that the Moor we had been told of did live in that house, that his name was Hadji Morato, that he was enormously rich, that he had one only daughter who was heiress to all his wealth, and that it was the general opinion throughout the city that she was the most beautiful woman in Barbary. Several of the viceroys who came there had sought her in marriage, but she had always been unwilling to marry. He had also learned that she had had a Christian slave woman who was now dead — all of which agreed with the contents of the paper. We immediately took counsel with the renegade about what means we should use to carry off the Moorish lady and bring us all to Christian territory. In the end it was agreed that for the present we should wait for a second message from Zoraida (that was the name of the woman who now wishes to be called Maria), because we saw clearly that she, and no one else, could find a way out of all these difficulties. Once we had decided this, the renegade told us not to worry, that he would either lose his life or restore us to liberty. For four days the baño was crowded with people, so the reed delayed its appearance for four days; but at the end of that time, when the baño was as usual empty, the reed reappeared with a cloth so bulky it promised a happy birth. Reed and cloth came down to me, and I found another paper and a hundred crowns in gold, with no other coin. The renegade was present, and in our cell we gave him the paper to read, which ran as follows:

"I cannot think of a plan, señor, for our going to Spain, nor has Lela Marien shown me one, though I have asked her. All that can be done is for me to give you plenty of gold from this window. Use it to ransom yourself and your friends, and let one of you go to the land of the Christians, buy a vessel there, and come back for the others. He will find me in my father's garden, which is at the Babazon gate near the seashore, where I shall be all this summer with my father and my servants. You can carry me away from there by night without any danger and bring me to the vessel. And remember you are to be my husband, or else I will pray to Marien to punish you. If you cannot trust anyone to go for the vessel, ransom yourself and you go, because I know you will return more surely than any other, since you are a gentleman and a Christian. Try to acquaint yourself with the garden; and when I see you walking out there, I shall know the baño is empty and I will give you plenty of money. Allah protect you, señor."

These were the words and contents of the second paper, and on hearing them each man declared himself willing to be the one ransomed and promised to go and return in scrupulous good faith. I made the same offer too. But the renegade objected to all this, saying he would on no account agree to one being set free before all went together, as experience had taught him how badly those who were set free kept the promises they had made in captivity. Captives of distinction frequently used this trick, he said, paying the ransom of one who was to go to Valencia or Majorca with money to fit out a bark and return for the others who had ransomed him — only never to come back; for recovered liberty, and the dread of losing it again, wipe from the memory every obligation in the world. To prove what he said, he told us briefly what had happened to a certain Christian gentleman almost at that very time — the strangest case that had ever occurred even there, where astonishing and marvellous things happen every moment. In short, he ended by saying that what could and ought to be done was for us to give him the money intended for the ransom of one of us Christians, so that he could buy a vessel in Algiers under the pretext of becoming a merchant trading at Tetuan and along the coast. As master of the vessel it would be easy for him to find some way of getting us all out of the baño and on board, especially if the Moorish lady gave, as she said, enough money to ransom us all — because once free it would be the simplest thing in the world for us to embark even in broad daylight. But the great difficulty was that the Moors do not allow any renegade to buy or own any craft, unless it be a large vessel for raiding expeditions, because they fear that anyone who buys a small vessel, especially a Spaniard, only wants it to escape to Christian territory. He could get around this, however, by arranging with a Tagarin Moor to share with him in buying the vessel and in the profit on the cargo. Under this cover he could become master of the vessel, in which case he considered all the rest as good as done. Now, although my comrades and I thought it would be a better plan to send to Majorca for the vessel, as the Moorish lady suggested, we did not dare oppose him, fearing that if we did not do as he said he would denounce us and put us all in danger of losing our lives, if he revealed our dealings with Zoraida, for whose life we would have all given our own. So we resolved to put ourselves in the hands of God and in the renegade's; and at the same time an answer was sent to Zoraida, telling her we would do everything she advised, since she had given us as good counsel as if Lela Marien had spoken it, and that it depended on her alone whether we deferred the business or carried it out at once. I renewed my promise to be her husband; and so, the next day the baño chanced to be empty, she gave us at different times, by means of the reed and cloth, two thousand gold crowns and a paper saying that the next Juma — that is, Friday — she was going to her father's garden, but that before she went she would give us more money. If it was not enough we were to let her know, and she would give us as much as we asked, because her father had so much he would not miss it, and besides she kept all the keys.

We at once gave the renegade five hundred crowns to buy the vessel, and with eight hundred I ransomed myself, giving the money to a Valencian merchant who happened to be in Algiers at the time. He had me released on his word, pledging that on the arrival of the first ship from Valencia he would pay my ransom; for if he had handed over the money at once it would have made the king suspect that my ransom money had been in Algiers for a long time, and that the merchant had kept it secret for his own gain. In fact my master was so hard to deal with that I dared not on any account pay the money down at once. The Thursday before the Friday on which the fair Zoraida was to go to the garden, she gave us another thousand crowns and warned us of her departure, begging me, if I were ransomed, to find out her father's garden at once and to seek every opportunity of going there to see her. I answered briefly that I would do so, and that she must remember to commend us to Lela Marien with all the prayers the captive woman had taught her. This done, steps were taken to ransom our three comrades, so as to get them out of the baño; for otherwise, seeing me ransomed and themselves not, even though the money was forthcoming, they might make a fuss about it, and the devil might prompt them to do something that would harm Zoraida. Although their station might have been enough to relieve me of this fear, I was unwilling to take any risk in the matter, and so I had them ransomed in the same way I was, handing over all the money to the merchant so that he could give security with safety and confidence — without, however, confiding our arrangement and secret to him, which might have been dangerous.

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 41
paragraphs: In which the captive continues his adventures

Before fifteen days were up our renegade had already purchased an excellent vessel with room for more than thirty people. To make the transaction safe and give it cover, he thought it best to make, as he did, a voyage to a place called Shershel, twenty leagues from Algiers on the Oran side, where there is an extensive trade in dried figs. He made this voyage two or three times in company with the Tagarin already mentioned. (The Moors of Aragon are called Tagarins in Barbary, and those of Granada Mudéjares; but in the Kingdom of Fez they call the Mudéjares Elches, and they are the people the king mostly employs in war.) Each time he passed with his vessel he anchored in a cove not two crossbow shots from the garden where Zoraida was waiting. There the renegade, together with the two Moorish lads who rowed, used to station himself on purpose, either saying his prayers or rehearsing what he meant to do for real. He would also go to Zoraida's garden and ask for fruit, which her father gave him, not knowing him. But although, as he afterwards told me, he tried to speak to Zoraida and tell her who he was, and that by my orders he was to take her to the land of the Christians so she might feel reassured, he had never been able to: Moorish women do not allow themselves to be seen by any Moor or Turk unless their husband or father bids them; with Christian captives they permit freedom of intercourse and communication, even more than might be considered proper. For my part I would have been sorry if he had spoken to her, since it might have alarmed her to find her affairs being discussed by renegades. But God, who ordered things otherwise, gave our renegade no opportunity for his well-meant attempt. Seeing how safely he could go to Shershel and back, anchoring when and where and how he liked, and that the Tagarin his partner had no will but his — and now that I was ransomed, all we needed was to find some Christians to row — he told me to look out for any I would be willing to take with me, beyond those who had been ransomed, and to engage them for the next Friday, which he had set for our departure. So I spoke to twelve Spaniards, all stout rowers and the sort who could most easily slip out of the city; but it was no easy matter to find that many just then, because there were twenty ships out cruising and they had taken all the rowers with them. These would not have been found if it had not been that their master had stayed at home that summer without going to sea, in order to finish a galliot he had on the stocks. I said nothing more to these men than that the next Friday in the evening they were to come out stealthily one by one and hang about Hadji Morato's garden, waiting for me until I came. I gave each one these directions separately, with orders that if they saw any other Christians there, they were to say nothing to them except that I had directed them to wait at that spot.

With this preliminary settled, another, still more necessary step had to be taken: to let Zoraida know how matters stood, so that she might be prepared and not be taken by surprise if we were suddenly to seize her before she thought the Christians' vessel could have returned. I decided, therefore, to go to the garden and try to speak to her. The day before my departure I went there on the pretext of gathering herbs. The first person I met was her father, who addressed me in the language that all over Barbary and even in Constantinople serves as the medium between captives and Moors — neither Morisco nor Castilian, nor of any other nation, but a mixture of all languages by which we can all understand one another. In this sort of language, I say, he asked me what I wanted in his garden and to whom I belonged. I replied that I was a slave of the Arnaut Mami (I knew for a certainty that this man was a great friend of his), and that I wanted some herbs to make a salad. He then asked me whether I was being held for ransom and what my master was asking for me. While these questions and answers were going on, the fair Zoraida, who had spotted me some time before, came out of the house in the garden; and as Moorish women are by no means particular about being seen by Christians, or, as I said before, at all coy, she had no hesitation in coming over to where her father was standing with me. Moreover her father, seeing her approach slowly, called her to come. It would be beyond me to describe now the great beauty, the high-bred air, the brilliant attire of my beloved Zoraida as she presented herself before my eyes. I will content myself with saying that more pearls hung from her fair neck, her ears, and her hair than she had hairs on her head. On her ankles — which, as is customary, were bare — she had carcajes (which is the Morisco word for bracelets or anklets) of the purest gold, set with so many diamonds that, she told me afterwards, her father valued them at ten thousand doubloons, and those on her wrists were worth as much again. The pearls were abundant and very fine, since the highest display and adornment of Moorish women is to deck themselves with rich pearls and seed-pearls; and so there are more such pearls among the Moors than among any other people. Zoraida's father had the reputation of owning a great number, and the purest in all Algiers, and also of having more than two hundred thousand Spanish crowns; and she, who is now mistress of me alone, was mistress of all that. Whether thus adorned she would have been beautiful or not, and what she must have been in her prosperity, may be imagined from the beauty that remains to her after so many hardships. As everyone knows, the beauty of some women has its times and its seasons, increased or diminished by chance causes; and naturally the emotions of the mind heighten or impair it, though more often they completely destroy it. In a word, she presented herself before me that day attired with the utmost splendour, and supremely beautiful — at any rate, she seemed to me the most beautiful thing I had ever seen; and when I added to that everything I owed her, I felt as though I had before me some heavenly being come to earth to bring me relief and happiness.
As she came over her father told her in his own language that I was a captive belonging to his friend the Arnaut Mami, and that I had come for salad.
She took up the conversation, and in that mixture of tongues I have spoken of she asked me if I was a gentleman, and why I was not ransomed.

I answered that I was already ransomed, and that the price showed what value my master set on me, since they had been paid one thousand five hundred zoltanis for me. To which she replied, "If you had been my father's, I tell you I would not have let him part with you for twice as much, because you Christians always tell lies about yourselves and make yourselves out poor to cheat the Moors."
"That may be, lady," I said; "but I really did deal truthfully with my master, as I do and mean to do with everybody in the world."
"And when do you go?" said Zoraida.
"Tomorrow, I think," I said, "because there is a vessel here from France that sails tomorrow, and I think I shall go in her."
"Would it not be better," said Zoraida, "to wait for the arrival of ships from Spain and go with them, and not with the French, who are not your friends?"

"No," I said; "though if there were word that a Spanish ship was now coming, it is true I might perhaps wait for it. But it is more likely I shall leave tomorrow, because the longing I feel to return to my country and to those I love is so strong that it will not let me wait for another opportunity, however better, if it is delayed."
"No doubt you are married in your own country," said Zoraida, "and so you are anxious to go and see your wife."
"I am not married," I replied, "but I have given my promise to marry when I arrive there."
"And is the lady to whom you have given it beautiful?" said Zoraida.
"So beautiful," I said, "that to describe her properly and tell you the truth, she is very like you."

At this her father laughed very heartily and said, "By Allah, Christian, she must be very beautiful if she is like my daughter, who is the most beautiful woman in all this kingdom. Just look at her well, and you will see I am telling the truth."

Zoraida's father, as the better linguist, helped interpret most of these words and phrases, because although she spoke that bastard language used there, she expressed her meaning more by signs than by words.

While we were still engaged in this conversation, a Moor came running up shouting that four Turks had leaped over the fence or wall of the garden and were gathering the fruit, even though it was not yet ripe. The old man was alarmed and Zoraida too, for the Moors commonly — almost instinctively — dread the Turks, but particularly the soldiers, who are so insolent and domineering to the Moors under their power that they treat them worse than if they were their slaves. Her father said to Zoraida, "Daughter, go into the house and shut yourself in while I go and speak to these dogs. And you, Christian, pick your herbs and go in peace, and may Allah bring you safe to your own country."

I bowed, and he went off to look for the Turks, leaving me alone with Zoraida, who pretended to be about to retire as her father had told her. But the moment he was hidden by the trees of the garden, she turned to me with her eyes full of tears and said, "Tameji, cristiano, tameji?" — that is, "Are you going, Christian, are you going?"
I answered, "Yes, lady, but not without you, come what may. Watch out for me on the next Juma, and don't be alarmed when you see us, for we shall most certainly go to the land of the Christians."

I said this in such a way that she perfectly understood everything that had passed between us. Throwing her arm round my neck, she began with feeble steps to move towards the house; but as fate would have it (and it might have gone very badly if heaven had not otherwise ordered it), just as we were moving on in the manner and position I have described, with her arm round my neck, her father, returning after having sent the Turks away, saw how we were walking, and we saw that he saw us. But Zoraida, ready and quick-witted, did not take her arm from my neck — on the contrary, she drew closer to me and laid her head on my breast, bending her knees a little and showing every sign of fainting, while I at the same time made it look as though I were supporting her against my will. Her father came running up to where we were, and seeing his daughter in this state asked what was the matter with her. Since she gave no answer, he said, "No doubt she has fainted in alarm at the entrance of those dogs," and taking her from me he drew her to his own breast, while she, sighing, her eyes still wet with tears, said again, "Ameji, cristiano, ameji" — "Go, Christian, go." To which her father replied, "There is no need, daughter, for the Christian to go, because he has done you no harm, and the Turks have now gone. Do not be alarmed, there is nothing to hurt you, for, as I say, the Turks at my request have gone back the way they came."

"It was they who terrified her, as you said, señor," I said to her father; "but since she tells me to go, I have no wish to displease her. Peace be with you, and with your leave I will come back to this garden for herbs if need be, because my master says nowhere are there better herbs for salad than here."

"Come back for any you need," replied Hadji Morato, "for my daughter does not speak this way because she is displeased with you or with any Christian. She only meant that the Turks should go, not you; or that it was time for you to look for your herbs."

With this I at once took my leave of both, and she, looking as though her heart were breaking, withdrew with her father. While pretending to look for herbs I made my way around the garden at my ease, studying carefully all the approaches and exits, and the fastenings of the house, and everything that could be used to make our task easier.

Having done so, I went and gave an account of all that had happened to the renegade and my comrades, and looked forward impatiently to the hour when, all fear at an end, I should find myself in possession of the prize fortune was holding out to me in the fair and lovely Zoraida. The time passed at last, and the appointed day we so longed for arrived; and, all following the arrangement and plan we had decided on after careful consideration and many long discussions, we succeeded as fully as we could have wished. On the Friday following the day on which I had spoken to Zoraida in the garden, the renegade anchored his vessel at nightfall almost opposite the spot where she was. The Christians who were to row were ready and hiding in different places round about, all waiting for me, anxious and elated, eager to attack the vessel they had before their eyes; for they did not know the renegade's plan and expected to gain their liberty by force of arms and by killing the Moors on board the vessel. As soon, then, as I and my comrades made our appearance, all those in hiding saw us and came to join us. By now it was the time when the city gates are shut, and no one was to be seen in all the space outside.
