Once we were gathered together, we debated whether it would be better first to go for Zoraida or to take the Moorish rowers prisoner on the vessel; but while we were still undecided our renegade came up asking what was keeping us, since it was now the time and all the Moors were off their guard, most of them asleep. We told him why we were hesitating, but he said it was more important first to secure the vessel, which could be done with the greatest ease and without any danger, and then we could go for Zoraida. We all approved of what he said, and so without further delay, with him as our guide, we made for the vessel. He leaped on board first, drew his cutlass, and said in Morisco, "Let no one stir from here unless he wants it to cost him his life." By this time almost all the Christians were on board, and the Moors, who were fainthearted, hearing their captain speak this way were cowed; and without one of them taking up arms (and they had few or hardly any), they submitted without a word to being bound by the Christians, who quickly secured them, warning them that if they raised any kind of outcry they would all be put to the sword. With this accomplished, and half of our party left to keep guard over them, the rest of us, again taking the renegade as our guide, hurried to Hadji Morato's garden. As good luck would have it, on trying the gate it opened as easily as if it had not been locked; and so, quietly and in silence, we reached the house without being noticed by anyone. The lovely Zoraida was watching for us at a window, and as soon as she saw there were people there she asked in a low voice if we were "Nizarani," meaning to ask if we were Christians. I answered that we were, and begged her to come down. As soon as she recognised me she did not delay an instant, but without answering a word came down immediately, opened the door, and presented herself before us all, so beautiful and so richly attired that I cannot attempt to describe her. The moment I saw her I took her hand and kissed it, and the renegade and my two comrades did the same; and the rest, who knew nothing of the circumstances, did as they saw us do, since it only looked as if we were thanking her and recognising her as the giver of our liberty. The renegade asked her in Morisco whether her father was in the house. She replied that he was and that he was asleep.
"Then we will have to wake him and take him with us," said the renegade, "and everything of value in this fair house."

"No," said she, "my father must not on any account be touched, and there is nothing in the house except what I shall take, and that will be enough to enrich and satisfy all of you. Wait a little and you shall see." And with that she went in, telling us she would return immediately and asking us to keep quiet and not make any noise.

I asked the renegade what had passed between them, and when he told me, I declared that nothing should be done except in accordance with Zoraida's wishes. She now came back with a little trunk so full of gold crowns that she could barely carry it. Unfortunately her father woke up while this was going on, and hearing a noise in the garden came to the window. At once seeing that all those out there were Christians, he raised a tremendous outcry, calling out in Arabic, "Christians, Christians! Thieves, thieves!" — cries that threw us all into the greatest fear and confusion. But the renegade, seeing the danger we were in and how important it was for him to carry out his purpose before we were heard, rushed up to where Hadji Morato was, and some of our party went with him. I, however, did not dare to leave Zoraida, who had fallen almost fainting in my arms. To be brief, those who had gone upstairs acted so quickly that in an instant they came down carrying Hadji Morato with his hands bound and a napkin tied over his mouth to keep him from uttering a word, warning him at the same time that any attempt to speak would cost him his life. When his daughter caught sight of him she covered her eyes so as not to see him, and her father was horror-struck, not knowing how willingly she had placed herself in our hands. But now it was crucial for us to be on the move, and carefully and quickly we regained the vessel, where those who had remained on board were waiting in fear that some mishap had befallen us. It was barely two hours after nightfall when we were all on board the vessel, where the cords were removed from the hands of Zoraida's father, and the napkin from his mouth; but the renegade once more told him not to utter a word, or they would take his life. He, when he saw his daughter there, began to sigh piteously, and still more when he saw that I held her closely embraced and that she lay quiet, without resisting or complaining, or showing any reluctance; nevertheless he remained silent, lest they should carry out the repeated threats the renegade had made.

Finding herself now on board, and that we were about to push off with the oars, Zoraida, seeing her father there and the other Moors bound, asked the renegade to beg me as a favour to release the Moors and set her father at liberty, for she would rather drown herself in the sea than see a father who had loved her so dearly carried away captive before her eyes and on her account. The renegade repeated this to me, and I replied that I was very willing to do so; but he answered that it was not advisable, because if they were left there they would at once raise the country and stir up the city, and lead to the despatch of swift cruisers in pursuit, with us being taken by sea or land without any possibility of escape; and that the most that could be done was to set them free at the first Christian ground we reached. On this we all agreed; and Zoraida, when it was explained to her, along with the reasons that prevented us from doing what she wanted at once, was satisfied likewise. Then in glad silence and with cheerful eagerness each of our stout rowers took his oar, and commending ourselves to God with all our hearts, we began to shape our course for the island of Majorca, the nearest Christian land. However, with the Tramontana wind rising a little and the sea growing somewhat rough, it was impossible for us to keep a straight course for Majorca, and we were forced to coast in the direction of Oran — not without great unease, for fear we should be sighted from the town of Shershel, which lies on that coast not more than sixty miles from Algiers. We were also afraid of meeting on that course one of the galliots that usually come with goods from Tetuan; although each of us individually and all of us together felt confident that, if we met a merchant galliot (provided it was not a cruiser), not only would we not be lost, but we should take a vessel in which we could more safely make our voyage. As we pursued our course, Zoraida kept her head between my hands so as not to see her father, and I felt that she was praying to Lela Marien to help us.

We must have made about thirty miles when daybreak found us some three musket-shots off the land, which seemed to us deserted, without anyone to see us. For all that, however, by hard rowing we put a little farther out to sea, since it was now somewhat calmer; and having gained about two leagues, the word was given to row by batches while we ate something, for the vessel was well stocked. But the rowers said it was no time to take any rest: let food be served to those who were not rowing, but they would not leave their oars on any account. This was done. But now a stiff breeze began to blow, which obliged us to leave off rowing and make sail at once and steer for Oran, since it was impossible to keep any other course. All this was done very promptly, and under sail we ran more than eight miles an hour without any fear, except of coming across some vessel out on a raiding expedition. We gave the Moorish rowers some food, and the renegade comforted them by saying they were not being held captive, that we would set them free at the first opportunity.

The same was said to Zoraida's father, who replied, "Anything else, Christian, I might hope for or think likely from your generosity and good behaviour, but do not think me so simple as to imagine you will give me my liberty; for you would never have exposed yourselves to the danger of taking it from me only to restore it to me so generously, especially as you know who I am and the sum you can expect to receive for restoring it. If you will name that sum, I here offer you all you ask, for myself and for my unhappy daughter — or for her alone, since she is the greatest and most precious part of my soul."

As he said this he began to weep so bitterly that he filled us all with compassion and forced Zoraida to look at him. When she saw him weeping she was so moved that she rose from my feet and ran to throw her arms round him, and pressing her face to his they both gave way to such an outburst of tears that several of us were forced to keep them company.

But when her father saw her in full dress and with all her jewels on, he said to her in his own language, "What does this mean, my daughter? Last night, before this terrible misfortune that has fallen on us, I saw you in your everyday and indoor clothes; and now, without having had time to dress yourself, and without my bringing you any joyful news to occasion adorning and bedecking yourself, I see you arrayed in the finest attire it would be in my power to give you when fortune was kindest to us. Answer me this; it troubles and surprises me more than even this misfortune itself."

The renegade interpreted to us what the Moor said to his daughter; she, however, returned him no answer. But when he noticed in one corner of the vessel the little trunk in which she kept her jewels — which he knew very well he had left in Algiers and had not brought to the garden — he was still more amazed, and asked her how that trunk had come into our hands, and what was in it. To which the renegade, without waiting for Zoraida to reply, answered, "Do not trouble yourself by asking your daughter Zoraida so many questions, señor, for one answer I will give you will serve for all. I would have you know that she is a Christian, and that it is she who has been the file for our chains and our deliverer from captivity. She is here of her own free will, and as glad, I imagine, to find herself in this position as one who escapes from darkness into the light, from death to life, and from suffering to glory."
"Daughter, is this true, what he says?" cried the Moor.
"It is," replied Zoraida.
"That you are truly a Christian," said the old man, "and that you have given your father into the power of his enemies?"
To which Zoraida answered, "A Christian I am, but it is not I who have placed you in this position, for it was never my wish to leave you or do you harm, but only to do good to myself."
"And what good have you done yourself, daughter?" said he.
"Ask that," said she, "of Lela Marien, for she can tell you better than I can."

The Moor had hardly heard these words when with remarkable speed he flung himself headfirst into the sea, where no doubt he would have drowned had not the long and full robe he wore held him up for a little on the surface of the water. Zoraida cried out to us to save him, and we all hurried to help, and seizing him by his robe we drew him in half drowned and unconscious. Zoraida was so distressed that she wept over him as piteously and bitterly as if he were already dead. We turned him face down and he discharged a great quantity of water, and at the end of two hours he came to. Meanwhile, the wind having changed, we were forced to head for the land and ply our oars to avoid being driven on shore; but it was our good fortune to reach a creek on one side of a small promontory or cape called by the Moors that of the "Cava rumia," which in our language means "the wicked Christian woman." Their tradition is that La Cava — the woman through whom Spain was lost — lies buried at that spot; _cava_ in their language meaning "wicked woman," and _rumia_ "Christian." Moreover, they count it unlucky to anchor there when need compels them, and they never do so otherwise. For us, however, it was not the resting-place of the wicked woman but a haven of safety for our relief, so much had the sea now got up. We posted a lookout on shore, never let the oars out of our hands, ate of the stores the renegade had laid in, and implored God and Our Lady with all our hearts to help and protect us, so that we might bring to a happy ending so prosperous a beginning. At Zoraida's entreaty, orders were given to set on shore her father and the other Moors who were still bound, for she could not bear, nor could her tender heart endure, to see her father in bonds and her fellow-countrymen prisoners before her eyes. We promised her to do this at the moment of departure, since the place was uninhabited and we ran no risk in releasing them there.

Our prayers were not so far in vain as to go unheard by heaven, for after a while the wind changed in our favour, made the sea calm, and invited us once more to resume our voyage with good heart. Seeing this, we untied the Moors, and one by one put them ashore, at which they were filled with amazement. But when we came to land Zoraida's father, who had now completely recovered his senses, he said:

"Why do you suppose, Christians, that this wicked woman is glad you are giving me my liberty? Do you think it is because of the affection she bears me? No, indeed — it is only because of the hindrance my presence is to the carrying out of her base designs. And do not imagine that it is her belief that yours is better than ours that has led her to change her religion; it is only because she knows that immodesty is more freely practised in your country than in ours." Then turning to Zoraida, while I and another of the Christians held him fast by both arms in case he should do some mad act, he said to her, "Infamous girl, misguided maiden, where in your blindness and madness are you going, in the hands of these dogs, our natural enemies? Cursed be the hour I begot you! Cursed the luxury and indulgence in which I raised you!"

Seeing that he was not likely to stop any time soon, I hurried to put him on shore, and from there he kept up his curses and lamentations aloud, calling on Mohammed to pray Allah to destroy us, to confound us, to make an end of us. When, having set sail, we could no longer hear what he said, we could still see what he did — how he plucked out his beard and tore his hair and lay writhing on the ground. Once he raised his voice to such a pitch that we were able to hear what he said: "Come back, dear daughter, come back to shore; I forgive you everything. Let those men have the money — it is theirs now — and come back to comfort your sorrowing father, who will give up his life on this barren strand if you leave him."

All this Zoraida heard, and heard with sorrow and tears, and all she could say in answer was, "May Allah grant that Lela Marien, who has made me become a Christian, give you comfort in your sorrow, my father. Allah knows that I could not do otherwise than I have done, and that these Christians owe nothing to my will; for even had I wished not to go with them but to remain at home, it would have been impossible for me, so eagerly did my soul urge me on to the accomplishment of this purpose, which I feel to be as righteous as to you, dear father, it seems wicked."

But neither could her father hear her nor we see him when she said this. And so, while I consoled Zoraida, we turned our attention to our voyage, in which a breeze from the right point so favoured us that we made sure of finding ourselves off the coast of Spain by daybreak the next morning. But as good seldom or never comes pure and unmixed, without being followed by some disturbing evil that gives it a shock, our fortune — or perhaps the curses the Moor had hurled at his daughter, for whatever kind of father they come from these are always to be dreaded — brought it about that, when we were now in mid-sea about three hours into the night, running with all sail set and oars lashed (the favouring breeze saving us the trouble of using them), we saw by the light of the moon, which shone brilliantly, a square-rigged vessel in full sail close to us, luffing up and standing across our course, and so close that we had to strike sail to avoid running foul of her, while they too put the helm hard up to let us pass. They came to the side of the ship to ask who we were, where we were bound, and where we came from; but as they asked this in French our renegade said, "Let no one answer, for no doubt these are French corsairs who plunder all comers."

On this warning no one said a word; but after we had drawn a little ahead and the vessel was now lying to leeward, suddenly they fired two guns, apparently both loaded with chain-shot, for with one they cut our mast in half and brought it and the sail down into the sea, and the other, fired at the same moment, sent a ball into our vessel amidships, staving her in completely but without doing any further damage. We, however, finding ourselves sinking, began to shout for help and call on those in the ship to pick us up as we were beginning to fill. They then lay to, and lowering a skiff or boat, as many as a dozen Frenchmen, well armed with matchlocks and their matches burning, got into it and came alongside. Seeing how few we were, and that our vessel was going down, they took us in, telling us this had come to us through our incivility in not giving them an answer. Our renegade took the trunk containing Zoraida's wealth and dropped it into the sea without anyone noticing what he did. In short, we went on board with the Frenchmen, who, after finding out everything they wanted to know about us, rifled us of everything we had, as if they had been our bitterest enemies; and from Zoraida they took even the anklets she wore on her feet. But the distress they caused her did not distress me as much as the fear I was in that, after robbing her of her rich and precious jewels, they would go on to rob her of the most precious jewel of all, the one she valued more than any other. The desires of those people, however, do not go beyond money, but their greed for that is insatiable, and on this occasion was carried to such a pitch that they would have taken even the clothes we wore as captives if they had been worth anything to them. It was the advice of some of them to throw us all into the sea wrapped up in a sail, because they planned to trade at some of the ports of Spain, giving themselves out as Bretons, and if they brought us in alive they would be punished as soon as the robbery was discovered. But the captain (the one who had plundered my beloved Zoraida) said he was satisfied with the prize he had got, and that he would not touch at any Spanish port but pass the Straits of Gibraltar by night, or as best he could, and make for La Rochelle, from which he had sailed. So they agreed by common consent to give us the skiff belonging to their ship and everything we needed for the short voyage that remained to us; and they did so the next day on coming in sight of the Spanish coast — at which, with the joy we felt, all our sufferings and miseries were as completely forgotten as if they had never been endured, such is the delight of recovering lost liberty.

It may have been about midday when they put us in the boat, giving us two kegs of water and some biscuit. The captain, moved by I know not what compassion, as the lovely Zoraida was about to embark, gave her some forty gold crowns and would not let his men take from her the same garments she has on now. We got into the boat, returning them thanks for their kindness to us, and showing ourselves grateful rather than indignant. They stood out to sea, steering for the straits; we, looking to no compass other than the land in front of us, set to rowing with such energy that by sunset we were so near it that we thought we might easily land before the night was far advanced. But as the moon did not show that night, and the sky was clouded, and we did not know where we were, it did not seem prudent to make for the shore, as several of us advised, saying we ought to run ourselves ashore even if it were on rocks and far from any habitation, since this way we should be relieved from the anxiety we naturally felt of the prowling vessels of the Tetuan corsairs, who leave Barbary at nightfall and are on the Spanish coast by daybreak, where they commonly take some prize and then go home to sleep in their own houses. But of the conflicting counsels the one adopted was that we should approach gradually and land where we could if the sea was calm enough to permit it. This was done, and a little before midnight we drew near to the foot of a huge, lofty mountain, not so close to the sea that it did not leave a narrow space where we could land conveniently. We ran our boat up on the sand, all sprang out and kissed the ground, and with tears of joyful satisfaction returned thanks to God our Lord for all his incomparable goodness to us on our voyage. We took the provisions out of the boat, drew it up on the shore, and then climbed a long way up the mountain, for even there we could not feel easy in our hearts, nor persuade ourselves that it was Christian soil now under our feet.

The dawn came more slowly, I think, than we could have wished. We completed the ascent in order to see if from the summit any habitation or any shepherds' huts could be made out, but strain our eyes as we might, we could see neither dwelling nor human being, nor path nor road. We decided, however, to push on farther, since before long we must surely see someone who could tell us where we were. But what distressed me most was to see Zoraida going on foot over that rough ground; for though I once carried her on my shoulders, she was more wearied by my weariness than rested by the rest, and so she would never again let me undergo the exertion, and went on very patiently and cheerfully while I led her by the hand. We had gone rather less than a quarter of a league when the sound of a little bell fell on our ears, a clear proof that there were flocks nearby. Looking about carefully to see if any were within view, we saw a young shepherd quietly and unsuspectingly trimming a stick with his knife at the foot of a cork tree. We called to him, and he, raising his head, sprang nimbly to his feet — for, as we afterwards learned, the first people he saw were the renegade and Zoraida, and seeing them in Moorish dress he imagined that all the Moors of Barbary were upon him. Plunging into the thicket in front of him with remarkable speed, he began to raise a tremendous outcry, shouting, "The Moors — the Moors have landed! To arms, to arms!" We were all thrown into perplexity by these cries, not knowing what to do; but reflecting that the shepherd's shouts would raise the country and that the mounted coast-guard would come at once to see what was the matter, we agreed that the renegade must strip off his Turkish garments and put on a captive's jacket or coat, which one of our party gave him at once, though he himself was reduced to his shirt. And so, commending ourselves to God, we followed the same road we saw the shepherd take, expecting every moment that the coast-guard would be on us. Nor did our expectation deceive us, for two hours had not passed when, coming out of the brushwood into the open ground, we saw some fifty mounted men swiftly approaching at a hand-gallop. As soon as we saw them we stopped, waiting for them; but as they came close and, instead of the Moors they were after, saw a band of poor Christians, they were taken aback, and one of them asked if it could be we who were the reason the shepherd had raised the alarm. I said "Yes," and as I was about to explain to him what had happened, and where we came from and who we were, one of the Christians in our party recognised the horseman who had asked the question, and before I could say anything more he exclaimed:

"Thanks be to God, sirs, for bringing us to such good quarters! Unless I am much mistaken, the ground we stand on is that of Velez Malaga, unless all my years of captivity have made me unable to remember that you, señor, who ask who we are, are Pedro de Bustamante, my uncle."
The Christian captive had hardly uttered these words when the horseman threw himself off his horse and ran to embrace the young man, crying:

"Nephew of my soul and life! I recognise you now; and long have I mourned you as dead — I, and my sister, your mother, and all your kin still alive, whom God has been pleased to preserve so they may enjoy the happiness of seeing you. We knew long since that you were in Algiers, and from the look of your clothes and those of all this company, I conclude that you have had a miraculous restoration to liberty."
"It is true," replied the young man, "and by-and-by we will tell you everything."

As soon as the horsemen understood we were Christian captives, they dismounted, and each offered his horse to carry us to the city of Velez Malaga, a league and a half away. Some of them went to fetch the boat to the city, after we had told them where we had left it; others took us up behind them, and Zoraida was placed on the horse of the young man's uncle. The whole town came out to meet us, for by this time they had heard of our arrival from someone who had gone on ahead. They were not astonished to see liberated captives or captive Moors, since people on that coast are well used to seeing both; but they were astonished at the beauty of Zoraida, which was just then heightened both by the exertion of travelling and by joy at finding herself on Christian soil and relieved of all fear of being lost. This had brought such a glow to her face that — unless my affection for her was deceiving me — I would venture to say there was not a more beautiful creature in the world, at least none that I had ever seen. We went straight to the church to return thanks to God for the mercies we had received, and when Zoraida entered it she said there were faces there like Lela Marien's. We told her they were her images, and as well as he could the renegade explained to her what they meant, that she might adore them as if each of them were the very same Lela Marien who had spoken to her. Having great intelligence and a quick, clear instinct, she understood at once everything he said to her about them. From there they took us away and distributed us among different houses in the town; but as for the renegade, Zoraida, and myself, the Christian who had come with us brought us to the house of his parents, who had a fair share of the gifts of fortune and treated us with as much kindness as they did their own son.

We remained six days in Velez, at the end of which the renegade, having found out everything he needed to do, set out for the city of Granada to restore himself to the sacred bosom of the Church through the medium of the Holy Inquisition. The other freed captives took their leave, each going the way that seemed best to him; and Zoraida and I were left alone, with nothing more than the crowns the courtesy of the Frenchman had given Zoraida, with which I bought the beast she rides. Attending her for now as her father and squire rather than as her husband, we are now going to find out if my father is still living, or if any of my brothers has had better fortune than mine; though, since heaven has made me Zoraida's companion, I think no other lot, however happy, could be given to me that I would rather have. The patience with which she endures the hardships poverty brings with it, and the eagerness she shows to become a Christian, are such that they fill me with admiration and bind me to serve her all my life — though the happiness I feel in seeing myself hers, and her mine, is disturbed and marred by not knowing whether I shall find any corner to shelter her in my own country, or whether time and death may have made such changes in the fortunes and lives of my father and brothers that I shall hardly find anyone who knows me, if they are not alive.

I have no more of my story to tell you, gentlemen. Whether it has been an interesting or a curious one, let your better judgments decide; all I can say is that I would gladly have told it to you more briefly, although my fear of wearying you has made me leave out more than one detail.

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 42
paragraphs: Which treats of what further took place at the inn, and several other things worth knowing

With these words the captive fell silent, and Don Fernando said to him, "In truth, captain, the way you have told this remarkable adventure has been entirely fitting to the novelty and strangeness of the matter. The whole story is curious and uncommon, full of incidents that fill the hearers with wonder and astonishment, and so great is the pleasure we have found in listening to it that we should be glad if it were to begin again, even if tomorrow were to find us still occupied with the same tale." While he said this Cardenio and the rest offered to be of service to him in any way that lay in their power, in words and language so kindly and sincere that the captain was much gratified by their good will. In particular Don Fernando offered, if the captain would go back with him, to have his brother the marquis become godfather at the baptism of Zoraida, and on his own part to provide him the means of appearing in his own country with the credit and comfort he was entitled to. For all this the captive returned thanks very courteously, although he would not accept any of their generous offers.

By this time night closed in, and as it did, a coach came up to the inn attended by some men on horseback, who asked for accommodation. The landlady replied that there was not a hand's breadth of the whole inn unoccupied.
"Still, for all that," said one of those who had ridden up, "room must be found for his lordship the Judge here."

At this name the landlady was taken aback, and said, "Señor, the fact is I have no beds; but if his lordship the Judge brings one with him, as no doubt he does, let him come in and welcome; my husband and I will give up our room to accommodate his worship."

"Very good, so be it," said the squire. But in the meantime a man had got out of the coach whose dress indicated at a glance the office he held: the long robe with ruffled sleeves he wore showed that he was, as his servant had said, a Judge of appeal. He led by the hand a young girl in travelling dress, apparently about sixteen years old, of such a high-bred air, so beautiful and so graceful, that all were filled with admiration when she appeared; and but for having seen Dorothea, Luscinda, and Zoraida, who were there in the inn, they would have thought a beauty like this maiden's would have been hard to find. Don Quixote was present at the entrance of the Judge with the young lady, and as soon as he saw him he said, "Your worship may with confidence enter and take your ease in this castle; for though the accommodation be scanty and poor, there are no quarters so cramped or inconvenient that they cannot make room for arms and letters — especially if arms and letters have beauty for a guide and leader, as letters represented by your worship have in this fair maiden, to whom not only should castles throw themselves open and yield themselves up, but rocks should split themselves asunder and mountains divide and bow themselves down to give her a reception. Enter, your worship, I say, into this paradise, for here you will find stars and suns to accompany the heaven your worship brings with you; here you will find arms in their supreme excellence, and beauty in its highest perfection."

The Judge was struck with amazement at Don Quixote's language and scrutinised him very carefully, no less astonished by his figure than by his talk; and before he could find words to answer him he had a fresh surprise on seeing opposite him Luscinda, Dorothea, and Zoraida, who, having heard of the new guests and of the beauty of the young lady, had come out to see her and welcome her. Don Fernando, Cardenio, and the curate, however, greeted him in a more intelligible and polished style. In short, the Judge made his entrance in a state of bewilderment, both at what he saw and what he heard, and the fair ladies of the inn gave the fair damsel a cordial welcome. On the whole he could see that all who were there were people of quality; but with the figure, countenance, and bearing of Don Quixote he was at his wits' end. After all civilities had been exchanged and the accommodation of the inn inquired into, it was settled, as it had been before, that all the women should retire to the garret already mentioned, and that the men should remain outside as if to guard them. The Judge therefore was very pleased to allow his daughter, for such the damsel was, to go with the ladies, which she did very willingly; and with part of the host's narrow bed and half of what the Judge had brought with him, they made a more comfortable arrangement for the night than they had expected.

The captive, whose heart had leaped within him the instant he saw the Judge, somehow telling him that this was his brother, asked one of the servants who came with him what his name was and whether he knew what part of the country he came from. The servant replied that he was called the Licentiate Juan Perez de Viedma, and that he had heard he came from a village in the mountains of Leon. From this statement, and from what he himself had seen, he was convinced that this was his brother who had taken up letters on their father's advice. Excited and rejoicing, he called Don Fernando, Cardenio, and the curate aside, and told them how things stood, assuring them that the judge was his brother. The servant had also told him that he was now going to the Indies with the appointment of Judge of the Supreme Court of Mexico; and he had learned likewise that the young lady was his daughter, whose mother had died giving birth to her, and that he was very rich in consequence of the dowry left him with the daughter. He asked their advice as to what means he should adopt to make himself known — or to find out beforehand whether, when he had made himself known, his brother, seeing him so poor, would be ashamed of him or would receive him warmly.

"Leave it to me to find that out," said the curate. "Although, señor captain, there is no reason to suppose you will not be kindly received, because the worth and wisdom your brother's bearing shows him to possess do not make it likely that he will prove haughty or insensible, or that he will not know how to value the accidents of fortune at their proper weight."
"Still," said the captain, "I would not make myself known abruptly, but in some indirect way."
"I have told you already," said the curate, "that I will manage it in a way that will satisfy us all."
By this time supper was ready, and they all took their seats at the table, except the captive and the ladies, who supped by themselves in their own room. In the middle of supper the curate said:

"I had a comrade of your worship's name, Señor Judge, in Constantinople, where I was a captive for several years; and that same comrade was one of the stoutest soldiers and captains in the whole Spanish infantry. But he had as large a share of misfortune as he had of gallantry and courage."
"And what was the captain's name, señor?" asked the Judge.

"He was called Ruy Perez de Viedma," replied the curate, "and he was born in a village in the mountains of Leon. He told me of a circumstance involving his father and his brothers which, had it not been told me by so truthful a man as he was, I would have set down as one of those fables old women tell over the fire in winter. He said his father had divided his property among his three sons, and had addressed words of advice to them sounder than any of Cato's. But I can say this much: the choice he made of going to the wars met with such success that, by his gallant conduct and courage, and without any help except his own merit, he rose in a few years to be captain of infantry, and to see himself on the high road and in position to be given the command of a regiment before long. But Fortune was against him, for where he might have expected her favour he lost it, and with it his liberty, on that glorious day when so many recovered theirs — at the battle of Lepanto. I lost mine at La Goletta, and after a variety of adventures we found ourselves comrades at Constantinople. From there he went to Algiers, where he met with one of the most extraordinary adventures that ever befell anyone in the world."

Here the curate went on to relate briefly his brother's adventure with Zoraida — to all of which the Judge gave such attentive hearing that he had never before been so much of a listener. The curate, however, only went so far as to describe how the Frenchmen plundered those in the boat, and the poverty and distress in which his comrade and the fair Moor were left, of whom he said he had been unable to learn what became of them, or whether they had reached Spain, or been carried to France by the Frenchmen.

The captain, standing a little to one side, was listening to everything the curate said, and watching every movement of his brother — who, as soon as he saw that the curate had finished his story, gave a deep sigh and said with his eyes full of tears, "Oh, señor, if you only knew what news you have given me, and how it strikes me to the heart, making me show how I feel it with these tears that spring from my eyes in spite of all my worldly wisdom and self-restraint! That brave captain you speak of is my eldest brother, who, being of a bolder and loftier mind than my other brother or myself, chose the honourable and worthy calling of arms — one of the three careers our father proposed to us, as your comrade mentioned in that fable you thought he was telling you. I followed letters, in which God and my own exertions have raised me to the position you see me in. My second brother is in Peru, so wealthy that with what he has sent to my father and to me he has fully repaid the share he took with him, and has even put in my father's hands the means to indulge his natural generosity, while I too have been able to pursue my studies in a more becoming and creditable fashion, and so to reach my present standing. My father is still alive, though dying with anxiety to hear of his eldest son, and prays God unceasingly that death may not close his eyes until he has looked upon those of his son. But about him, what surprises me is that, having so much common sense as he had, he should have failed to send any word of himself, whether in his troubles and sufferings or in his prosperity; for if his father or any of us had known of his condition he need not have waited for that miracle of the reed to obtain his ransom. But what now worries me is the uncertainty of whether those Frenchmen may have restored him to liberty, or murdered him to hide the robbery. All this will make me continue my journey not with the satisfaction in which I began it, but in the deepest melancholy and sadness. Oh dear brother! If I only knew where you are now, I would hurry to find you and deliver you from your sufferings, though it were to cost me suffering myself! Oh that I could bring news to our old father that you are alive, even if in the deepest dungeon of Barbary — for his wealth and my brother's and mine would rescue you from there! Oh beautiful and generous Zoraida, that I could repay your goodness to a brother! That I could be present at the new birth of your soul, and at your bridal that would give us all such happiness!"

All this and more the Judge uttered with such deep emotion at the news he had received of his brother that everyone who heard him shared in it, showing their sympathy with his sorrow. The curate, seeing then how well he had succeeded in carrying out his purpose and the captain's wishes, had no desire to keep them unhappy any longer. He rose from the table and went into the room where Zoraida was, took her by the hand, with Luscinda, Dorothea, and the Judge's daughter following her. The captain was waiting to see what the curate would do, when the latter, taking him with the other hand, advanced with both of them to where the Judge and the other gentlemen were and said, "Let your tears cease, Señor Judge, and the wish of your heart be granted as fully as you could desire, for you have before you your worthy brother and your good sister-in-law. He whom you see here is Captain Viedma, and this is the fair Moor who has been so good to him. The Frenchmen I told you of have reduced them to the state of poverty you see, that you may show the generosity of your kind heart."

The captain ran to embrace his brother, who placed both hands on his breast so as to have a good look at him, holding him a little way off; but as soon as he had fully recognised him he clasped him in his arms so closely, shedding such tears of heartfelt joy, that most of those present could not help joining in. The words the brothers exchanged, the emotion they showed, can scarcely be imagined, I fancy, much less put down in writing. They told each other in a few words the events of their lives; they showed the true affection of brothers in all its strength; then the judge embraced Zoraida, putting all he had at her disposal; then he had his daughter embrace her, and the fair Christian and the lovely Moor drew fresh tears from every eye. And there was Don Quixote, observing all these strange proceedings attentively without uttering a word, attributing the whole thing to chimeras of knight-errantry. Then they agreed that the captain and Zoraida should return with his brother to Seville, and send word to his father of his having been delivered and found, so as to enable him to come and be present at the marriage and baptism of Zoraida — since it was impossible for the Judge to put off his journey, as he had been informed that in a month from then the fleet was to sail from Seville for New Spain, and to miss the passage would have been a great inconvenience to him. In short, everybody was pleased and glad at the captive's good fortune; and since almost two-thirds of the night was now past, they decided to retire to rest for the remainder. Don Quixote offered to mount guard over the castle in case they should be attacked by some giant or other malevolent scoundrel, covetous of the great treasure of beauty the castle contained. Those who knew him thanked him for this service, and gave the Judge an account of his extraordinary humour, at which he was not a little amused. Sancho Panza alone was fuming at the lateness of the hour for going to bed; and he, of all, was the one who made himself most comfortable, stretching himself out on the trappings of his donkey, which, as will be told further on, cost him dear.

The ladies, then, having retired to their chamber, and the others having settled themselves with as little discomfort as they could, Don Quixote sallied out of the inn to act as sentinel of the castle as he had promised. It happened, however, that a little before dawn a voice so musical and sweet reached the ears of the ladies that it forced them all to listen attentively, but especially Dorothea, who had been awake, and at whose side Doña Clara de Viedma, for so the Judge's daughter was called, lay sleeping. No one could imagine who it was that sang so sweetly, and the voice was unaccompanied by any instrument. At one moment it seemed to them as if the singer were in the courtyard, at another in the stable; and as they were all attention, wondering, Cardenio came to the door and said, "Listen, whoever is not asleep, and you will hear a muleteer's voice that enchants as it chants."
"We are listening already, señor," said Dorothea; on which Cardenio went away. Dorothea, giving all her attention to it, made out the words of the song to be these:

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 43
paragraphs: Which relates the pleasant story of the muleteer, together with other strange things that came to pass at the inn
Ah me, Love's mariner am I / On Love's deep ocean sailing; / I know not where the haven lies, / I dare not hope to gain it.
One solitary distant star / Is all I have to guide me, / A brighter orb than those of old / That Palinurus lighted.
And vaguely drifting am I borne, / I know not where it leads me; / I fix my gaze on it alone, / Of all beside it heedless.
But over-cautious prudery, / And coyness cold and cruel, / When most I need it, these, like clouds, / Its longed-for light refuse me.
Bright star, goal of my yearning eyes / As thou above me beamest, / When thou shalt hide thee from my sight / I'll know that death is near me.
The singer had got this far when it struck Dorothea that it was not fair to let Clara miss hearing such a sweet voice, so, shaking her from side to side, she woke her, saying:
"Forgive me, child, for waking you, but I do it so that you may have the pleasure of hearing the best voice you have ever heard, perhaps, in your whole life."

Clara woke quite drowsy, and not understanding at the moment what Dorothea was saying, asked her what it was; Dorothea repeated what she had said, and Clara became attentive at once. But she had hardly heard two lines, as the singer continued, when a strange trembling seized her, as if she were suffering from a severe attack of quartan ague, and throwing her arms round Dorothea she said:
"Ah, dear lady of my soul and life! Why did you wake me? The greatest kindness fortune could do me now would be to close my eyes and ears so as neither to see nor hear that unhappy musician."
"What are you talking about, child?" said Dorothea. "Why, they say this singer is a muleteer!"
"No, he is the lord of many places," replied Clara, "and the one in my heart, which he holds so firmly, shall never be taken from him unless he is willing to surrender it."
Dorothea was amazed at the girl's ardent words, since they seemed far beyond such experience of life as her tender years gave any promise of, so she said:

"You speak in such a way that I cannot understand you, Señora Clara. Explain yourself more clearly, and tell me what is this you are saying about hearts and places and this musician whose voice has so moved you? But do not tell me anything now; I do not want to lose the pleasure I get from listening to the singer by giving my attention to your raptures, because I see he is starting a new strain and a new air."

"Let him, in heaven's name," returned Clara; and not to hear him she stopped both ears with her hands, at which Dorothea was again surprised. But turning her attention to the song, she found that it went like this:
Sweet Hope, my stay, / That onward to the goal of thy intent / Dost make thy way, / Heedless of hindrance or impediment, / Have thou no fear / If at each step thou findest death is near.
No victory, / No joy of triumph doth the faint heart know; / Unblest is he / That a bold front to Fortune dares not show, / But soul and sense / In bondage yieldeth up to indolence.
If Love his wares / Do dearly sell, his right must be contest; / What gold compares / With that whereon his stamp he hath imprest? / And all men know / What costeth little that we rate but low.
Love resolute / Knows not the word "impossibility;" / And though my suit / Beset by endless obstacles I see, / Yet no despair / Shall hold me bound to earth while heaven is there.

Here the voice ceased and Clara's sobs began afresh, all of which excited Dorothea's curiosity to know what could be the cause of such sweet singing and such bitter weeping. So she again asked her what she had been about to say before. On this Clara, afraid that Luscinda might overhear her, wound her arms tightly round Dorothea and put her mouth so close to her ear that she could speak without fear of being heard by anyone else, and said:

"This singer, dear señora, is the son of a gentleman of Aragon, lord of two villages, who lives opposite my father's house in Madrid. Although my father had curtains on his windows in winter and lattice-work in summer, somehow — I do not know how — this gentleman, who was pursuing his studies, saw me, whether in church or somewhere else, I cannot tell, and in fact fell in love with me, and let me know it from the windows of his house with so many signs and tears that I was forced to believe him, and even to love him, without knowing what it was he wanted of me. One of the signs he used to make me was to link one hand in the other, to show me he wished to marry me. Although I would have been glad if that were possible, being alone and motherless I had no one to open my mind to, and so I left it as it was, showing him no favour except, when my father and his too were away from home, to raise the curtain or lattice a little and let him see me plainly, at which he would show such delight that he seemed about to go mad. Meanwhile the time for my father's departure arrived, which he found out about, but not from me, since I had never been able to tell him. He fell sick, of grief I believe; and so the day we left I could not see him to take farewell of him, even with my eyes. But after we had been two days on the road, on entering the posada of a village a day's journey from here, I saw him at the inn door in the dress of a muleteer, and so well disguised that, if I did not carry his image graven on my heart, it would have been impossible for me to recognise him. But I knew him, and I was surprised, and glad; he watched me, unsuspected by my father, from whom he always hides himself when he crosses my path on the road, or in the posadas where we halt. And, knowing what he is, and reflecting that for love of me he is making this journey on foot in all this hardship, I am ready to die of sorrow; and where he sets foot there I set my eyes. I do not know what his object is in coming, or how he could have got away from his father, who loves him beyond measure, having no other heir, and because he deserves it, as you will see when you see him. And what is more, I can tell you, everything he sings is out of his own head, for I have heard them say he is a great scholar and poet. And what is more, every time I see him or hear him sing I tremble all over, and am terrified that my father will recognise him and find out about our love. I have never spoken a word to him in my life, and for all that I love him so that I could not live without him. This, dear señora, is all I have to tell you about the musician whose voice has so delighted you; and from this alone you may easily see he is no muleteer, but a lord of hearts and towns, as I told you already."

"Say no more, Doña Clara," said Dorothea at this, at the same time kissing her a thousand times over, "say no more, I tell you, but wait until day comes, when I trust in God to arrange this affair of yours so that it may have the happy ending such an innocent beginning deserves."

"Ah, señora," said Doña Clara, "what end can be hoped for when his father is of such lofty position and so wealthy that he would think I was not fit to be even a servant to his son, much less his wife? And as to marrying without my father's knowledge, I would not do it for all the world. I would not ask anything more than that this youth should go back and leave me; perhaps with not seeing him, and the long distance we have to travel, the pain I suffer now may grow easier — though I daresay the remedy I propose will do me very little good. I don't know how the devil this came about, or how this love I have for him got in; I such a young girl, and he such a mere boy. I truly believe we are both the same age, and I am not sixteen yet; for I will be sixteen on Michaelmas Day next, my father says."

Dorothea could not help laughing to hear how like a child Doña Clara spoke. "Let us go to sleep now, señora," she said, "for the little of the night I fancy is left to us. God will soon send us daylight, and we will set everything to rights, or it will go hard with me."

With this they fell asleep, and deep silence reigned through the inn. The only ones not asleep were the landlady's daughter and her servant Maritornes, who, knowing the weak point of Don Quixote's humour and that he was outside the inn standing guard in armour and on horseback, decided between them to play some trick on him, or at least amuse themselves for a while by listening to his nonsense. As it happened there was not a window in the whole inn that looked outwards except a hole in the wall of a straw-loft through which they used to throw out the straw. At this hole the two demi-damsels posted themselves, and observed Don Quixote on his horse, leaning on his pike and from time to time letting out such deep and doleful sighs that he seemed to pluck up his soul by the roots with each one. They could hear him saying in a soft, tender, loving tone, "Oh my lady Dulcinea del Toboso, perfection of all beauty, summit and crown of discretion, treasure house of grace, depositary of virtue, and finally, ideal of all that is good, honourable, and delightful in this world! What is your grace doing now? Are you, perchance, mindful of your enslaved knight who of his own free will has exposed himself to such great perils, and all to serve you? Give me tidings of her, oh luminary of the three faces! Perhaps at this moment, envious of hers, you are gazing at her, either as she paces some gallery of her sumptuous palaces, or leans over some balcony, considering how, while preserving her purity and greatness, she may ease the tortures this wretched heart of mine endures for her sake; what glory shall reward my sufferings, what repose my toil, and lastly what death my life, and what reward my services? And you, oh sun, that are now no doubt harnessing your steeds in haste to rise early and come forth to see my lady: when you see her, I beg you, salute her on my behalf. But take care, when you see and salute her, that you do not kiss her face; for I shall be more jealous of you than you were of that light-footed ingrate that made you sweat and run so on the plains of Thessaly, or on the banks of the Peneus (for I do not exactly recall where you ran on that occasion) in your jealousy and love."
Don Quixote had got this far in his pathetic speech when the landlady's daughter began to signal to him, saying, "Señor, come over here, please."

At these signals and that voice Don Quixote turned his head and saw, by the light of the moon, which was then in its full splendour, that someone was calling to him from the hole in the wall, which seemed to him to be a window — and what is more, with a gilt grating, such as rich castles like the one he believed the inn to be ought to have. It immediately occurred to his imagination that, as on the former occasion, the fair damsel, the daughter of the lady of the castle, overcome by love for him, was once more trying to win his affection; and with this idea, so as not to seem discourteous or ungrateful, he turned Rocinante's head and approached the hole. As he saw the two wenches, he said:

"I pity you, beauteous lady, that you should have directed your thoughts of love to a quarter from which it is impossible that such a return can be made to you as is due to your great merit and gentle birth. For this you must not blame this unhappy knight-errant, whom love renders incapable of submission to any other than the one whom, the first moment his eyes beheld her, he made absolute mistress of his soul. Forgive me, noble lady, and retire to your apartment; do not, by any further declaration of your passion, compel me to show myself more ungrateful. And if, of the love you bear me, you find that there is anything else in my power in which I can gratify you — provided it be not love itself — demand it of me; for I swear to you by that sweet absent enemy of mine to grant it this instant, even if you require of me a lock of Medusa's hair, which was all snakes, or even the very beams of the sun shut up in a vial."
"My mistress wants nothing of that sort, sir knight," said Maritornes at this.
"What then, discreet dame, is it that your mistress wants?" replied Don Quixote.

"Only one of your fair hands," said Maritornes, "to enable her to vent over it the great passion that has brought her to this loophole, so much at the risk of her honour; for if the lord her father had heard her, the least slice he would cut off her would be her ear."

"I should like to see that tried," said Don Quixote; "but he had better beware, if he does not want to meet the most disastrous end that ever father in the world met for having laid hands on the tender limbs of a love-stricken daughter."

Maritornes felt sure Don Quixote would offer the hand she had asked for, and making up her mind what to do, she got down from the hole and went into the stable, where she took the halter of Sancho Panza's donkey, and in all haste returned to the hole — just as Don Quixote had planted himself standing on Rocinante's saddle in order to reach the grated window where he supposed the lovelorn damsel to be. Giving her his hand, he said, "Lady, take this hand, or rather this scourge of the evil-doers of the earth; take, I say, this hand which no other hand of woman has ever touched, not even hers who has complete possession of my entire body. I present it to you, not that you may kiss it, but that you may observe the texture of the sinews, the close network of the muscles, the breadth and capacity of the veins, from which you may infer what must be the strength of the arm that has such a hand."

"That we shall see presently," said Maritornes; and making a running knot on the halter, she passed it over his wrist and, coming down from the hole, tied the other end very firmly to the bolt of the door of the straw-loft.

Don Quixote, feeling the roughness of the rope on his wrist, exclaimed, "Your grace seems to be grating rather than caressing my hand. Do not treat it so harshly, for it is not to blame for the offence my resolution has given you, nor is it just to wreak all your vengeance on so small a part. Remember that one who loves so well should not revenge herself so cruelly."

But there was no one left to listen to these words of Don Quixote's, for as soon as Maritornes had tied him she and the other made off, ready to die with laughing, leaving him fastened in such a way that it was impossible for him to release himself.

He was, as has been said, standing on Rocinante, with his arm passed through the hole and his wrist tied to the bolt of the door, and in mighty fear and dread of being left hanging by the arm if Rocinante were to move one way or the other; so he did not dare to make the slightest movement, although from Rocinante's patient and imperturbable disposition he had good reason to expect that he would stand without budging for a whole century. Finding himself fast, then, and that the ladies had retired, he began to imagine that all this was done by enchantment, as on the former occasion when in that same castle that enchanted Moor of a carrier had thrashed him; and he cursed in his heart his own want of sense and judgement in venturing to enter the castle again after having come off so badly the first time — it being a settled point with knights-errant that, when they have tried an adventure and not succeeded in it, it is a sign it is not reserved for them but for others, and that therefore they need not try it again. Nevertheless he pulled his arm to see if he could release himself, but it had been made so fast that all his efforts were in vain. It is true he pulled it gently, in case Rocinante should move; but try as he might to seat himself in the saddle, he had nothing for it but to stand upright or pull his hand off. Then it was that he wished for the sword of Amadis, against which no enchantment had any power; then he cursed his ill fortune; then he magnified the loss the world would sustain by his absence while he remained there enchanted, for he believed beyond doubt that he was; then he once more took to thinking of his beloved Dulcinea del Toboso; then he called to his worthy squire Sancho Panza, who, buried in sleep and stretched on the pack-saddle of his donkey, was oblivious at that moment of the mother that bore him; then he called on the sages Lirgandeo and Alquife to come to his aid; then he invoked his good friend Urganda to succour him. And then, at last, morning found him in such a state of desperation and perplexity that he was bellowing like a bull, for he had no hope that day would bring any relief to his suffering, which he believed would last forever, since he was enchanted. He was convinced of this by seeing that Rocinante never stirred, much or little, and he felt persuaded that he and his horse were to remain in this state, without eating or drinking or sleeping, until the malign influence of the stars was past, or until some other more skilful enchanter should disenchant him.

But he was very much deceived in this conclusion, because daylight had hardly begun to appear when there came up to the inn four men on horseback, well equipped and accoutred, with firelocks across their saddle-bows. They called out and knocked loudly at the gate of the inn, which was still shut. Seeing this, Don Quixote, even where he was, did not forget to act as sentinel, and said in a loud and imperious tone, "Knights, or squires, or whatever you be, you have no right to knock at the gates of this castle; for it is plain enough that those within are either asleep, or else are not in the habit of throwing open the fortress until the sun's rays have spread over the whole surface of the earth. Withdraw to a distance, and wait until it is broad daylight, and then we shall see whether it will be proper or not to open to you."

"What the devil fortress or castle is this," said one of them, "to make us stand on such ceremony? If you are the innkeeper, have them open to us; we are travellers who only want to feed our horses and go on, for we are in a hurry."
"Do you think, gentlemen, that I look like an innkeeper?" said Don Quixote.
"I don't know what you look like," replied the other; "but I know you are talking nonsense when you call this inn a castle."
"A castle it is," returned Don Quixote, "and more — one of the best in this whole province, and it has within it people who have had the sceptre in the hand and the crown on the head."

"It would be better if it were the other way," said the traveller, "the sceptre on the head and the crown in the hand; but if so, maybe there is within some company of players, with whom it is a common thing to have those crowns and sceptres you speak of — for in such a small inn as this, and where such silence is kept, I do not believe people entitled to crowns and sceptres can have taken up quarters."
"You know little of the world," returned Don Quixote, "since you are ignorant of what commonly happens in knight-errantry."

But the spokesman's companions, growing weary of the dialogue with Don Quixote, renewed their knocks with such vehemence that the host, and not only he but everybody in the inn, woke up, and he got up to ask who was knocking. It happened at this moment that one of the horses of the four who were seeking admittance went to smell Rocinante, who, melancholy and dejected and with drooping ears, stood motionless, supporting his sorely stretched master. As he was, after all, flesh, though he looked as if he were made of wood, he could not help giving way and in return smelling the one who had come to offer him attentions. But he had hardly moved at all when Don Quixote lost his footing; and slipping off the saddle, he would have come to the ground, except for being suspended by the arm, which caused him such agony that he believed either his wrist would be cut through or his arm torn off. He hung so near the ground that he could just touch it with his feet, which was all the worse for him; finding how little was wanted to enable him to plant his feet firmly, he struggled and stretched himself as much as he could to gain a footing — just like those undergoing the torture of the strappado, when they are fixed at "touch and no touch," who aggravate their own sufferings by their violent efforts to stretch themselves, deceived by the hope which makes them fancy that with a very little more they will reach the ground.

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 44
paragraphs: In which are continued the unheard-of adventures of the inn

So loud, in fact, were Don Quixote's shouts that the landlord, hurriedly opening the gate of the inn, came out in dismay and ran to see who was uttering such cries, and those who were outside joined him. Maritornes, who had been roused by the same outcry, suspecting what it was, ran to the loft and, without anyone seeing her, untied the halter by which Don Quixote was suspended, and down he came to the ground in full view of the landlord and the travellers, who came over and asked him what was the matter with him that he shouted so. Without saying a word in reply, he took the rope off his wrist and, rising to his feet, leaped onto Rocinante, braced his buckler on his arm, put his lance in rest, and making a considerable circuit of the plain came back at a half-gallop exclaiming:

"Whoever shall say that I have been enchanted with just cause — provided my lady the Princess Micomicona grants me permission to do so — I give him the lie, challenge him, and defy him to single combat."

The newly arrived travellers were amazed at Don Quixote's words; but the landlord removed their surprise by telling them who he was, and not to mind him as he was out of his senses. They then asked the landlord whether by any chance a youth of about fifteen, dressed like a muleteer and of such-and-such an appearance, had come to that inn — describing that of Doña Clara's lover. The landlord replied that there were so many people in the inn he had not noticed the person they were asking about; but one of them, spotting the coach in which the Judge had come, said, "He is here for certain, because this is the coach he is following. Let one of us stay at the gate, and the rest go in to look for him; or indeed it would be as well if one of us went round the inn, in case he should escape over the wall of the yard." "So be it," said another; and while two of them went in, one remained at the gate and the other made the circuit of the inn. The landlord, observing all this, could not guess why they were taking all these precautions, though he understood they were looking for the youth whose description they had given him.

It was by now broad daylight; and for that reason, as well as because of the noise Don Quixote had made, everybody was awake and up, but particularly Doña Clara and Dorothea, for they had been able to sleep but badly that night — the one from agitation at having her lover so near her, the other from curiosity to see him. Don Quixote, when he saw that not one of the four travellers took any notice of him or replied to his challenge, was furious and ready to die with indignation and wrath. If he could have found in the ordinances of chivalry that it was lawful for a knight-errant to undertake or engage in another enterprise when he had given his word and faith not to involve himself in any until he had made an end of the one he was pledged to, he would have attacked the whole lot of them and would have made them return an answer in spite of themselves. But considering that it would not become him, nor be right, to begin any new emprise until he had established Micomicona in her kingdom, he was forced to hold his peace and wait quietly to see what would come of the proceedings of those same travellers — one of whom found the youth they were seeking lying asleep by the side of a muleteer, without a thought of anyone coming in search of him, much less finding him.

The man laid hold of him by the arm, saying, "It becomes you well indeed, Señor Don Luis, to be in the clothes you are wearing, and well does the bed I find you in agree with the luxury in which your mother brought you up."

The youth rubbed his sleepy eyes and stared for a while at the one who held him, but presently recognised him as one of his father's servants. At this he was so taken aback that for some time he could not find or utter a word, while the servant went on, "There is nothing for it now, Señor Don Luis, but to submit quietly and return home — unless you want my lord, your father, to depart for the other world, since nothing else can be the consequence of the grief he is in at your absence."
"But how did my father know I had gone this road and in this dress?" said Don Luis.

"It was a student you confided your intentions to," answered the servant, "who disclosed them, touched with pity at the distress he saw your father suffer on missing you. He therefore dispatched four of his servants in search of you, and here we all are at your service, better pleased than you can imagine that we shall return so soon and be able to restore you to those eyes that so yearn for you."
"That shall be as I please, or as heaven orders," returned Don Luis.
"What can you please, or heaven order," said the other, "except to agree to go back? Anything else is impossible."

All this conversation between the two was overheard by the muleteer beside whom Don Luis lay, and rising, he went to report what had taken place to Don Fernando, Cardenio, and the others, who had by this time dressed themselves; and he told them how the man had addressed the youth as "Don," and what words had passed, and how he wanted him to go back to his father, which the youth was unwilling to do. With this, and what they already knew of the rare voice heaven had given him, they all felt very anxious to know more particularly who he was, and even to help him if it was attempted to use force against him. So they hurried to where he was still talking and arguing with his servant. Dorothea at this moment came out of her room, followed by Doña Clara all in a tremor; and calling Cardenio aside, she told him in a few words the story of the musician and Doña Clara, and he at the same time told her what had happened, how his father's servants had come in search of him. But in telling her this, he did not speak quietly enough but that Doña Clara heard what he said, at which she was so much agitated that, had Dorothea not hurried to support her, she would have fallen to the ground. Cardenio then asked Dorothea to return to her room, since he would try to make the whole matter right, and they did as he asked. All four who had come in quest of Don Luis had now come into the inn and surrounded him, urging him to return and console his father at once, without a moment's delay. He replied that he could not do so on any account until he had finished some business in which his life, honour, and heart were at stake. The servants pressed him, saying that most certainly they would not return without him, and that they would take him away whether he liked it or not.
"You shall not do that," replied Don Luis, "unless you take me dead; though however you take me, it will be without life."

By this time most of those in the inn had been drawn over by the dispute, but particularly Cardenio, Don Fernando, his companions, the Judge, the curate, the barber, and Don Quixote, who now considered there was no necessity for mounting guard over the castle any longer. Cardenio, already acquainted with the young man's story, asked the men who wanted to take him away what object they had in seeking to carry off this youth against his will.
"Our object," said one of the four, "is to save the life of his father, who is in danger of losing it through this gentleman's disappearance."
Upon this Don Luis exclaimed, "There is no need to make my affairs public here. I am free, and I will return if I please; and if not, none of you shall compel me."
"Reason will compel your worship," said the man, "and if it has no power over you, it has power over us, to make us do what we came for, and what it is our duty to do."

"Let us hear what the whole affair is about," said the Judge at this; but the man, who knew him as a neighbour of theirs, replied, "Do you not know this gentleman, Señor Judge? He is the son of your neighbour, who has run away from his father's house in a dress so unbecoming to his rank, as your worship may see."

The judge on this looked at him more carefully and recognised him, and embracing him said, "What folly is this, Señor Don Luis? What can have been the cause that could have induced you to come here in this way, and in this dress, which so ill becomes your station?"

Tears came into the young man's eyes, and he was unable to utter a word in reply to the Judge, who told the four servants not to be uneasy, that everything would be satisfactorily settled; and then taking Don Luis by the hand, he drew him aside and asked the reason for his having come there.

But while he was questioning him they heard a loud outcry at the gate of the inn. The cause of it was that two of the guests who had spent the night there, seeing everybody busy about finding out what the four men wanted, had got the idea of going off without paying what they owed; but the landlord, who minded his own affairs more than other people's, caught them going out of the gate and demanded his reckoning, abusing them for their dishonesty in such language that they were driven to reply with their fists. They began to lay on him in such a style that the poor man was forced to cry out and call for help. The landlady and her daughter could see no one freer to give aid than Don Quixote, and to him the daughter said, "Sir knight, by the virtue God has given you, help my poor father, for two wicked men are beating him to a pulp."

To which Don Quixote very deliberately and phlegmatically replied, "Fair damsel, at the present moment your request is inopportune, because I am barred from involving myself in any adventure until I have brought to a happy conclusion one to which my word has pledged me. But what I can do for you is what I will now tell you: run and tell your father to stand his ground as best he can in this battle, and on no account let himself be vanquished, while I go and request permission of the Princess Micomicona to come to his aid in his distress; and if she grants it, you may rest assured I will relieve him from it."
"Sinner that I am," exclaimed Maritornes, who stood by, "before you have got your permission my master will be in the other world."

"Give me leave, señora, to obtain the permission I speak of," returned Don Quixote; "and if I get it, it will matter very little if he is in the other world, because I will rescue him from there in spite of all that the same world can do; or at any rate I will give you such a revenge over those who shall have sent him there that you will be more than moderately satisfied." And without saying anything more he went and knelt before Dorothea, asking her Highness in knightly and errant phrase to be pleased to grant him permission to aid and succour the castellan of that castle, who now stood in grievous jeopardy. The princess granted it graciously, and at once, bracing his buckler on his arm and drawing his sword, he hurried to the inn gate, where the two guests were still handling the landlord roughly. But as soon as he reached the spot he stopped short and stood still, though Maritornes and the landlady asked him why he hesitated to help their master and husband.

"I hesitate," said Don Quixote, "because it is not lawful for me to draw sword against persons of squirely condition; but call my squire Sancho to me, for this defence and vengeance are his affair and business."

Thus matters stood at the inn gate, where there was a very lively exchange of fisticuffs and punches, to the sore damage of the landlord and to the wrath of Maritornes, the landlady, and her daughter, who were furious to see the pusillanimity of Don Quixote and the hard treatment their master, husband, and father was undergoing. But let us leave him there, for he will surely find someone to help him, and if not, let him suffer and hold his tongue who attempts more than his strength allows him to do; and let us go back fifty paces to see what Don Luis said in reply to the Judge, whom we left questioning him privately as to his reasons for coming on foot and so meanly dressed.
To which the youth, pressing his hand in a way that showed his heart was troubled by some great sorrow, and shedding a flood of tears, replied:

"Señor, I have no more to tell you than that, from the moment when, through heaven's will and our being near neighbours, I first saw Doña Clara, your daughter and my lady, from that instant I made her the mistress of my will; and if yours, my true lord and father, offers no objection, this very day she shall become my wife. For her I left my father's house, and for her I assumed this disguise, to follow her wherever she may go, as the arrow seeks its mark or the sailor the pole-star. She knows nothing more of my passion than what she may have learned from sometimes seeing from a distance that my eyes were filled with tears. You know already, señor, the wealth and noble birth of my parents, and that I am their sole heir; if this is a sufficient inducement for you to venture to make me completely happy, accept me at once as your son. For if my father, influenced by other aims of his own, should disapprove of this happiness I have sought for myself, time has more power to alter and change things than human will."

With this the love-smitten youth fell silent, while the Judge, after hearing him, was astonished, perplexed, and surprised, as well at the manner and intelligence with which Don Luis had confessed the secret of his heart as at the position in which he found himself, not knowing what course to take in a matter so sudden and unexpected. All the answer he gave him, therefore, was to tell him to set his mind at ease for the present, and to arrange with his servants not to take him back that day, so there might be time to consider what was best for all parties. Don Luis kissed his hands by force — nay, bathed them with his tears — in a way that would have touched a heart of marble, not to say that of the Judge, who, as a shrewd man, had already perceived how advantageous the marriage would be to his daughter; though, were it possible, he would have preferred that it be brought about with the consent of Don Luis's father, who he knew was looking for a title for his son.

The guests had by this time made peace with the landlord, since, more by persuasion and Don Quixote's fair words than by threats, they had paid him what he demanded. The servants of Don Luis were waiting for the end of the conversation with the Judge and their master's decision, when the devil, who never sleeps, contrived that the barber from whom Don Quixote had taken Mambrino's helmet, and from whom Sancho Panza had taken the trappings of his donkey in exchange for his own, should at this very moment enter the inn. As the said barber led his donkey to the stable, he noticed Sancho Panza repairing something or other belonging to the pack-saddle; and the moment he saw it he knew it, and made bold to attack Sancho, exclaiming, "Ha, sir thief, I have caught you! Hand over my basin and my pack-saddle, and all my trappings that you robbed me of."
