Almost the same civilities were exchanged between him and the student, who, listening to Don Quixote, took him to be a sensible, clear-headed man.

Here the author describes minutely everything belonging to Don Diego's mansion, putting before us in his picture the whole contents of a rich gentleman-farmer's house. But the translator of the history thought it best to pass over these and other details of the same sort in silence, as they aren't in keeping with the main purpose of the story, whose strong point is truth rather than dull digressions.

They led Don Quixote into a room, where Sancho removed his armour, leaving him in loose Walloon breeches and a chamois-leather doublet, all stained with the rust of his armour. His collar was a falling one of scholastic cut, without starch or lace; his buskins buff-coloured, his shoes polished. He wore his good sword, hung from a baldric of sea-wolf's skin, for he had suffered for many years, they say, from an ailment of the kidneys; and over it all he threw a long cloak of good grey cloth. But first, with five or six buckets of water (the exact number is disputed), he washed his head and face, and even then the water remained whey-coloured, thanks to Sancho's greed and his purchase of those unlucky curds that had turned his master so white. Thus arrayed, and with an easy, sprightly, gallant air, Don Quixote passed into another room, where the student was waiting to entertain him while the table was being laid. On the arrival of so distinguished a guest, Doña Cristina was anxious to show she knew how, and was able, to give a fitting reception to those who came to her house.

While Don Quixote was taking off his armour, Don Lorenzo (for that was Don Diego's son's name) seized the chance to say to his father, "What are we to make of this gentleman you've brought home, sir? His name, his appearance, and your describing him as a knight-errant have my mother and me completely puzzled."

"I don't know what to say, my son," Don Diego replied. "All I can tell you is that I have seen him perform the acts of the greatest madman in the world, and heard him make observations so sensible that they cancel out everything he does. You talk to him and feel the pulse of his wits, and as you are shrewd, draw the most reasonable conclusion you can about his wisdom or folly — though, to tell the truth, I am more inclined to take him to be mad than sane."

With this, Don Lorenzo went off to entertain Don Quixote as has been said, and in the course of their conversation, Don Quixote said to Don Lorenzo, "Your father, Señor Don Diego de Miranda, has told me of the rare abilities and subtle intellect you have, and, above all, that you are a great poet."

"A poet, perhaps," Don Lorenzo replied, "but a great one, by no means. It's true I am somewhat given to poetry and to reading good poets, but not enough to justify the title of 'great' my father gives me."
"I don't dislike that modesty," said Don Quixote; "for there is no poet who isn't conceited and doesn't think he's the best poet in the world."
"There is no rule without an exception," said Don Lorenzo; "there may be some who are poets and don't think they are."

"Very few," said Don Quixote; "but tell me, what verses are these you have in hand, the ones your father tells me keep you somewhat restless and absorbed? If it's some gloss, I know something about glosses, and I'd like to hear them; and if they're for a poetry contest, try to carry off the second prize — first always goes by favour or personal standing, second by simple justice; so the third comes to be second, and the first, reckoned this way, comes to be third, much as licentiate degrees are awarded at the universities. But for all that, the title of first is a great distinction."
"So far," said Don Lorenzo to himself, "I shouldn't take you for a madman; but let's go on." So he said to him, "You appear to have attended the schools; what sciences have you studied?"
"That of knight-errantry," said Don Quixote, "which is as good as that of poetry, and even a finger or two above it."
"I don't know what science that is," said Don Lorenzo, "and until now I have never heard of it."

"It is a science," said Don Quixote, "that comprehends in itself all or most of the sciences in the world. He who professes it must be a jurist, and must know the rules of justice, distributive and equitable, so as to give each one what belongs to him and is due to him. He must be a theologian, so as to be able to give a clear and distinctive reason for the Christian faith he professes, whenever it is asked of him. He must be a physician, and above all a herbalist, so that in wastes and solitudes he may know the herbs that have the property of healing wounds — a knight-errant can't go searching for someone to cure him at every step. He must be an astronomer, so as to know by the stars how many hours of the night have passed, and what region and quarter of the world he is in. He must know mathematics, for at every turn occasion for them will arise. And, leaving aside that he must be adorned with all the virtues, cardinal and theological, to come down to minor particulars, he must, I say, be able to swim as well as Nicholas or Nicolao the Fish, as the story goes; he must know how to shoe a horse, repair his saddle and bridle; and, to return to higher matters, he must be faithful to God and to his lady; he must be pure in thought, decorous in words, generous in works, valiant in deeds, patient in suffering, compassionate toward the needy, and, lastly, an upholder of the truth, even if defending it should cost him his life. Of all these qualities, great and small, a true knight-errant is made up; judge then, Señor Don Lorenzo, whether it is a contemptible science the knight who studies and professes it has to learn, and whether it may not compare with the very loftiest taught in the schools."
"If that be so," Don Lorenzo replied, "this science, I declare, surpasses them all."
"How, 'if that be so'?" said Don Quixote.
"What I mean to say," said Don Lorenzo, "is that I doubt whether there are now, or ever were, any knight-errants adorned with such virtues."

"Many a time," replied Don Quixote, "have I said what I now say again: that most of the world is of the opinion there never were any knight-errants in it. As it's my view that, unless heaven by some miracle brings home to them the truth that there were and are, all the pains one takes will be wasted (as experience has often shown me), I will not now stop to disabuse you of the error you share with the multitude. All I'll do is pray heaven to deliver you from it, and show you how beneficial and necessary knight-errants were in days of old, and how useful they would be in these days, were they but in fashion. But now, for the sins of the people, sloth and indolence, gluttony and luxury are triumphant."
"Our guest has broken out on our hands," said Don Lorenzo to himself at this point; "but for all that, he is a glorious madman, and I should be a dull blockhead to doubt it."

Here, being called to dinner, they brought their conversation to a close. Don Diego asked his son what he had been able to make out about their guest's wits. To which he replied, "All the doctors and clever scribes in the world won't make sense of the scrawl of his madness; he is a madman full of streaks, full of lucid intervals."

They went in to dinner, and the meal was just what Don Diego had said on the road he was in the habit of giving his guests — neat, plentiful, and tasty. But what pleased Don Quixote most was the marvellous silence that reigned throughout the house, which was like a Carthusian monastery.

When the cloth had been removed, grace said, and their hands washed, Don Quixote earnestly pressed Don Lorenzo to recite the verses for the poetry contest, to which he replied, "Not to be like those poets who refuse when they're asked to recite their verses and vomit them up when they're not, I'll repeat my gloss, for which I don't expect any prize, having composed it merely as an exercise in ingenuity."

"A discerning friend of mine," said Don Quixote, "was of the opinion that no one should waste effort glossing verses. His reason was that the gloss can never live up to the text, and that often — most often — it wanders away from the meaning and purpose of the lines being glossed. Besides, the laws of the gloss are too strict: they allow no questions, no 'said he' or 'I say,' no turning verbs into nouns, no altering the construction, not to mention other restrictions and limitations that fetter gloss-writers, as you no doubt know."
"Really, Señor Don Quixote," said Don Lorenzo, "I wish I could catch your worship tripping at full stretch, but I cannot — you slip through my fingers like an eel."
"I don't understand what you mean by 'slipping,'" said Don Quixote.
"I'll explain another time," said Don Lorenzo; "for the moment, please attend to the glossed verses and the gloss, which run as follows:
Could 'was' become an 'is' for me, / Then would I ask no more than this; / Or could, for me, the time that is / Become the time that is to be! —
GLOSS

Dame Fortune once upon a day / To me was bountiful and kind; / But all things change; she changed her mind, / And what she gave she took away. / O Fortune, long I've sued to thee; / The gifts thou gavest me restore, / For, trust me, I would ask no more, / Could 'was' become an 'is' for me.

No other prize I seek to gain, / No triumph, glory, or success, / Only the long-lost happiness, / The memory whereof is pain. / One taste, methinks, of bygone bliss / The heart-consuming fire might stay; / And, so it come without delay, / Then would I ask no more than this.

I ask what cannot be, alas! / That time should ever be, and then / Come back to us, and be again, / No power on earth can bring to pass; / For fleet of foot is he, I wis, / And idly, therefore, do we pray / That what for aye hath left us may / Become for us the time that is.

Perplexed, uncertain, to remain / 'Twixt hope and fear, is death, not life; / 'Twere better, sure, to end the strife, / And dying, seek release from pain. / And yet, thought were the best for me. / Anon the thought aside I fling, / And to the present fondly cling, / And dread the time that is to be."

When Don Lorenzo had finished reciting his gloss, Don Quixote stood up, and in a loud voice — almost a shout — exclaimed as he grasped Don Lorenzo's right hand in his, "By the highest heavens, noble youth, you are the best poet on earth, and deserve to be crowned with laurel — not by Cyprus or by Gaeta, as a certain poet, God forgive him, said, but by the Academies of Athens, if they still flourished, and by those that flourish now, Paris, Bologna, Salamanca. Heaven grant that the judges who rob you of the first prize — may Phœbus pierce them with his arrows, and the Muses never cross the thresholds of their doors. Recite me some of your long-measure verses, señor, if you would be so good, for I want to feel the pulse of your rare genius thoroughly."

Is there any need to say that Don Lorenzo enjoyed hearing himself praised by Don Quixote, even though he looked on him as a madman? Power of flattery, how far-reaching you are, and how wide are the bounds of your pleasant jurisdiction! Don Lorenzo gave proof of it, for he agreed to Don Quixote's request and recited to him this sonnet on the fable or story of Pyramus and Thisbe.
SONNET

The lovely maid, she pierces now the wall; / Heart-pierced by her young Pyramus doth lie; / And Love spreads wing from Cyprus isle to fly, / A chink to view so wondrous great and small. / There silence speaketh, for no voice at all / Can pass so strait a strait; but love will ply / Where to all other power 'twere vain to try; / For love will find a way whate'er befall. / Impatient of delay, with reckless pace / The rash maid wins the fatal spot where she / Sinks not in lover's arms but death's embrace. / So runs the strange tale, how the lovers twain / One sword, one sepulchre, one memory, / Slays, and entombs, and brings to life again.

"Blessed be God," said Don Quixote when he had heard Don Lorenzo's sonnet, "that among the hosts of irritable poets I have found one consummate one — which, señor, the artistry of this sonnet proves to me that you are!"

For four days Don Quixote was most lavishly entertained at Don Diego's house, at the end of which he asked his permission to leave, telling him he was grateful for the kindness and hospitality he had received there, but that, since it didn't suit knight-errants to give themselves up for long to idleness and luxury, he was eager to fulfil the duties of his calling by seeking adventures, of which he was told there were plenty in that neighbourhood, where he hoped to occupy his time until the day came round for the jousts at Saragossa, which was his proper destination. First of all, he meant to enter the cave of Montesinos, of which so many marvellous things were reported all through the country, and at the same time to investigate and explore the origin and true source of the seven lakes commonly called the lakes of Ruidera.

Don Diego and his son praised his commendable resolution, and told him to take from their house and belongings whatever he wanted, as they would most gladly be of service to him — which indeed his personal worth and his honourable profession made incumbent on them.

The day of his departure came at last, as welcome to Don Quixote as it was sad and sorrowful to Sancho Panza, who was very well satisfied with the abundance of Don Diego's house, and objected to returning to the starvation of the woods and wilds and the short rations of his ill-stocked alforjas. These, however, he filled and packed with what he considered necessary. On taking leave, Don Quixote said to Don Lorenzo, "I don't know if I have told you already, but if I have I'll tell you again: if you want to spare yourself fatigue and toil in reaching the inaccessible summit of the temple of fame, you have only to step off the somewhat narrow path of poetry and take the still narrower one of knight-errantry — wide enough, however, to make you an emperor in the twinkling of an eye."

In this speech Don Quixote wrapped up the evidence of his madness, but even better in what he added when he said, "God knows, I would gladly take Don Lorenzo with me, to teach him how to spare the humble and trample the proud underfoot — virtues that are part and parcel of the profession I belong to. But since his tender age does not allow it, and his praiseworthy pursuits do not permit it, I'll simply content myself with impressing on your worship that you'll become famous as a poet if you are guided by the opinion of others rather than by your own. For no fathers or mothers ever think their own children ugly, and this kind of deception prevails still more strongly in the case of the children of the brain."

Father and son were amazed afresh at the strange medley Don Quixote talked, at one moment sense, at another nonsense, and at the pertinacity and persistence he showed in going through thick and thin in quest of his unlucky adventures, which he made the end and aim of his desires. There was a renewal of offers of service and civilities, and then, with the gracious permission of the lady of the castle, they took their leave — Don Quixote on Rocinante, Sancho on Dapple.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 19
paragraphs: In which is told the adventure of the lovesick shepherd, together with other truly droll incidents

Don Quixote had gone only a short distance beyond Don Diego's village when he ran into a couple of either priests or students, and a couple of peasants, mounted on four asses. One of the students carried, wrapped up in a piece of green buckram by way of a portmanteau, what seemed to be a little linen and a couple of pairs of ribbed stockings; the other carried nothing but a pair of new fencing-foils with buttons. The peasants carried various articles that showed they were on their way home from some large town where they had bought them. Both students and peasants were struck with the same amazement everyone felt who saw Don Quixote for the first time, and were dying to know who this man, so different from ordinary men, could be. Don Quixote greeted them, and after finding out that their road was the same as his, offered them his company, asking them to slacken their pace, as their young asses travelled faster than his horse. To oblige them, he told them in a few words who he was and the calling and profession he followed — that of a knight-errant seeking adventures in all parts of the world. He informed them that his own name was Don Quixote of La Mancha, and that he was called, by way of surname, the Knight of the Lions.

All this was Greek or gibberish to the peasants, but not to the students, who very soon spotted the crack in Don Quixote's pate. For all that, they regarded him with admiration and respect, and one of them said to him, "If you, sir knight, have no fixed road — as is the way with those who seek adventures — let your worship come with us. You'll see one of the finest and richest weddings ever celebrated to this day in La Mancha, or for many a league around."

Don Quixote asked if it was some prince's, that he spoke of it in such terms. "Not at all," said the student. "It's the wedding of a farmer and a farmer's daughter — he the richest in all this country, she the fairest mortal ever set eyes on. The display will be something rare and out of the ordinary, because it's to be held in a meadow next to the bride's town. She is called, _par excellence_, Quiteria the fair; the bridegroom is called Camacho the rich. She is eighteen, he twenty-two, and they are fairly matched, though some knowing types — who carry every pedigree in the world by heart — insist that the family of fair Quiteria is better than Camacho's; but nobody minds that nowadays, since wealth can solder a great many flaws. At any rate, Camacho is open-handed, and it's his fancy to roof in the whole meadow with branches, so the sun will have hard work getting in to reach the grass on the ground. He has provided dancers too — not just sword-dancers but also bell-dancers, for in his own town there are people who ring the changes and jingle the bells to perfection. Of shoe-dancers I say nothing, because of those he has hired a host. But none of these things, nor of the many others I've left out, will do more to make this a memorable wedding than the part I suspect the despairing Basilio will play in it. This Basilio is a young man of the same village as Quiteria, and he lived in the house next door to her parents — a circumstance Love seized on to reproduce, to the letter, the long-forgotten loves of Pyramus and Thisbe. Basilio loved Quiteria from his earliest years, and she answered his passion with countless modest tokens of affection, so the loves of the two children, Basilio and Quiteria, were the talk and amusement of the town. As they grew up, Quiteria's father decided to refuse Basilio his usual freedom of access to the house, and to spare himself constant doubts and suspicions, he arranged a match for his daughter with the rich Camacho, not approving of marrying her to Basilio, who had less of fortune's gifts than of nature's. To tell the truth ungrudgingly, Basilio is the most agile youth we know — a mighty thrower of the bar, a first-rate wrestler, a great ball-player. He runs like a deer, leaps better than a goat, knocks down the ninepins as if by magic, sings like a lark, plays the guitar so as to make it speak, and above all handles a sword as well as the best."

"For that excellence alone," Don Quixote put in, "the young man deserves to marry not merely the fair Quiteria, but Queen Guinevere herself, were she alive now, in spite of Lancelot and all who would try to prevent it."

"Say that to my wife," said Sancho, who had until now listened in silence, "because she won't hear of anything but each one marrying his equal, holding with the proverb 'each ewe to her like.' What I would like is for this good Basilio (for I'm beginning to take a fancy to him already) to marry this lady Quiteria. And a blessing and good luck — I meant to say the opposite — on people who would stop those who love one another from marrying."

"If everyone who loved one another were to marry," said Don Quixote, "it would deprive parents of the right to choose, and to marry their children to the proper person at the proper time. If daughters were left to choose husbands as they pleased, one would be for choosing her father's servant, and another some fellow she's seen passing in the street and fancies gallant and dashing, even if he's a drunken bully; for love and infatuation easily blind the eyes of judgment, which are so much needed in choosing one's way of life. The choice of a spouse is very liable to error, and it needs great caution and the special favour of heaven to make it a good one. A man who has to make a long journey, if he is wise, will look for some trusty and pleasant companion to go with him before he sets out. Why, then, should he not do the same who has to make the whole journey of life down to the final halting-place of death — especially when the companion has to be his companion in bed, at the table, and everywhere, as the wife is to her husband? The companionship of one's wife is no article of merchandise that, once bought, may be returned, bartered, or exchanged. It is an inseparable accident that lasts as long as life. It is a noose that, once put round your neck, turns into a Gordian knot, which, if the scythe of Death does not cut it, there is no untying. I could say a great deal more on this subject, were I not held back by the wish to know whether the señor licentiate has anything more to tell about Basilio."

To this the student, bachelor — or, as Don Quixote called him, licentiate — replied, "I have nothing more to say, except that from the moment Basilio learned that fair Quiteria was to marry Camacho the rich, he has never been seen to smile, or heard to utter a rational word. He goes about moody and dejected, talking to himself in a way that shows plainly he is out of his senses. He eats little and sleeps little; all he eats is fruit, and when he sleeps, if he sleeps at all, it is in the field on the bare ground like a brute beast. Sometimes he stares at the sky, at other times he fixes his eyes on the ground in such an abstracted way that he might be taken for a clothed statue, with its drapery stirred by the wind. In short, he shows such signs of a heart crushed by suffering that all of us who know him believe that when fair Quiteria says 'yes' tomorrow, it will be his sentence of death."

"God will guide it better," said Sancho. "God who gives the wound gives the salve; nobody knows what will happen. There are a good many hours between now and tomorrow, and any one of them, or any moment, the house may fall. I have seen the rain coming down and the sun shining at the same time; many a man goes to bed in good health who can't stir the next day. Tell me, is there anyone who can boast of having driven a nail into the wheel of Fortune? No, by my faith. And between a woman's 'yes' and 'no' I wouldn't venture to put the point of a pin — there wouldn't be room for it. If you tell me Quiteria loves Basilio heart and soul, then I'll give him a bag of good luck — for love, I've heard say, looks through spectacles that make copper look like gold, poverty wealth, and bleary eyes pearls."

"What are you driving at, Sancho? Curses on you!" said Don Quixote. "When you take to stringing proverbs and sayings together, nobody can understand you but Judas himself, and I wish he had you. Tell me, you animal, what do you know about nails or wheels or anything else?"

"Oh, if you don't understand me," Sancho replied, "it's no wonder my words are taken for nonsense. But no matter; I understand myself, and I know I haven't said anything very foolish in what I've said — only your worship, señor, is always cavilling at everything I say, indeed everything I do."
"Cavilling, not gravelling," said Don Quixote, "you mangler of honest language — God confound you!"

"Don't find fault with me, your worship," Sancho returned, "for you know I haven't been brought up at court or trained at Salamanca, to know whether I'm adding or dropping a letter in my words. Why, God bless me, it's not fair to force a man from Sayago to speak like a man from Toledo; and maybe there are Toledans who don't hit it off when it comes to polished talk either."

"That is true," said the licentiate, "because those who have been brought up in the Tanneries and the Zocodover can't talk like those who spend nearly all day pacing the cathedral cloisters, and yet they're all Toledans. Pure, correct, elegant, and lucid language will be found in men of courtly breeding and discrimination, even if they were born in Majalahonda. I say of discrimination, because there are many who lack it, and discrimination is the grammar of good language, if accompanied by practice. I, sirs, for my sins, have studied canon law at Salamanca, and I rather pride myself on expressing my meaning in clear, plain, and intelligible language."

"If you didn't pride yourself more on your skill with those foils you carry than on dexterity of tongue," said the other student, "you would have been head of the degrees, where you are now at the tail."
"Look here, bachelor Corchuelo," the licentiate returned, "you have the most mistaken idea in the world about skill with the sword, if you think it useless."

"It's no mere idea on my part, but an established truth," Corchuelo replied. "And if you want me to prove it to you by experiment, you have swords there, and this is a good opportunity. I have a steady hand and a strong arm, and these joined with my resolution, which is not small, will make you admit I am not mistaken. Get down and put your positions and circles and angles and science to work, for I hope to make you see stars at noonday with my rough, raw swordsmanship — in which, next to God, I trust that the man is yet to be born who'll make me turn my back, and that there is no one in the world I won't force to give ground."

"As to whether you turn your back or not, I don't concern myself," the master of fencing replied; "though it might well be that your grave would be dug on the spot where you planted your foot the first time. I mean that you'd be stretched dead there for despising skill with the sword."
"We shall soon see," Corchuelo replied, and getting briskly off his ass he drew out furiously one of the swords the licentiate carried on his beast.

"It mustn't be that way," Don Quixote put in. "I'll be the director of this fencing match, and judge of this often-disputed question." Dismounting from Rocinante and grasping his lance, he planted himself in the middle of the road, just as the licentiate, with an easy, graceful bearing and step, advanced toward Corchuelo, who came on against him darting fire from his eyes, as the saying goes. The other two of the party, the peasants, without dismounting from their asses, served as spectators of the mortal tragedy. The cuts, thrusts, downstrokes, backstrokes, and doubles Corchuelo delivered were past counting, and came faster than hops or hail. He attacked like an angry lion, but was met by a tap on the mouth from the button of the licentiate's sword that checked him in the middle of his furious onset, and made him kiss it as if it were a relic, though not as devoutly as relics are and ought to be kissed. The end of it was that the licentiate counted off for him by thrusts every button on the short cassock he wore, tore the skirts into strips, like the tails of a cuttlefish, knocked off his hat twice, and so completely tired him out that, in vexation, anger, and rage, he took the sword by the hilt and flung it away with such force that one of the peasants there — a notary, who went to retrieve it — afterwards made an affidavit that he had sent it nearly three-quarters of a league; which testimony has served, and serves, to show and establish with full certainty that strength is overcome by skill.

Corchuelo sat down exhausted, and Sancho, approaching, said, "By my faith, señor bachelor, if your worship takes my advice, you'll never challenge anyone to fence again — only to wrestle and throw the bar, for you have the youth and strength for that. But as for these fencers, as they call them, I've heard say they can put the point of a sword through the eye of a needle."

"I'm satisfied with having tumbled off my donkey," said Corchuelo, "and with having had the truth I was so ignorant of proved to me by experience." Getting up, he embraced the licentiate, and they were better friends than ever; and not caring to wait for the notary who had gone for the sword, since they saw he'd be a long time about it, they resolved to push on so as to reach Quiteria's village, where they all belonged, in good time.

During the rest of the journey the licentiate held forth on the excellences of the sword, with such conclusive arguments and such figures and mathematical proofs that all were convinced of the value of the science, and Corchuelo cured of his dogmatism.

It grew dark; but before they reached the town it seemed to all of them as if there was a heaven full of countless glittering stars in front of it. They heard, too, the pleasant mingled notes of a variety of instruments — flutes, drums, psalteries, pipes, tabors, and timbrels — and as they drew near they could see that the trees of a leafy arcade built at the entrance of the town were filled with lights unaffected by the wind, the breeze at the time being so gentle that it had no power to stir the leaves. The musicians were the life of the wedding, wandering through the pleasant grounds in separate bands, some dancing, some singing, others playing the various instruments already mentioned. In short, it seemed as though mirth and merriment were frisking and gambolling all over the meadow. Several other people were busy erecting raised benches from which guests might conveniently watch the plays and dances that were to be performed the next day on the spot dedicated to the celebration of the marriage of Camacho the rich and the obsequies of Basilio. Don Quixote would not enter the village, although both the peasant and the bachelor pressed him; he excused himself, in his own opinion amply, on the grounds that it was the custom of knight-errants to sleep in the fields and woods in preference to towns, even were it under gilded ceilings. So he turned aside a little out of the road, very much against Sancho's will, as the good quarters he had enjoyed in the castle or house of Don Diego came back to his mind.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 20
paragraphs: Giving an account of the wedding of Camacho the rich, together with the incident of Basilio the poor

Scarcely had fair Aurora given bright Phœbus time to dry the liquid pearls upon her golden locks with the heat of his fervent rays, when Don Quixote, shaking sloth from his limbs, sprang to his feet and called to his squire Sancho, who was still snoring. Seeing this, Don Quixote, before rousing him, addressed him thus: "Happy you, above all the dwellers on the face of the earth, who, without envying or being envied, sleep with a tranquil mind, and whom neither enchanters persecute nor enchantments frighten. Sleep, I say, and will say a hundred times, with no jealous thoughts of your mistress to make you keep ceaseless vigils, and no cares about how to pay the debts you owe or find tomorrow's food for yourself and your needy little family to interfere with your rest. Ambition does not break your rest, nor does this world's empty pomp disturb you; the utmost reach of your anxiety is to provide for your ass, since upon my shoulders you have laid the support of yourself, the counterweight and burden that nature and custom have imposed on masters. The servant sleeps, and the master lies awake thinking how to feed him, advance him, and reward him. The distress of seeing the sky turn brazen and withhold its needful moisture from the earth is felt not by the servant but by the master, who in times of scarcity and famine must support the one who served him in times of plenty and abundance."

To all this Sancho made no reply, because he was asleep; nor would he have wakened up so soon as he did, had not Don Quixote brought him round with the butt of his lance. He woke at last, drowsy and lazy, and casting his eyes about in every direction, observed, "From the direction of that arcade comes, if I'm not mistaken, a steam and a smell a great deal more like fried rashers than galingale or thyme. A wedding that begins with smells like that, by my faith, ought to be plentiful and unstinting."
"Enough, glutton," said Don Quixote. "Come, let us go and witness this wedding, and see what the rejected Basilio does."

"Let him do what he likes," Sancho returned. "If he weren't poor, he would marry Quiteria. To make a grand match for himself, and he without a farthing — is there nothing else? By my faith, señor, it's my view that the poor man should be content with what he can get, and not go looking for dainties at the bottom of the sea. I'll bet my arm that Camacho could bury Basilio in reales; and if that's so, as no doubt it is, what a fool Quiteria would be to refuse the fine dresses and jewels Camacho must have given her and will give her, and take instead Basilio's bar-throwing and swordplay. They won't give a pint of wine at the tavern for a good cast of the bar or a neat thrust of the sword. Talents and accomplishments that can't be turned into money — let Count Dirlos have them. But when such gifts fall on someone with hard cash, I only wish my own station in life were as becoming as those gifts. On a good foundation you can raise a good building, and the best foundation in the world is money."

"For God's sake, Sancho," said Don Quixote here, "stop that harangue. I believe that if you were allowed to go on with everything you start every other minute, you'd have no time left for eating or sleeping; you'd spend it all in talking."

"If your worship had a good memory," Sancho replied, "you'd remember the articles of our agreement before we set out from home this last time. One of them was that I was to be allowed to say all I liked, so long as it was not against my neighbour or your worship's authority; and so far, it seems to me, I have not broken that article."

"I remember no such article, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "and even if it were so, I want you to hold your tongue and come along, for the instruments we heard last night are already starting to enliven the valleys again, and no doubt the marriage will take place in the cool of the morning, and not in the heat of the afternoon."

Sancho did as his master told him, and putting the saddle on Rocinante and the pack-saddle on Dapple, they both mounted and at a leisurely pace entered the arcade. The first thing that met Sancho's eyes was a whole ox spitted on a whole elm tree, and in the fire over which it was to be roasted was burning a middling-sized mountain of faggots. Six stewpots that stood around the blaze had not been made in the ordinary mould of common pots: they were six half wine-jars, each fit to hold the contents of a slaughter-house — they swallowed whole sheep and hid them away inside without showing any more sign of them than if they were pigeons. Countless hares lay ready skinned, and plucked fowls hung from the trees ready for burial in the pots; numberless wildfowl and game of various sorts were suspended from the branches so the air might keep them cool. Sancho counted more than sixty wineskins of over six gallons each, all filled, as proved afterwards, with generous wines. There were also piles of the whitest bread, like the heaps of grain one sees on threshing-floors. There was a wall made of cheeses arranged like open brickwork, and two cauldrons full of oil, bigger than those of a dyer's shop, served for cooking fritters, which when fried were taken out with two mighty shovels and plunged into another cauldron of prepared honey standing close by. Of cooks and cook-maids there were more than fifty, all clean, brisk, and cheerful. In the capacious belly of the ox were a dozen soft little sucking-pigs, which, sewn up there, served to give it tenderness and flavour. The spices of various kinds did not seem to have been bought by the pound but by the quarter, and all lay open to view in a great chest. In short, all the preparations for the wedding were in rustic style, but plentiful enough to feed an army.

Sancho observed all, contemplated all, and everything won his heart. The first to captivate and take his fancy were the pots, out of which he would have very gladly helped himself to a moderate pipkinful; then the wineskins secured his affections; and lastly, the produce of the frying-pans — if indeed such imposing cauldrons can be called frying-pans. Unable to control himself or bear it any longer, he approached one of the busy cooks and civilly but hungrily begged permission to soak a scrap of bread in one of the pots. The cook answered, "Brother, this is not a day on which hunger is to have any sway, thanks to the rich Camacho. Get down and look about for a ladle and skim off a hen or two, and much good may they do you."
"I don't see one," said Sancho.

"Wait a moment," said the cook; "sinner that I am, how particular and shy you are!" So saying, he seized a bucket and plunging it into one of the half-jars took up three hens and a couple of geese, and said to Sancho, "Fall to, friend, and take the edge off your appetite with these skimmings until dinnertime comes."
"I have nothing to put them in," said Sancho.
"Well then," said the cook, "take spoon and all — for Camacho's wealth and happiness furnish everything."

While Sancho was thus occupied, Don Quixote was watching the entrance, at one end of the arcade, of some twelve peasants, all in holiday and gala dress, mounted on twelve beautiful mares with rich, handsome field trappings and a number of little bells attached to their petrals. Marshalled in regular order, they ran not one but several courses over the meadow, with jubilant shouts and cries of "Long live Camacho and Quiteria! He as rich as she is fair, and she the fairest on earth!"
Hearing this, Don Quixote said to himself, "It's easy to see these folk have never seen my Dulcinea del Toboso; for if they had, they'd be more moderate in their praises of this Quiteria of theirs."

Shortly after this, several bands of dancers of various sorts began to enter the arcade at different points, and among them one of sword-dancers, composed of some twenty-four lads of gallant and high-spirited bearing, dressed in the finest and whitest of linen, and with handkerchiefs embroidered in various colours with fine silk. One of those on the mares asked an active youth who led them whether any of the dancers had been wounded. "As yet, thank God, no one has been wounded," he said; "we are all safe and sound." And he at once began to execute complicated figures with the rest of his comrades, with so many turns and so great dexterity that, although Don Quixote was well used to seeing dances of the same kind, he thought he had never seen any so good as this. He also admired another that came in, made up of fair young maidens, none of whom seemed to be under fourteen or over eighteen, all dressed in green stuff, with their hair partly braided, partly flowing loose, but all of such bright gold as to vie with the sunbeams; and over their hair they wore garlands of jasmine, roses, amaranth, and honeysuckle. At their head were a venerable old man and an ancient dame, more brisk and active, however, than might have been expected from their years. The notes of a Zamora bagpipe accompanied them, and with modesty in their faces and in their eyes, and lightness in their feet, they looked the best dancers in the world.

Following these came an artistic dance of the sort they call "speaking dances." It was composed of eight nymphs in two files, with the god Cupid leading one and Interest the other — the former furnished with wings, bow, quiver, and arrows, the latter in a rich dress of gold and silk of various colours. The nymphs who followed Love bore their names written on white parchment in large letters on their backs. "Poetry" was the name of the first, "Wit" of the second, "Birth" of the third, and "Valour" of the fourth. Those who followed Interest were distinguished in the same way: the badge of the first announced "Liberality," that of the second "Largess," the third "Treasure," the fourth "Peaceful Possession." In front of them all came a wooden castle drawn by four wild men, all clad in ivy and hemp dyed green, and looking so lifelike that they nearly terrified Sancho. On the front of the castle and on each of the four sides of its frame it bore the inscription "Castle of Caution." Four skilful tabor and flute players accompanied them, and the dance having been opened, Cupid, after executing two figures, raised his eyes and bent his bow against a damsel who stood between the turrets of the castle, and addressed her thus:

I am the mighty God whose sway / Is potent over land and sea. / The heavens above us own me; nay, / The shades below acknowledge me. / I know not fear, I have my will, / Whate'er my whim or fancy be; / For me there's no impossible, / I order, bind, forbid, set free.

Having concluded the stanza he discharged an arrow at the top of the castle, and went back to his place. Interest then came forward and went through two more figures; and as soon as the tabors ceased, he said:

But mightier than Love am I, / Though Love it be that leads me on, / Than mine no lineage is more high, / Or older, underneath the sun. / To use me rightly few know how, / To act without me fewer still, / For I am Interest, and I vow / For evermore to do thy will.
Interest retired, and Poetry came forward; and when she had gone through her figures like the others, fixing her eyes on the damsel of the castle, she said:

With many a fanciful conceit, / Fair Lady, winsome Poesy / Her soul, an offering at thy feet, / Presents in sonnets unto thee. / If thou my homage wilt not scorn, / Thy fortune, watched by envious eyes, / On wings of poesy upborne / Shall be exalted to the skies.
Poetry withdrew, and on the side of Interest, Liberality advanced; and after going through her figures she said:

To give, while shunning each extreme, / The sparing hand, the over-free, / Therein consists, so wise men deem, / The virtue Liberality. / But thee, fair lady, to enrich, / Myself a prodigal I'll prove, / A vice not wholly shameful, which / May find its fair excuse in love.

In the same manner all the characters of the two bands advanced and retired, and each executed its figures and delivered its verses, some of them graceful, some burlesque; but Don Quixote's memory (although he had an excellent one) only carried away those just quoted. Then all mingled together, forming chains and breaking off again with graceful, unconstrained gaiety; and whenever Love passed in front of the castle he shot his arrows up at it, while Interest broke gilded pellets against it. At length, after they had danced a good while, Interest drew out a great purse, made of the skin of a large brindled cat and to all appearance full of money, and flung it at the castle; and with the force of the blow the boards fell asunder and tumbled down, leaving the damsel exposed and unprotected. Interest and the characters of his band advanced, and throwing a great chain of gold over her neck, pretended to lead her away captive. On seeing this, Love and his supporters made as though they would release her, the whole action being to the accompaniment of the tabors and in the form of a regular dance. The wild men made peace between them, and with great dexterity readjusted and fixed the boards of the castle, and the damsel once more ensconced herself within; and with this the dance wound up, to the great enjoyment of the spectators.

Don Quixote asked one of the nymphs who it was that had composed and arranged it. She replied that it was a beneficiary of the town who had a nice taste in devising things of the sort. "I would lay a wager," said Don Quixote, "that this same bachelor or beneficiary is a greater friend of Camacho's than of Basilio's, and that he is better at satire than at vespers; he has worked the accomplishments of Basilio and the riches of Camacho very neatly into the dance." Sancho Panza, who was listening to all this, exclaimed, "The king is my cock — I stick to Camacho." "It's easy to see you're a peasant, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and one of the sort that cry 'Long life to the conqueror.'"

"I don't know what sort I am," Sancho returned, "but I know very well that I'll never get such elegant skimmings off Basilio's pots as these I've got off Camacho's." And he showed him the bucketful of geese and hens, and seizing one began to eat with great gusto and appetite, saying, "A fig for the accomplishments of Basilio! As much as you have, so much are you worth; and as much as you are worth, so much do you have. As a grandmother of mine used to say, there are only two families in the world, the Haves and the Have-nots; and she stuck to the Haves. And to this day, Señor Don Quixote, people would sooner feel the pulse of 'Have' than of 'Know'; an ass covered with gold looks better than a horse with a pack-saddle. So once more I say I stick to Camacho — whose bountiful pot-skimmings are geese and hens, hares and rabbits — and not to Basilio's, whose, if any ever come to hand, or even to foot, will only be rinsings."

"Have you finished your harangue, Sancho?" said Don Quixote. "Of course I have finished it," Sancho replied, "because I see your worship takes offence at it; but if it weren't for that, there was work enough cut out for three days."
"God grant I may see you dumb before I die, Sancho," said Don Quixote.

"At the rate we are going," said Sancho, "I'll be chewing clay before your worship dies; and then, maybe, I'll be so dumb that I won't say a word until the end of the world, or at least till the day of judgment."

"Even if that happens, O Sancho," said Don Quixote, "your silence will never make up for all you have talked, are talking, and will talk all your life. Besides, it stands to reason that my death will come before yours; so I never expect to see you dumb, not even when you are drinking or sleeping, and that is the utmost I can say."

"In good faith, señor," Sancho replied, "there's no trusting that fleshless one — I mean Death — who devours the lamb as soon as the sheep, and, as I've heard our curate say, treads with equal foot upon the lofty towers of kings and the lowly huts of the poor. That lady is more mighty than dainty; she's in no way squeamish, she devours everything and is ready for everything, and fills her alforjas with people of all sorts, ages, and ranks. She's no reaper that sleeps out the noontide; at all hours she is reaping and cutting down the dry grass as well as the green. She never seems to chew, but bolts and swallows everything put before her, for she has a canine appetite that is never satisfied. And though she has no belly, she shows she has a dropsy and is thirsty to drink the lives of all who live, as one would drink a jug of cold water."

"Say no more, Sancho," said Don Quixote here; "don't try to better it, and risk a fall. In truth, what you have said about death in your rustic phrase is what a good preacher might have said. I tell you, Sancho, if you had discretion to match your native wit, you might take a pulpit in hand, and go about the world preaching fine sermons." "He preaches well who lives well," said Sancho, "and I know no more theology than that."
"Nor need you," said Don Quixote, "but I cannot conceive or make out how it is that, the fear of God being the beginning of wisdom, you, who are more afraid of a lizard than of Him, know so much."

"Pass judgment on your chivalries, señor," Sancho returned, "and don't set yourself up to judge of other men's fears or braveries, for I am as good a fearer of God as my neighbours. But leave me to finish off these skimmings, for all the rest is only idle talk that we'll be called to account for in the other world." And so saying, he began a fresh attack on the bucket with such hearty appetite that he aroused Don Quixote's, who no doubt would have helped him had he not been prevented by what must be told further on.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 21
paragraphs: In which Camacho's wedding is continued, with other delightful incidents

While Don Quixote and Sancho were engaged in the discussion set out in the last chapter, they heard loud shouts and a great noise. These were made by the men on the mares as they went at full gallop, shouting, to receive the bride and bridegroom, who were approaching with musical instruments and pageantry of all sorts around them, accompanied by the priest and the relatives of both, and all the most distinguished people of the surrounding villages. When Sancho saw the bride, he exclaimed, "By my faith, she's not dressed like a country girl, but like some fine court lady. By God, as well as I can make out, the patena she wears is rich coral, and her green Cuenca stuff is thirty-pile velvet; and then the white linen trimming — by my oath, it's satin! Look at her hands — jet rings on them! May I never have luck if they aren't gold rings, and real gold, set with pearls as white as curdled milk, and every one of them worth an eye out of your head! Whoreson baggage, what hair she has! If it's not a wig, I never saw longer or fairer all the days of my life. See how bravely she carries herself — and her shape! Wouldn't you say she was like a walking palm tree loaded with clusters of dates? — for the trinkets she has hanging from her hair and neck look just like them. I swear in my heart she's a brave lass, fit 'to pass over the banks of Flanders.'"

Don Quixote laughed at Sancho's boorish eulogies and thought that, except for his lady Dulcinea del Toboso, he had never seen a more beautiful woman. The fair Quiteria looked somewhat pale, no doubt because of the bad night brides always pass dressing themselves up for the morrow's wedding. They advanced toward a stage that stood on one side of the meadow, decked with carpets and boughs, where they were to plight their troth and from which they were to watch the dances and plays. But at the moment of their arrival they heard a loud outcry behind them, and a voice exclaiming, "Wait a little, you who are as inconsiderate as you are hasty!" At these words everyone turned around, and saw that the speaker was a man dressed in what looked like a loose black coat trimmed with crimson patches like flames. He was crowned (as was presently seen) with a crown of gloomy cypress, and in his hand he held a long staff. As he approached he was recognised by everyone as the dashing Basilio, and all waited anxiously to see what would come of his words, dreading some disaster as a result of his appearance at such a moment. He came up at last, weary and breathless, and planting himself in front of the bridal pair, drove his staff, which had a steel spike at the end, into the ground; and with a pale face and his eyes fixed on Quiteria, he addressed her thus in a hoarse, trembling voice:

"You know well, ungrateful Quiteria, that according to the holy law we acknowledge, as long as I live you can take no husband. Nor are you ignorant either that, hoping that time and my own efforts would improve my fortune, I have never failed to observe the respect due to your honour. But you, throwing aside all you owe to my true love, would surrender what is mine to another whose wealth brings him not only good fortune but supreme happiness. And now to complete it (not that I think he deserves it, but inasmuch as heaven is pleased to bestow it on him), I will, with my own hands, do away with the obstacle that may interfere with it, and remove myself from between you. Long live the rich Camacho! Many a happy year may he live with the ungrateful Quiteria! And let the poor Basilio die — Basilio whose poverty clipped the wings of his happiness and brought him to the grave!"

So saying, he seized the staff he had driven into the ground, and leaving half of it fixed there, showed it to be a sheath that concealed a fairly long rapier. And, with what may be called its hilt planted in the ground, he swiftly, coolly, and deliberately threw himself upon it. In an instant the bloody point and half the steel blade appeared at his back, the unhappy man falling to the earth bathed in his blood, and transfixed by his own weapon.

His friends at once ran to his aid, filled with grief at his misery and sad fate, and Don Quixote, dismounting from Rocinante, hurried to support him, taking him in his arms, and found he had not yet stopped breathing. They were about to draw out the rapier, but the priest who stood by objected to its being withdrawn before Basilio had confessed, as the instant of its withdrawal would be that of his death. Basilio, however, reviving slightly, said in a weak voice, as if in pain, "If you would consent, cruel Quiteria, to give me your hand as my bride in this last fatal moment, I might still hope that my rashness would find pardon, in that by it I attained the bliss of being yours."

Hearing this, the priest told him to think of the welfare of his soul rather than the cravings of the body, and earnestly to implore God's pardon for his sins and for his rash act. To which Basilio replied that he was determined not to confess unless Quiteria first gave him her hand in marriage, because that happiness would compose his mind and give him courage to make his confession.

Don Quixote, hearing the wounded man's plea, exclaimed aloud that what Basilio asked was just and reasonable, and moreover a request easily complied with; and that it would be as much to Señor Camacho's honour to receive the lady Quiteria as the widow of the brave Basilio as if he received her direct from her father.
"In this case," he said, "it will only be to say 'yes,' and no consequences can follow the utterance of the word, since the nuptial bed of this marriage must be the grave."

Camacho was listening to all this, perplexed and bewildered, not knowing what to say or do. But so urgent were the entreaties of Basilio's friends, imploring him to allow Quiteria to give Basilio her hand so that his soul, quitting this life in despair, should not be lost, that they moved — indeed, forced — him to say that if Quiteria were willing to give it, he was satisfied, as it was only putting off the fulfilment of his wishes for a moment. At once everyone fell on Quiteria and pressed her — some with prayers, others with tears, others with persuasive arguments — to give her hand to poor Basilio. But she, harder than marble and more unmoved than any statue, seemed unable or unwilling to utter a word; nor would she have given any reply had the priest not told her to decide quickly what she meant to do, as Basilio now had his soul at his teeth, and there was no time for hesitation.

On this the fair Quiteria, to all appearance distressed, grieved, and repentant, advanced without a word to where Basilio lay, his eyes already turned in his head, his breathing short and painful, murmuring Quiteria's name between his teeth, and apparently about to die like a heathen and not like a Christian. Quiteria approached him, and kneeling, demanded his hand by signs without speaking. Basilio opened his eyes, and gazing fixedly at her, said, "O Quiteria, why have you turned compassionate at a moment when your compassion will serve as a dagger to rob me of life? For I have no strength left now either to bear the happiness you give me in accepting me as yours, or to suppress the pain that is rapidly drawing the dread shadow of death over my eyes. What I beg of you, fatal star to me, is that the hand you demand of me and would give me be not given out of complaisance, nor to deceive me afresh, but that you confess and declare that without any constraint upon your will you give it to me as to your lawful husband; for it is not right that you should trifle with me at such a moment as this, or have recourse to falsehoods with one who has dealt so truly by you."

While he was uttering these words he showed such weakness that the bystanders expected each return of faintness to take his life with it. Then Quiteria, overcome with modesty and shame, holding the hand of Basilio in her right hand, said, "No force would bend my will; as freely, therefore, as it is possible for me to do so, I give you the hand of a lawful wife, and take yours if you give it to me of your own free will, untroubled and unaffected by the calamity your hasty act has brought upon you."
"Yes, I give it," said Basilio, "not agitated or distracted, but with the unclouded reason heaven is pleased to grant me — thus do I give myself to be your husband."
"And I give myself to be your wife," said Quiteria, "whether you live many years, or they carry you from my arms to the grave."

"For one so badly wounded," Sancho remarked at this point, "this young man has a great deal to say. They should make him leave off billing and cooing, and attend to his soul; for to my thinking he has it more on his tongue than at his teeth."

Basilio and Quiteria having joined hands, the priest, deeply moved and with tears in his eyes, pronounced the blessing on them, and implored heaven to grant an easy passage to the soul of the newly wedded man. Who, the instant he received the blessing, started nimbly to his feet and with unparalleled effrontery pulled out the rapier that had been sheathed in his body. All the bystanders were astounded, and some, more simple than inquiring, began shouting, "A miracle, a miracle!" But Basilio replied, "No miracle, no miracle — only a trick, a trick!" The priest, perplexed and amazed, made haste to examine the wound with both hands, and found that the blade had passed not through Basilio's flesh and ribs, but through a hollow iron tube full of blood, which he had adroitly fixed at the spot — the blood, as was afterwards established, having been so prepared as not to congeal. In short, the priest and Camacho and most of those present saw they had been tricked and made fools of. The bride showed no sign of displeasure at the deception; on the contrary, hearing them say that the marriage, being fraudulent, would not be valid, she said that she confirmed it afresh, from which they all concluded that the whole thing had been planned by agreement and understanding between the pair. Camacho and his supporters were so mortified at this that they proceeded to revenge themselves by violence, and a great number of them drew their swords and attacked Basilio, in whose defence as many more swords were instantly unsheathed; and Don Quixote, taking the lead on horseback, with his lance over his arm and well covered with his shield, made everyone give way before him. Sancho, who never found any pleasure or enjoyment in such doings, retreated to the wine-jars from which he had taken his delectable skimmings, considering that, as a holy place, that spot would be respected.

"Hold, sirs, hold!" cried Don Quixote in a loud voice. "We have no right to take vengeance for wrongs that love may do us. Remember, love and war are the same thing, and as in war it is allowable and common to use wiles and stratagems to overcome the enemy, so in the contests and rivalries of love the tricks and devices employed to attain the desired end are justifiable, provided they are not to the discredit or dishonour of the loved object. Quiteria belonged to Basilio and Basilio to Quiteria by the just and beneficent disposal of heaven. Camacho is rich, and can purchase his pleasure when, where, and as it pleases him. Basilio has but this ewe-lamb, and no one, however powerful, shall take her from him. These two whom God has joined, man cannot separate; and he who attempts it must first pass the point of this lance." So saying, he brandished it so stoutly and dexterously that he overawed all who did not know him.

But so deep an impression had Quiteria's rejection made on Camacho's mind that it drove her at once from his thoughts; and so the counsels of the priest, who was a wise and kindly disposed man, prevailed with him, and by his means he and his partisans were pacified and calmed; and to prove it they put up their swords again, inveighing more against Quiteria's pliancy than against Basilio's craftiness. Camacho maintained that, if Quiteria as a maiden had had such a love for Basilio, she would have loved him too as a married woman, and that he ought to thank heaven more for having taken her than for having given her.

Camacho and those of his following being thus consoled and pacified, those on Basilio's side were appeased. And the rich Camacho, to show he felt no resentment for the trick and didn't care about it, desired the festival to go on as if he were married in fact. Neither Basilio, however, nor his bride, nor their followers would take any part in it, and they withdrew to Basilio's village; for the poor, if they are persons of virtue and good sense, have those who follow, honour, and uphold them, just as the rich have those who flatter and dance attendance on them. With them they took Don Quixote, regarding him as a man of worth and a stout one. Sancho alone had a cloud on his soul, for he found himself debarred from waiting for Camacho's splendid feast and festival, which lasted until night; and thus dragged away, he moodily followed his master, who accompanied Basilio's party, and left behind him the flesh-pots of Egypt — though in his heart he took them with him, and their now nearly finished skimmings that he carried in the bucket conjured up before his eyes visions of the glory and abundance of the good cheer he was losing. And so, vexed and dejected though not hungry, without dismounting from Dapple, he followed in Rocinante's footsteps.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 22
paragraphs: Which tells of the grand adventure of the cave of Montesinos in the heart of La Mancha, which the valiant Don Quixote brought to a happy conclusion

Many and great were the attentions shown to Don Quixote by the newly married couple, who felt under obligation to him for coming forward in defence of their cause; and they raised his wisdom to the same level as his courage, rating him a Cid in arms and a Cicero in eloquence. Worthy Sancho enjoyed himself for three days at the expense of the pair, from whom they learned that the sham wound was not a scheme arranged with the fair Quiteria, but a device of Basilio's, who had counted on exactly the outcome they had seen. He admitted, it is true, that he had confided his idea to some of his friends, so that at the proper time they might aid him in his purpose and ensure the success of the deception.

"That," said Don Quixote, "is not, and ought not to be called, deception, which aims at virtuous ends." And the marriage of lovers he maintained to be a most excellent end, reminding them, however, that love has no greater enemy than hunger and constant want. For love is all gaiety, enjoyment, and happiness, especially when the lover is in possession of the object of his love, and poverty and want are the declared enemies of all these — which he said in order to urge Señor Basilio to abandon the practice of those accomplishments he was skilled in, since though they brought him fame, they brought him no money, and to apply himself instead to the acquisition of wealth by legitimate industry, which will never fail those who are prudent and persevering. The poor man who is a man of honour (if indeed a poor man can be a man of honour) has a jewel when he has a fair wife, and if she is taken from him, his honour is taken from him and slain. The fair woman who is a woman of honour, and whose husband is poor, deserves to be crowned with the laurels and crowns of victory and triumph. Beauty by itself attracts the desires of all who behold it, and the royal eagles and birds of towering flight stoop on it as on a dainty lure; but if beauty be accompanied by want and penury, then the ravens and the kites and other birds of prey assail it, and she who stands firm against such attacks well deserves to be called the crown of her husband. "Remember, prudent Basilio," Don Quixote added, "it was the opinion of a certain sage — I know not whom — that there was not more than one good woman in the whole world; and his advice was that each man should think and believe that this one good woman was his own wife, and in this way he would live happy. I myself am not married, nor, so far, has it ever entered my thoughts to be so; nevertheless I would venture to give advice to anyone who might ask it, as to the manner in which he should seek a wife such as he would be content to marry. The first thing I would recommend would be to look to good name rather than to wealth, for a good woman does not win a good name merely by being good, but by letting it be seen that she is so; and open looseness and freedom do much more damage to a woman's honour than secret depravity. If you take a good woman into your house, it will be an easy matter to keep her good, and even to make her still better; but if you take a bad one, you will find it hard work to mend her, for it is no easy matter to pass from one extreme to another. I do not say it is impossible, but I look on it as difficult."

Sancho, listening to all this, said to himself, "This master of mine, when I say anything that has weight and substance, says I might take a pulpit in hand and go about the world preaching fine sermons. But of him I say that, when he begins stringing maxims together and giving advice, not only might he take one pulpit in hand, but two on each finger, and go into the market-places to his heart's content. Devil take you for a knight-errant, what a lot of things you know! I used to think in my heart that the only thing he knew was what belonged to his chivalry; but there is nothing he won't have a finger in."
Sancho muttered this somewhat aloud, and his master overheard him and asked, "What are you muttering there, Sancho?"

"I'm not saying anything or muttering anything," said Sancho. "I was only saying to myself that I wish I'd heard what your worship just said before I married; perhaps I'd say now, 'The ox that's loose licks himself well.'"
"Is your Teresa so bad then, Sancho?"
"She's not very bad," Sancho replied, "but she's not very good either; at least she's not as good as I could wish."

"You do wrong, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "to speak ill of your wife, for after all she is the mother of your children." "We are quits," Sancho returned; "for she speaks ill of me whenever she takes it into her head, especially when she's jealous — and Satan himself could not put up with her then."

In short, they remained three days with the newly married couple, by whom they were entertained and treated like kings. Don Quixote begged the fencing licentiate to find him a guide to show him the way to the cave of Montesinos, as he had a great desire to enter it and see with his own eyes whether the wonderful tales told of it all over the country were true. The licentiate said he would get him a cousin of his own, a famous scholar, and very much given to reading books of chivalry, who would have great pleasure in leading him to the mouth of the very cave, and would show him the lakes of Ruidera, which were likewise famous all over La Mancha, and even all over Spain. And he assured him he would find him entertaining, for he was a young man who could write books good enough to be printed and dedicated to princes. The cousin arrived at last, leading an ass in foal, with a pack-saddle covered with a parti-coloured carpet or sackcloth. Sancho saddled Rocinante, got Dapple ready, and stocked his alforjas — along with which went those of the cousin, likewise well filled — and so, commending themselves to God and bidding farewell to all, they set out, taking the road for the famous cave of Montesinos.

On the way, Don Quixote asked the cousin what sort and character his pursuits, avocations, and studies were. The cousin replied that he was by profession a humanist, and his pursuits and studies were making books for the press, all of great utility and no less entertainment to the nation. One was called "The Book of Liveries," in which he described seven hundred and three liveries, with their colours, mottoes, and ciphers, from which gentlemen of the court might pick and choose any they fancied for festivals and revels, without having to go begging for them from anyone, or, as the saying is, racking their brains to make them suitable to their objects and purposes. "For," he said, "I give the jealous, the rejected, the forgotten, the absent, what will suit and fit them without fail. I have another book, too, which I shall call 'Metamorphoses, or the Spanish Ovid,' one of rare and original invention; for, imitating Ovid in burlesque style, I show in it who the Giralda of Seville and the Angel of the Magdalena were, what the sewer of Vecinguerra at Cordova was, what the bulls of Guisando, the Sierra Morena, the Leganitos and Lavapies fountains at Madrid, were — not forgetting those of the Piojo, of the Caño Dorado, and of the Priora; and all with their allegories, metaphors, and changes, so that they are amusing, interesting, and instructive all at once. Another book I have, which I call 'The Supplement to Polydore Vergil,' which treats of the invention of things, and is a work of great erudition and research; for I establish and elucidate elegantly some matters of great importance that Polydore failed to mention. He forgot to tell us who was the first man in the world to have a cold in the head, and who was the first to try salivation for the French disease; but I give it accurately set forth, and quote more than twenty-five authors in proof of it — so you may see I have laboured to good purpose, and that the book will be of service to the whole world."

Sancho, who had been very attentive to the cousin's words, said to him, "Tell me, señor — and may God give you luck in printing your books — can you tell me (for of course you know, since you know everything) who was the first man that scratched his head? For to my thinking it must have been our father Adam."
"So it must," the cousin replied; "for there's no doubt Adam had a head and hair, and being the first man in the world, he would have scratched himself sometimes."
"So I think," said Sancho; "but now tell me, who was the first tumbler in the world?"

"Really, brother," the cousin answered, "I couldn't say for certain at this moment without having investigated it. I'll look it up when I get back to where my books are, and satisfy you the next time we meet, for this won't be the last."

"Look here, señor," said Sancho, "don't trouble yourself about it, for I have just this minute hit upon what I asked you. The first tumbler in the world, you must know, was Lucifer, when they cast or pitched him out of heaven — for he came tumbling down into the bottomless pit."
"You are right, friend," said the cousin; and Don Quixote said, "Sancho, that question and answer are not your own; you have heard them from someone else."

"Hold your peace, señor," said Sancho. "Faith, if I take to asking questions and answering, I'll go on from this till tomorrow morning. To ask foolish things and answer nonsense I don't need to go looking for help from my neighbours."

"You have said more than you are aware of, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "For there are some who wear themselves out learning and proving things that, once known and proved, aren't worth a farthing to the understanding or the memory."

In this and other pleasant conversation the day went by, and that night they put up at a small hamlet, from which it was, the cousin told Don Quixote, no more than two leagues to the cave of Montesinos, adding that if he was bent on entering it, he'd need to provide himself with ropes so he could be tied and lowered into its depths. Don Quixote said that even if it reached to the bottomless pit, he meant to see where it went; so they bought about a hundred fathoms of rope, and the next day at two in the afternoon they arrived at the cave, the mouth of which is spacious and wide, but full of thorn and wild-fig bushes and brambles and briars, so thick and matted that they completely close it up and cover it over.

On coming within sight of it, the cousin, Sancho, and Don Quixote dismounted, and the first two immediately tied the third very firmly with the ropes. As they were girding and swathing him, Sancho said, "Mind what you are about, master mine; don't go burying yourself alive, or putting yourself where you'll be like a bottle put to cool in a well. It's no affair or business of your worship's to become the explorer of this place, which must be worse than a Moorish dungeon."

"Tie me and hold your peace," said Don Quixote, "for an enterprise like this, friend Sancho, was reserved for me." And the guide said, "I beg you, Señor Don Quixote, to observe carefully and examine with a hundred eyes everything inside; there may be some things for me to put into my book of 'Transformations.'"
"The drum is in hands that will know how to beat it well enough," said Sancho Panza.

When this was said and the tying finished (which was not over the armour but only over the doublet), Don Quixote observed, "It was careless of us not to have provided ourselves with a small cattle-bell to be tied to the rope close to me, the sound of which would show that I was still descending and alive. But since that's out of the question now, in God's hand be it to guide me." He then fell on his knees and in a low voice offered up a prayer to heaven, imploring God to aid him and grant him success in this apparently perilous and untried adventure; and then exclaimed aloud, "O mistress of my actions and movements, illustrious and peerless Dulcinea del Toboso, if so be the prayers and supplications of this fortunate lover can reach your ears, by your incomparable beauty I beg you to listen to them, for they ask nothing but that you do not refuse me your favour and protection now that I stand in such need of them. I am about to precipitate, to sink, to plunge myself into the abyss here before me, only to let the world know that while you favour me, there is no impossibility I will not attempt and accomplish." With these words he approached the cavern, and saw that it was impossible to lower himself in or gain entrance except by sheer force, or by hewing a passage; so, drawing his sword, he began to demolish and cut away the brambles at the mouth of the cave. At the noise, a vast multitude of crows and choughs flew out of it so thick and so fast that they knocked Don Quixote down; and if he had been as much of a believer in augury as he was a Catholic Christian he would have taken it as a bad omen and declined to bury himself in such a place. He got up, however, and as no more crows came out, nor night-birds like the bats that had flown out at the same time as the crows, the cousin and Sancho giving him rope, he lowered himself into the depths of the dread cavern. As he entered it, Sancho sent his blessing after him, making a thousand crosses over him and saying, "God, and the Peña de Francia, and the Trinity of Gaeta guide you, flower and cream of knight-errants. There you go, you dare-devil of the earth, heart of steel, arm of brass; once more, God guide you and send you back safe, sound, and unhurt to the light of this world you are leaving to bury yourself in the darkness you are seeking there." And the cousin offered up almost the same prayers and supplications.

Don Quixote kept calling to them to give him rope and more rope, and they gave it out little by little. By the time the calls, which came out of the cave as out of a pipe, ceased to be heard, they had let down the hundred fathoms of rope. They were inclined to pull Don Quixote up again, as they could give him no more rope; however, they waited about half an hour, at the end of which time they began to gather in the rope again with great ease and without feeling any weight, which made them think Don Quixote was remaining below; and persuaded that this was the case, Sancho wept bitterly and hauled away in great haste to settle the question. When, however, they had come to what seemed rather more than eighty fathoms, they felt a weight, at which they were greatly delighted; and at last, at ten fathoms more, they saw Don Quixote distinctly, and Sancho called out to him, saying, "Welcome back, señor, for we had begun to think you were going to stay down there to found a family." But Don Quixote answered not a word, and drawing him out entirely they saw he had his eyes shut and every appearance of being fast asleep.

They stretched him on the ground and untied him, but still he did not awake; however, they rolled him back and forwards and shook and pulled him about, so that after some time he came to himself, stretching himself just as if he were waking up from a deep, sound sleep, and looking about him said, "God forgive you, friends; you have taken me away from the sweetest and most delightful existence and spectacle any human being ever enjoyed or beheld. Now indeed do I know that all the pleasures of this life pass away like a shadow and a dream, or fade like the flower of the field. O ill-fated Montesinos! O sore-wounded Durandarte! O unhappy Belerma! O tearful Guadiana, and you, hapless daughters of Ruidera, who show in your waves the tears that flowed from your beautiful eyes!"

The cousin and Sancho Panza listened with deep attention to the words of Don Quixote, who uttered them as if with immense pain he were drawing them up from his very bowels. They begged him to explain himself, and tell them what he had seen in that hell down there.
"Hell do you call it?" said Don Quixote. "Call it by no such name, for it doesn't deserve it, as you shall soon see."

He then asked them to give him something to eat, as he was very hungry. They spread the cousin's sackcloth on the grass, brought out the stores of the alforjas, and all three sitting down lovingly and sociably, they made a luncheon and a supper of it all in one; and when the sackcloth was removed, Don Quixote of La Mancha said, "Let no one rise, and attend to me, my sons, both of you."

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 23
paragraphs: About the wonderful things the incomparable Don Quixote said he saw in the deep cave of Montesinos — the impossibility and magnitude of which cause this adventure to be deemed apocryphal

It was about four in the afternoon when the sun, veiled in clouds, with softened light and tempered beams, let Don Quixote tell his two distinguished listeners what he had seen in the cave of Montesinos without heat or discomfort. He began as follows:

"About twelve or fourteen times a man's height down inside that pit, on the right-hand side, there's a recess or open space large enough to hold a big cart with its mules. A little light reaches it through some chinks or crevices that open to the surface of the earth. I noticed this recess when I was already growing tired and disgusted at finding myself hanging suspended by the rope, travelling downward into that dark region with no certainty or knowledge of where I was going. So I decided to enter it and rest for a while. I called out, telling you not to let out more rope until I gave the signal, but you must not have heard me.
