I then gathered in the rope you were sending me, made a coil of it, and sat down on it, thinking and considering what I should do to lower myself to the bottom, since I had no one to hold me up. And while I was deep in that perplexity, suddenly and without warning a profound sleep fell upon me, and when I least expected it — I don't know how — I woke and found myself in the middle of the most beautiful and delightful meadow that nature could produce or the most vivid human imagination conceive. I opened my eyes, I rubbed them, and I realised I was not asleep but thoroughly awake. Even so, I felt my head and chest to be sure it was really me there and not some empty deceiving phantom; but touch, feeling, and the steady thoughts running through my mind all convinced me that I was the same man then and there that I am at this moment. Next there appeared before my sight a stately royal palace or castle, with walls that seemed built of clear transparent crystal; and through two great doors which opened wide in it, I saw a venerable old man coming out and advancing toward me, dressed in a long mulberry-coloured serge gown that trailed on the ground. On his shoulders and chest he wore a green satin collegiate hood, and on his head a black Milanese bonnet; his snow-white beard fell below his belt. He carried no weapon at all, only a rosary of beads bigger than fair-sized hazelnuts, every tenth bead like a moderate ostrich egg; his bearing, his gait, his dignity and imposing presence held me spellbound and wondering. He came up to me, and the first thing he did was embrace me closely, and then he said, 'For a long time now, O valiant knight Don Quixote of La Mancha, we who are held enchanted in these solitudes have been hoping to see you, so that you might make known to the world what is shut up and hidden in this deep cavern, called the cave of Montesinos, which you have entered — an achievement reserved for your invincible heart and stupendous courage alone to attempt. Come with me, illustrious sir, and I will show you the marvels hidden within this transparent castle, of which I am the alcaide and perpetual warden; for I am Montesinos himself, from whom the cave takes its name.'

"The moment he told me he was Montesinos, I asked him if the story they tell up in the world above was true — that he had taken out the heart of his great friend Durandarte from his breast with a little dagger, and carried it to the lady Belerma, as his friend had commanded him at the point of death. He answered that they were right in every respect except about the dagger, since it was not a dagger, nor a little one, but a burnished poniard sharper than an awl."
"That poniard must have been made by Ramon de Hoces of Seville," said Sancho.

"I don't know," said Don Quixote; "but it could not have been made by that poniard-maker, because Ramon de Hoces was a man of yesterday, and the affair at Roncesvalles, where this mishap happened, was long ago. The question is of no great importance, though, and it doesn't affect or alter the truth or substance of the story."
"That's true," said the cousin; "go on, Señor Don Quixote, for I am listening to you with the greatest pleasure in the world."

"And I tell the tale with no less pleasure," said Don Quixote. "So, to continue — the venerable Montesinos led me into the crystal palace, where, in a lower chamber, strangely cool and made entirely of alabaster, there was an elaborately wrought marble tomb. Stretched at full length upon it I saw a knight — not of bronze, marble, or jasper, as are seen on other tombs, but of actual flesh and bone. His right hand (which struck me as somewhat hairy and sinewy, a sign of great strength in its owner) lay on the side of his heart. Before I could put any question to Montesinos, he, seeing me gazing at the tomb in amazement, said to me, 'This is my friend Durandarte, flower and mirror of the true lovers and valiant knights of his day. He is held enchanted here, as I myself and many others are, by that French enchanter Merlin who, they say, was the devil's son; but my belief is, not that he was the devil's son, but that he knew, as the saying is, a point more than the devil. How or why he enchanted us, no one knows; but time will tell, and I suspect that time is not far off. What I marvel at is this: I know it as surely as I know it's now day that Durandarte ended his life in my arms, and that after his death I took out his heart with my own hands — and it must have weighed more than two pounds, for, according to the naturalists, the man who has a large heart is more largely endowed with valour than the man who has a small one. Then how, given all that, and given that the knight really did die, does he now moan and sigh from time to time, as if he were still alive?'
"As he said this, the wretched Durandarte cried out in a loud voice:

O cousin Montesinos! 'Twas my last request of thee, When my soul hath left the body, And that lying dead I be, With thy poniard or thy dagger Cut the heart from out my breast, And bear it to Belerma. This was my last request."

"On hearing this, the venerable Montesinos fell on his knees before the unhappy knight and, with tearful eyes, exclaimed, 'Long since, Señor Durandarte, my beloved cousin, long since have I done what you bade me on that sad day when I lost you; I took out your heart as best I could, leaving not an atom of it in your breast. I wiped it with a lace handkerchief and took the road to France with it, having first laid you in the bosom of the earth with tears enough to wash and cleanse my hands of the blood that covered them after going through your innards. And, what's more, O cousin of my soul, at the first village I came to after leaving Roncesvalles, I sprinkled a little salt on your heart to keep it sweet, and bring it, if not fresh, at least pickled, into the presence of the lady Belerma — whom, together with you, myself, your squire Guadiana, the duenna Ruidera and her seven daughters and two nieces, and many more of your friends and acquaintances, the sage Merlin has kept enchanted here these many years. And although more than five hundred have gone by, not one of us has died; only Ruidera and her daughters and nieces are missing, and these, because of the tears they shed, Merlin — out of the compassion he seems to have felt for them — changed into so many lakes, which to this day in the world of the living, and in the province of La Mancha, are called the Lakes of Ruidera. The seven daughters belong to the kings of Spain and the two nieces to the knights of a very holy order called the Order of St. John. Your squire Guadiana, likewise bewailing your fate, was changed into a river of his own name; but when he came to the surface and saw the sun of another heaven, so great was his grief at finding he was leaving you that he plunged into the bowels of the earth. Since he cannot help following his natural course, however, he comes forth from time to time and shows himself to the sun and the world. The lakes I mentioned send him their waters, and with these, and others that come to him, he makes a grand and imposing entrance into Portugal; but for all that, wherever he goes he shows his melancholy and sadness, and takes no pride in breeding choice fish — only coarse and tasteless sorts, very different from those of the golden Tagus. All this that I'm telling you now, O cousin of mine, I have told you many times before; and since you make no answer, I fear that either you don't believe me or you don't hear me, which causes me God knows what grief. I have news to give you now which, if it doesn't serve to ease your suffering, will at least not increase it. Know that you have here before you (open your eyes and you will see) that great knight of whom the sage Merlin has prophesied such great things — that Don Quixote of La Mancha, I mean, who has again, and to better purpose than in past times, revived in these days the long-forgotten knight-errantry, and by whose intervention and aid we may yet be disenchanted; for great deeds are reserved for great men.'

"'And if that may not be,' said the wretched Durandarte in a low, feeble voice, 'if that may not be, then, my cousin, I say _patience and shuffle_;' and turning over on his side, he relapsed into his former silence without uttering another word."

"And now there was a great outcry and lamentation, accompanied by deep sighs and bitter sobs. I looked around, and through the crystal wall I saw a procession passing through another chamber — two lines of fair damsels all dressed in mourning, with white Turkish-style turbans on their heads. Behind them, in the rear, came a lady — for so her dignity made her seem — also dressed in black, with a white veil so long and full that it swept the ground. Her turban was twice as large as the largest of the others; her eyebrows met, her nose was rather flat, her mouth was large but with ruddy lips, and her teeth, of which she allowed an occasional glimpse, were seen to be sparse and badly set, though as white as peeled almonds. She carried in her hands a fine cloth, and in it, as well as I could make out, a heart that had been mummified, so parched and dried was it. Montesinos told me that all those in the procession were the attendants of Durandarte and Belerma, who were enchanted there with their master and mistress, and that the last one, the one carrying the heart in the cloth, was the lady Belerma. With her damsels, four days a week, she went in procession singing — or rather weeping — dirges over the body and miserable heart of his cousin; and if she appeared to me somewhat plain or not as beautiful as fame reported her, it was because of the bad nights and worse days she passed in that enchantment, as I could see from the great dark circles round her eyes and her sickly complexion. 'Her sallowness, and the rings round her eyes,' he said, 'are not caused by the monthly ailment usual with women — for it's been many months, even years, since she has had any — but by the grief her own heart suffers over the one she holds in her hand perpetually, which reminds her and brings back the sad fate of her lost lover. Were it not for this, hardly would the great Dulcinea del Toboso, so celebrated in all these parts and even in the world, come up to her in beauty, grace, and gaiety.'"

"'Hold hard!' I said at this. 'Tell your story as you ought, Señor Don Montesinos, for you know very well that all comparisons are odious, and there's no need to compare one person to another. The peerless Dulcinea del Toboso is what she is, and the lady Doña Belerma is what _she_ is and has been, and that's enough.' To which he replied, 'Forgive me, Señor Don Quixote; I own I was wrong, and spoke unadvisedly in saying that the lady Dulcinea could scarcely come up to the lady Belerma. It is enough for me to have learned, by what means I don't know, that you are her knight, to make me bite my tongue out before I would compare her to anything save heaven itself.' After this apology that the great Montesinos made me, my heart recovered from the shock it had taken at hearing my lady compared with Belerma."
"Still, I wonder," said Sancho, "that your worship didn't climb on the old fellow and bruise every bone of him with kicks, and pluck his beard until you didn't leave a hair in it."

"No, Sancho, my friend," said Don Quixote, "that would not have been right of me, for we are all bound to pay respect to the aged, even though they aren't knights — but especially to those who are, and who are enchanted. I only know I gave him as good as he brought in the many other questions and answers we exchanged."

"I can't understand, Señor Don Quixote," the cousin remarked here, "how it is that your worship, in such a short space of time as you have been below there, could have seen so many things, and said and answered so much."
"How long is it since I went down?" asked Don Quixote.
"Little more than an hour," replied Sancho.

"That can't be," returned Don Quixote, "because night overtook me while I was there, and day came, and it was night again and day again three times; so by my reckoning I have been three days in those remote regions beyond our ken."
"My master must be right," replied Sancho; "for since everything that has happened to him is by enchantment, maybe what seems to us an hour would seem three days and nights there."
"That's it," said Don Quixote.
"And did your worship eat anything all that time, señor?" asked the cousin.
"I never touched a morsel," answered Don Quixote, "nor did I feel hunger, or even think of it."
"And do the enchanted eat?" said the cousin.
"They neither eat," said Don Quixote, "nor are they subject to the grosser bodily needs, though it is thought their nails, beards, and hair do grow."
"And do the enchanted sleep, señor?" asked Sancho.
"Certainly not," replied Don Quixote; "at least, in the three days I was with them, not one of them closed an eye, nor did I either."

"The proverb 'Tell me what company you keep and I'll tell you what you are' fits the case here," said Sancho. "Your worship keeps company with enchanted people who are always fasting and watching; what wonder is it, then, that you neither eat nor sleep while you are with them? But forgive me, señor, if I say that of all this you've told us, may God take me — I was about to say the devil — if I believe a single particle."
"What!" said the cousin. "Has Señor Don Quixote been lying? Why, even if he wanted to, he hasn't had time to imagine and put together such a host of lies."
"I don't believe my master lies," said Sancho.
"If not, then what do you believe?" asked Don Quixote.

"I believe," replied Sancho, "that this Merlin, or those enchanters who enchanted the whole crowd your worship says you saw and spoke with down there, stuffed your imagination or your mind with all this rigmarole you've been treating us to, and all that's still to come."

"All that might be, Sancho," replied Don Quixote; "but it isn't so, because everything I've told you I saw with my own eyes and touched with my own hands. But what will you say when I tell you now how, among the countless other marvellous things Montesinos showed me (of which at the proper time, in the course of our journey, I will give you an account, for they wouldn't all fit here), he showed me three country girls who went skipping and capering like goats across the pleasant fields there — and the instant I saw them I knew one to be the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso, and the other two those same country girls who were with her, the ones we spoke to on the road from El Toboso? I asked Montesinos if he knew them, and he said he did not, but he thought they must be some enchanted ladies of distinction, for they had only made their appearance in those meadows a few days before. I was not to be surprised at that, because there were a great many other ladies there, of times past and present, enchanted in various strange shapes — and among them he had recognised Queen Guinevere and her dame Quintañona, the one who poured out the wine for Lancelot when he came from Britain."

When Sancho Panza heard his master say this, he was ready to take leave of his senses, or die laughing. Since he knew the real truth about the pretended enchantment of Dulcinea — having himself been the enchanter and the concocter of all the evidence — he made up his mind at last that, beyond all doubt, his master was out of his wits and stark mad. So he said to him, "It was an evil hour, a worse season, and a sorrowful day, dear master mine, when your worship went down to the other world, and an unlucky moment when you met Señor Montesinos, who has sent you back to us like this. You were well enough up here in your full senses, such as God had given you, delivering maxims and giving advice at every turn — not as you are now, talking the greatest nonsense imaginable."
"As I know you, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "I pay no attention to your words."

"Nor I to your worship's," said Sancho, "whether you beat me or kill me for the ones I've spoken, or will speak, if you don't correct and mend your own. But tell me, while we're still at peace, how or by what did you recognise the lady our mistress? And if you spoke to her, what did you say, and what did she answer?"

"I recognised her," said Don Quixote, "by her wearing the same garments she had on when you pointed her out to me. I spoke to her, but she didn't utter a word in reply; on the contrary, she turned her back on me and took to flight at such a pace that a crossbow bolt couldn't have overtaken her. I wanted to follow her, and would have, had Montesinos not advised me not to bother, as it would be useless, particularly since the time was drawing near when I'd have to leave the cavern. He told me, moreover, that in time he would let me know how he and Belerma, and Durandarte, and all who were there, were to be disenchanted. But of all I saw and observed down there, what gave me most pain was this: while Montesinos was speaking to me, one of the two companions of the hapless Dulcinea came up to me on one side without my having seen her coming, and with tears in her eyes said to me, in a low, agitated voice, 'My lady Dulcinea del Toboso kisses your worship's hands and begs you to do her the favour of letting her know how you are; and, being in great need, she also begs your worship as earnestly as she can to be so good as to lend her half a dozen reals — or as much as you may have on you — on this new dimity petticoat I have here; and she promises to repay them very soon.' I was amazed and taken aback by such a message, and turning to Señor Montesinos I asked him, 'Is it possible, Señor Montesinos, that persons of distinction under enchantment can be in need?' To which he replied, 'Believe me, Señor Don Quixote, what is called need is to be met with everywhere, and penetrates all quarters and reaches everyone, and does not spare even the enchanted; and since the lady Dulcinea del Toboso sends to ask for those six reals, and the pledge is to all appearance a good one, there's nothing for it but to give them to her, for no doubt she must be in some great strait.' 'I will take no pledge from her,' I replied, 'nor can I give her what she asks, for all I have is four reals' — which I gave (they were the ones you, Sancho, gave me the other day to hand out as alms to the poor I met along the road) — 'and I said, Tell your mistress, my dear, that I am grieved to the heart over her distresses, and wish I were a Fugger to remedy them, and that I would have her know that I cannot, and ought not to, be in good health while deprived of the happiness of seeing her and enjoying her discreet conversation; and that I implore her as earnestly as I can to allow herself to be seen and addressed by this captive servant and forlorn knight of hers. Tell her too that when she least expects it she will hear it announced that I have made an oath and vow after the fashion of the one the Marquis of Mantua made to avenge his nephew Baldwin when he found him at the point of death in the heart of the mountains — namely, not to eat bread off a tablecloth, and other trifling matters which he added, until he had avenged him; and I will make the same vow, to take no rest and to roam the seven regions of the earth more thoroughly than the Infante Don Pedro of Portugal ever roamed them, until I have disenchanted her.' 'All that and more you owe my lady,' was the damsel's answer to me; and taking the four reals, instead of curtseying she cut a caper, springing two full yards into the air."

"O blessed God!" exclaimed Sancho aloud at this. "Is it possible that such things can be in the world, and that enchanters and enchantments can have such power in it as to have changed my master's right senses into a craze so full of absurdity? O señor, señor, for God's sake, think of yourself, have a care for your honour, and give no credit to this silly stuff that has left you scant and short of wits."

"You talk this way because you love me, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "and not being experienced in the things of the world, everything that has some difficulty about it seems to you impossible. But time will pass, as I said before, and I will tell you some of the things I saw down there that will make you believe what I've related now, the truth of which admits of neither reply nor question."

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 24
paragraphs: Wherein are related a thousand trifling matters, as trivial as they are necessary to the right understanding of this great history

The man who translated this great history from the original written by its first author, Cide Hamete Benengeli, says that on coming to the chapter giving the adventures of the cave of Montesinos he found these exact words written in the margin in Hamete's own hand:

"I cannot convince or persuade myself that everything written in the preceding chapter could have happened precisely to the valiant Don Quixote — and for this reason: that all the adventures that have occurred up to now have been possible and probable; but as for this one of the cave, I see no way of accepting it as true, since it passes all reasonable bounds. To believe that Don Quixote could lie, he being the most truthful gentleman and the noblest knight of his time, is impossible; he would not have told a lie though he were shot to death with arrows. On the other hand, I reflect that he related and told the story with all the details given, and that he could not in so short a space have fabricated such a vast complication of absurdities. If, then, this adventure seems apocryphal, that's no fault of mine; and so, without affirming its falsehood or its truth, I write it down. Decide for yourself in your wisdom, reader; I am not bound, nor is it in my power, to do more — though it's certain they say that at the time of his death he retracted, and said he had invented it, thinking it matched and fitted the adventures he had read of in his histories." And then he goes on to say:

The cousin was amazed both at Sancho's boldness and at the patience of his master, and concluded that the good temper Don Quixote displayed came from the happiness he felt at having seen his lady Dulcinea, even enchanted as she was; because otherwise the words and language Sancho had used to him deserved a thrashing, for he really did seem to have been rather impudent. Now the cousin said to him, "I, Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha, look upon the time I have spent in travelling with your worship as very well spent, for I have gained four things from it. The first is that I have made your acquaintance, which I consider great good fortune; the second, that I have learned what the cave of Montesinos contains, together with the transformations of the Guadiana and of the lakes of Ruidera — which will be useful to me for the Spanish Ovid I have in hand; the third, to have discovered the antiquity of cards — that they were in use at least in the time of Charlemagne, as may be inferred from the words you say Durandarte uttered when, at the end of that long spell while Montesinos was talking to him, he woke up and said, 'Patience and shuffle.' He could not have learned that phrase and expression while he was enchanted, only before he became so, in France, in the time of the said emperor Charlemagne. And this demonstration is just the thing for that other book I'm writing, the 'Supplement to Polydore Vergil on the Invention of Antiquities;' for I believe he never thought of including cards in his book, as I mean to do in mine — and it will be a matter of great importance, particularly when I can cite so grave and truthful an authority as Señor Durandarte. And the fourth thing is that I have established the source of the river Guadiana, until now unknown to mankind."
"You are right," said Don Quixote; "but I'd like to know, if by God's favour they grant you a licence to print those books of yours — which I doubt — to whom do you mean to dedicate them?"
"There are lords and grandees in Spain to whom they can be dedicated," said the cousin.

"Not many," said Don Quixote; "not that they are unworthy of it, but because they don't care to accept books and take on the obligation of making the return that seems due to the author's labour and courtesy. One prince I know who makes up for all the rest, and more — how much more, if I ventured to say, would perhaps stir up envy in many a noble breast; but let this stand over for some more convenient time, and let's go and look for some place to shelter ourselves in tonight."

"Not far from here," said the cousin, "there is a hermitage where a hermit lives who they say was once a soldier, and who has the reputation of being a good Christian and a very intelligent and charitable man. Next to the hermitage he has a small house that he built at his own cost, but though small it's large enough to receive guests."
"Has this hermit any hens, do you think?" asked Sancho.

"Few hermits are without them," said Don Quixote; "for those we see nowadays are not like the hermits of the Egyptian deserts, who dressed in palm-leaves and lived on the roots of the earth. But don't think that by praising these I am disparaging the others; all I mean is that the penances of those today don't come up to the asceticism and austerity of former times; but it doesn't follow from this that they are not all worthy — at least I think them so; and at the worst, the hypocrite who pretends to be good does less harm than the open sinner."

At this point they saw a man on foot approaching the spot where they stood, moving at a rapid pace and beating a mule loaded with lances and halberds. When he came up to them he greeted them and passed on without stopping. Don Quixote called to him, "Stay, good fellow; you seem to be in more of a hurry than suits that mule."

"I cannot stop, señor," the man answered; "the arms you see I'm carrying here are to be used tomorrow, so I mustn't delay. God be with you. But if you want to know what I am carrying them for, I mean to lodge tonight at the inn beyond the hermitage, and if you're going the same way you will find me there, and I will tell you some curious things. Once more, God be with you;" and he urged his mule on at such a pace that Don Quixote had no time to ask what these curious things were that he meant to tell them. Since Don Quixote was somewhat inquisitive and always tortured by his anxiety to learn something new, he decided to set out at once and pass the night at the inn instead of stopping at the hermitage, where the cousin had wanted them to halt. So they mounted, and all three took the direct road for the inn, which they reached a little before nightfall. On the way the cousin proposed that they go up to the hermitage for a quick drink. The moment Sancho heard this he steered his Dapple toward it, and Don Quixote and the cousin did the same. But it seems Sancho's bad luck so ordered it that the hermit was not at home, for so a sub-hermit they found at the hermitage told them. They called for some of the best. She replied that her master had none, but that if they liked cheap water she would give it with great pleasure.
"If I'd been after water," said Sancho, "there are wells along the road where I could have had enough of it. Ah, Camacho's wedding, and the plentiful house of Don Diego — how I miss you!"

Leaving the hermitage, they pushed on toward the inn, and a little further on they came upon a youth who was walking ahead of them at no great speed, so they overtook him. He carried a sword over his shoulder, with a bundle slung on it — apparently his clothes, probably his breeches or trousers, and his cloak and a shirt or two; for he had on a short jacket of velvet with a satiny gloss in places, and his shirt was hanging out; his stockings were silk, and his shoes square-toed in the court style. He might have been eighteen or nineteen, with a merry face and an apparently energetic manner, and he walked along singing seguidillas to lighten the tedium of the road. As they came up with him he was just finishing one, which the cousin learned by heart and which is said to run as follows —
I'm off to the wars For the want of pence, Oh, had I but money I'd show more sense.
The first to address him was Don Quixote, who said, "You travel very lightly, sir gallant; where are you bound, may we ask, if it's your pleasure to tell us?"
To which the youth replied, "The heat and my poverty are the reason for my travelling so lightly, and it's to the wars that I'm bound."
"How poverty?" asked Don Quixote; "the heat one can understand."

"Señor," replied the youth, "in this bundle I'm carrying velvet trousers to match this jacket; if I wear them out on the road, I won't be able to make a decent appearance in them in the city, and I haven't the money to buy others; so for this reason, as well as to keep myself cool, I'm making my way in this fashion to catch up with some companies of infantry that are not twelve leagues off, in which I'll enlist; and after that there will be no lack of baggage trains to travel with to the place of embarkation, which they say will be Cartagena. I'd rather have the King for a master, and serve him in the wars, than serve some court pauper."
"And did you get any bonus, now?" asked the cousin.

"If I had been in the service of some grandee of Spain or some distinguished personage," replied the youth, "I'd surely have got it; for that's the advantage of serving good masters — out of the servants' hall men come to be ancients or captains, or get a good pension. But to my misfortune I always served place-hunters and adventurers whose keep and wages were so miserable and scanty that half went on paying for the starching of one's collars; it would be a miracle indeed if a page-volunteer ever got anything like a reasonable bonus."
"And tell me, for heaven's sake," asked Don Quixote, "is it possible, my friend, that in all the time you served you never got any livery?"

"They gave me two," replied the page; "but just as when you leave a religious community before taking your vows, they strip you of the dress of the order and give you back your own clothes — so did my masters return mine to me. As soon as the business that had brought them to court was finished, they went home and took back the liveries they had given merely for show."

"What _spilorceria_, as an Italian would say," said Don Quixote; "but for all that, consider yourself happy in having left court with as worthy an object as you have, for there's nothing on earth more honourable or more profitable than serving, first of all God, and then one's king and natural lord, particularly in the profession of arms — by which, if not more wealth, at least more honour is to be won than by letters, as I have said many a time. For though letters may have founded more great houses than arms, still those founded by arms have I know not what superiority over those founded by letters, and a certain splendour belonging to them that distinguishes them above all. And bear in mind what I'm about to say to you, for it will be of great use and comfort to you in time of trouble: don't let your mind dwell on the bad chances that may befall you, for the worst of all is death, and if it is a good death, the best of all is to die. They asked Julius Caesar, the valiant Roman emperor, what was the best death. He answered, the unexpected one, the one that comes suddenly and unforeseen; and though he answered like a pagan and one without knowledge of the true God, still, as far as sparing our feelings is concerned, he was right; for suppose you're killed in the first engagement or skirmish, whether by a cannonball or blown up by a mine — what does it matter? It's only dying, and all is over. According to Terence, a soldier looks better dead in battle than alive and safe in flight; and the good soldier wins fame in proportion as he is obedient to his captains and those in command over him. And remember, my son, that it's better for the soldier to smell of gunpowder than of civet, and that if old age should come upon you in this honourable calling — though you may be covered with wounds and crippled and lame — it will not come upon you without honour, and such as poverty cannot lessen; especially now that provisions are being made for supporting and relieving old and disabled soldiers. For it isn't right to deal with them after the fashion of those who set free and get rid of their black slaves when they are old and useless, turning them out of their houses under the pretence of making them free and making them slaves to hunger, from which they cannot expect to be released except by death. But for now I won't say more than this: get up behind me on my horse as far as the inn, sup with me there, and tomorrow you shall pursue your journey, and God give you as good speed as your intentions deserve."

The page did not accept the invitation to mount, though he did accept the one to supper at the inn; and here they say Sancho said to himself, "God be with you for a master; is it possible that a man who can say things so many and so good as he has said just now can say that he saw the impossible absurdities he reports about the cave of Montesinos? Well, well, we shall see."

And now, just as night was falling, they reached the inn, and Sancho was not displeased to notice that his master took it for a real inn and not for a castle as usual. The moment they entered, Don Quixote asked the landlord after the man with the lances and halberds, and was told that he was in the stable seeing to his mule — which is what Sancho and the cousin proceeded to do for their own beasts, giving the best manger and the best place in the stable to Rocinante.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 25
paragraphs: Wherein is set down the braying adventure, and the droll one of the puppet-showman, together with the memorable divinations of the divining ape

Don Quixote's bread would not bake, as the common saying is, until he had heard and learned the curious things the man with the arms had promised. He went to find him where the innkeeper said he was, and having found him, bade him say now, at any rate, what he had to say in answer to the question he had asked him on the road. "The tale of my wonders must be taken more leisurely and not standing up," said the man; "let me finish feeding my beast, good sir, and then I'll tell you things that will astonish you."

"Don't wait for that," said Don Quixote; "I'll help you with everything." And so he did, sifting the barley for him and cleaning out the manger — a degree of humility that made the other feel bound to tell him with a good grace what he had asked. So, seating himself on a bench with Don Quixote beside him, and the cousin, the page, Sancho Panza, and the landlord for a senate and an audience, he began his story this way:

"You must know that in a village four and a half leagues from this inn, it so happened that one of the regidors, by the tricks and roguery of a servant girl of his (it's too long a story to tell), lost an ass; and though he did everything he possibly could to find it, it was all in vain. A fortnight may have gone by, so the story goes, since the ass had been missing, when, as the regidor who had lost it was standing in the plaza, another regidor of the same town said to him, 'Pay me for good news, gossip; your ass has turned up.' 'That I will, and well, gossip,' said the other; 'but tell us, where has he turned up?' 'In the forest,' said the finder; 'I saw him this morning without pack-saddle or harness of any sort, and so lean it broke your heart to see him. I tried to drive him before me and bring him to you, but he is already so wild and shy that when I went near him he made off into the thickest part of the forest. If you have a mind that the two of us should go back and look for him, let me put up this she-ass at my house and I'll be back at once.' 'You'd be doing me a great kindness,' said the owner of the ass, 'and I'll try to repay it in the same coin.' It's with all these details, and in the very same way I'm telling it now, that those who know all about it tell the story. Well then, the two regidors set off on foot, arm in arm, for the forest, and when they came to the place where they hoped to find the ass they could not find him, nor was he to be seen anywhere about, search as they might. Seeing, then, that there was no sign of him, the regidor who had seen him said to the other, 'Look here, gossip; a plan has occurred to me, by which beyond a doubt we shall manage to discover the animal, even if he's stowed away in the bowels of the earth, not to say the forest. Here it is: I can bray to perfection, and if you can even a little, the thing's as good as done.' 'Even a little, did you say, gossip?' said the other; 'by God, I won't give in to anybody, not even to the asses themselves.' 'We'll soon see,' said the second regidor, 'for my plan is that you go to one side of the forest and I to the other, so as to make a full circuit; and every now and then you will bray and I will bray; and the ass will surely hear us and answer us if he's in the forest.' To which the owner of the ass replied, 'It's an excellent plan, I declare, gossip, and worthy of your great genius;' and the two separating as agreed, it so happened that they brayed at almost the same moment, and each, deceived by the braying of the other, ran to look, thinking the ass had turned up at last. When they came in sight of one another, the loser said, 'Is it possible, gossip, that it wasn't my ass that brayed?' 'No, it was me,' said the other. 'Well then, I can tell you, gossip,' said the ass's owner, 'that between you and an ass there is not an atom of difference where braying is concerned, for in all my life I never saw or heard anything more natural.' 'Those praises and compliments belong to you more justly than to me, gossip,' said the inventor of the plan; 'for, by the God that made me, you could give a couple of brays' odds to the best and most finished brayer in the world; the tone you have is deep, your voice is well kept up as to time and pitch, and your finishing notes come thick and fast. In fact, I own myself beaten, and yield the palm to you, and give in to you in this rare accomplishment.' 'Well then,' said the owner, 'I'll set a higher value on myself from now on and consider that I know something, since I have an excellence of some sort; for though I always thought I brayed well, I never supposed I came up to the pitch of perfection you describe.' 'And I say too,' said the second, 'that there are rare gifts going to waste in the world, and that they are ill bestowed on those who don't know how to use them.' 'Ours,' said the owner of the ass, 'unless in cases like the one we have in hand now, can be of no service to us; and even in this, God grant they may be of some use.' So saying, they separated and took to their braying again — but every moment they were deceiving one another and coming to meet again, until they arranged a countersign — so as to know that it was them and not the ass — to give two brays, one after the other. In this way, doubling the brays at every step, they made the complete circuit of the forest, but the lost ass never gave them an answer or even a sign of one. How could the poor ill-starred brute have answered, when, in the thickest part of the forest, they found him devoured by wolves? As soon as he saw him, his owner said, 'I was wondering he didn't answer, for if he wasn't dead he'd have brayed when he heard us, or he wouldn't have been an ass; but for the sake of hearing you bray so perfectly, gossip, I count the trouble I've taken in looking for him well bestowed, even though I've found him dead.' 'It's in a good hand, gossip,' said the other; 'if the abbot sings well, the acolyte is not much behind him.' So they returned, disconsolate and hoarse, to their village, where they told their friends, neighbours, and acquaintances what had befallen them in their search for the ass, each praising the other's perfection in braying. The whole story came to be known and spread abroad through the villages of the neighbourhood; and the devil, who never sleeps, with his love for sowing dissensions and scattering discord everywhere, blowing mischief about and making quarrels out of nothing, contrived to make the people of the other towns fall to braying whenever they saw anyone from our village, as if to throw the braying of our regidors in our teeth. Then the boys took it up, which was as bad as falling into the hands and mouths of all the devils of hell; and braying spread from one town to another in such a way that the men of the braying town are as easy to recognise as blacks are to be known from whites, and the unlucky joke has gone so far that several times the mocked have come out in arms and as a body to do battle with the mockers, and neither king nor rook, fear nor shame, can mend matters. Tomorrow or the day after, I believe, the men of my town — that is, of the braying town — are going to take the field against another village two leagues away from ours, one of the ones that persecute us most; and so that we may turn out well prepared, I have bought these lances and halberds you have seen. These are the curious things I told you I had to tell, and if you don't think they are, I have got no others;" and with that the worthy fellow brought his story to a close.

Just at this moment there came in at the gate of the inn a man entirely dressed in chamois leather — hose, breeches, and doublet — who said in a loud voice, "Señor host, have you room? Here's the divining ape and the show of the Release of Melisendra just coming."

"Body of me!" said the landlord, "why, it's Master Pedro! We're in for a grand night!" I forgot to mention that Master Pedro had his left eye and nearly half his cheek covered with a patch of green taffeta, showing that something ailed all that side. "Your worship is welcome, Master Pedro," the landlord went on; "but where are the ape and the show, for I don't see them?" "They are close at hand," said the man in the chamois leather, "but I came on ahead to find out if there was any room." "I'd make the Duke of Alva himself clear out to make room for Master Pedro," said the landlord; "bring in the ape and the show; there's company in the inn tonight that will pay to see that and the cleverness of the ape." "So be it, by all means," said the man with the patch; "I'll lower the price, and be well satisfied if I only pay my expenses; and now I'll go back and hurry on the cart with the ape and the show;" and with that he went out of the inn.

Don Quixote at once asked the landlord what this Master Pedro was, and what was the show and what was the ape he had with him; to which the landlord replied, "This is a famous puppet-showman who for some time now has been going about this Mancha de Aragon, exhibiting a show of the release of Melisendra by the famous Don Gaiferos — one of the best and best-presented stories that have been seen in this part of the kingdom for many a year. He also has an ape with the most extraordinary gift ever seen in an ape or imagined in a human being. If you ask him anything, he listens attentively to the question, then jumps onto his master's shoulder and, pressing close to his ear, tells him the answer that Master Pedro then delivers. He says a great deal more about things past than about things to come; and though he doesn't always hit the truth in every case, most of the time he is not far wrong, so that he makes us fancy he has got the devil in him. He gets two reals for every question if the ape answers — I mean if his master answers for him after he has whispered in his ear; and so it's believed that this same Master Pedro is very rich. He is a 'gallant man,' as they say in Italy, and good company, and leads the finest life in the world; talks more than six, drinks more than a dozen, all by means of his tongue, his ape, and his show."

Master Pedro now came back, and in a cart followed the show and the ape — a big one, without a tail, with buttocks as bare as felt, but not vicious-looking. As soon as Don Quixote saw him, he asked, "Can you tell me, sir fortune-teller, what fish do we catch, and how will it be with us? See, here are my two reals," and he bade Sancho give them to Master Pedro; but he answered for the ape and said, "Señor, this animal does not give any answer or information concerning things that are to come; of things past he knows something, and more or less of things present."

"By God," said Sancho, "I wouldn't give a farthing to be told what's past with me, for who knows that better than I do myself? And to pay for being told what I know would be mighty foolish. But since you know things present, here are my two reals, and tell me, most excellent sir ape, what is my wife Teresa Panza doing now, and what is she amusing herself with?"

Master Pedro refused to take the money, saying, "I won't receive payment in advance, or until the service has first been rendered;" and then with his right hand he gave a couple of slaps on his left shoulder, and with one spring the ape perched himself there, and putting his mouth to his master's ear began chattering his teeth rapidly. Having kept this up about as long as it would take to say a creed, with another spring he was on the ground, and at the same instant Master Pedro ran in great haste and fell upon his knees before Don Quixote, and embracing his legs exclaimed, "These legs I embrace as I would embrace the two pillars of Hercules, O illustrious reviver of knight-errantry, so long consigned to oblivion! O never yet duly extolled knight, Don Quixote of La Mancha, courage of the faint-hearted, prop of the tottering, arm of the fallen, staff and counsel of all who are unfortunate!"

Don Quixote was thunderstruck, Sancho astounded, the cousin staggered, the page astonished, the man from the braying town agape, the landlord in perplexity — in short, everyone amazed at the words of the puppet-showman, who went on to say, "And you, worthy Sancho Panza, the best squire and squire to the best knight in the world! Be of good cheer, for your good wife Teresa is well, and at this very moment she is hackling a pound of flax; and more by token, she has at her left hand a jug with a broken spout that holds a good drop of wine, with which she comforts herself at her work."

"That I can well believe," said Sancho. "She is a lucky one, and if it weren't for her jealousy I wouldn't swap her for the giantess Andandona, who by my master's account was a very clever and worthy woman; my Teresa is one of those who won't let themselves go without anything, even if their heirs may have to pay for it."

"Now I declare," said Don Quixote, "he who reads much and travels much sees and knows a great deal. I say so because what amount of persuasion could have persuaded me that there are apes in the world who can divine, as I have just seen with my own eyes? For I am that very Don Quixote of La Mancha this worthy animal refers to — though he has gone rather too far in my praise; but whatever I may be, I thank heaven that it has endowed me with a tender and compassionate heart, always disposed to do good to all and harm to none."
"If I had money," said the page, "I would ask señor ape what will happen to me on the journey I'm making."

To which Master Pedro, who had by now risen from Don Quixote's feet, replied, "I have already said that this little beast gives no answer as to the future; but if he did, not having money would be of no consequence, for to oblige Señor Don Quixote here, I would give up all the profits in the world. And now, because I have promised it, and to afford him pleasure, I will set up my show and offer entertainment to all who are in the inn, without any charge whatever." As soon as he heard this, the landlord, delighted beyond measure, pointed out a place where the show could be set up, which was done at once.

Don Quixote was not very satisfied with the divinations of the ape, since he didn't think it proper that an ape should divine anything, either past or future; so while Master Pedro was arranging the show, he withdrew with Sancho into a corner of the stable, where, without being overheard by anyone, he said to him, "Look here, Sancho, I've been seriously thinking over this ape's extraordinary gift, and I've come to the conclusion that beyond doubt this Master Pedro, his master, has a pact, tacit or express, with the devil."
"If the packet is express from the devil," said Sancho, "it must be a very dirty packet no doubt; but what good can it do Master Pedro to have such packets?"

"You don't understand me, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "I only mean he must have made some compact with the devil to infuse this power into the ape, so he may earn his living, and once he has grown rich the devil will collect his soul — which is what the enemy of mankind wants. What leads me to believe this is that the ape only answers about things past or present, and the devil's knowledge extends no further; for the future he knows only by guesswork, and that not always — it is reserved for God alone to know the times and seasons, for whom there is neither past nor future; all is present. This being so, it is clear that this ape speaks by the spirit of the devil; and I'm astonished they haven't denounced him to the Holy Office, and put him to the question, and forced it out of him by whose virtue it is that he divines. Because it is certain this ape is not an astrologer; neither his master nor he sets up — or knows how to set up — those figures they call judiciary, which are now so common in Spain that there isn't a jade, or page, or old cobbler who won't undertake to set up a figure as readily as picking up a knave of cards from the ground, bringing to nothing the marvellous truth of the science by their lies and ignorance. I know of a lady who asked one of these figure-schemers whether her little lap-dog would be in pup and would breed, and how many and what colour the little pups would be. To which señor astrologer, after setting up his figure, answered that the bitch would be in pup and would drop three pups — one green, another bright red, and the third parti-coloured — provided she conceived between eleven and twelve, either of the day or night, and on a Monday or Saturday. But as things turned out, two days after this the bitch died of a surfeit, and señor planet-ruler had the credit all over the place of being a most profound astrologer, as most of these planet-rulers have."

"Still," said Sancho, "I would be glad if your worship would have Master Pedro ask his ape whether what happened to your worship in the cave of Montesinos is true; for, begging your worship's pardon, I, for my part, take it to have been all flam and lies, or at any rate something you dreamed."
"That may be," replied Don Quixote; "however, I'll do what you suggest, though I have my own scruples about it."

At this point Master Pedro came up looking for Don Quixote, to tell him the show was now ready and to come and see it, for it was worth seeing. Don Quixote explained his wish, and asked him to have his ape tell him at once whether certain things that had happened to him in the cave of Montesinos were dreams or realities — for they seemed to him to partake of both. Upon this Master Pedro, without answering, went back to fetch the ape, and having placed it in front of Don Quixote and Sancho, said, "See here, señor ape, this gentleman wishes to know whether certain things that happened to him in the cave called the cave of Montesinos were false or true." On his making the usual sign, the ape climbed onto his left shoulder and seemed to whisper in his ear, and Master Pedro said at once, "The ape says that the things you saw, or that happened to you, in that cave are, part of them false, part true; and that he only knows this and no more as regards your question; but if your worship wishes to know more, on Friday next he will answer everything that may be asked him, for his virtue is at present exhausted, and won't return to him till Friday, as he has said."
"Did I not say, señor," said Sancho, "that I couldn't bring myself to believe that all your worship said about the adventures in the cave was true, or even half of it?"

"The course of events will tell, Sancho," replied Don Quixote; "time, which discloses all things, leaves nothing it doesn't drag into the light of day, though it be buried in the bosom of the earth. But enough of that for now; let us go and see Master Pedro's show, for I'm sure there must be something novel in it."

"Something!" said Master Pedro; "this show of mine has sixty thousand novel things in it; let me tell you, Señor Don Quixote, it is one of the best-worth-seeing things in the world today; but _operibus credite et non verbis_, and now let's get to work, for it's growing late, and we have a great deal to do and to say and show."

Don Quixote and Sancho obeyed him and went over to where the show was already set up and uncovered, ringed all around with lighted wax tapers that made it look splendid and bright. When they came to it Master Pedro positioned himself inside it, since he was the one who had to work the puppets, and a boy, a servant of his, posted himself outside to act as showman and explain the mysteries of the exhibition, holding a wand in his hand to point to the figures as they came out. And so, all who were in the inn being arranged in front of the show — some standing, and Don Quixote, Sancho, the page, and the cousin given the best seats — the interpreter began to say what whoever reads or hears the next chapter will hear or see.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 26
paragraphs: Wherein is continued the droll adventure of the puppet-showman, together with other things in truth right good

All were silent, Tyrians and Trojans; I mean, all who were watching the show were hanging on the lips of the interpreter of its wonders, when drums and trumpets were heard sounding inside it and cannon going off. The noise was soon over, and then the boy raised his voice and said, "This true story which is here represented before your worships is taken word for word from the French chronicles and from the Spanish ballads on everybody's lips, and on the lips of the boys about the streets. Its subject is the release by Señor Don Gaiferos of his wife Melisendra, a captive in Spain at the hands of the Moors in the city of Sansueña — for so they then called what is now called Saragossa; and there you may see how Don Gaiferos is playing at the tables, just as they sing it —
At tables playing Don Gaiferos sits, For Melisendra is forgotten now.

And that personage who appears there with a crown on his head and a sceptre in his hand is the Emperor Charlemagne, the supposed father of Melisendra, who, angered to see his son-in-law's inaction and unconcern, comes in to chide him; and observe with what vehemence and energy he chides him, so that you'd fancy he was going to give him half a dozen raps with his sceptre; and indeed there are authors who say he did give them, and sound ones too; and after saying a great deal to him about endangering his honour by not effecting the release of his wife, he said, so the tale runs,
Enough I've said, see to it now.

Observe, too, how the emperor turns away and leaves Don Gaiferos fuming; and now see how, in a burst of anger, he flings the table and the board far from him and calls in haste for his armour, and asks his cousin Don Roland for the loan of his sword, Durindana, and how Don Roland refuses to lend it, offering him his company in the difficult enterprise he is undertaking; but he, in his valour and anger, will not accept it, and says that he alone will be enough to rescue his wife, even though she were imprisoned deep in the centre of the earth; and with this he retires to arm himself and set out on his journey at once. Now let your worships turn your eyes to that tower over there, which is supposed to be one of the towers of the alcazar of Saragossa, now called the Aljaferia; that lady who appears on that balcony dressed in Moorish fashion is the peerless Melisendra, for many a time she used to gaze from there upon the road to France, and seek consolation in her captivity by thinking of Paris and her husband. Observe, too, a new incident which now occurs, the like of which perhaps was never seen. Do you not see that Moor, who silently and stealthily, with his finger on his lip, approaches Melisendra from behind? Observe now how he plants a kiss upon her lips, and what a hurry she is in to spit and wipe them with the white sleeve of her smock, and how she bewails herself and tears her fair hair as though it were to blame for the wrong. Observe, too, that the stately Moor who is in that corridor is King Marsilio of Sansueña, who, having seen the Moor's insolence, at once orders him (though his kinsman and a great favourite of his) to be seized and given two hundred lashes, while carried through the streets of the city according to custom, with criers going before him and officers of justice behind; and here you see them come out to execute the sentence, although the offence has been scarcely committed; for among the Moors there are no indictments nor remands as with us."

Here Don Quixote called out, "Child, child, go straight on with your story and don't run into curves and slants, for to establish a fact clearly there is need of a great deal of proof and confirmation;" and Master Pedro said from within, "Boy, stick to your text and do as the gentleman bids you; that's the best plan; keep to your plain song and don't attempt harmonies, for they are apt to break down from being too fine."

"I will," said the boy, and he went on to say, "This figure that you see here on horseback, covered with a Gascon cloak, is Don Gaiferos himself, whom his wife — now avenged for the insult of the amorous Moor, and taking her stand on the balcony of the tower with a calmer and more tranquil countenance — has spotted without recognising him; and she addresses her husband, supposing him to be some traveller, and holds with him all that conversation and colloquy in the ballad that runs —
If you, sir knight, to France are bound, Oh! for Gaiferos ask —

which I won't repeat here, because prolixity breeds disgust; suffice it to observe how Don Gaiferos reveals himself, and that by her joyful gestures Melisendra shows us she has recognised him; and what's more, we now see her lowering herself from the balcony to place herself on the haunches of her good husband's horse. But ah! unhappy lady, the edge of her petticoat has caught on one of the bars of the balcony and she is left hanging in the air, unable to reach the ground. But you see how compassionate heaven sends aid in our sorest need: Don Gaiferos advances, and without minding whether the rich petticoat is torn or not, he seizes her and by force brings her to the ground, and then with one jerk places her on the haunches of his horse, astraddle like a man, and bids her hold on tight and clasp her arms round his neck, crossing them on his breast so as not to fall, for the lady Melisendra was not used to that style of riding. You see, too, how the neighing of the horse shows his satisfaction with the gallant and beautiful burden he bears in his lord and lady. You see how they wheel round and quit the city, and in joy and gladness take the road to Paris. Go in peace, O peerless pair of true lovers! May you reach your longed-for fatherland in safety, and may fortune put no obstacle in the way of your prosperous journey; may the eyes of your friends and kinsmen behold you enjoying in peace and tranquillity the remaining days of your life — and may they be as many as those of Nestor!"
Here Master Pedro called out again and said, "Simplicity, boy! None of your high flights; all affectation is bad."

The interpreter made no answer but went on to say, "There was no shortage of idle eyes that see everything, to see Melisendra come down and mount, and word was brought to King Marsilio, who at once gave orders to sound the alarm; and see what a stir there is, and how the city is drowned with the sound of the bells pealing in the towers of all the mosques."

"No, no," said Don Quixote at this; "on that point of the bells, Master Pedro is very inaccurate, for bells are not in use among the Moors; only kettledrums, and a kind of small trumpet somewhat like our clarion. To ring bells this way in Sansueña is unquestionably a great absurdity."

On hearing this, Master Pedro stopped ringing and said, "Don't look into trifles, Señor Don Quixote, or want to have things up to a pitch of perfection that is out of reach. Are there not almost every day a thousand comedies put on all around us, full of thousands of inaccuracies and absurdities — and for all that, they have a successful run, and are listened to not only with applause but with admiration and all the rest? Go on, boy, and don't mind; for as long as I fill my pouch, no matter if I show as many inaccuracies as there are motes in a sunbeam."

"True enough," said Don Quixote; and the boy went on, "See what a numerous and glittering crowd of horsemen issues from the city in pursuit of the two faithful lovers, what a blowing of trumpets there is, what sounding of horns, what beating of drums and tabors; I fear they will overtake them and bring them back tied to the tail of their own horse, which would be a dreadful sight."

Don Quixote, however, seeing such a swarm of Moors and hearing such a din, thought it would be right to aid the fugitives; and standing up he exclaimed in a loud voice, "Never, while I live, will I permit foul play to be practised in my presence on such a famous knight and fearless lover as Don Gaiferos. Halt! ill-born rabble, follow him not nor pursue him, or you will have to reckon with me in battle!" And suiting the action to the word, he drew his sword, and with one bound placed himself close to the show, and with unexampled rapidity and fury began to rain down blows on the puppet troop of Moors, knocking some over, decapitating others, maiming this one and demolishing that; and among many more he delivered one downward stroke that, if Master Pedro hadn't ducked, made himself small, and got out of the way, would have sliced his head off as easily as if it had been made of almond-paste. Master Pedro kept shouting, "Hold hard! Señor Don Quixote! can't you see they're not real Moors you're knocking down and killing and destroying, but only little pasteboard figures! Look — sinner that I am! — how you're wrecking and ruining all that I'm worth!" But in spite of this, Don Quixote did not stop discharging a continuous rain of cuts, slashes, downstrokes, and backstrokes; and at length, in less than the time it takes to say two creeds, he brought the whole show to the ground, with all its fittings and figures shivered and knocked to pieces, King Marsilio badly wounded, and the Emperor Charlemagne with his crown and head split in two. The whole audience was thrown into confusion, the ape fled to the roof of the inn, the cousin was frightened, and even Sancho Panza himself was in mighty fear, for, as he swore after the storm was over, he had never seen his master in such a furious passion.

The complete destruction of the show being thus accomplished, Don Quixote became a little calmer and said, "I wish I had here before me now all those who do not or will not believe how useful knights-errant are in the world; just think, if I had not been here, what would have become of the brave Don Gaiferos and the fair Melisendra? Depend upon it, by this time those dogs would have overtaken them and inflicted some outrage upon them. So then, long live knight-errantry beyond everything living on earth this day!"
"Let it live, and welcome," said Master Pedro at this in a feeble voice, "and let me die, for I am so unfortunate that I can say with King Don Rodrigo —
Yesterday was I lord of Spain To-day I've not a turret left That I may call mine own.

Not half an hour, nay, barely a minute ago, I saw myself lord of kings and emperors, with my stables filled with countless horses, and my trunks and bags with gay dresses unnumbered; and now I find myself ruined and laid low, destitute and a beggar, and above all without my ape — for, by my faith, my teeth will have to sweat for it before I get him caught again; and all through the reckless fury of sir knight here, who, they say, protects the fatherless, and rights wrongs, and does other charitable deeds; but whose generous intentions have been found wanting in my case only — blessed and praised be the highest heavens! Verily, knight of the rueful figure he must be, to have disfigured mine."

Sancho Panza was touched by Master Pedro's words and said to him, "Don't weep and lament, Master Pedro; you break my heart. Let me tell you, my master Don Quixote is so catholic and scrupulous a Christian that, if he can be made to see he has done you any wrong, he will own it, and be willing to pay for it and make it good, and something over and above."

"Only let Señor Don Quixote pay me for some part of the work he has destroyed," said Master Pedro, "and I'd be content, and his worship would ease his conscience; for he cannot be saved who keeps what is another's against the owner's will, and makes no restitution."
"That is true," said Don Quixote; "but at the moment I am not aware that I have anything of yours, Master Pedro."

"What!" returned Master Pedro; "and these relics lying here on the bare hard ground — what scattered and shattered them but the invincible strength of that mighty arm? And whose were the bodies they belonged to but mine? And what did I earn my living by but by them?"

"Now am I fully convinced," said Don Quixote, "of what I had many times before believed: that the enchanters who persecute me do nothing more than put figures like these before my eyes, and then change and turn them into whatever they please. In truth and earnest, I assure you gentlemen who now hear me, that to me everything that has taken place here seemed to take place literally — that Melisendra was Melisendra, Don Gaiferos was Don Gaiferos, Marsilio was Marsilio, and Charlemagne was Charlemagne. That was why my anger was roused; and to be faithful to my calling as a knight-errant I sought to give aid and protection to those who fled, and with this good intention I did what you have seen. If the result has been the opposite of what I intended, it is no fault of mine, but of those wicked beings that persecute me; but, for all that, I am willing to condemn myself in costs for this error of mine, though it did not proceed from malice; let Master Pedro see what he wants for the spoiled figures, and I agree to pay it at once in good and current money of Castile."

Master Pedro made him a bow, saying, "I expected no less of the rare Christianity of the valiant Don Quixote of La Mancha, true helper and protector of all destitute and needy vagabonds; the landlord here and the great Sancho Panza shall be the arbitrators and appraisers between your worship and me of what these dilapidated figures are worth, or may be worth."

The landlord and Sancho consented, and then Master Pedro picked up from the ground King Marsilio of Saragossa with his head off, and said, "Here you see how impossible it is to restore this king to his former state, so I think, saving your better judgments, that for his death, decease, and demise, four reals and a half may be given me."
"Proceed," said Don Quixote.
"Well then, for this split from top to bottom," continued Master Pedro, taking up the split Emperor Charlemagne, "it wouldn't be much if I were to ask five reals and a quarter."
"It's not a little," said Sancho.
"Nor is it much," said the landlord; "make it even, and say five reals."

"Let him have the whole five and a quarter," said Don Quixote; "for the sum total of this notable disaster does not stand on a quarter more or less; and make an end of it quickly, Master Pedro, for it's getting on toward supper-time, and I have some hints of hunger."
"For this figure," said Master Pedro, "which is without a nose, and missing an eye, and is the fair Melisendra, I ask — and I am being reasonable in my charge — two reals and twelve maravedis."

"The very devil must be in it," said Don Quixote, "if Melisendra and her husband aren't by this time at least on the French border, for the horse they rode on seemed to me to fly rather than gallop; so don't try to sell me the cat for the hare, showing me here a noseless Melisendra when she's now, maybe, enjoying herself at her ease with her husband in France. God help every one to his own, Master Pedro, and let us all proceed fairly and honestly; and now go on."

Master Pedro, seeing that Don Quixote was beginning to wander and return to his original fancy, was not disposed to let him escape, so he said to him, "This cannot be Melisendra; it must be one of the damsels that waited on her; so if I'm given sixty maravedis for her, I'll be content and sufficiently paid."

And so he went on, putting prices on ever so many more smashed figures, which, after the two arbitrators had adjusted them to the satisfaction of both parties, came to forty reals and three-quarters; and over and above this sum, which Sancho at once paid out, Master Pedro asked for two reals for his trouble in catching the ape.

"Let him have them, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "not for catching the ape, but for getting drunk; and two hundred would I give this minute as good news to anyone who could tell me positively that the lady Doña Melisendra and Señor Don Gaiferos were now in France and with their own people."

"No one could tell us that better than my ape," said Master Pedro; "but there's no devil that could catch him now; though I suspect that affection and hunger will drive him to come looking for me tonight; tomorrow will soon be here, and we shall see."

In short, the puppet-show storm passed off, and they all supped in peace and good fellowship at Don Quixote's expense, for he was the height of generosity. Before daylight the man with the lances and halberds took his departure, and soon after daybreak the cousin and the page came to bid Don Quixote farewell — the former returning home, the latter resuming his journey, toward which, to help him, Don Quixote gave him twelve reals. Master Pedro did not care to engage in any more talk with Don Quixote, whom he knew right well; so he rose before the sun, and having got together the remains of his show and caught his ape, he too went off to seek his adventures. The landlord, who did not know Don Quixote, was as much astonished at his mad freaks as at his generosity. To conclude, Sancho, on his master's orders, paid him very liberally, and taking leave of him they quitted the inn at about eight in the morning and took to the road, where we'll leave them to pursue their journey — for this is necessary, to allow certain other matters to be set forth, which are needed to clear up this famous history.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 27
paragraphs: Wherein it is shown who Master Pedro and his ape were, together with the mishap Don Quixote had in the braying adventure, which he did not conclude as he would have liked or as he had expected

Cide Hamete, the chronicler of this great history, begins this chapter with the words, "I swear as a Catholic Christian;" with regard to which his translator says that Cide Hamete's swearing as a Catholic Christian — he being, as no doubt he was, a Moor — only meant that, just as a Catholic Christian taking an oath swears, or ought to swear, what is true, and tell the truth in what he avers, so he was telling the truth, as much as if he swore as a Catholic Christian, in all he chose to write about Quixote, especially in declaring who Master Pedro was and what was the divining ape that astonished all the villages with his divinations. He says, then, that whoever has read the First Part of this history will remember well enough the Gines de Pasamonte whom, with the other galley slaves, Don Quixote set free in the Sierra Morena — a kindness for which he afterwards got poor thanks and worse payment from that evil-minded, ill-conditioned set. This Gines de Pasamonte — Don Ginesillo de Parapilla, Don Quixote called him — was the one who stole Dapple from Sancho Panza. Because, by the fault of the printers, neither the how nor the when was stated in the First Part, this has been a puzzle to many people, who attribute to the bad memory of the author what was the error of the press. In fact, however, Gines stole him while Sancho Panza was asleep on his back, using the same plan and trick Brunello used when he stole Sacripante's horse from between his legs at the siege of Albracca; and, as has been told, Sancho afterwards recovered him. This Gines, then, afraid of being caught by the officers of justice — who were looking for him to punish him for his numberless rascalities and offences (which were so many and so great that he himself wrote a big book giving an account of them) — resolved to shift his quarters into the kingdom of Aragon, cover up his left eye, and take up the trade of a puppet-showman; for this, as well as juggling, he knew how to practise to perfection. From some released Christians returning from Barbary, it so happened, he bought the ape, which he taught to climb onto his shoulder at a certain sign, and to whisper, or seem to whisper, in his ear. Thus prepared, before entering any village where he was bound with his show and his ape, he used to inform himself at the nearest village, or from the most likely person he could find, as to what particular things had happened there, and to whom; and bearing them well in mind, the first thing he did was put on his show, sometimes one story, sometimes another, but all lively, amusing, and familiar. As soon as the show was over, he brought forward the accomplishments of his ape, assuring the public that he divined all the past and the present, but as for the future he had no skill. For each question answered he charged two reals, and for some he made a reduction, depending on how he felt the pulse of the questioners; and when now and then he came to houses where things he knew about had happened to the people living there, even if they did not ask him a question, not caring to pay for it, he would make the sign to the ape and then declare that it had said so-and-so — which fitted the case exactly. In this way he acquired a prodigious name and everyone ran after him; on other occasions, being very crafty, he would answer in such a way that the answers suited the questions; and since no one cross-questioned him or pressed him to tell how his ape divined, he made fools of them all and filled his pouch. The instant he entered the inn he recognised Don Quixote and Sancho, and with that recognition it was easy for him to astonish them and all who were there; but it would have cost him dear had Don Quixote brought his hand down a little lower when he cut off King Marsilio's head and destroyed all his horsemen, as related in the preceding chapter.

So much for Master Pedro and his ape; and now to return to Don Quixote of La Mancha. After he had left the inn he decided to visit, first of all, the banks of the Ebro and that neighbourhood, before entering the city of Saragossa, for there was plenty of time still before the jousts. With this object in view he followed the road and travelled along it for two days without meeting any adventure worth writing down, until on the third day, as he was climbing a hill, he heard a great noise of drums, trumpets, and musket-shots. At first he thought some regiment of soldiers was passing that way, and to see them he spurred Rocinante and reached the top of the hill. From there he saw at the foot of it over two hundred men, as it seemed to him, armed with weapons of various sorts — lances, crossbows, partisans, halberds, and pikes, and a few muskets and a great many bucklers. He descended the slope and approached the band close enough to see distinctly the flags, make out the colours, and recognise the devices they bore — especially one on a standard or ensign of white satin, on which was painted in a very lifelike style an ass like a little sard, with its head up, its mouth open, and its tongue out, as if it were in the act and attitude of braying; and around it were inscribed in large letters these two lines —
They did not bray in vain, Our alcaldes twain.

From this device Don Quixote concluded that these people must be from the braying town, and he said so to Sancho, explaining to him what was written on the standard. At the same time he observed that the man who had told them about the matter was wrong in saying that the two who brayed were regidors, for according to the lines of the standard they were alcaldes. To which Sancho replied, "Señor, there's nothing to stick at in that, for maybe the regidors who brayed back then came to be alcaldes of their town afterwards, and so they may go by both titles; besides, it has nothing to do with the truth of the story whether the brayers were alcaldes or regidors, provided at any rate they did bray — for an alcalde is just as likely to bray as a regidor." In short, they perceived clearly that the town which had been twitted had turned out to do battle with another that had jeered at it more than was fair or neighbourly.

Don Quixote proceeded to join them, not a little to Sancho's uneasiness, for he never relished mixing himself up in expeditions of that sort. The members of the troop received him into their midst, taking him to be someone on their side. Don Quixote, putting up his visor, advanced with an easy bearing and demeanour to the standard with the ass, and all the chief men of the army gathered round him to look at him, staring with the usual amazement everyone felt on seeing him for the first time. Don Quixote, seeing them examining him so attentively, and that none of them spoke to him or put any question to him, decided to take advantage of their silence. So, breaking his own, he lifted up his voice and said, "Worthy sirs, I beg you as earnestly as I can not to interrupt an argument I wish to put to you, until you find it displeases or wearies you; and if that should happen, on the slightest hint you give me I will put a seal upon my lips and a gag upon my tongue."
They all told him to say what he liked, for they would listen to him willingly.

With this permission, Don Quixote went on to say, "I, sirs, am a knight-errant whose calling is arms, and whose profession is to protect those who need protection and give help to those who stand in need of it. Some days ago I learned of your misfortune and the cause that drives you to take up arms again and again to revenge yourselves on your enemies; and having many times thought over your case in my mind, I find that, according to the laws of combat, you are mistaken in holding yourselves insulted; for a private individual cannot insult an entire community — unless it be by defying it collectively as a traitor, because he cannot tell who in particular is guilty of the treason for which he defies it.
