Of this we have an example in Don Diego Ordoñez de Lara, who defied the whole town of Zamora because he did not know that Vellido Dolfos alone had committed the treachery of slaying his king; and so he defied them all, and the vengeance and the reply concerned all — though, to be sure, Señor Don Diego went rather too far, indeed very much beyond the limits of a defiance, for he had no occasion to defy the dead, or the waters, or the fishes, or those yet unborn, and all the rest of it as set forth; but let that pass, for when anger breaks out there's no father, governor, or bridle to check the tongue. The case being, then, that no one person can insult a kingdom, province, city, state, or entire community, it is clear there is no reason for going out to avenge the defiance of such an insult, since it is not one. A fine thing it would be if the people of the clock town were to be at loggerheads every moment with everyone who called them by that name — or the Cazoleros, Berengeneros, Ballenatos, Jaboneros, or the bearers of all the other names and titles that are always in the mouths of boys and common people! It would be a nice business indeed if all these illustrious cities were to take huff and revenge themselves and go about perpetually making trombones of their swords in every petty quarrel! No, no; God forbid! There are four things for which sensible men and well-ordered states ought to take up arms, draw their swords, and risk their persons, lives, and properties. The first is to defend the Catholic faith; the second, to defend one's life, which is in accordance with natural and divine law; the third, in defence of one's honour, family, and property; the fourth, in the service of one's king in a just war; and if to these we choose to add a fifth (which may be included in the second), in defence of one's country. To these five, as it were capital causes, may be added some others that may be just and reasonable, and make it a duty to take up arms; but to take them up for trifles and things to laugh at and be amused by rather than offended by, looks as though the one doing it were altogether wanting in common sense. Moreover, to take an unjust revenge (and there cannot be any just one) is directly opposed to the sacred law that we acknowledge, in which we are commanded to do good to our enemies and to love those that hate us — a command which, though it seems somewhat difficult to obey, is only so to those who have in them less of God than of the world, and more of the flesh than of the spirit; for Jesus Christ, God and true man, who never lied, and could not and cannot lie, said, as our law-giver, that his yoke was easy and his burden light; he would not, therefore, have laid any command upon us that was impossible to obey. Thus, sirs, you are bound to keep quiet by both human and divine law."
"The devil take me," said Sancho to himself at this, "but this master of mine is a theologian; or, if not, faith, he's as like one as one egg is like another."

Don Quixote stopped to take breath, and, observing that silence was still preserved, had a mind to continue his discourse, and would have done so had Sancho not interposed with his smartness; for he, seeing his master pause, took the lead, saying, "My lord Don Quixote of La Mancha, who once was called the Knight of the Rueful Countenance but is now called the Knight of the Lions, is a gentleman of great discretion who knows Latin and his mother tongue like a bachelor of arts, and in everything that he handles or advises proceeds like a good soldier, and has all the laws and ordinances of what they call combat at his fingers' ends; so you have nothing to do but let yourselves be guided by what he says, and on my head be it if it is wrong. Besides which, you have been told that it is folly to take offence at merely hearing a bray. I remember when I was a boy I brayed as often as I had a fancy to, without anyone hindering me, and so elegantly and naturally that when I brayed all the asses in the town would bray; but I was none the less for that the son of my parents, who were greatly respected; and though I was envied because of the gift by more than one of the high and mighty ones of the town, I didn't care two farthings for it; and that you may see I am telling the truth, wait a bit and listen — for this art, like swimming, once learned is never forgotten;" and then, taking hold of his nose, he began to bray so vigorously that all the valleys around rang again.

One of those standing near him, however, fancying he was mocking them, lifted up a long staff he had in his hand and gave him such a blow with it that Sancho dropped helpless to the ground. Don Quixote, seeing him so roughly handled, attacked the man who had struck him, lance in hand; but so many men thrust themselves between them that he could not avenge him. Far from it: finding a shower of stones rained upon him, and crossbows and muskets unnumbered levelled at him, he wheeled Rocinante round and, as fast as his best gallop could take him, fled from their midst, commending himself to God with all his heart to deliver him out of this peril, in dread every step of some ball coming in at his back and out at his chest, and every minute drawing his breath to see whether it had gone from him. The members of the band, however, were satisfied with seeing him take flight and did not fire on him. They put Sancho, scarcely restored to his senses, on his ass and let him go after his master — not that he was sufficiently in his wits to guide the beast, but Dapple followed the footsteps of Rocinante, from whom he could not remain a moment separated. Don Quixote, having got some way off, looked back; and seeing Sancho coming, waited for him, since he perceived that no one was following him. The men of the troop stood their ground till night, and as the enemy did not come out to battle, they returned to their town exulting; and had they been aware of the ancient custom of the Greeks, they would have erected a trophy on the spot.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 28
paragraphs: Of matters that Benengeli says he who reads them will know, if he reads them with attention

When the brave man flees, treachery is manifest, and it is for wise men to reserve themselves for better occasions. This proved to be the case with Don Quixote who, giving way before the fury of the townsfolk and the hostile intentions of the angry troop, took to flight, and without a thought of Sancho or the danger he was leaving him in, retreated to such a distance as he thought made him safe. Sancho, lying across his ass, followed him, as has been said, and at length came up, by which time he had recovered his senses; and on joining him let himself drop off Dapple at Rocinante's feet, sore, bruised, and battered. Don Quixote dismounted to examine his wounds, but finding him whole from head to foot, he said to him, angrily enough, "In an evil hour did you take to braying, Sancho! Where have you learned that it's a good idea to mention the rope in the house of the man who's been hanged? To the music of brays what harmonies could you expect to get but cudgels? Give thanks to God, Sancho, that they signed the cross on you just now with a stick, and did not mark you _per signum crucis_ with a cutlass."

"I'm not equal to answering," said Sancho, "for I feel as if I were speaking through my shoulders. Let us mount and get away from here; I'll keep from braying, but not from saying that knights-errant fly and leave their good squires to be pounded like privet, or made meal of, at the hands of their enemies."

"He does not fly who retires," returned Don Quixote; "for I would have you know, Sancho, that the valour which is not based on a foundation of prudence is called rashness, and the exploits of the rash man are to be attributed rather to good fortune than to courage; and so I own that I retired, but not that I fled; and in this I have followed the example of many valiant men who have reserved themselves for better times; the histories are full of instances of this, but as it would not be any good to you or any pleasure to me, I won't recount them to you now."

Sancho was by this time mounted with the help of Don Quixote, who then mounted Rocinante himself, and at a leisurely pace they proceeded to take shelter in a grove which was in sight about a quarter of a league off. Every now and then Sancho gave vent to deep sighs and dismal groans; and on Don Quixote asking him what caused such acute suffering, he replied that, from the end of his backbone up to the nape of his neck, he was so sore it nearly drove him out of his senses.

"The cause of that soreness," said Don Quixote, "will no doubt be that, since the staff with which they struck you was a very long one, it caught you all the way down the back, where all the parts that are sore are located; and if it had reached any further you would be sorer still."

"By God," said Sancho, "your worship has relieved me of a great doubt and cleared up the point for me in elegant style! Body of me! is the cause of my soreness such a mystery that you have to tell me I am sore everywhere the staff hit me? If it was my ankles that hurt, there might be something in divining why they did, but it doesn't take much divining to know I'm sore where they thrashed me. By my faith, master mine, the ills of others hang by a hair; every day I'm discovering more and more how little I have to hope for from keeping company with your worship. For if this time you've allowed me to be drubbed, next time, or a hundred times more, we'll have the blanketings of the other day all over again, and all the other pranks which, if they've fallen on my shoulders now, will be thrown in my teeth by and by. I would do a great deal better — if I weren't an ignorant brute who'll never do any good all my life — I would do a great deal better, I say, to go home to my wife and children and support them and bring them up on whatever God may please to give me, instead of following your worship along roads that lead nowhere and paths that are no paths at all, with little to drink and less to eat. And then when it comes to sleeping! Measure out seven feet on the earth, brother squire, and if that's not enough for you, take as many more, for you may have it all your own way and stretch yourself to your heart's content. Oh that I could see burnt and turned to ashes the first man who meddled with knight-errantry — or at any rate the first who chose to be squire to such fools as all the knights-errant of past times must have been! Of those of today I say nothing, because, since your worship is one of them, I respect them, and because I know your worship knows a point more than the devil in all you say and think."

"I would lay a good wager with you, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that now you are talking on without anyone to stop you, you don't feel a pain in your whole body. Talk away, my son, say whatever comes into your head or mouth; for so long as you feel no pain, the irritation your impertinences give me will be a pleasure to me; and if you are so anxious to go home to your wife and children, God forbid that I should prevent you; you have money of mine — see how long it is since we left our village this third time, and how much you can and ought to earn every month, and pay yourself out of your own hand."

"When I worked for Tom Carrasco, the father of the bachelor Samson Carrasco that your worship knows," replied Sancho, "I used to earn two ducats a month besides my food; I can't tell what I can earn with your worship, though I know a knight-errant's squire has harder times of it than the one who works for a farmer; for after all, those of us who work for farmers, however much we toil all day, at worst, at night, we have our olla supper and sleep in a bed — which I haven't slept in since I've been in your worship's service, except for the short time we were in Don Diego de Miranda's house, and the feast I had with the skimmings I took off Camacho's pots, and what I ate, drank, and slept in Basilio's house; all the rest of the time I have been sleeping on the hard ground under the open sky, exposed to what they call the inclemencies of heaven, keeping life in me with scraps of cheese and crusts of bread, and drinking water either from the brooks or from the springs we come to on these by-paths we travel."
"I admit, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that all you say is true; how much, do you think, ought I to give you over and above what Tom Carrasco gave you?"

"I think," said Sancho, "that if your worship was to add on two reals a month I'd consider myself well paid — that is, as far as the wages of my labour go; but to make up to me for your worship's pledge and promise to give me the government of an island, it would be fair to add six reals more, making thirty in all."

"Very good," said Don Quixote; "it is twenty-five days since we left our village, so reckon up, Sancho, according to the wages you have made out for yourself, and see how much I owe you in proportion, and pay yourself, as I said before, out of your own hand."

"O body of me!" said Sancho, "but your worship is very much out in that reckoning; for when it comes to the promise of the island we must count from the day your worship promised it to me to this present hour we are at now."
"Well, how long is it, Sancho, since I promised it to you?" said Don Quixote.
"If I remember rightly," said Sancho, "it must be over twenty years, three days more or less."

Don Quixote gave himself a great slap on the forehead and began to laugh heartily, and said, "Why, I have not been wandering, either in the Sierra Morena or in the whole course of our sallies, but barely two months — and you say, Sancho, that it is twenty years since I promised you the island. I believe now you'd have all the money you have of mine go on your wages. If so, and if that is your pleasure, I give it to you now, once and for all, and much good may it do you; for so long as I see myself rid of such a good-for-nothing squire I'll be glad to be left a pauper without a rap. But tell me, you perverter of the squirely rules of knight-errantry, where have you ever seen or read that any knight-errant's squire made terms with his lord, 'you must give me so much a month for serving you'? Plunge, scoundrel, rogue, monster — for such I take you to be — plunge, I say, into the _mare magnum_ of their histories; and if you shall find that any squire ever said or thought what you have said now, I will let you nail it on my forehead, and give me, over and above, four sound slaps in the face. Turn the rein, or the halter, of your Dapple, and begone home; for one single step further you shall not make in my company. O bread thanklessly received! O promises ill-bestowed! O man more beast than human being! Now, when I was about to raise you to such a position that, in spite of your wife, they would call you 'my lord,' you are leaving me? You are going now when I had a firm and fixed intention of making you lord of the best island in the world? Well, as you yourself have said before now, honey is not for the mouth of the ass. Ass you are, ass you will be, and ass you will end when the course of your life is run; for I know it will come to its close before you perceive or discern that you are a beast."

Sancho regarded Don Quixote earnestly while he was giving him this rating, and was so touched by remorse that tears came to his eyes; and in a piteous and broken voice he said to him, "Master mine, I confess that, to be a complete ass, all I want is a tail; if your worship will only fix one on me, I'll look on it as rightly placed, and I'll serve you as an ass all the remaining days of my life. Forgive me and have pity on my folly, and remember I know but little; and if I talk much, it's more from infirmity than malice; but he who sins and mends commends himself to God."

"I should have been surprised, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "if you hadn't slipped some bit of a proverb into your speech. Well, well, I forgive you, provided you mend and don't show yourself in future so fond of your own interest, but try to be of good cheer and take heart, and encourage yourself to look forward to the fulfilment of my promises — which, by being delayed, does not become impossible."

Sancho said he would do so, and keep up his heart as best he could. They then entered the grove, and Don Quixote settled himself at the foot of an elm, and Sancho at the foot of a beech, for trees of this kind and others like them always have feet but no hands. Sancho passed the night in pain, for with the evening dews the blow of the staff made itself felt all the more. Don Quixote passed it in his never-failing meditations; but, for all that, they had some winks of sleep, and with the appearance of daylight they pursued their journey in quest of the banks of the famous Ebro, where what will be told in the following chapter befell them.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 29
paragraphs: Of the famous adventure of the enchanted bark

By stages already described or left undescribed, two days after quitting the grove Don Quixote and Sancho reached the river Ebro, and the sight of it was a great delight to Don Quixote as he contemplated and gazed at the charms of its banks, the clearness of its stream, the gentleness of its current, and the abundance of its crystal waters; and the pleasant view revived a thousand tender thoughts in his mind. Above all, he dwelt upon what he had seen in the cave of Montesinos; for though Master Pedro's ape had told him that of those things part was true, part false, he clung more to their truth than to their falsehood — the very reverse of Sancho, who held them all to be downright lies.

As they were going along this way, they spotted a small boat, without oars or any other gear, that lay at the water's edge tied to the trunk of a tree growing on the bank. Don Quixote looked all round, and seeing nobody, at once, without more ado, dismounted from Rocinante and told Sancho to get down from Dapple and tie both beasts securely to the trunk of a poplar or willow that stood there. Sancho asked the reason for this sudden dismounting and tying. Don Quixote replied, "You must know, Sancho, that this bark is plainly, and without any possibility of an alternative, calling and inviting me to enter it, and to go in it to give aid to some knight or other person of distinction in need of it, who is no doubt in some sore strait. For this is the way of the books of chivalry and of the enchanters who figure and speak in them. When a knight is involved in some difficulty from which he cannot be delivered except by the hand of another knight, though they may be at a distance of two or three thousand leagues or more one from the other, they either take him up on a cloud, or they provide a bark for him to get into, and in less than the twinkling of an eye they carry him where they will and where his help is required; and so, Sancho, this bark is placed here for the same purpose; this is as true as that it is now day, and before it passes, tie Dapple and Rocinante together, and then in God's hand be it to guide us; for I would not hold back from embarking, though barefoot friars were to beg me."

"As that's the case," said Sancho, "and your worship chooses to give in to these — I don't know if I may call them absurdities — at every turn, there's nothing for it but to obey and bow the head, bearing in mind the proverb, 'Do as your master bids you, and sit down to table with him;' but for all that, for the sake of easing my conscience, I warn your worship that it is my opinion this bark is no enchanted one, but belongs to some of the fishermen of the river, for they catch the best shad in the world here."

As Sancho said this, he tied the beasts, leaving them to the care and protection of the enchanters with sorrow enough in his heart. Don Quixote told him not to be uneasy about leaving the animals, "for he who would carry their owners over such longinquous roads and regions would take care to feed them."
"I don't understand that logiquous," said Sancho, "nor have I ever heard the word in all the days of my life."
"Longinquous," replied Don Quixote, "means far off; but it's no wonder you don't understand it, for you aren't bound to know Latin, like some who pretend to know it and don't."
"Now they are tied," said Sancho; "what are we to do next?"

"What?" said Don Quixote, "cross ourselves and weigh anchor; I mean, embark and cut the moorings by which the bark is held;" and the bark began to drift slowly away from the bank. But when Sancho saw himself somewhere about two yards out in the river, he began to tremble and give himself up for lost; but nothing distressed him more than hearing Dapple bray and seeing Rocinante struggling to get loose, and he said to his master, "Dapple is braying in grief at our leaving him, and Rocinante is trying to escape and plunge in after us. O dear friends, peace be with you, and may this madness that is taking us away from you, turned into sober sense, bring us back to you." And with that he fell weeping so bitterly that Don Quixote said to him, sharply and angrily, "What are you afraid of, cowardly creature? What are you weeping at, heart of butter-paste? Who is pursuing or molesting you, soul of a tame mouse? What do you want, unsatisfied in the very heart of abundance? Are you, perchance, tramping barefoot over the Riphaean mountains, instead of being seated on a bench like an archduke on the tranquil stream of this pleasant river, from which in a short space we shall come out upon the broad sea? But we must already have come out and gone seven hundred or eight hundred leagues; and if I had here an astrolabe to take the altitude of the pole, I could tell you how many we have travelled — though either I know little, or we have already crossed or shall shortly cross the equinoctial line, which parts the two opposite poles midway."
"And when we come to that line your worship speaks of," said Sancho, "how far shall we have gone?"

"Very far," said Don Quixote, "for of the three hundred and sixty degrees that this terraqueous globe contains, as computed by Ptolemy, the greatest cosmographer known, we shall have travelled one half when we come to the line I spoke of."
"By God," said Sancho, "your worship gives me a nice authority for what you say, putrid Dolly something transmogrified, or whatever it is."

Don Quixote laughed at the interpretation Sancho put upon "computed," and the name of the cosmographer Ptolemy, and said, "You must know, Sancho, that with the Spaniards and those who embark at Cadiz for the East Indies, one of the signs they have to show them when they have passed the equinoctial line I told you of is that the lice die upon everybody on board the ship, and not a single one is left, or to be found in the whole vessel if they gave its weight in gold for it; so, Sancho, you may as well pass your hand down your thigh, and if you come upon anything alive we shall be no longer in doubt; if not, then we have crossed."

"I don't believe a bit of it," said Sancho; "still, I'll do as your worship bids me; though I don't know what need there is for trying these experiments, for I can see with my own eyes that we have not moved five yards from the bank, or shifted two yards from where the animals are standing, for there are Rocinante and Dapple in the very same place where we left them; and keeping a watch as I am now, I swear by all that's good, we are not stirring or moving at the pace of an ant."

"Try the test I told you of, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and don't mind any other, for you know nothing about colures, lines, parallels, zodiacs, ecliptics, poles, solstices, equinoxes, planets, signs, bearings, or the measures of which the celestial and terrestrial spheres are composed. If you were acquainted with all these things, or any portion of them, you would see clearly how many parallels we have cut, what signs we have seen, and what constellations we have left behind and are now leaving behind. But again I tell you, feel and hunt, for I am certain you are cleaner than a sheet of smooth white paper."

Sancho felt, and passing his hand gently and carefully down to the hollow of his left knee, he looked up at his master and said, "Either the test is a false one, or we have not come to where your worship says, nor within many leagues of it."
"Why, how so?" asked Don Quixote; "have you come upon anything?"

"Ay, and somethings," replied Sancho; and shaking his fingers he washed his whole hand in the river along which the boat was quietly gliding in midstream, not moved by any occult intelligence or invisible enchanter, but simply by the current, just there smooth and gentle.

They now came in sight of some large water mills that stood in the middle of the river, and the instant Don Quixote saw them he cried out, "Do you see there, my friend? There stands the castle or fortress, where there is, no doubt, some knight in durance, or ill-used queen, or infanta, or princess, in whose aid I am brought here."
"What the devil city, fortress, or castle is your worship talking about, señor?" said Sancho; "don't you see that those are mills that stand in the river to grind corn?"

"Hold your peace, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "though they look like mills they are not so; I have already told you that enchantments transform things and change their proper shapes; I don't mean to say they really change them from one form into another, but that it seems as though they did, as experience proved in the transformation of Dulcinea, sole refuge of my hopes."

By this time, the boat, having reached the middle of the stream, began to move less slowly than before. The millers, when they saw the boat coming down the river and on the point of being sucked in by the draft of the wheels, ran out in haste — several of them, with long poles to stop it; and being all mealy, with faces and garments covered with flour, they presented a sinister appearance. They raised loud shouts, crying, "Devils of men, where are you going? Are you mad? Do you want to drown yourselves, or dash yourselves to pieces among these wheels?"

"Did I not tell you, Sancho," said Don Quixote at this, "that we had reached the place where I am to show what the might of my arm can do? See what ruffians and villains come out against me; see what monsters oppose me; see what hideous countenances come to frighten us! You shall soon see, scoundrels!" And then standing up in the boat he began in a loud voice to hurl threats at the millers, exclaiming, "Ill-conditioned and worse-counselled rabble, restore to liberty and freedom the person you hold in durance in this your fortress or prison, high or low, or of whatever rank or quality he may be; for I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, otherwise called the Knight of the Lions, for whom, by the disposition of heaven above, it is reserved to give a happy issue to this adventure;" and so saying he drew his sword and began making passes in the air at the millers, who, hearing but not understanding all this nonsense, strove to stop the boat, which was now getting into the rushing channel of the wheels. Sancho fell upon his knees devoutly appealing to heaven to deliver him from such imminent peril; which it did by the activity and quickness of the millers, who, pushing against the boat with their poles, stopped it — not, however, without overturning and throwing Don Quixote and Sancho into the water. Lucky it was for Don Quixote that he could swim like a goose, though the weight of his armour carried him twice to the bottom; and had it not been for the millers, who plunged in and hoisted them both out, it would have been Troy town with the pair of them. As soon as they were landed, more drenched than thirsty, Sancho went down on his knees and with clasped hands and eyes raised to heaven, prayed a long and fervent prayer to God to deliver him evermore from the rash projects and attempts of his master. The fishermen, the owners of the boat — which the mill-wheels had knocked to pieces — now came up, and seeing it smashed, they proceeded to strip Sancho and demand payment for it from Don Quixote; but he, with great calmness, just as if nothing had happened to him, told the millers and fishermen that he would pay for the bark most cheerfully, on condition that they delivered up to him, free and unhurt, the person or persons that were in durance in that castle of theirs.
"What persons or what castle are you talking of, madman? Are you for carrying off the people who come to grind corn in these mills?"

"That's enough," said Don Quixote to himself, "it would be preaching in the desert to attempt by entreaties to induce this rabble to do any virtuous action. In this adventure two mighty enchanters must have encountered one another, and one frustrates what the other attempts; one provided the bark for me, and the other upset me. God help us, this world is all machinations and schemes at cross purposes one with the other. I can do no more." And then turning toward the mills he said aloud, "Friends, whoever you are that are immured in that prison, forgive me that, to my misfortune and yours, I cannot deliver you from your misery; this adventure is doubtless reserved and destined for some other knight."

So saying he settled with the fishermen, and paid fifty reals for the boat, which Sancho handed over very much against the grain, saying, "With a couple more bark businesses like this we shall have sunk our whole capital."

The fishermen and the millers stood staring in amazement at the two figures, so very different to all appearance from ordinary men, and were wholly unable to make out the drift of the observations and questions Don Quixote addressed to them; and coming to the conclusion that they were madmen, they left them and betook themselves, the millers to their mills, and the fishermen to their huts. Don Quixote and Sancho returned to their beasts, and to their life of beasts, and so ended the adventure of the enchanted bark.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 30
paragraphs: Of Don Quixote's adventure with a fair huntress

They reached their beasts in low spirits and bad humour enough, knight and squire — Sancho particularly, for with him what touched the stock of money touched his heart, and when any was taken from him he felt as if he were robbed of the apples of his eyes. In short, without exchanging a word, they mounted and quitted the famous river — Don Quixote absorbed in thoughts of his love, Sancho in thinking of his advancement, which just then, it seemed to him, he was very far from securing; for, fool as he was, he saw clearly enough that his master's acts were all, or most of them, utterly senseless; and he began to cast about for an opportunity of retiring from his service and going home some day, without entering into any explanations or taking any farewell of him. Fortune, however, ordered matters in a fashion very much the opposite of what he contemplated.

It so happened that the next day toward sunset, on coming out of a wood, Don Quixote cast his eyes over a green meadow, and at the far end of it observed some people. Drawing nearer, he saw it was a hawking party. Coming closer, he distinguished among them a lady of graceful bearing, on a pure white palfrey or hackney, caparisoned with green trappings and a silver-mounted side-saddle. The lady was also in green, so richly and splendidly dressed that splendour itself seemed personified in her. On her left hand she bore a hawk — proof to Don Quixote's mind that she must be some great lady and the mistress of the whole hunting party, which was the fact. So he said to Sancho, "Run, Sancho my son, and tell that lady on the palfrey with the hawk that I, the Knight of the Lions, kiss the hands of her exalted beauty, and if her excellence will grant me leave I will go and kiss them in person and place myself at her service for anything that may be in my power and her highness may command; and mind, Sancho, how you speak, and take care not to thrust any of your proverbs into your message."
"You've got a likely one here to thrust any in!" said Sancho; "leave me alone for that! Why, this isn't the first time in my life I have carried messages to high and exalted ladies."
"Except that you carried to the lady Dulcinea," said Don Quixote, "I know not that you have carried any other, at least in my service."

"That is true," replied Sancho; "but pledges don't distress a good payer, and in a house where there's plenty, supper is soon cooked; I mean, there's no need of telling or warning me about anything; for I'm ready for everything and know a little of everything."
"That I believe, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "go and good luck to you, and God speed you."

Sancho went off at top speed, forcing Dapple out of his regular pace, and came to where the fair huntress was standing; and dismounting, he knelt before her and said, "Fair lady, that knight you see there, the Knight of the Lions by name, is my master, and I am a squire of his, and at home they call me Sancho Panza. This same Knight of the Lions, who not long since was called the Knight of the Rueful Countenance, sends by me to say may it please your highness to give him leave that, with your permission, approval, and consent, he may come and carry out his wishes, which are, as he says and I believe, to serve your exalted loftiness and beauty; and if you give it, your ladyship will do a thing that will redound to your honour, and he will receive a most distinguished favour and happiness."

"You have indeed, squire," said the lady, "delivered your message with all the formalities such messages require; rise up, for it isn't right that the squire of a knight so great as he of the Rueful Countenance — of whom we have heard a great deal here — should remain on his knees; rise, my friend, and tell your master he is welcome to the services of myself and the duke my husband, in a country house we have here."

Sancho got up, charmed as much by the beauty of the good lady as by her high-bred air and her courtesy, but above all by what she had said about having heard of his master, the Knight of the Rueful Countenance; for if she did not call him Knight of the Lions, it was no doubt because he had only just taken the name. "Tell me, brother squire," asked the duchess (whose title, however, is not known), "this master of yours, is he not one of whom there is a history extant in print, called 'The Ingenious Gentleman, Don Quixote of La Mancha,' who has for the lady of his heart a certain Dulcinea del Toboso?"

"He is the same, señora," replied Sancho; "and that squire of his who figures, or ought to figure, in the said history under the name of Sancho Panza, is myself — unless they have changed me in the cradle, I mean in the press."
"I am delighted at all this," said the duchess; "go, brother Panza, and tell your master that he is welcome to my estate, and that nothing could happen to me that could give me greater pleasure."

Sancho returned to his master mightily pleased with this gratifying answer, and told him everything the great lady had said to him, lauding to the skies in his rustic phrase her rare beauty, her graceful gaiety, and her courtesy. Don Quixote drew himself up briskly in his saddle, fixed himself in his stirrups, settled his visor, gave Rocinante the spur, and with an easy bearing advanced to kiss the hands of the duchess, who, having sent for the duke her husband, told him while Don Quixote was approaching all about the message; and as both of them had read the First Part of this history and from it were aware of Don Quixote's crazy turn, they awaited him with the greatest delight and anxiety to make his acquaintance, meaning to fall in with his humour and agree with everything he said, and, as long as he stayed with them, to treat him as a knight-errant, with all the ceremonies usual in the books of chivalry they had read — for they themselves were very fond of them.

Don Quixote now came up with his visor raised, and as he seemed about to dismount Sancho hurried to go and hold his stirrup for him; but in getting down off Dapple he was so unlucky as to hitch his foot in one of the ropes of the pack-saddle in such a way that he was unable to free it, and was left hanging by it with his face and chest on the ground. Don Quixote, who was not used to dismount without having the stirrup held, thinking Sancho had by this time come to hold it for him, threw himself off with a lurch and brought Rocinante's saddle after him — which was no doubt badly girthed — and saddle and he both came to the ground; not without embarrassment to him and abundant curses muttered between his teeth against the unlucky Sancho, who still had his foot in the shackles. The duke ordered his huntsmen to go to the help of knight and squire, and they raised Don Quixote, sorely shaken by his fall; and he, limping, advanced as best he could to kneel before the noble pair. This, however, the duke would by no means permit; on the contrary, dismounting from his horse, he went and embraced Don Quixote, saying, "I am grieved, Sir Knight of the Rueful Countenance, that your first experience on my ground should have been such an unfortunate one as we have seen; but the carelessness of squires is often the cause of worse accidents."

"What has happened to me in meeting you, mighty prince," replied Don Quixote, "cannot be unfortunate, even if my fall had not stopped short of the depths of the bottomless pit, for the glory of having seen you would have lifted me up and delivered me from it. My squire, God's curse upon him, is better at loosing his tongue in talking impertinence than at tightening the girths of a saddle to keep it steady; but however I may be, fallen or raised up, on foot or on horseback, I shall always be at your service and that of my lady the duchess, your worthy consort, worthy queen of beauty and paramount princess of courtesy."
"Gently, Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha," said the duke; "where my lady Doña Dulcinea del Toboso is, it is not right that other beauties should be praised."

Sancho, by this time released from his entanglement, was standing by, and before his master could answer he said, "There is no denying — and it must be maintained — that my lady Dulcinea del Toboso is very beautiful; but the hare jumps up where one least expects it; and I have heard say that what we call nature is like a potter that makes vessels of clay, and he who makes one fair vessel can as well make two, or three, or a hundred; I say so because, by my faith, my lady the duchess is in no way behind my mistress the lady Dulcinea del Toboso."

Don Quixote turned to the duchess and said, "Your highness may believe that never had knight-errant in this world a more talkative or a droller squire than I have, and he will prove the truth of what I say, if your highness is pleased to accept of my services for a few days."

To which the duchess answered, "that worthy Sancho is droll I consider a very good thing, because it is a sign that he is shrewd; for drollery and sprightliness, Señor Don Quixote, as you very well know, do not take up their abode with dull wits; and since good Sancho is droll and sprightly I here set him down as shrewd."
"And talkative," added Don Quixote.
"So much the better," said the duke, "for many droll things cannot be said in few words; but not to lose time in talking, come, great Knight of the Rueful Countenance —"
"Of the Lions, your highness must say," said Sancho, "for there is no Rueful Countenance nor any such character now."

"Of the Lions be it," continued the duke; "I say, let Sir Knight of the Lions come to a castle of mine close by, where he shall be given that reception which is due to so exalted a personage, and which the duchess and I are accustomed to give to all knights-errant who come there."

By this time Sancho had fixed and girthed Rocinante's saddle, and Don Quixote having got on his back and the duke having mounted a fine horse, they placed the duchess in the middle and set out for the castle. The duchess asked Sancho to come to her side, for she found infinite enjoyment in listening to his shrewd remarks. Sancho required no urging, but pushed himself in between them and the duke, who thought it rare good fortune to receive such a knight-errant and such a homely squire in their castle.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 31
paragraphs: Which treats of many great matters

Sancho's satisfaction was supreme at finding himself, as it seemed, an established favourite with the duchess. He was looking forward to discovering in her castle what he had found in Don Diego's house and Basilio's: he had always been fond of good living, and always seized any chance of feasting himself the moment one presented itself. The history tells us, then, that before they reached the country house or castle, the duke rode on ahead and instructed all his servants on how they were to treat Don Quixote. So the instant Don Quixote came up to the castle gates with the duchess, two lackeys or equerries, dressed in what they call morning gowns of fine crimson satin reaching down to their feet, hurried out, caught Don Quixote in their arms before he had seen or heard them, and said to him, "Your highness should go and help my lady the duchess down from her horse."

Don Quixote obeyed, and a great exchange of compliments followed between the two of them over the matter; but in the end the duchess's determination won, and she refused to dismount from her palfrey except in the arms of the duke, saying she did not consider herself worthy to impose so unnecessary a burden on so great a knight. At length the duke came out to help her down, and as they entered a spacious courtyard two beautiful young women came forward and threw a large mantle of the finest scarlet cloth over Don Quixote's shoulders. At the same instant all the galleries of the courtyard were lined with the menservants and maidservants of the household, crying, "Welcome, flower and cream of knight-errantry!" while all or most of them flung little pellets filled with scented water over Don Quixote and the duke and duchess. Don Quixote was utterly astonished at all this, and this was the first time he truly felt and believed himself to be a knight-errant in reality and not merely in his imagination, now that he saw himself treated in the same way he had read of such knights being treated in days of old.

Sancho, abandoning Dapple, hung on to the duchess and entered the castle, but feeling a twinge of conscience at having left the donkey on his own, he approached a respectable duenna who had come out with the rest to receive the duchess, and in a low voice he said to her, "Señora Gonzalez, or whatever your grace may be called—"

"I am called Doña Rodriguez de Grijalba," replied the duenna. "What is it you want, brother?" To which Sancho answered, "I'd be grateful if you could do me the favour of going out to the castle gate, where you'll find a grey donkey of mine; please have them put him in the stable, or put him there yourself, because the poor little beast is easily frightened and can't bear being alone at all."

"If the master is as wise as the servant," said the duenna, "we've struck a fine bargain. Be off with you, brother, and bad luck to you and to whoever brought you here. Go look after your donkey yourself — we, the duennas of this house, are not used to that sort of work."

"Well now, honestly," Sancho returned, "I've heard my master, who is the very treasure-house of stories, tell the story of Lancelot when he came from Britain, and he said that ladies waited on Lancelot and duennas waited on his horse. As for my donkey, I wouldn't trade him for Señor Lancelot's horse."
"If you're a comedian, brother," said the duenna, "save your jokes for somewhere they'll pass for wit and be paid for; from me you'll get nothing but a fig."
"At any rate it'll be a very ripe one," said Sancho, "because you won't lose the trick in years by even a point."

"Son of a bitch," said the duenna, blazing with anger, "whether I'm old or not is something I'll settle with God, not with you, you garlic-stuffed scoundrel!" — and she said it so loudly that the duchess heard her, and turning round and seeing the duenna in such a state of agitation, with her eyes flashing, asked her who she was quarrelling with.

"With this fellow here," said the duenna, "who has gone out of his way to demand that I go and put a donkey of his that's at the castle gate into the stable, holding it up to me as an example that they did the same I don't know where — that some ladies waited on one Lancelot, and duennas on his horse; and to top it all off, he called me old."

"That," said the duchess, "I would have considered the gravest insult that could be offered me." And addressing Sancho, she said, "You should know, friend Sancho, that Doña Rodriguez is very youthful, and she wears that hood more for the sake of authority and custom than because of her years."

"May all the rest of my years be unlucky," said Sancho, "if that's how I meant it. I only spoke because I'm so fond of my donkey, and I thought I couldn't commend him to a kinder-hearted person than the lady Doña Rodriguez."
Don Quixote, who was listening, said to him, "Is this appropriate conversation for the place, Sancho?"

"Señor," replied Sancho, "everyone has to mention what concerns him wherever he happens to be. I thought of Dapple here, and I spoke of him here; if I had thought of him in the stable I would have spoken there."

At which the duke observed, "Sancho is quite right, and there's no reason at all to find fault with him. Dapple shall be fed to his heart's content, and Sancho can rest easy — he'll be treated just as well as Sancho himself."

While this conversation, amusing to everyone except Don Quixote, was going on, they climbed the staircase and ushered Don Quixote into a chamber hung with rich gold cloth and brocade. Six young women relieved him of his armour and waited on him like pages, all of them prepared and instructed by the duke and duchess on what they were to do and how they were to treat Don Quixote, so that he might see and believe they were treating him like a knight-errant. When his armour was removed, there stood Don Quixote in his tight-fitting breeches and chamois doublet — lean, lanky, and long, with cheeks that looked as if they were kissing each other inside his mouth. He was such a figure that if the damsels waiting on him had not taken care to stifle their laughter (one of the particular instructions their master and mistress had given them), they would have burst out laughing. They asked him to let himself be undressed so they could put a shirt on him, but he absolutely refused, saying that modesty became knights-errant as much as valour did. However, he said they could give the shirt to Sancho. He shut himself in with Sancho in a room where there was a sumptuous bed, undressed, and put on the shirt; and then, finding himself alone with Sancho, he said to him, "Tell me, you newly fledged buffoon and old fool, do you think it right to offend and insult a duenna as deserving of reverence and respect as that one back there? Was that a moment to be thinking of your Dapple? Are these noble people likely to let the beasts fare badly when they treat their owners in such elegant style? For God's sake, Sancho, restrain yourself, and don't expose the threadbare weave so they can see what coarse, boorish stuff you're made of. Remember, sinner that you are, that a master is the more esteemed the more respectable and well-bred his servants are; and one of the greatest advantages princes have over other men is that they have servants as good as themselves to wait on them. Don't you see — shortsighted creature that you are, and unlucky mortal that I am! — that if they perceive you to be a coarse clown or a dull blockhead, they'll suspect me of being some impostor or swindler? No, no, Sancho my friend, keep clear, oh keep clear of these stumbling-blocks! Whoever lets himself become a chatterbox and a clown sinks into wretched buffoonery the first time he trips. Bridle your tongue, weigh your words before they escape your mouth, and bear in mind that we are now in quarters from which, by God's help and the strength of my arm, we shall come out mightily advanced in fame and fortune."

Sancho earnestly promised him he would keep his mouth shut and bite off his tongue before uttering a single word that wasn't entirely to the purpose and well considered, and told him he could rest easy on that point — it would never come out through Sancho who they really were.

Don Quixote got dressed, put on his baldric with his sword, threw the scarlet mantle over his shoulders, placed on his head a green satin cap the damsels had given him, and thus arrayed walked out into the great hall, where he found the damsels lined up in double file, the same number on each side, all with the equipment for washing his hands, which they presented to him with elaborate bows and ceremonies. Then twelve pages came in, together with the seneschal, to lead him to dinner, as his hosts were already waiting for him. They placed him in their midst and with great pomp and ceremony escorted him into another room, where a sumptuous table had been laid with just four place settings. The duchess and the duke came to the doorway to receive him, and with them a grave ecclesiastic — one of those who manage noblemen's households; one of those who, not being born great themselves, never know how to teach those who are how to behave as such; one of those who would have the greatness of great folk measured by their own narrowness of mind; one of those who, when they try to introduce economy into the household they run, lead it into pettiness. One of this sort, I say, must have been the grave churchman who came out with the duke and duchess to receive Don Quixote.

A great many polite speeches were exchanged, and at last, taking Don Quixote between them, they went to sit down at the table. The duke pressed Don Quixote to take the head of the table, and though he refused, the duke's pleas were so urgent he had to accept it.

The ecclesiastic sat down opposite him, and the duke and duchess at the sides. All this time Sancho stood by, gaping with amazement at the honour he saw shown to his master by these illustrious persons. Observing all the ceremonious back-and-forth between the duke and Don Quixote over who would take the head of the table, he said, "If your worship will give me leave, I'll tell you a story of what happened in my village about this business of seats."

The moment Sancho said this, Don Quixote trembled, sure he was about to come out with something foolish. Sancho glanced at him and, guessing his thoughts, said, "Don't worry that I'll go astray, señor, or say anything that isn't to the point. I haven't forgotten the advice your worship gave me just now about talking much or little, well or badly."
"I don't remember any of it, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "Say what you like, but say it quickly."
"Well then," said Sancho, "what I'm about to say is so true that my master Don Quixote, who is here present, will keep me from lying."
"Lie as much as you like for all I care, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "I'm not going to stop you, but think about what you're going to say."
"I've considered and reconsidered so much," said Sancho, "that the bell-ringer's in a safe berth — as will be seen by what follows."
"It would be a good idea," said Don Quixote, "if your highnesses would order them to throw this idiot out, because he'll spout a heap of nonsense."
"By the duke's life, Sancho is not to be taken away from me for a single moment," said the duchess. "I'm very fond of him, because I know he is very shrewd."

"May your holiness's days be shrewd ones too," said Sancho, "for the good opinion you have of my wit, though there's none in me. But the story I want to tell is this: there was an invitation given by a gentleman in my town, a very rich one, of good family — for he was one of the Alamos of Medina del Campo, married to Doña Mencia de Quiñones, the daughter of Don Alonso de Marañon, Knight of the Order of Santiago, who was drowned at the Herradura — the one there was that quarrel about years ago in our village, which my master Don Quixote was mixed up in, to the best of my recollection, the one in which Tomasillo the scapegrace, son of Balbastro the blacksmith, was wounded. Isn't all this true, master mine? On your life, say so, so these gentlefolk don't take me for some lying chatterbox."
"So far," said the ecclesiastic, "I take you to be more of a chatterbox than a liar; but I don't know what I'll take you for by the time you're done."

"You cite so many witnesses and proofs, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that I have no choice but to say you must be telling the truth. Get on with it, and cut the story short, because at this rate you won't reach the end for two days."

"He's not to cut it short," said the duchess. "On the contrary, to please me he is to tell it just as he knows it, even if he doesn't finish for six days; and if he took that long they would be the most pleasant days I ever spent."
"Well then, sirs, I say," Sancho went on, "that this same gentleman, whom I know as well as I know my own hands — it's not a bowshot from my house to his — invited a poor but respectable labourer—"
"Get on, brother," said the churchman; "at the rate you're going, your story won't end this side of the next world."

"I'll stop short of halfway, God willing," said Sancho. "And so I say, this labourer, coming to the house of the gentleman I mentioned, the one who had invited him — God rest his soul, he's dead now; and what's more they say he died the death of an angel, though I wasn't there, because just at that time I had gone off to reap at Tembleque—"
"On your life, my son," said the churchman, "hurry back from Tembleque, and finish your story without burying the gentleman, unless you want to make more funerals."
"Well then, it so happened," said Sancho, "that as the pair of them were about to sit down to table — and I can see them now plainer than ever—"

The duke and duchess were greatly entertained by the irritation the worthy churchman showed at the long-winded, halting way Sancho had of telling his story, while Don Quixote was burning with rage and vexation.

"So, as I was saying," Sancho continued, "as the pair of them were about to sit down to table — as I said — the labourer insisted that the gentleman take the head of the table, and the gentleman insisted that the labourer take it, because his orders had to be obeyed in his own house. But the labourer, who prided himself on his politeness and good breeding, would not on any account, until the gentleman, out of patience, put his hands on his shoulders and forced him down into the seat, saying, 'Sit down, you stupid lout, because wherever I sit will be the head for you.' And that's the story, and honestly, I don't think it's been brought up out of place here."

Don Quixote turned every colour, and on his sunburnt face it left him mottled like jasper. The duke and duchess suppressed their laughter so as not to humiliate Don Quixote completely, because they saw through Sancho's impertinence. To change the subject and keep Sancho from coming out with more absurdities, the duchess asked Don Quixote what news he had of the lady Dulcinea, and whether he had sent her any gifts of giants or villains lately, because surely he must have defeated a good many.

To which Don Quixote replied, "Señora, my misfortunes, though they had a beginning, will never have an end. I have defeated giants and I have sent her ruffians and villains; but where are they to find her, if she is enchanted and turned into the most ill-favoured peasant wench imaginable?"

"I don't know about that," said Sancho Panza. "To me she looks like the fairest creature in the world; at any rate, in nimbleness and jumping she won't yield to an acrobat. By my faith, señora duchess, she can spring from the ground onto the back of a donkey like a cat."
"You've seen her enchanted, Sancho?" asked the duke.
"Seen her? Well!" said Sancho. "Why, who the devil was it but me that first thought up the enchantment business in the first place? She's as enchanted as my father is."

The ecclesiastic, hearing them talk of giants and villains and enchantments, began to suspect this must be the Don Quixote of La Mancha whose story the duke was always reading. He had often rebuked the duke for it, telling him it was foolish to read such foolery. And becoming convinced his suspicion was correct, he turned to the duke and said very angrily, "Señor, your excellency will have to account to God for what this good man does. This Don Quixote, or Don Simpleton, or whatever his name is, cannot, I imagine, be quite such a blockhead as your excellency makes him out to be, holding out encouragement to him to keep going with his lunacies and follies." Then turning to address Don Quixote, he said, "And you, numskull — who put it into your head that you're a knight-errant, that you defeat giants and capture villains? Go your way and good luck to you. Go home and bring up your children if you have any, look after your business, and stop wandering about the world, gaping and making a laughing-stock of yourself to everyone who knows you and everyone who doesn't. In heaven's name, where did you discover that there are or ever were knights-errant? Where are there giants in Spain or villains in La Mancha, or enchanted Dulcineas, or any of the other silly things they tell about you?"

Don Quixote listened attentively to the reverend gentleman's words, and as soon as he saw he had finished speaking, regardless of the presence of the duke and duchess, he sprang to his feet with an angry look and an agitated face, and said — but the reply deserves a chapter of its own.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 32
paragraphs: About the reply Don Quixote gave his critic, with other incidents grave and droll

Don Quixote, then, having risen to his feet, trembling from head to foot like a man dosed with mercury, said in a hurried, agitated voice, "The place I am in, the presence I stand in, and the respect I have always had for the profession to which your worship belongs, hold and bind the hands of my just indignation. For these reasons, and because I know, as everyone knows, that a clergyman's weapon is the same as a woman's — the tongue — I will with mine engage in equal combat with your worship, from whom one might have expected good advice instead of foul abuse. Pious, well-meant reproof requires a different bearing and arguments of another sort; in any case, to have reproved me in public, and so roughly, oversteps the bounds of proper reproof — that comes better with gentleness than with rudeness. And it isn't fitting to call the sinner an outright blockhead and fool, without knowing anything about the sin being reproved. Come, tell me — for which of the stupidities you have observed in me do you condemn and abuse me, and order me home to look after my house and wife and children, without knowing whether I have any? Is nothing more needed than to wangle one's way into other people's houses to rule over the masters — and that, perhaps, after having been brought up in all the narrowness of some seminary, without ever having seen more of the world than may lie within twenty or thirty leagues around — to be fit to lay down the law rashly for chivalry, and pass judgment on knights-errant? Is it perhaps an idle occupation, or is the time ill-spent that is spent in roaming the world in quest, not of its pleasures, but of those arduous toils by which the good rise upwards to the abodes of everlasting life? If gentlemen, great lords, nobles, men of high birth, were to rate me a fool, I should take it as an irreparable insult; but I don't care a farthing if clerics who have never entered upon or trod the paths of chivalry should think me foolish. A knight I am, and a knight I will die, if it pleases the Most High. Some take the broad road of overweening ambition; others that of mean and servile flattery; others that of deceitful hypocrisy, and some that of true religion. But I, guided by my star, follow the narrow path of knight-errantry, and in pursuit of that calling I despise wealth, but not honour. I have redressed injuries, righted wrongs, punished insolences, defeated giants, and crushed monsters. I am in love, for no other reason than that knights-errant are required to be so; but though I am, I am no carnal-minded lover — I am one of the chaste, platonic sort. My intentions are always directed to worthy ends: to do good to all and evil to none. And if a man who means this, does this, and makes this his practice deserves to be called a fool, then it is for your highnesses to say, most excellent duke and duchess."

"Good, by God!" cried Sancho. "Say no more in your own defence, master mine, because there's nothing more in the world to be said, thought, or insisted on. And besides — when this gentleman denies, as he has, that there are or ever have been knights-errant in the world, is it any wonder if he knows nothing of what he's been talking about?"
"Are you, perhaps, brother," said the ecclesiastic, "that Sancho Panza they mention, the one to whom your master has promised an island?"

"Yes, I am," said Sancho, "and what's more, I'm one who deserves it as much as anyone. I'm one of the sort — 'Attach yourself to the good, and you'll be one of them,' and of those who 'Not with whom you're bred, but with whom you're fed,' and of those who 'Lean against a good tree, and good shade covers them.' I've leant on a good master, and I've been going about with him for months, and please God I'll turn out to be just like him; long life to him and long life to me, because he won't be short of empires to rule, or I of islands to govern."
"No, friend Sancho, certainly not," said the duke. "In the name of Señor Don Quixote, I confer on you the government of one — not a small one either — that I have at my disposal."
"Down on your knees, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and kiss the feet of his excellency for the favour he has granted you."

Sancho obeyed, and on seeing this the ecclesiastic stood up from the table completely out of temper, exclaiming, "By the gown I wear, I'm almost ready to say that your excellency is as big a fool as these sinners. No wonder they're mad, when people in their senses sanction their madness! I leave your excellency to them, because as long as they are in the house, I will stay in my own and spare myself the trouble of reproving what I cannot remedy." And without uttering another word or eating another bite, he stalked off, the entreaties of the duke and duchess being entirely useless to stop him — not that the duke said much to him, because he couldn't, on account of the laughter the man's uncalled-for anger provoked.

When he had stopped laughing, he said to Don Quixote, "You have replied on your own behalf so stoutly, Sir Knight of the Lions, that there's no need to seek further satisfaction for this, which, though it may look like an offence, is not so at all — because, as women can give no offence, no more can ecclesiastics, as you very well know."

"That is true," said Don Quixote, "and the reason is that he who is not liable to offence cannot give offence to anyone. Women, children, and ecclesiastics, since they cannot defend themselves, though they may receive offence cannot be insulted — because between the offence and the insult there is, as your excellency very well knows, this difference: the insult comes from someone capable of offering it, who does so, and maintains it; the offence may come from any quarter without carrying insult with it. To take an example: a man is standing unsuspectingly in the street, and ten others come up armed and beat him; he draws his sword and conducts himself like a man, but the number of his opponents makes it impossible for him to achieve his purpose and avenge himself; this man suffers an offence but not an insult. Another example will make the same thing plain: a man is standing with his back turned, another comes up and strikes him, and after striking him takes to flight without waiting an instant, and the first man pursues him but does not overtake him; the one who received the blow received an offence, but not an insult, because an insult must be maintained. If the man who struck him, even though he did so sneakingly and treacherously, had drawn his sword and stood and faced him, then the one who was struck would have received offence and insult at the same time — offence because he was struck treacherously, insult because the striker maintained what he had done, standing his ground without running away. And so, according to the laws of the accursed duel, I may have received offence, but not insult, since neither women nor children can maintain it, nor can they wound, nor have they any way of standing their ground — and it's just the same with those who belong to religion. These three sorts of persons are without arms offensive or defensive, and so, although by nature they are bound to defend themselves, they have no right to offend anybody. And although I said just now that I might have received offence, I now say certainly not, because he who cannot receive an insult can still less give one. For these reasons I ought not to feel, nor do I feel, aggrieved at what that good man said to me. I only wish he had stayed a little longer, so I might have shown him the mistake he makes in supposing and maintaining that there are not and never have been any knights-errant in the world; if Amadis or any of his countless descendants had heard him say as much, I am sure it would not have gone well with his worship."

"I'll take my oath of that," said Sancho. "They would have given him a slash that would have split him from top to toe like a pomegranate or a ripe melon; they were just the fellows to put up with jokes of that sort! By my faith, I'm certain if Reinaldos of Montalban had heard the little man's words, he'd have given him such a smack on the mouth that he wouldn't have spoken for the next three years. Let him tackle them, and he'll see how he gets out of their hands!"
The duchess, listening to Sancho, was ready to die laughing, and in her own mind she set him down as droller and madder than his master; and there were quite a few just then who shared that opinion.

Don Quixote finally calmed down, and dinner came to an end, and as the tablecloth was being cleared, four damsels came in: one with a silver basin, another with a jug also of silver, a third with two fine white towels over her shoulder, and the fourth with her arms bared to the elbows and in her white hands (white they certainly were) a round ball of Naples soap. The one with the basin approached, and with arch composure and impudence thrust it under Don Quixote's chin. Wondering at such a ceremony, he said never a word, supposing it was the custom of that country to wash beards instead of hands. So he stretched his out as far as he could, and at that instant the jug began to pour and the damsel with the soap rubbed his beard briskly, raising snowflakes — for the soap lather was no less white — not only over his beard but all over his face, even over the eyes of the submissive knight, so that he was forced to keep them shut. The duke and duchess, who had known nothing about this, waited to see how the strange washing would end. The barber-damsel, when she had him a hand's breadth deep in lather, pretended there was no more water, and told the one with the jug to go and fetch some, while Señor Don Quixote waited. She did so, and Don Quixote was left the strangest and most ridiculous figure imaginable. Everyone present — and there were quite a few — was watching him, and as they saw him there with half a yard of neck on display, uncommonly brown, his eyes shut, and his beard full of soap, it was a great wonder, and only by enormous self-discipline, that they were able to keep from laughing. The damsels, the engineers of the joke, kept their eyes down, not daring to look at their master and mistress; and as for the duke and duchess, laughter and anger struggled within them, and they didn't know what to do — whether to punish the audacity of the girls or to reward them for the amusement they had had from seeing Don Quixote in such a state.

At length the damsel with the jug returned and they finished washing Don Quixote, and the one carrying the towels very deliberately wiped him and dried him; and all four together, making him a profound bow and curtsy, were about to leave when the duke, lest Don Quixote see through the joke, called out to the one with the basin, saying, "Come and wash me, and make sure there's water enough." The girl, sharp-witted and quick, came and placed the basin for the duke just as she had for Don Quixote, and they soon had him well soaped and washed, and after wiping him dry they made their bow and withdrew. It came out afterwards that the duke had sworn that if they had not washed him as they had Don Quixote, he would have punished them for their impudence — which they cleverly atoned for by soaping him as well.

Sancho watched the washing ceremony very attentively and said to himself, "God bless me, if only it were the custom in this country to wash squires' beards too as well as knights'. Because by God and on my soul, I want it badly; and if they gave me a scrape of the razor besides, I'd take it as an even greater kindness."
"What are you saying to yourself, Sancho?" asked the duchess.

"I was saying, señora," he replied, "that in the courts of other princes, I've always heard that when the cloth is taken away, they give water for the hands, but not lye for the beard; and that shows it's good to live long so you can see a lot. To be sure they say too that whoever lives a long life must endure a lot of evil, though to endure a washing of that sort is pleasure rather than pain."
"Don't be uneasy, friend Sancho," said the duchess. "I'll see to it that my damsels wash you, and even put you in the tub if necessary."
"I'll settle for the beard," said Sancho, "at least for now; and as for the future, God has decided what will be."
"Attend to worthy Sancho's request, seneschal," said the duchess, "and do exactly what he wishes."

The seneschal replied that Señor Sancho would be obeyed in everything; and with that he went off to dinner and took Sancho along with him, while the duke and duchess and Don Quixote remained at the table discussing a great variety of things, all bearing on the calling of arms and knight-errantry.

The duchess begged Don Quixote, since he seemed to have a sharp memory, to describe and portray for her the beauty and features of the lady Dulcinea del Toboso, because, judging by what rumour trumpeted abroad of her beauty, she felt sure Dulcinea must be the fairest creature in the world, indeed in all La Mancha.

Don Quixote sighed on hearing the duchess's request, and said, "If I could pluck out my heart and lay it on a plate on this table here before your highness's eyes, it would spare my tongue the pain of telling what can hardly be thought, for in it your excellency would see her portrayed in full. But why should I attempt to depict and describe in detail, feature by feature, the beauty of the peerless Dulcinea — a burden worthy of other shoulders than mine, an enterprise in which the brushes of Parrhasius, Timantes, and Apelles, and the chisel of Lysippus ought to be employed, to paint it in pictures and carve it in marble and bronze, and Ciceronian and Demosthenian eloquence to sound its praises?"
"What does Demosthenian mean, Señor Don Quixote?" said the duchess. "It's a word I never heard in all my life."
"Demosthenian eloquence," said Don Quixote, "means the eloquence of Demosthenes, as Ciceronian means that of Cicero, who were the two most eloquent orators in the world."

"True," said the duke; "you must have lost your wits to ask such a question. Nevertheless, Señor Don Quixote would greatly gratify us if he would depict her for us; never fear, even in an outline or sketch she'll be something to make the fairest envious."

"I would do so, certainly," said Don Quixote, "had she not been blurred to my mind's eye by the misfortune that fell upon her a short time ago — one of such a nature that I am more ready to weep over it than to describe it. Your highnesses must know that, going a few days back to kiss her hands and receive her blessing, approval, and permission for this third sally, I found her altogether a different being from the one I sought. I found her enchanted and changed from a princess into a peasant, from fair to foul, from an angel into a devil, from fragrant to foul-smelling, from refined to clownish, from a dignified lady into a leaping tomboy — in a word, from Dulcinea del Toboso into a coarse Sayago wench."

"God bless me!" cried the duke aloud at this. "Who can have done the world such an injury? Who can have robbed it of the beauty that gladdened it, of the grace and gaiety that charmed it, of the modesty that gave it lustre?"

"Who?" replied Don Quixote. "Who could it be but some malignant enchanter, one of the many who persecute me out of envy — that accursed race born into the world to obscure and bring to nothing the achievements of the good, and to glorify and exalt the deeds of the wicked? Enchanters have persecuted me, enchanters persecute me still, and enchanters will continue to persecute me until they have sunk me and my lofty chivalry in the deep abyss of oblivion; and they injure and wound me where they know I feel it most. Because to deprive a knight-errant of his lady is to deprive him of the eyes he sees with, of the sun that gives him light, of the food by which he lives. I've said it many times before, and I say it once more now: a knight-errant without a lady is like a tree without leaves, a building without a foundation, or a shadow without the body that casts it."

"There's no denying it," said the duchess. "But still, if we are to believe the history of Don Quixote that has come out here lately to general applause, it is to be inferred from it, if I'm not mistaken, that you never saw the lady Dulcinea, and that she is nothing in the world but an imaginary lady — one you yourself begot and gave birth to in your brain, and adorned with whatever charms and perfections you chose."

"There's a good deal to be said on that point," said Don Quixote. "God knows whether there is a Dulcinea in the world or not, or whether she is imaginary or not imaginary; these are matters whose proof must not be pushed to extreme lengths. I have not begotten nor given birth to my lady, though I see her as she has to be — a lady who contains in herself all the qualities that would make her famous throughout the world: beautiful without blemish, dignified without haughtiness, tender and yet modest, gracious from courtesy and courteous from good breeding, and finally, of exalted lineage, because beauty shines forth and excels with a higher degree of perfection in those of good blood than in the fair of low birth."

"That is true," said the duke. "But Señor Don Quixote will give me leave to say what I am compelled to say by the story of his exploits that I've read, from which one infers that, granting there is a Dulcinea in El Toboso, or out of it, and that she is in the highest degree beautiful as you have described her to us, as for the loftiness of her lineage she is not on a par with the Orianas, Alastrajareas, Madasimas, or others of that sort, with whom, as you well know, the histories abound."

"To that I may reply," said Don Quixote, "that Dulcinea is the daughter of her own deeds, that virtues rectify blood, and that lowly virtue is more to be regarded and esteemed than exalted vice. Besides, Dulcinea has something in her that may raise her to be a crowned and sceptred queen — because the merit of a fair and virtuous woman is capable of performing greater miracles than that. And though not formally, she virtually has higher fortunes within herself."

"I declare, Señor Don Quixote," said the duchess, "that in everything you say, you proceed most cautiously and with the bridle in hand, as the saying goes. From now on I'll believe in her myself, and I'll see to it that everyone in my house believes — even my lord the duke if necessary — that there is a Dulcinea in El Toboso, that she is alive today, that she is beautiful and nobly born and deserves to have such a knight as Señor Don Quixote in her service, which is the highest praise I have it in my power to give her, or that I can think of. But I can't help having a small doubt, and a certain grudge against Sancho Panza. The doubt is this: the aforesaid history declares that the said Sancho Panza, when he carried a letter on your worship's behalf to the said lady Dulcinea, found her sifting a sack of wheat; and what's more, it says it was red wheat — a thing which makes me doubt the loftiness of her lineage."

To this Don Quixote made answer, "Señora, your highness must know that everything, or almost everything, that happens to me transcends the ordinary limits of what happens to other knights-errant, whether it's directed by the inscrutable will of destiny, or by the malice of some jealous enchanter. Now it's an established fact that all or most famous knights-errant have some special gift — one is invulnerable to enchantment, another is made of such impenetrable flesh that he cannot be wounded, like the famous Roland, one of the twelve peers of France, of whom it's said he could not be wounded except in the sole of his left foot, and only with the point of a stout pin and no other sort of weapon. And so, when Bernardo del Carpio slew him at Roncesvalles, finding that he couldn't wound him with steel, he lifted him up from the ground in his arms and strangled him, calling to mind in good time the death Hercules inflicted on Antaeus, the fierce giant said to be the son of Terra. I would infer from what I've mentioned that perhaps I may have some gift of this kind — not that of being invulnerable, because experience has proved to me many times that I am of tender flesh and not at all impenetrable; nor that of being proof against enchantment, because I've already seen myself thrust into a cage in which all the world would not have been able to confine me except by force of enchantments. But since I delivered myself from that one, I'm inclined to believe there's no other that can harm me. And so, these enchanters, seeing they can't exert their vile craft against my person, take revenge on what I love most, and try to rob me of life by maltreating that of Dulcinea, in whom I live. And therefore I am convinced that when my squire carried my message to her, they changed her into a common peasant girl, engaged in such a mean occupation as sifting wheat; but as I have already said, that wheat was not red wheat, nor wheat at all, but grains of oriental pearl. And as a proof of all this, I must tell your highnesses that, coming to El Toboso a short time ago, I was altogether unable to find the palace of Dulcinea; and the next day, though Sancho my squire saw her in her own proper shape, which is the fairest in the world, to me she appeared to be a coarse, ill-favoured farm-girl, by no means well-spoken either — she who is propriety itself.
