They travel nearly all over it, and there is no town out of which they do not go full up of meat and drink, as the saying is, and with a real, at least, in money, and they come off at the end of their travels with more than a hundred crowns saved, which, changed into gold, they smuggle out of the kingdom either in the hollow of their staves or in the patches of their pilgrim's cloaks or by some device of their own, and carry to their own country in spite of the guards at the posts and passes where they are searched. Now my purpose is, Sancho, to carry away the treasure I left buried, which, since it is outside the town, I shall be able to do without risk, and to write, or cross over from Valencia, to my daughter and wife, who I know are at Algiers, and find some means of bringing them to some French port and from there to Germany, there to await whatever it may be God's will to do with us; for, after all, Sancho, I know well that Ricota my daughter and Francisca Ricota my wife are Catholic Christians, and though I am not so much so, still I am more of a Christian than a Moor, and it is always my prayer to God that he will open the eyes of my understanding and show me how I am to serve him; but what amazes me and I cannot understand is why my wife and daughter should have gone to Barbary rather than to France, where they could live as Christians."

To this Sancho replied, "Remember, Ricote, that may not have been open to them, for Juan Tiopieyo your wife's brother took them, and being a true Moor he went where he could go most easily; and another thing I can tell you — it is my belief you are going in vain to look for what you have left buried, for we heard they took from your brother-in-law and your wife a great quantity of pearls and money in gold which they had brought to be inspected."

"That may be," said Ricote; "but I know they did not touch my hoard, for I did not tell them where it was, for fear of accidents; and so, if you will come with me, Sancho, and help me to take it away and conceal it, I will give you two hundred crowns with which you may relieve your needs, and, as you know, I know they are many."

"I would do it," said Sancho; "but I am not at all covetous, for I gave up an office this morning in which, if I had been, I might have made the walls of my house of gold and dined off silver plates before six months were out; and so for this reason, and because I feel I would be guilty of treason to my king if I helped his enemies, I would not go with you, even if instead of promising me two hundred crowns you were to give me four hundred here in hand."
"And what office is this you've given up, Sancho?" asked Ricote.
"I have given up being governor of an island," said Sancho, "and such a one, faith, as you won't find the like of easily."
"And where is this island?" said Ricote.
"Where?" said Sancho. "Two leagues from here, and it is called the island of Barataria."
"Nonsense, Sancho," said Ricote; "islands are away out in the sea; there are no islands on the mainland."

"What? No islands!" said Sancho. "I tell you, friend Ricote, I left it this morning, and yesterday I was governing there as I pleased like a sagittarius; but for all that I gave it up, for it seemed to me a dangerous office, a governor's."
"And what have you gained by the government?" asked Ricote.

"I have gained," said Sancho, "the knowledge that I am no good for governing, unless it is a drove of cattle, and that the riches to be got by these governments are got at the cost of one's rest and sleep — ay, and even one's food; for in islands the governors must eat little, especially if they have doctors to look after their health."

"I don't understand you, Sancho," said Ricote; "but it seems to me all nonsense you're talking. Who would give you islands to govern? Is there any shortage in the world of cleverer men than you for governors? Hold your peace, Sancho, and come back to your senses, and consider whether you will come with me as I said to help me to take away the treasure I left buried (for indeed it may be called a treasure, it is so large), and I will give you wherewithal to keep you, as I told you."

"And I've told you already, Ricote, that I will not," said Sancho; "let it content you that by me you shall not be betrayed, and go your way in God's name and let me go mine; for I know that well-gotten gain may be lost, but ill-gotten gain is lost, itself and its owner likewise."
"I will not press you, Sancho," said Ricote; "but tell me, were you in our village when my wife and daughter and brother-in-law left it?"

"I was so," said Sancho; "and I can tell you your daughter left it looking so lovely that all the village turned out to see her, and everybody said she was the fairest creature in the world. She wept as she went, and embraced all her friends and acquaintances and those who came out to see her, and she begged them all to commend her to God and Our Lady his mother, and this in such a touching way that it made me weep myself, though I'm not much given to tears commonly; and, faith, many a one would have liked to hide her, or go out and carry her off on the road; but the fear of going against the king's command kept them back. The one who showed himself most moved was Don Pedro Gregorio, the rich young heir you know of, and they say he was deep in love with her; and since she left he has not been seen in our village again, and we all suspect he has gone after her to steal her away, but so far nothing has been heard of it."

"I always had a suspicion that gentleman had a passion for my daughter," said Ricote; "but as I felt sure of my Ricota's virtue, it gave me no uneasiness to know that he loved her; for you must have heard it said, Sancho, that the Morisco women seldom or never engage in love affairs with the old Christians; and my daughter, who I fancy thought more of being a Christian than of lovemaking, would not trouble herself about the attentions of this heir."
"God grant it," said Sancho, "for it would be a bad business for both of them; but now let me be off, friend Ricote, for I want to reach where my master Don Quixote is tonight."

"God be with you, brother Sancho," said Ricote; "my comrades are beginning to stir, and it is time, too, for us to continue our journey." And then they both embraced, and Sancho mounted Dapple, and Ricote leant upon his staff, and so they parted.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 55
paragraphs: What happened to Sancho on the road, and other things that cannot be surpassed

His long delay with Ricote kept Sancho from reaching the duke's castle that day, though he was within half a league of it when night, somewhat dark and cloudy, overtook him. As it was summer, that did not trouble him much, and he turned off the road meaning to wait for morning; but his bad luck and hard fate so arranged it that, while he was looking for a comfortable spot, he and Dapple fell into a deep, dark hole among some very old ruined buildings. As he fell he commended himself with all his heart to God, convinced he would not stop until he hit the bottom of the bottomless pit. But it didn't turn out that way: at little more than three times a man's height Dapple struck bottom, and Sancho found himself sitting on him without the slightest hurt or scrape. He felt himself all over and held his breath to check whether he was sound or had a hole punched in him somewhere, and finding himself whole and in perfect health he poured out thanks to God our Lord for the mercy shown him, since he had been sure he was broken into a thousand pieces. He also ran his hands along the walls of the pit to see if he could get out without help, but they were quite smooth and offered no hold anywhere, which distressed him terribly — especially when he heard how piteously and mournfully Dapple was bemoaning himself, and no wonder he complained, nor was it bad temper, for in truth he was in a very poor state. "Alas," said Sancho, "what unexpected disasters happen at every turn to those who live in this miserable world! Who would have said that a man who saw himself yesterday seated on a throne, governor of an island, ordering servants and vassals about, would see himself today buried in a pit without a soul to help him, without servant or vassal to come to his rescue? Here we must perish of hunger, my ass and I, if indeed we don't die first, he of his bruises and injuries, and I of grief and sorrow. At any rate I won't be as lucky as my master Don Quixote of La Mancha, when he went down into the cave of that enchanted Montesinos, where he found people who made more fuss over him than if he had been in his own house — they say he came in for a table laid out and a bed ready made. There he saw fair and pleasant visions, but here I expect I'll see toads and adders. Unlucky wretch that I am, what an end my follies and fancies have come to! They'll dig up my bones out of this, when heaven wills that I'm found, picked clean, white and polished, and my good Dapple's with them, and by that, perhaps, it will be discovered who we are, at least by those who have heard that Sancho Panza never parted from his ass, nor his ass from Sancho Panza. Unlucky wretches, I say again, that our hard fate should not let us die in our own country and among our own people, where if there was no remedy for our misfortune, at least there would be someone to grieve over it and to close our eyes as we passed away! O comrade and friend, how badly have I repaid your faithful service! Forgive me, and beg Fortune, as best you can, to deliver us out of this miserable strait we are both in; and I promise to set a crown of laurel on your head, and make you look like a poet laureate, and give you double feeds."

In this strain Sancho bewailed himself, and his ass listened but never answered a word, such was the distress and anguish the poor beast was in. At last, after a night spent in bitter moaning and lamentation, day came, and by its light Sancho saw it was wholly impossible to climb out of that pit without help, and he fell to bemoaning his fate and shouting loudly to find out if anyone was within hearing; but all his shouting was crying in the wilderness, for there was not a soul anywhere nearby to hear him, and at last he gave himself up for dead. Dapple was lying on his back, and Sancho got him to his feet, which he could barely keep; and then taking a piece of bread out of his saddlebags that had shared their fortunes in the fall, he gave it to the ass, who was not at all sorry to have it, and said to him as if he understood, "With bread all sorrows are less."

Then he noticed on one side of the pit a hole large enough to admit a person if he stooped and squeezed himself small. Sancho went over and crept through, and found it wide and spacious inside, which he was able to see because a ray of sunlight that came through what you might call the roof showed it all plainly. He saw too that it opened out and widened into another spacious cavity; so he made his way back to where the ass was, and with a stone began to pick the clay away from the hole until in a short time he had made room for the beast to pass easily. Then taking him by the halter, he set off through the cavern to see if there was any way out at the other end. He advanced, sometimes in the dark, sometimes without light, but never without fear. "God Almighty help me!" he said to himself; "what is a misadventure to me would make a fine adventure for my master Don Quixote. He would have been sure to take these depths and dungeons for flowery gardens or the palaces of Galiana, and would have counted on emerging from this darkness and confinement into some blooming meadow; but I, unlucky as I am, hopeless and dispirited, expect at every step another pit deeper than the first to open under my feet and swallow me up for good — 'welcome evil, if you come alone.'"

In this way and with these reflections he seemed to himself to have travelled a bit more than half a league when at last he made out a faint glimmer that looked like daylight finding its way in on one side, showing that this road, which seemed to him the road to the other world, led to some opening.

Here Cide Hamete leaves him and returns to Don Quixote, who in high spirits and contentment was looking forward to the day set for the battle he was to fight with the man who had robbed Doña Rodriguez's daughter of her honour, for whom he hoped to obtain satisfaction for the wrong and injury so shamefully done her. So it happened that, having ridden out one morning to practise and exercise what he would have to do in the encounter awaiting him the next day, as he was putting Rocinante through his paces or pressing him to the charge, he brought the horse's hooves so close to a pit that, but for reining him in tightly, there would have been no avoiding a fall into it. He pulled him up without going down, and coming a little closer examined the hole without dismounting; but as he was looking at it he heard loud cries coming from below, and by listening carefully was able to make out that whoever was uttering them was saying, "Hey, up there! is there any Christian who hears me, or any charitable gentleman who will take pity on a sinner buried alive, on a disgoverned, unfortunate governor?"

It struck Don Quixote that it was Sancho Panza's voice he heard, at which he was taken aback and astonished, and raising his own voice as much as he could, he called out, "Who is down there? Who is that complaining?"

"Who should be here, or who should complain," came the answer, "but the forlorn Sancho Panza, for his sins and for his bad luck governor of the island of Barataria, squire-that-was to the famous knight Don Quixote of La Mancha?"

When Don Quixote heard this his astonishment was redoubled and his agitation grew greater than ever, for it occurred to him that Sancho must be dead and his soul in torment down there; and carried away by the idea he exclaimed, "I conjure you by everything I as a Catholic Christian can conjure you by, tell me who you are; and if you are a soul in torment, tell me what you would have me do for you, for since my profession is to give aid and succour to those in need in this world, it will extend also to aiding and succouring the distressed of the other world, who cannot help themselves."
"In that case," the voice answered, "your worship who speaks to me must be my master Don Quixote of La Mancha; in fact, from the tone of the voice it is plainly nobody else."

"Don Quixote I am," replied Don Quixote, "he whose profession it is to aid and succour the living and the dead in their needs; therefore tell me who you are, for you are keeping me in suspense — because if you are my squire Sancho Panza, and you are dead, since the devils have not carried you off and by God's mercy you are in purgatory, our holy mother the Roman Catholic Church has intercessory means enough to release you from the pains you are in; and I for my part will plead with her to that end, as far as my resources will allow. Without further delay, then, declare yourself and tell me who you are."

"By all that's good," was the answer, "and by the birth of whomever your worship chooses, I swear, Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha, that I am your squire Sancho Panza, and that I've never died in all my life; but that, having given up my government for reasons that would take more time to explain, I fell last night into this pit where I am now, and Dapple is my witness and won't let me lie about it, because here he is with me, what's more."
And that wasn't all: you would have thought the ass understood what Sancho said, because at that very moment he began to bray so loudly that the whole cave rang.

"Splendid testimony!" exclaimed Don Quixote; "I know that bray as well as if I were its mother, and your voice too, my Sancho. Wait while I go to the duke's castle, which is close by, and I'll bring someone to pull you out of this pit your sins no doubt have landed you in."
"Go, your worship," said Sancho, "and come back quickly, for God's sake; I can't stand being buried alive any longer, and I'm dying of fear."

Don Quixote left him and hurried to the castle to tell the duke and duchess what had happened to Sancho, and they were not a little astonished at it; they could easily understand his having fallen, given the confirming fact of a cave that had been there since time immemorial, but they couldn't imagine how he had quit the government without their getting any notice of his coming. To cut it short, they fetched ropes and tackle, as the saying goes, and by dint of many hands and much labour they hauled Dapple and Sancho Panza out of the darkness into the light of day. A student who saw him remarked, "That's the way all bad governors should come out of their governments, as this sinner comes out of the depths of the pit — dead with hunger, pale, and I'd guess without a penny to his name."

Sancho overheard him and said, "It's eight or ten days, brother growler, since I entered upon the government of the island they gave me, and in all that time I never had a bellyful of food, not even for an hour; doctors persecuted me and enemies crushed my bones; nor had I any chance to take bribes or collect taxes; and if that's the case, as it is, I don't think I deserve to come out in this fashion; but 'man proposes and God disposes'; and God knows what is best, and what suits each one best; and 'as the occasion, so the behaviour'; and 'let nobody say "I won't drink of this water"'; and 'where you think there are bacon flitches, there are no pegs to hang them on'; God knows my meaning and that's enough; I say no more, though I could."

"Don't be angry or annoyed at what you hear, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "or there'll never be an end of it; keep a safe conscience and let them say what they like, for trying to stop slanderers' tongues is like trying to put gates on the open plain. If a governor comes out of his government rich, they say he's been a thief; and if he comes out poor, that he's been a fool and a blockhead."
"They'll be pretty sure this time," said Sancho, "to set me down as a fool rather than a thief."

Talking thus, and surrounded by boys and a crowd of people, they reached the castle, where in one of the corridors the duke and duchess stood waiting for them; but Sancho would not go up to see the duke until he had first stabled Dapple, for he said the poor beast had passed a very bad night in his last quarters. Then he went upstairs to see his lord and lady, and kneeling before them said, "Because it was your highnesses' pleasure, and not from any merit of my own, I went to govern your island of Barataria, which 'I entered naked, and naked I find myself; I neither lose nor gain.' Whether I have governed well or ill, I have had witnesses who will say what they please. I have answered questions, I have decided cases, and always dying of hunger, for Doctor Pedro Recio of Tirteafuera, the island's and governor's doctor, would have it so. Enemies attacked us by night and put us in a great fix, but the people of the island say they came out safe and victorious by the might of my arm — may God give them as much health as there is truth in what they say. In short, during that time I have weighed the cares and responsibilities of governing, and by my reckoning my shoulders can't bear them, nor are they a load for my loins or arrows for my quiver; and so, before the government threw me over, I preferred to throw the government over; and yesterday morning I left the island as I found it, with the same streets, houses, and roofs it had when I came in. I asked no loan of anyone, nor did I try to fill my pocket; and though I meant to make some useful laws, I made hardly any, since I was afraid they wouldn't be kept; for in that case it comes to the same thing to make them or not to make them. I quit the island, as I said, with no escort except my ass; I fell into a pit, I pressed on through it, until this morning by the light of the sun I saw a way out, but not so easy a one but that, had not heaven sent me my master Don Quixote, I'd have stayed there till the end of the world. So now my lord and lady duke and duchess, here is your governor Sancho Panza, who in the bare ten days he has held the government has come by the knowledge that he wouldn't give anything to be governor, not to say of an island, but of the whole world; and that point being settled, kissing your worships' feet, and imitating the game of the boys when they say, 'jump and give me one,' I take a leap out of the government and pass into the service of my master Don Quixote; for after all, though there I eat my bread in fear and trembling, at least I eat my fill; and for my part, so long as I'm full, it's all the same to me whether it's with carrots or with partridges."

Here Sancho brought his long speech to an end, Don Quixote having been the whole time in dread of his uttering a host of absurdities; and when he found him leave off with so few, he gave heartfelt thanks to heaven. The duke embraced Sancho and told him he was heartily sorry he had given up the government so soon, but that he would see to it he was provided with some other post on his estate less burdensome and more profitable. The duchess also embraced him, and gave orders that he should be taken good care of, for it was plain to see he had been badly treated and worse bruised.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 56
paragraphs: The prodigious and unparalleled battle that took place between Don Quixote of La Mancha and the lacquey Tosilos in defence of the daughter of Doña Rodriguez

The duke and duchess had no reason to regret the joke played on Sancho Panza in giving him the government, especially as their majordomo returned the same day and gave them a minute account of nearly every word and deed Sancho uttered or did during the time; and to wind up with, eloquently described the attack on the island and Sancho's fright and departure, all of which amused them a great deal. After this the history goes on to say that the day fixed for the battle arrived, and that the duke, after repeatedly instructing his lacquey Tosilos how to deal with Don Quixote so as to vanquish him without killing or wounding him, gave orders to have the heads removed from the lances, telling Don Quixote that Christian charity, on which he prided himself, could not allow the battle to be fought with so much risk and danger to life, and that he must be content with the offer of a battlefield on his territory (though that was against the decree of the holy Council, which prohibits all challenges of the sort) and not push such an arduous venture to its extreme. Don Quixote bid his excellence arrange every detail of the affair as he pleased, since for his part he would obey him in everything. The dread day having arrived, then, and the duke having ordered a spacious stand to be set up facing the castle courtyard for the judges of the field and the appellant duennas, mother and daughter, vast crowds streamed in from all the villages and hamlets of the neighbourhood to see the novel spectacle of the battle; nobody, dead or alive, in those parts had ever seen or heard of one like it.

The first to enter the field and the lists was the master of ceremonies, who surveyed and paced the whole ground to see that there was nothing unfair and nothing concealed that might make the combatants stumble or fall; then the duennas entered and took their seats, wrapped in mantles that covered their eyes — even their bosoms — and displaying no slight emotion as Don Quixote appeared in the lists. Shortly afterwards, accompanied by several trumpets and mounted on a powerful steed that looked like it would crush the whole place, the great lacquey Tosilos made his appearance on one side of the courtyard with his visor down, stiffly cased in a suit of stout, shining armour. The horse was plainly a Frieslander, broad-backed and dapple-grey, with half a pound of wool hanging from each fetlock. The gallant combatant came well primed by his master the duke as to how he was to behave against the valiant Don Quixote of La Mancha, warned that he must on no account kill him, but should try to shirk the first encounter to avoid the risk of killing him, as he was sure to do if he met him full tilt. He crossed the courtyard at a walk, and reaching the spot where the duennas were placed stopped to look at the one who demanded him for a husband. The marshal of the field summoned Don Quixote, who had already presented himself in the courtyard, and standing by Tosilos's side he addressed the duennas and asked if they consented that Don Quixote of La Mancha should do battle for their right. They said they did, and that whatever he did on their behalf they declared rightly done, final, and valid. By this time the duke and duchess had taken their places in a gallery overlooking the enclosure, which was packed to overflowing with a multitude eager to see this perilous and unparalleled encounter. The conditions of the combat were that if Don Quixote proved the victor, his opponent was to marry the daughter of Doña Rodriguez; but if he should be vanquished, his opponent was released from the promise that was claimed against him and from all obligation to give satisfaction. The master of ceremonies divided the sun between them and stationed them, each on the spot where he was to stand. The drums beat, the sound of the trumpets filled the air, the earth trembled underfoot, the hearts of the watching crowd were full of suspense, some hoping for a happy outcome, some apprehensive of an untoward ending; and at last Don Quixote, commending himself with all his heart to God our Lord and to the lady Dulcinea del Toboso, stood waiting for the signal for the onset. Our lacquey, however, was thinking of something very different; he was thinking only of what I am now about to tell.

It seems that as he stood contemplating his enemy she struck him as the most beautiful woman he had ever seen in his life; and the little blind boy whom in our streets they commonly call Love had no mind to let slip the chance of triumphing over a lacquey heart and adding it to his trophies. So, stealing gently up on him unseen, he drove a dart two yards long into the poor lacquey's left side and pierced his heart through and through — which he was able to do quite at his ease, for Love is invisible, and comes in and goes out as he likes, without anyone calling him to account for what he does. Well then, when they gave the signal for the onset our lacquey was in an ecstasy, musing on the beauty of her whom he had already made mistress of his liberty, and so he paid no attention to the trumpet, unlike Don Quixote, who was off the instant he heard it and, at the highest speed Rocinante could manage, set off to meet his enemy. His good squire Sancho shouted lustily as he saw him start, "God guide you, cream and flower of knights-errant! God give you the victory, for the right is on your side!" But although Tosilos saw Don Quixote coming at him, he never stirred a step from the spot where he was posted; instead, he called loudly to the marshal of the field, and when the marshal came up to see what he wanted, Tosilos said, "Señor, isn't this battle to decide whether I marry or do not marry that lady?" "Just so," was the answer. "Well then," said the lacquey, "I feel qualms of conscience, and I'd put a heavy burden on it if I went any further with the combat; so I declare that I yield myself vanquished and that I am willing to marry the lady at once."

The marshal of the field was lost in astonishment at Tosilos's words; and as he was one of those who were in on the arrangement of the affair, he didn't know what to say in reply. Don Quixote pulled up in mid-career when he saw that his enemy was not coming on to the attack. The duke couldn't make out why the battle wasn't going on, but the marshal of the field hurried over to let him know what Tosilos had said, and he was amazed and extremely angry at it. Meanwhile Tosilos advanced to where Doña Rodriguez sat and said in a loud voice, "Señora, I am willing to marry your daughter, and I have no wish to obtain by strife and fighting what I can obtain in peace and without any risk to my life."

The valiant Don Quixote heard him and said, "As that is the case I am released and absolved from my promise; let them marry by all means, and as 'God our Lord has given her, may Saint Peter add his blessing.'"

The duke had now come down to the castle courtyard, and going up to Tosilos he said, "Is it true, sir knight, that you yield yourself vanquished, and that out of scruples of conscience you wish to marry this damsel?"
"It is, señor," replied Tosilos.
"And he does well," said Sancho, "for what you have to give to the mouse, give to the cat, and it will save you all the trouble."

Tosilos meanwhile was trying to unlace his helmet, and he begged them to come to his help at once, as he was running short of breath and could not remain so long shut up in that confined space. They removed it in haste, and his lacquey features were revealed to public view. At this sight Doña Rodriguez and her daughter raised a mighty outcry, exclaiming, "This is a trick! This is a trick! They have put Tosilos, my lord the duke's lacquey, on us in place of the real husband. The justice of God and the king against such trickery — not to say roguery!"

"Do not distress yourselves, ladies," said Don Quixote; "this is no trickery or roguery, or if it is, it is not the duke who is at the bottom of it but those wicked enchanters who persecute me, and who, jealous of my reaping the glory of this victory, have turned your husband's features into those of this person, who you say is the duke's lacquey. Take my advice, and despite the malice of my enemies marry him, for beyond a doubt he is the one you want for a husband."

When the duke heard this his anger all but vanished in a fit of laughter, and he said, "The things that happen to Señor Don Quixote are so extraordinary that I am ready to believe this lacquey of mine is not one; but let us adopt this plan and stratagem: let us put off the marriage for, say, a fortnight, and let us keep this person we are uncertain about in close confinement, and perhaps in the course of that time he may return to his original shape; for the spite the enchanters bear Señor Don Quixote can't last so long, especially as it is of so little benefit to them to practise these deceptions and transformations."

"Oh, señor," said Sancho, "those scoundrels are well used to changing whatever concerns my master from one thing into another. A knight he overcame some time back, called the Knight of the Mirrors, they turned into the shape of the bachelor Sansón Carrasco of our town and a great friend of ours; and my lady Dulcinea del Toboso they have turned into a common country girl; so I suspect this lacquey will have to live and die a lacquey all the days of his life."

Here Rodriguez's daughter exclaimed, "Whoever this man is who claims me for a wife, I am thankful to him for it, for I'd rather be the lawful wife of a lacquey than the cheated mistress of a gentleman — though the one who played me false was no real gentleman either."

To be brief, all the talk and all that had happened ended in Tosilos being shut up until it was seen how his transformation turned out. All hailed Don Quixote as victor, but the greater number were vexed and disappointed to find that the combatants they had been so anxiously waiting for had not battered one another to pieces — just as boys are disappointed when the man they are waiting to see hanged does not come out because the prosecution or the court has pardoned him. The crowd dispersed, the duke and Don Quixote returned to the castle, Tosilos was locked up, Doña Rodriguez and her daughter remained perfectly contented to see that the affair must end in a marriage one way or another, and Tosilos wanted nothing else.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 57
paragraphs: Which treats of how Don Quixote took leave of the duke, and of what happened with the witty and impudent Altisidora, one of the duchess's maids

Don Quixote now felt it right to quit a life of such idleness as he was leading in the castle, for he fancied he was making himself sorely missed by letting himself remain shut up and inactive amid the countless luxuries and enjoyments his hosts lavished on him as a knight; and he felt too that he would have to give heaven a strict account of that indolence and seclusion; and so one day he asked the duke and duchess to grant him permission to take his leave. They gave it, showing at the same time that they were very sorry he was leaving them.

The duchess gave his wife's letters to Sancho Panza, who shed tears over them and said, "Who would have thought that such grand hopes as the news of my government bred in my wife Teresa Panza's breast would end in my going back now to the vagabond adventures of my master Don Quixote of La Mancha? Still, I'm glad to see my Teresa behaved as she ought in sending the acorns, because if she hadn't sent them I'd have been sorry, and she'd have shown herself ungrateful. It's a comfort to me that they can't call that present a bribe, for I had got the government already when she sent them, and it's only reasonable that those who have had a good turn done them should show their gratitude, if only with a trifle. After all, I went into the government naked, and I come out of it naked; so I can say with a safe conscience — and that's no small matter — 'naked I was born, naked I find myself, I neither lose nor gain.'"

So did Sancho soliloquise on the day of their departure, while Don Quixote, who had the night before taken leave of the duke and duchess, came out and made his appearance at an early hour in full armour in the castle courtyard. The whole household of the castle was watching him from the corridors, and the duke and duchess too came out to see him. Sancho was mounted on his Dapple, with his saddlebags, valise, and provisions, and supremely happy because the duke's majordomo — the same who had played the part of the Trifaldi — had given him a little purse with two hundred gold crowns to meet the necessary expenses of the road; though of this Don Quixote knew nothing as yet. While all were, as has been said, watching him, suddenly from among the duennas and handmaidens the impudent and witty Altisidora lifted up her voice and said in pathetic tones:

Give ear, cruel knight; / Draw rein; where's the need / Of spurring the flanks / Of that ill-broken steed? / From what art thou flying? / No dragon I am, / Not even a sheep, / But a tender young lamb. / Thou hast jilted a maiden / As fair to behold / As nymph of Diana / Or Venus of old. / Bireno, Æneas, what worse shall I call thee? / Barabbas go with thee! All evil befall thee!

In thy claws, ruthless robber, / Thou bearest away / The heart of a meek / Loving maid for thy prey, / Three kerchiefs thou stealest, / And garters a pair, / From legs than the whitest / Of marble more fair; / And the sighs that pursue thee / Would burn to the ground / Two thousand Troy Towns, / If so many were found. / Bireno, Æneas, what worse shall I call thee? / Barabbas go with thee! All evil befall thee!

May no bowels of mercy / To Sancho be granted, / And thy Dulcinea / Be left still enchanted, / May thy falsehood to me / Find its punishment in her, / For in my land the just / Often pays for the sinner. / May thy grandest adventures / Discomfitures prove, / May thy joys be all dreams, / And forgotten thy love. / Bireno, Æneas, what worse shall I call thee? / Barabbas go with thee! All evil befall thee!

May thy name be abhorred / For thy conduct to ladies, / From London to England, / From Seville to Cadiz; / May thy cards be unlucky, / Thy hands contain ne'er a / King, seven, or ace / When thou playest primera; / When thy corns are cut / May it be to the quick; / When thy grinders are drawn / May the roots of them stick. / Bireno, Æneas, what worse shall I call thee? / Barabbas go with thee! All evil befall thee!

All the while the unhappy Altisidora was bewailing herself in this strain, Don Quixote stood staring at her; and without saying a word in reply he turned to Sancho and said, "Sancho my friend, I conjure you by the life of your forefathers tell me the truth — have you by any chance taken the three kerchiefs and the garters this love-sick maid speaks of?"
To this Sancho made answer, "The three kerchiefs I have; but the garters, as much as 'over the hills of Úbeda.'"

The duchess was amazed at Altisidora's nerve; she knew she was bold, lively, and impudent, but not so much so as to venture to take such liberties; and not being prepared for the joke, her astonishment was all the greater. The duke had a mind to keep up the sport, so he said, "It does not seem well done to me, sir knight, that after receiving the hospitality offered you in this very castle, you should have ventured to carry off even three kerchiefs, not to mention my handmaid's garters. It shows a bad heart and does not tally with your reputation. Restore her garters, or else I defy you to mortal combat, for I am not afraid of rascally enchanters changing or altering my features as they changed his who encountered you into those of my lacquey, Tosilos."

"God forbid," said Don Quixote, "that I should draw my sword against your illustrious person, from which I have received such great favours. The kerchiefs I will return, since Sancho says he has them; as for the garters that is impossible, for I do not have them, neither does he; and if your handmaid here will look in her hiding-places, depend upon it she will find them. I have never been a thief, my lord duke, nor do I mean to be so long as I live, if God ceases not to keep me in his care. This damsel by her own confession speaks as one in love, for which I am not to blame, and therefore need ask pardon neither of her nor of your excellence — whom I entreat to have a better opinion of me, and once more to give me leave to pursue my journey."

"And may God so prosper it, Señor Don Quixote," said the duchess, "that we may always hear good news of your exploits; God speed you, for the longer you stay the more you inflame the hearts of the damsels who behold you; and as for this one of mine, I will so chastise her that she will not transgress again, either with her eyes or with her words."

"One word and no more, O valiant Don Quixote, I ask you to hear," said Altisidora, "and that is that I beg your pardon about the theft of the garters, for by God and upon my soul I have got them on, and I have fallen into the same blunder as the man who went looking for his ass while mounted on it."
"Didn't I say so?" said Sancho. "I'm a likely one to hide thefts! Why, if I'd wanted to deal in them, opportunities came ready enough to me in my government."

Don Quixote bowed his head, saluted the duke and duchess and all the bystanders, and wheeling Rocinante round, with Sancho following him on Dapple, he rode out of the castle, shaping his course for Saragossa.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 58
paragraphs: Which tells how adventures came crowding on Don Quixote in such numbers that they gave one another no breathing-space

When Don Quixote saw himself in open country, free, and relieved of Altisidora's attentions, he felt at his ease and in fresh spirits to take up the pursuit of chivalry once more; and turning to Sancho, he said, "Freedom, Sancho, is one of the most precious gifts heaven has bestowed on mankind; no treasures the earth holds buried or the sea conceals can compare with it; for freedom, as for honour, life may and should be ventured; and on the other hand, captivity is the greatest evil that can fall to the lot of man. I say this, Sancho, because you have seen the good cheer and abundance we enjoyed in this castle we are leaving; well then, amid those dainty banquets and snow-cooled drinks I felt as though I were suffering the pangs of hunger, because I did not enjoy them with the same freedom as if they were mine; for the sense of being under an obligation to repay benefits and favours received is a restraint that checks the independence of the spirit. Happy the man to whom heaven has given a piece of bread for which he is not bound to give thanks to any but heaven itself!"

"For all your worship says," said Sancho, "it isn't right that there should be no thanks on our part for two hundred gold crowns the duke's majordomo has given me in a little purse I carry next my heart, like a warming plaster or a comforter, to meet any chance calls; for we won't always find castles where they'll entertain us — now and then we may light on roadside inns where they'll cudgel us."

In conversation of this sort the knight and squire errant were pursuing their journey when, after they had gone a little more than half a league, they spotted some dozen men dressed like labourers stretched out on their cloaks on the grass of a green meadow eating their dinner. They had beside them what seemed to be white sheets covering some objects, standing upright or lying flat and arranged at intervals. Don Quixote went up to the diners, and after saluting them courteously, asked what those cloths covered. "Señor," answered one of the party, "under these cloths are some images carved in relief intended for an altarpiece we are setting up in our village; we carry them covered up so they won't be soiled, and on our shoulders so they won't be broken."
"With your good leave," said Don Quixote, "I should like to see them; for images carried so carefully must be fine ones."

"I should think they are!" said the other; "let the money they cost speak for that, since the fact is there is not one of them that doesn't stand us in more than fifty ducats; and that your worship may judge for yourself, wait a moment and you shall see with your own eyes." And getting up from his dinner he went and uncovered the first image, which proved to be one of Saint George on horseback, with a serpent writhing at his feet and the lance thrust down its throat with all that fierceness that is usually depicted. The whole group was one blaze of gold, as the saying is. On seeing it Don Quixote said, "That knight was one of the finest knights-errant the army of heaven ever owned; he was called Don Saint George, and he was moreover a defender of maidens. Let us see this next one."

The man uncovered it, and it turned out to be Saint Martin on his horse, dividing his cloak with the beggar. The instant Don Quixote saw it he said, "This knight too was one of the Christian adventurers, but I believe he was generous rather than valiant, as you can see, Sancho, by his dividing his cloak with the beggar and giving him half of it; no doubt it was winter at the time, for otherwise he would have given him the whole of it, so charitable was he."
"It was not that, most likely," said Sancho, "but that he held with the proverb that says, 'For giving and keeping there's need of brains.'"

Don Quixote laughed, and asked them to take off the next cloth, under which appeared the image of the patron saint of the Spains seated on horseback, his sword stained with blood, trampling on Moors and treading heads underfoot; and on seeing it Don Quixote exclaimed, "Ay, this is a knight, and one of the squadrons of Christ! This one is called Don Saint James the Moorslayer, one of the bravest saints and knights the world ever had or heaven has now."

They then raised another cloth that turned out to cover Saint Paul falling from his horse, with all the details usually given in representations of his conversion. When Don Quixote saw it, rendered so lifelike that one would have said Christ was speaking and Paul answering, "This," he said, "was in his time the greatest enemy that the Church of God our Lord had, and the greatest champion it will ever have: a knight-errant in life, a steadfast saint in death, an untiring labourer in the Lord's vineyard, a teacher of the Gentiles, whose school was heaven, and whose instructor and master was Jesus Christ himself."

There were no more images, so Don Quixote told them to cover them up again, and said to those who had brought them, "I take it as a happy omen, brothers, to have seen what I have, for these saints and knights were of the same profession as myself — the calling of arms — only with this difference between them and me, that they were saints and fought with divine weapons, and I am a sinner and fight with human ones. They won heaven by force of arms, for heaven suffers violence; and I, so far, don't know what I have won by dint of my sufferings; but if my Dulcinea del Toboso were released from hers, perhaps with mended fortunes and a mind restored to itself I might direct my steps in a better path than I am following at present."
"May God hear and sin be deaf," said Sancho to that.

The men were filled with wonder, as much at his figure as at his words, though they didn't understand the half of what he meant by them. They finished their dinner, took their images on their backs, and bidding farewell to Don Quixote resumed their journey.

Sancho was amazed afresh at the extent of his master's knowledge, as much as if he had never known him, for it seemed to him that there was no story or event in the world that he didn't have at his fingertips and fixed in his memory; and he said to him, "In truth, master mine, if what has happened to us today is to be called an adventure, it has been one of the sweetest and pleasantest that have befallen us in the whole course of our travels; we've come out of it unbelaboured and undismayed, we haven't drawn sword, we haven't smitten the earth with our bodies, nor have we been left famishing; blessed be God that he has let me see such a thing with my own eyes!"

"You speak well, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "but remember all times are not alike and they don't always run the same way; and these things the vulgar commonly call omens, which are not based on any natural reason, the wise man will simply count as happy accidents. One of these believers in omens will get up of a morning, leave his house, and meet a friar of the order of the blessed Saint Francis, and, as if he had met a griffin, he will turn around and go home. With another Mendoza the salt is spilled on his table, and gloom is spilled over his heart, as if nature were obliged to give warning of coming misfortunes by means of such trifles. The wise man and the Christian should not trifle with what it may please heaven to do. Scipio on coming to Africa stumbled as he leaped on shore; his soldiers took it as a bad omen; but he, clasping the soil with his arms, exclaimed, 'You cannot escape me, Africa, for I hold you tight between my arms.' So, Sancho, meeting those images has been to me a most happy occurrence."

"I can well believe it," said Sancho; "but I wish your worship would tell me why it is that the Spaniards, when they are about to give battle, in calling on that Saint James the Moorslayer, say 'Santiago and close Spain!' Is Spain, then, open, so that it needs to be closed? Or what is the meaning of this form?"

"You are very simple, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "God, you see, gave that great knight of the Red Cross to Spain as her patron saint and protector, especially in those hard struggles the Spaniards had with the Moors; and therefore they invoke and call upon him as their defender in all their battles; and in these he has been many a time seen beating down, trampling underfoot, destroying and slaughtering the Hagarene squadrons in plain sight of all; of which fact I could give you many examples recorded in truthful Spanish histories."

Sancho changed the subject and said to his master, "I marvel, señor, at the boldness of Altisidora, the duchess's handmaid; he whom they call Love must have cruelly pierced and wounded her; they say he is a little blind urchin who, though blear-eyed — or more properly speaking, sightless — if he aims at a heart, no matter how small, hits it and pierces it through with his arrows. I have heard it said too that the arrows of Love are blunted and robbed of their points by maidenly modesty and reserve; but with this Altisidora it seems they are sharpened rather than blunted."

"Bear in mind, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that love yields to no consideration, recognises no restraints of reason, and is of the same nature as death, that assails alike the lofty palaces of kings and the humble cabins of shepherds; and when it takes full possession of a heart, the first thing it does is to banish fear and shame from it; and so without shame Altisidora declared her passion, which excited in my mind embarrassment rather than commiseration."

"Notable cruelty!" exclaimed Sancho; "unheard-of ingratitude! I can only say for myself that the very smallest loving word of hers would have subdued me and made a slave of me. The devil! What a heart of marble, what bowels of brass, what a soul of mortar! But I can't imagine what this damsel saw in your worship that could have conquered and captivated her so. What gallant figure was it, what bold bearing, what sprightly grace, what fine features — which of these things by itself, or what all together, could have made her fall in love with you? Indeed and in truth, many a time I stop to look at your worship from the sole of your foot to the topmost hair of your head, and I see more to frighten one than to make one fall in love; moreover I have heard say that beauty is the first and main thing that excites love, and since your worship has none at all, I don't know what the poor creature fell in love with."

"Recollect, Sancho," replied Don Quixote, "there are two sorts of beauty, one of the mind, the other of the body; that of the mind displays and exhibits itself in intelligence, in modesty, in honourable conduct, in generosity, in good breeding; and all these qualities are possible and may exist in an ugly man; and when it is this sort of beauty and not that of the body that is the attraction, love is apt to spring up suddenly and violently. I, Sancho, perceive clearly enough that I am not beautiful, but at the same time I know I am not hideous; and it is enough for an honest man not to be a monster to be an object of love, if only he possesses the endowments of mind I have mentioned."

While engaged in this discussion they were making their way through a wood that lay beyond the road when suddenly, without expecting anything of the kind, Don Quixote found himself caught in some nets of green cord stretched from one tree to another; and unable to imagine what it could be, he said to Sancho, "Sancho, it strikes me this affair of these nets will prove one of the strangest adventures imaginable. May I die if the enchanters that persecute me are not trying to entangle me in them and delay my journey, by way of revenge for my obduracy toward Altisidora. Well then, let me tell them that if these nets, instead of being green cord, were made of the hardest diamonds, or were stronger than the net the jealous god of blacksmiths used to ensnare Venus and Mars, I would break them as easily as if they were made of rushes or cotton threads." But just as he was about to press forward and break through, suddenly from among some trees two shepherdesses of surpassing beauty appeared in his sight — or at least damsels dressed like shepherdesses, except that their jerkins and skirts were of fine brocade; that is to say, the skirts were rich farthingales of gold-embroidered tabby. Their hair, which in its golden brightness rivalled the beams of the sun itself, fell loose on their shoulders and was crowned with garlands twined with green laurel and red everlasting; and they looked to be not under fifteen years old nor over eighteen.

Such was the spectacle that filled Sancho with amazement, fascinated Don Quixote, made the sun halt in his course to behold them, and held all four in a strange silence. One of the shepherdesses was the first to speak, and said to Don Quixote, "Hold, sir knight, and do not break these nets, for they are not spread here to do you any harm but only for our amusement; and since I know you will ask why they have been put up and who we are, I will tell you in a few words. In a village some two leagues from here, where there are many people of quality and rich gentlefolk, it was agreed among a number of friends and relations to come with their wives, sons and daughters, neighbours, friends and kinsmen, and make holiday in this spot, one of the pleasantest in the whole neighbourhood, setting up among ourselves a new pastoral Arcadia, we maidens dressing as shepherdesses and the youths as shepherds. We have prepared two eclogues, one by the famous poet Garcilasso, the other by the most excellent Camoens in its own Portuguese tongue, but we have not yet acted them. Yesterday was the first day of our coming here; we have a few of what they call field-tents pitched among the trees on the bank of an ample brook that fertilises all these meadows; last night we spread these nets in the trees here to snare the silly little birds that, startled by the noise we make, may fly into them. If you please to be our guest, señor, you will be welcomed heartily and courteously, for here just now neither care nor sorrow shall enter."

She held her peace and said no more, and Don Quixote answered, "In truth, fairest lady, Actaeon when he unexpectedly beheld Diana bathing in the stream could not have been more fascinated and wonderstruck than I at the sight of your beauty. I commend your mode of entertainment, and thank you for the kindness of your invitation; and if I can serve you, you may command me with full confidence of being obeyed, for my profession is none other than to show myself grateful and ready to serve persons of all conditions, but especially persons of quality such as your appearance indicates; and if, instead of taking up, as they probably do, only a small space, these nets took up the whole surface of the globe, I would seek out new worlds to pass through so as not to break them; and that you may give some degree of credence to this exaggerated language of mine, know that the one declaring it to you is no less than Don Quixote of La Mancha, if indeed that name has reached your ears."

"Ah, friend of my soul," the other shepherdess instantly exclaimed, "what great good fortune has befallen us! Do you see this gentleman before us? Well, let me tell you he is the most valiant and the most devoted and the most courteous gentleman in all the world, unless a history of his achievements that has been printed and that I have read is telling lies and deceiving us. I'll lay a wager this good fellow with him is one Sancho Panza his squire, whose drolleries none can equal."
"That's true," said Sancho; "I am that same droll and squire you speak of, and this gentleman is my master Don Quixote of La Mancha, the same who's in the history and that they talk about."

"Oh, my friend," said the other, "let us entreat him to stay, for it will give our fathers and brothers infinite pleasure; I too have heard just what you have told me of the valour of the one and the drolleries of the other; and what is more, of him they say that he is the most constant and loyal lover that was ever heard of, and that his lady is one Dulcinea del Toboso, to whom all over Spain the palm of beauty is awarded."

"And justly awarded," said Don Quixote, "unless, indeed, your unequalled beauty makes it a matter of doubt. But spare yourselves the trouble, ladies, of pressing me to stay, for the urgent calls of my profession do not allow me to take rest under any circumstances."

At this moment there came up to the spot where the four stood a brother of one of the two shepherdesses, like them in shepherd costume, and as richly and gaily dressed as they were. They told him that their companion was the valiant Don Quixote of La Mancha, and the other Sancho his squire, of whom he knew already from having read their history. The gay shepherd offered him his services and begged he would accompany him to their tents, and Don Quixote had to give way and comply. And now the game was started, and the nets were filled with a variety of birds that, deceived by the colour, fell into the danger they were flying from. Upwards of thirty persons, all gaily attired as shepherds and shepherdesses, assembled on the spot, and were at once informed who Don Quixote and his squire were, at which they were not a little delighted, since they already knew of him through his history. They went off to the tents, where they found tables laid out, and choicely, plentifully, and neatly furnished. They treated Don Quixote as a person of distinction, giving him the place of honour, and all watched him, full of astonishment at the spectacle. At last the cloth being removed, Don Quixote with great composure lifted up his voice and said:

"One of the greatest sins men are guilty of is — some will say pride — but I say ingratitude, going by the common saying that hell is full of ingrates. This sin, as far as it has lain in my power, I have tried to avoid ever since I have enjoyed the faculty of reason; and if I cannot repay good deeds done me with other deeds, I substitute the desire to do so; and if that is not enough, I make them publicly known, for he who declares and makes known the good deeds done to him would repay them with other deeds if it were in his power, and for the most part those who receive are inferior to those who give. Thus, God is superior to all because he is the supreme giver, and the offerings of man fall short by an infinite distance of being a full return for the gifts of God; but gratitude in some degree makes up for this deficiency and shortcoming. I therefore, grateful for the favour shown me here, and unable to make a return in the same measure, restricted as I am by the narrow limits of my power, offer what I can and what I have to offer in my own way; and so I declare that for two full days I will maintain in the middle of this highway leading to Saragossa, that these ladies disguised as shepherdesses, who are here present, are the fairest and most courteous maidens in the world, excepting only the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso, sole mistress of my thoughts — be it said without offence to those who hear me, ladies and gentlemen."

On hearing this Sancho, who had been listening with great attention, cried out in a loud voice, "Is it possible there is anyone in the world who will dare to say and swear that this master of mine is a madman? Say, gentlemen shepherds, is there a village priest, however wise or learned, who could say what my master has said; or is there a knight-errant, whatever his renown as a man of valour, who could offer what my master has offered now?"

Don Quixote turned on Sancho with a face glowing with anger and said to him, "Is it possible, Sancho, there is anyone in the whole world who will say you are not a fool, with a lining to match, and I know not what trimmings of impertinence and roguery? Who asked you to meddle in my affairs, or to inquire whether I am a wise man or a blockhead? Hold your peace; answer me not a word; saddle Rocinante if he is unsaddled; and let us go to put my offer into execution; for with the right that I have on my side you may count as vanquished all who venture to question it." And in a great rage, and showing his anger plainly, he rose from his seat, leaving the company lost in wonder, and making them doubt whether to regard him as a madman or a rational being. In the end, though they tried to dissuade him from involving himself in such a challenge, assuring him that they accepted his gratitude as fully established and needed no fresh proofs to be convinced of his valiant spirit, since those related in the history of his exploits were sufficient, still Don Quixote persisted in his resolve; and mounted on Rocinante, bracing his buckler on his arm and grasping his lance, he posted himself in the middle of a high road not far from the green meadow. Sancho followed on Dapple, together with all the members of the pastoral gathering, eager to see how this vainglorious and extraordinary proposal would end.

Don Quixote, having, as has been said, planted himself in the middle of the road, made the sky ring with words to this effect: "Ho, you travellers and wayfarers, knights, squires, folk on foot or on horseback, who pass this way or shall pass in the course of the next two days! Know that Don Quixote of La Mancha, knight-errant, is posted here to maintain by arms that the beauty and courtesy of the nymphs that dwell in these meadows and groves surpass all upon earth, the lady of my heart, Dulcinea del Toboso, alone excepted. Therefore, let any who hold the opposite opinion come on, for here I await him."

Twice he repeated the same words, and twice they fell unheard by any adventurer; but fate, that was guiding affairs for him from better to better, so ordered it that shortly afterwards there appeared on the road a crowd of men on horseback, many of them with lances in their hands, all riding in a compact body and in great haste. The moment those who were with Don Quixote saw them they turned about and withdrew some distance from the road, knowing that if they stayed some harm might come to them; but Don Quixote with intrepid heart stood his ground, and Sancho Panza shielded himself behind Rocinante's hindquarters. The troop of lancers came up, and one of them in advance began shouting to Don Quixote, "Get out of the way, you son of the devil, or these bulls will trample you to pieces!"

"Rabble!" returned Don Quixote, "I care nothing for bulls, be they the fiercest the Jarama breeds on its banks. Confess at once, scoundrels, that what I have declared is true; otherwise you have to deal with me in combat."

The herdsman had no time to reply, nor Don Quixote to get out of the way even if he had wished; and so the drove of fierce bulls and tame bullocks, together with the crowd of herdsmen and others who were taking them to be penned up in a village where they were to be run the next day, passed over Don Quixote and over Sancho, Rocinante and Dapple, hurling them all to the earth and rolling them over on the ground. Sancho was left crushed, Don Quixote scared, Dapple belaboured, and Rocinante in no very sound condition.

They all got up at last, however, and Don Quixote in great haste, stumbling here and falling there, started off running after the drove, shouting, "Hold! stay! you rascally rabble, a single knight awaits you, and he is not of the temper or opinion of those who say, 'For a flying enemy make a bridge of silver.'" The retreating party in their haste, however, did not stop for that, or heed his threats any more than last year's clouds. Weariness brought Don Quixote to a halt, and more enraged than avenged he sat down on the road to wait until Sancho, Rocinante, and Dapple came up. When they reached him, master and man mounted once more, and without going back to bid farewell to the mock or imitation Arcadia, more in humiliation than contentment, they continued their journey.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 59
paragraphs: Which relates the strange thing, which may be regarded as an adventure, that happened to Don Quixote

A clear, limpid spring they discovered in a cool grove relieved Don Quixote and Sancho of the dust and fatigue brought on by the discourteous behaviour of the bulls, and by the side of this, having turned Dapple and Rocinante loose without headstall or bridle, the forlorn pair, master and man, sat themselves down. Sancho had recourse to the larder of his saddlebags and took out what he called the grub; Don Quixote rinsed his mouth and bathed his face, by which cooling process his flagging energies were revived. Out of pure vexation he did not eat, and out of pure politeness Sancho didn't venture to touch a morsel of what was in front of him, but waited for his master to take the first bite. Seeing, however, that, lost in thought, Don Quixote was forgetting to lift the bread to his mouth, Sancho said never a word, and trampling every sort of good breeding underfoot, began to stow away in his paunch the bread and cheese that came to hand.

"Eat, Sancho my friend," said Don Quixote; "sustain your life, which is of more consequence to you than to me, and leave me to die under the pain of my thoughts and pressure of my misfortunes. I was born, Sancho, to live dying, and you to die eating; and to prove the truth of what I say, look at me: printed in histories, famed in arms, courteous in behaviour, honoured by princes, courted by maidens — and after all, just when I was looking forward to palms, triumphs, and crowns won and earned by my valiant deeds, I have this morning seen myself trampled on, kicked, and crushed by the feet of unclean and filthy animals. This thought blunts my teeth, paralyses my jaws, cramps my hands, and robs me of all appetite for food; so much so that I have a mind to let myself die of hunger, the cruelest of all deaths."

"So then," said Sancho, munching hard all the time, "your worship doesn't agree with the proverb that says, 'Let Martha die, but let her die with a full belly.' I, at any rate, have no mind to kill myself; far from it, I mean to do what the cobbler does, who stretches the leather with his teeth until he makes it reach as far as he wants. I'll stretch out my life by eating until it reaches the end heaven has fixed for it; and let me tell you, señor, there's no greater folly than to think of dying of despair as your worship does; take my advice, and after eating lie down and sleep a bit on this green grass-mattress, and you'll see that when you wake you'll feel somewhat better."

Don Quixote did as he advised, for it struck him that Sancho's reasoning was more like a philosopher's than a blockhead's, and said he, "Sancho, if you will do for me what I am going to tell you, my ease of mind would be more assured and my heaviness of heart not so great, and it is this: to go aside a little while I am sleeping in accordance with your advice, and, baring your carcass to the air, give yourself three or four hundred lashes with Rocinante's reins, on account of the three thousand and odd you are to give yourself for the disenchantment of Dulcinea; for it is a great pity that the poor lady should be left enchanted through your carelessness and negligence."

"There's a good deal to be said on that point," said Sancho; "let us both go to sleep now, and after that, God has decreed what will happen. Let me tell your worship that for a man to whip himself in cold blood is a hard thing, especially if the stripes fall on an ill-nourished and worse-fed body. Let my lady Dulcinea have patience, and when she's least expecting it she'll see me made into a riddle with whipping, and 'until death it's all life'; I mean, I have still life in me and the desire to make good what I have promised."

Don Quixote thanked him, and ate a little, and Sancho a great deal, and then they both lay down to sleep, leaving those two inseparable friends and comrades, Rocinante and Dapple, to their own devices and to feed unrestrained on the abundant grass with which the meadow was furnished. They woke up rather late, mounted once more, and resumed their journey, pushing on to reach an inn that was in sight, apparently a league off. I say an inn, because Don Quixote called it so, contrary to his usual practice of calling all inns castles. They reached it and asked the landlord if they could put up there. He said yes, with as much comfort and as good fare as they could find in Saragossa. They dismounted, and Sancho stowed away his larder in a room of which the landlord gave him the key. He took the beasts to the stable, fed them, and came back to see what orders Don Quixote, who was seated on a bench at the door, had for him, giving special thanks to heaven that this inn had not been taken for a castle by his master. Supper-time came, and they went to their room, and Sancho asked the landlord what he had to give them for supper. To this the landlord replied that his mouth should be the measure; he had only to ask what he would, for that inn was provided with the birds of the air and the fowls of the earth and the fish of the sea.
"There's no need of all that," said Sancho; "if they'll roast us a couple of chickens we'll be satisfied, for my master is delicate and eats little, and I'm not over and above gluttonous."
The landlord replied that he had no chickens, for the kites had stolen them.
"Well then," said Sancho, "let señor landlord tell them to roast a pullet, so long as it's a tender one."
"Pullet! My father!" said the landlord; "indeed and in truth, only yesterday I sent over fifty to the city to sell; but apart from pullets, ask what you will."
"In that case," said Sancho, "you won't be without veal or kid."
"Just now," said the landlord, "there's none in the house, for it's all finished; but next week there will be enough and to spare."
"Much good that does us," said Sancho; "I'll lay a bet that all these shortages are going to wind up in plenty of bacon and eggs."

"By God," said the landlord, "my guest's wits must be precious dull; I tell him I have neither pullets nor hens, and he wants me to have eggs! Talk of other dainties, if you please, and don't ask for hens again."
"Body o' me!" said Sancho, "let's settle the matter; just say at once what you have, and let us have no more words about it."

"In truth and earnest, señor guest," said the landlord, "all I have is a couple of cow-heels like calves' feet, or a couple of calves' feet like cow-heels; they are boiled with chickpeas, onions, and bacon, and at this very moment they are crying 'Come eat me, come eat me.'"

"I mark them for mine on the spot," said Sancho; "let nobody touch them; I'll pay better for them than anyone else, for I could not wish for anything more to my taste; and I don't care a pin whether they are feet or heels."
"Nobody shall touch them," said the landlord; "the other guests I have, being persons of high quality, bring their own cook and caterer and larder with them."

"If you come to people of quality," said Sancho, "there's nobody more so than my master; but the calling he follows doesn't allow of larders or store-rooms; we lie down in the middle of a meadow and fill ourselves with acorns or medlars."
Here ended Sancho's conversation with the landlord, Sancho not caring to carry it any further by answering him, for he had already asked him what calling or what profession his master was of.

Supper-time having come, then, Don Quixote went to his room, the landlord brought in the stew-pan just as it was, and he sat down to sup very resolutely. It seems that in another room next to Don Quixote's, with nothing but a thin partition to separate them, he overheard these words: "As you live, Señor Don Jeronimo, while they are bringing supper, let us read another chapter of the Second Part of 'Don Quixote of La Mancha.'"

The instant Don Quixote heard his own name he started to his feet and listened with open ears to catch what they said about him, and heard the Don Jeronimo who had been addressed reply, "Why would you have us read that absurd stuff, Don Juan, when it is impossible for anyone who has read the First Part of the history of 'Don Quixote of La Mancha' to take any pleasure in reading this Second Part?"

"For all that," said he who was addressed as Don Juan, "we shall do well to read it, for there is no book so bad that it doesn't have something good in it. What displeases me most about it is that it represents Don Quixote as now cured of his love for Dulcinea del Toboso."

On hearing this Don Quixote, full of wrath and indignation, lifted up his voice and said, "Whoever he may be that says Don Quixote of La Mancha has forgotten or can forget Dulcinea del Toboso, I will teach him with equal arms that what he says is very far from the truth; for neither can the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso be forgotten, nor can forgetfulness have a place in Don Quixote; his motto is constancy, and his profession to maintain that with his life and never wrong it."
"Who is this that answers us?" said they in the next room.
"Who should it be," said Sancho, "but Don Quixote of La Mancha himself, who will make good all he has said and all he will say; for pledges don't trouble a good payer."

Sancho had hardly uttered these words when two gentlemen, for such they seemed to be, entered the room, and one of them, throwing his arms around Don Quixote's neck, said to him, "Your appearance can leave no question as to your name, nor can your name fail to identify your appearance; unquestionably, señor, you are the real Don Quixote of La Mancha, lodestar and morning star of knight-errantry, in defiance of him who has tried to usurp your name and bring your achievements to naught, as the author of this book which I here present to you has done." And with this he put into Don Quixote's hands a book which his companion was carrying. Don Quixote took it, and without replying began to run his eye over it; but he soon returned it saying, "In the little I have seen I have discovered three things in this author that deserve to be censured. The first is some words I have read in the preface; the next is that the language is Aragonese, since sometimes he writes without articles; and the third, which above all stamps him as ignorant, is that he goes wrong and departs from the truth in the most important part of the history, for here he says that my squire Sancho Panza's wife is called Mari Gutierrez, when she is called nothing of the sort, but Teresa Panza; and when a man errs on so important a point as this, there is good reason to fear he is in error on every other point in the history."

"A nice sort of historian, indeed!" exclaimed Sancho at this; "he must know a deal about our affairs when he calls my wife Teresa Panza, Mari Gutierrez; take the book again, señor, and see if I'm in it and if he has changed my name."
"From your talk, friend," said Don Jeronimo, "no doubt you are Sancho Panza, Señor Don Quixote's squire."
"Yes, I am," said Sancho; "and I'm proud of it."

"Faith, then," said the gentleman, "this new author does not handle you with the decency that displays itself in your person; he makes you out a heavy feeder and a fool, and not in the least droll, and a very different being from the Sancho described in the First Part of your master's history."
"God forgive him," said Sancho; "he might have left me in my corner without troubling his head about me; 'let him who knows how ring the bells; Saint Peter is very well in Rome.'"

The two gentlemen pressed Don Quixote to come into their room and have supper with them, as they knew very well there was nothing in that inn fit for one of his sort. Don Quixote, who was always polite, yielded to their request and supped with them. Sancho stayed behind with the stew, and invested with plenary delegated authority seated himself at the head of the table, and the landlord sat down with him, for he was no less fond of cow-heels and calves' feet than Sancho was.

While at supper Don Juan asked Don Quixote what news he had of the lady Dulcinea del Toboso — was she married, had she been brought to bed, or was she with child, or did she in maidenhood, still preserving her modesty and delicacy, cherish the memory of Señor Don Quixote's tender passion?

To this he replied, "Dulcinea is a maiden still, and my passion more firmly rooted than ever, our communication as unsatisfactory as before, and her beauty transformed into that of a foul country wench;" and then he proceeded to give them a full and particular account of the enchantment of Dulcinea, and of what had happened to him in the cave of Montesinos, together with what the sage Merlin had prescribed for her disenchantment, namely the scourging of Sancho.

Exceedingly great was the amusement the two gentlemen derived from hearing Don Quixote recount the strange incidents of his history; and if they were amazed by his absurdities they were equally amazed by the elegant style in which he delivered them. On the one hand they regarded him as a man of wit and sense, and on the other he seemed to them a maundering blockhead, and they could not make up their minds whereabouts between wisdom and folly they ought to place him.

Sancho having finished his supper, and left the landlord in the X condition, came to the room where his master was, and as he entered said, "May I die, sirs, if the author of the book your worships have got has any mind that we should agree; since he calls me glutton (according to what your worships say), I hope he doesn't call me a drunkard too."

"But he does," said Don Jeronimo; "I can't remember in what way, however, though I know his words are offensive, and what is more, lying, as I can plainly see by the physiognomy of the worthy Sancho before me."

"Believe me," said Sancho, "the Sancho and the Don Quixote of this history must be different persons from those who appear in the one Cide Hamete Benengeli wrote, who are ourselves; my master valiant, wise, and true in love, and I simple, droll, and neither glutton nor drunkard."

"I believe it," said Don Juan; "and were it possible, an order should be issued that no one should have the presumption to deal with anything relating to Don Quixote save his original author Cide Hamete, just as Alexander commanded that no one should presume to paint his portrait save Apelles."
"Let whoever will paint me," said Don Quixote; "but let him not abuse me, for patience will often break down when they heap insults upon it."

"None can be offered to Señor Don Quixote," said Don Juan, "that he himself will not be able to avenge, if he does not ward it off with the shield of his patience, which, I take it, is great and strong."

A considerable portion of the night passed in conversation of this sort, and though Don Juan wanted Don Quixote to read more of the book to see what it was all about, he was not to be prevailed upon, saying he treated it as read and pronounced it utterly silly; and, if by any chance it should come to its author's ears that he had it in his hand, he did not want him to flatter himself with the idea that he had read it, for our thoughts, and still more our eyes, should keep themselves aloof from what is obscene and filthy.

They asked him where he intended to direct his steps. He replied, to Saragossa, to take part in the harness jousts held in that city every year. Don Juan told him that the new history described how Don Quixote, whoever he might be, took part there in a tilting at the ring, utterly devoid of invention, poor in mottoes, very poor in costume, though rich in sillinesses.

"For that very reason," said Don Quixote, "I will not set foot in Saragossa; and by that means I shall expose to the world the lie of this new history writer, and people will see that I am not the Don Quixote he speaks of."
"You will do quite right," said Don Jeronimo; "and there are other jousts at Barcelona in which Señor Don Quixote may display his prowess."

"That is what I mean to do," said Don Quixote; "and as it is now time, I pray your worships to give me leave to retire to bed, and to place and retain me among the number of your greatest friends and servants."
"And me too," said Sancho; "maybe I'll be good for something."

With this they exchanged farewells, and Don Quixote and Sancho retired to their room, leaving Don Juan and Don Jeronimo amazed to see the medley he made of his good sense and his craziness; and they felt thoroughly convinced that these, and not those their Aragonese author described, were the genuine Don Quixote and Sancho.
